abstract_original: Living systems exhibit emergent organization that bridges molecular and evolutionary scales. Genetic variation, regulatory control, and metabolic dynamics interact across levels of complexity to produce coordinated cellular behavior, yet most datasets capture only one layer at a time. Despite vast genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic resources across species and environments, no synthesis framework connects these data to reveal how evolutionary forces shape the mesoscale—the intermediate level where genes, proteins, and metabolites assemble into adaptive networks. The SynEvo Working Group will develop a machine-learning–driven synthesis framework that unites population-genetic and multi-omics data to uncover conserved and divergent axes of molecular organization. Using well-characterized human and mosquito datasets, we will identify how genetic variation, regulatory control, and metabolic flux interact to produce conserved mesoscale modules reflecting evolutionary constraint and innovation. These contrasting systems serve as testbeds for uncovering evolutionary design principles of molecular coordination—how selection and constraint shape regulatory–metabolic organization across life. SynEvo integrates interpretable machine learning with genome-scale metabolic (GEM) and MiReN (Minimal Regulatory Network; MILP-based regulatory inference) approaches, producing an open SynEvo Atlas hosted within NCEMS infrastructure—a reusable resource for evolutionary systems biology. By revealing both species- specific adaptations and conserved mesoscale design principles, SynEvo will advance conceptual and computational frontiers, providing fundamental insight into how life organizes itself across molecular, physiological, and evolutionary dimensions, with applications to human health, malaria transmission, and environmental resilience.

title: A Unified Framework for Analyses of Proteome Turnover Dynamics
title_norm: a unified framework for analyses of proteome turnover dynamics
abstract_text: Proteins vary widely in how long they persist within cells, from minutes to years, and this variation plays a central role in regulating biological function and maintaining cellular homeostasis. Decades of research have revealed several mechanisms that influence protein half-lives across the kingdoms of life. However, the differential impact of these mechanisms on protein half-lives within and between species remains incompletely understood. This knowledge gap can be addressed by comprehensive analyses of global proteome stability datasets enabled by recent advances in mass spectrometry-based proteomics. However, these datasets are currently fragmented across heterogeneous studies that are not easily amenable to meta-analysis. [Abstract]
Proteins vary widely in how long they persist within cells, from minutes to years, and this variation plays a central role in regulating biological function and maintaining cellular homeostasis. Decades of research have revealed several mechanisms that influence protein half-lives across the kingdoms of life. However, the differential impact of these mechanisms on protein half-lives within and between species remains incompletely understood. This knowledge gap can be addressed by comprehensive analyses of global proteome stability datasets enabled by recent advances in mass spectrometry-based proteomics. However, these datasets are currently fragmented across heterogeneous studies that are not easily amenable to meta-analysis. This Working Group will bring together complementary expertise in proteomics, computational biology, systems biochemistry, and evolution to systematically harmonize and integrate publicly available datasets on protein turnover across four representative species across two kingdoms of life - E. coli, S. cerevisiae, M. musculus, and H. sapiens. By reanalyzing existing data using consistent approaches and unifying metadata standards, we will generate a comprehensive, comparable, and publicly accessible resource, the Protein Stability Database (PSD). This database will enable us to identify the molecular and evolutionary principles that govern protein stability and assess how turnover patterns vary across different cell types and organisms. Beyond addressing these core questions, our Working Group aims to establish best practices and a shared vocabulary for measuring and reporting protein turnover, enabling seamless incorporation of future datasets and integration with other NCEMS data resources.

[Full Proposal]
Introduction and Goals Protein turnover, the continual balance between synthesis and degradation, defines the lifetime of every protein in the cell and is a fundamental determinant of proteome homeostasis. The half-life of a protein reflects the integrated effects of its sequence, structure, post- translational modifications, and interactions with cellular protein quality-control pathways (1-4). Despite its central importance, our understanding of what governs protein turnover kinetics remains incomplete. Although many of the underlying mechanisms regulating protein stability are well characterized and broadly conserved, the extent to which these mechanisms shape the observed diversity of protein half-lives across species remains unclear. For example, it remains unknown whether long-lived bacterial proteins are also long-lived in eukaryotes, or how bacterial orthologs of ubiquitin-tagged proteins in eukaryotes achieve regulated stability despite lacking the ubiquitin– proteasome system. Likewise, while sequence-encoded degradation signals such as degrons and N-end rule motifs are conserved across life, their specific recognition and implementation differ widely. Our goal is to integrate existing proteome turnover datasets to identify shared and species-specific determinants of protein stability across eukaryotic and prokaryotic species. Figure 1. Project overview Recent advances in bottom-up proteomics have enabled proteome-wide measurements of protein half- lives through dynamic labeling techniques such as pulsed SILAC and dynamic isotopic labeling (5-7). These approaches have revealed that turnover rates vary by several orders of magnitude, even within a single cell type. However, despite the proliferation of such datasets, most studies have been conducted independently, focused on only one or a few cell types or closely related organisms, analyzed using different kinetic models, and published in heterogeneous formats. Consequently, the field lacks an integrated, quantitative framework that connects turnover rates to molecular features and evolutionary context. The fragmented nature of existing datasets has hindered meta-analyses and limited our understanding of how protein stability is organized across species. More broadly, there are no unified resources for examining how diverse sequence and structural properties, such as intrinsic disorder, folding stability, and domain organization, collectively determine protein lifetimes in vivo. The harmonized datasets produced through this project will enable systematic cross-species and mechanistic comparisons of protein turnover. A major unresolved question in the field of proteostasis is the degree to which protein half-lives are conserved across species and cell types. Comparative studies within eukaryotes have revealed that some protein classes, such as ribosomal proteins and metabolic enzymes, maintain remarkably consistent turnover rates across evolution, whereas others, including regulatory and stress-response proteins, show considerable variation (18). This variability likely reflects adaptation to organismal traits such as metabolic rate, lifespan, and optimal growth temperature. However, to date, no cross-kingdom comparisons have been conducted, and it remains unknown how turnover patterns differ between the major domains of life. In particular, it is unclear how the distinct proteostasis architectures of prokaryotes and eukaryotes (e.g., protease networks vs. ubiquitin–proteasome and autophagy systems) differentially shape proteome stabilities at a global level. Systematically comparing turnover dynamics across species will clarify how conserved degradation principles are adapted to different cellular and evolutionary contexts and may identify shared and species-specific rules governing protein half-lives. Understanding the determinants of protein half-lives requires integrating diverse layers of biological information. Sequence-encoded features, such as degrons, amino-terminal residues, charge, hydrophobicity, and predicted disorder, are known to influence degradation susceptibility; however, these effects are modulated by higher-order properties, including domain organization, folding energetics, and the presence of intrinsically disordered regions (8, 9). Structural proteomics techniques such as SPROX, TPP, LiP and CETSA now provide global measures of thermodynamic stability that can be directly compared to turnover rates (10-12), while advances in structure prediction (AlphaFold, ESMFold) make it possible to extract biophysical descriptors for nearly every protein (13, 14). At the same time, proteostasis networks, including chaperones, E3 ubiquitin ligases, and autophagy pathways, play central roles in determining whether a misfolded or damaged protein is refolded or degraded (15-17). However, these data layers have not been combined systematically, and the relative contributions of diverse sequence and structure predictors of protein longevity across kingdoms of life remain to be quantified in a unified framework. Quantifying cross-species trends in protein half-lives requires a systematic, cross-species comparison grounded in a consistent methodology, which no existing resource currently provides. At present, turnover data are fragmented across studies that differ in scope, methodology, and analytical treatment. For example, protein half-life measurements, structural stability data, and thermal stability datasets are typically stored in separate repositories and analyzed using distinct pipelines and reference proteomes, complicating direct comparison. Moreover, turnover rates have been analyzed based on a variety of kinetic models and normalization procedures, resulting in incompatible parameters across datasets. Even when comparable data exist, meaningful biological variations in relative protein half-lives may be obscured by systematic shifts in absolute half-lives resulting from differences in global factors, such as metabolic rate and growth dynamics. Addressing these challenges requires harmonizing datasets, refitting kinetic models using unified procedures, and normalizing turnover estimates to account for species-specific physiological scaling factors. We propose to address these gaps by establishing a comprehensive, harmonized database of protein half-lives and associated molecular features across four well-studied organisms: E. coli, S. cerevisiae, M. musculus, and H. sapiens. These species were chosen because they span the major evolutionary transitions from prokaryotic to eukaryotic proteostasis systems and collectively account for the majority of available quantitative turnover data. By limiting the initial analysis to this set, we can ensure both data depth and biological interpretability while developing scalable workflows that can later be extended to additional species and experimental contexts. Our Working Group will harmonize existing datasets, re-analyze them using consistent kinetic models, and integrate them with structural, biophysical, and proteostasis-related annotations to uncover the molecular and evolutionary determinants of protein stability. This synthesis will address two overarching questions: (1) To what extent are protein half-lives conserved across species? and (2) What shared and species-specific molecular and biophysical properties determine protein half-lives across organisms? Answering these questions will not only advance our mechanistic understanding of proteome dynamics but also create the first community- accessible, metadata-rich resource for studying protein turnover at scale. Ultimately, we envision that this framework will enable new hypotheses about how protein longevity shapes cellular adaptation, aging, and evolution, and will provide a foundation for integrating turnover measurements with other NCEMS data resources on protein folding, interactions, and post-translational regulation. Proposed Activities 1. Gathering and re-analysis of protein half-life data We will systematically assemble and harmonize all publicly available quantitative protein half-life datasets for the five selected species using a unified computational workflow. Dynamic-labeling studies employing pulsed SILAC and related approaches will be identified from repositories such as PRIDE and curated with detailed metadata. An initial NCEMS data-scouting analysis has identified several key turnover datasets from bacteria (19, 20) (Source ID 1), S. cerevisiae (21, 22) (Source ID 2), and mammalian systems (23-26) (Source ID 3-4). In this initial phase, datasets will be reanalyzed where raw intensity or labeling data are available. Turnover rates will be refitted using single- and multi-exponential decay models implemented in Python, following established approaches from previous proteome dynamics studies. In doing so, we will explicitly account for two key parameters that may affect the accuracy and comparability of turnover measurements across datasets. First, we will correct for variations in amino acid precursor enrichment kinetics due to differences in labeling strategies, ensuring that turnover rates derived from different experimental designs can be meaningfully compared (27, 28). Second, our turnover fitting models will accommodate deviations from first-order kinetics by allowing for the presence of multiple degradation phases (29). Such deviations may reflect the presence of distinct protein pools that differ in stability, or coexisting protein isoforms and post-translational variants with heterogeneous turnover behavior. Confidence intervals and quality metrics will be derived through non-linear least squares and Bayesian sampling methods. Rather than developing new algorithms, our goal is to uniformly apply well-established models and quality control metrics to ensure comparability across datasets and species. Each dataset will be standardized to include controlled vocabulary fields describing the organism, cell type, growth rate, temperature, labeling duration, and kinetic model used to derive half-lives. The harmonized datasets will be stored in interoperable formats to facilitate reuse and integration with complementary molecular features. The final outcome will be a comprehensive, metadata-rich resource of high-quality, normalized turnover measurements across the five focal organisms, publicly released through NCEMS cyberinfrastructure to ensure open access and reproducibility. 2. Conservation of protein half-lives across species We will then analyze the evolutionary conservation of protein stability. Orthologous proteins will be mapped among E. coli, S. cerevisiae, mouse, and human using OrthoDB and UniProt annotations. Cross-species comparisons will quantify how half-lives vary among orthologs and functional classes, revealing which aspects of proteome stability are evolutionarily conserved and which are tuned to lineage-specific physiology. We will also explore how organismal traits, such as optimal growth temperature, metabolic rate, and lifespan, correlate with global turnover patterns, providing insights into the selective pressures that shape proteome stability. These comparative analyses will generate a quantitative framework for understanding how evolution and environment jointly influence the dynamics of protein maintenance. 3. Uncovering predictors of conserved and species-specific protein half-lives Finally, we will use the unified dataset described above and our insights on evolutionary conservation of protein stabilities to conduct multivariate analyses to identify molecular and biophysical determinants of protein stability. First, we will integrate protein-intrinsic properties, such as degron motifs, terminal residues, charge distribution, hydrophobicity, predicted disorder, and amino acid composition, with higher-order features derived from omics, structural, and thermodynamic data. These include domain organization, intrinsically disordered regions, contact order, and model confidence metrics (pLDDT) from multiple structural prediction algorithms such as AlphaFold, OmegaFold, and ESMFold. Folding energetics will be incorporated from proteome-wide stability measurements obtained using SPROX, TPP, and CETSA experiments. Extrinsic cellular factors, including chaperone interactions, ubiquitination, E3- ligase targeting, and autophagy substrate status, will be analyzed in parallel to assess the role of proteostasis networks. Regression and machine-learning approaches will be applied to quantify the relative contributions of these features and to identify conserved versus lineage-specific predictors. In parallel, we will evaluate more advanced architectures, such as using deep neural nets with a cross- attention mechanism to learn half-life across sample types from protein embeddings, which are transformer-based lower-dimension representations of protein sequences and structures from large protein language models such as ESM2, ProtT5. We will next perform multi-target prediction models that will aim to simultaneously predict protein half-life, folding stability, and other proteostatic parameters directly from sequence and structural features. Training will be performed on CyVerse GPU nodes using PyTorch/PyTorch Lightning framework. Performance will be evaluated using a variety of metrics, e.g., reconstruction loss for finding fast-turnover regulatory proteins, and comparison of prediction accuracy against baseline models such as existing degron databases. Together, these analyses will take advantage of the harmonized data set to provide the most comprehensive examination to date of the molecular features that govern protein half-lives across biological systems. From there, we will explore explainability/interpretability analysis, including using gradient or attention-based methods or ablation methods. Expected Outcomes and Broader Impacts This project will lead to the establishment of the Protein Stability Database (PSD), the first harmonized, metadata-rich database of protein half-lives across multiple species. The specific short-term applications of PSD include the identification of conserved stability determinants and the establishment of quantitative models linking sequence and structure to degradation kinetics. Beyond these immediate research goals, the PSD will serve as a valuable resource for evaluating kinetic models, training machine learning frameworks in protein turnover prediction, and developing quantitative theories of proteostasis. We note that PSD is envisioned as a static, versioned database that will not require NCEMS support for web interfaces, update pipelines, or ongoing maintenance. The database will be released in an archival format and hosted through NCEMS-supported infrastructure and institutional repositories. Our long-term vision for this effort is not to develop a continuously updated resource, but rather to establish a uniform set of best practices for conducting and reporting protein half-life measurements. By defining a shared vocabulary and standardized metadata schema, this effort will facilitate the seamless incorporation of future datasets generated by the protein turnover community, ensuring that subsequent data can be integrated using consistent and interoperable formats without requiring additional NCEMS resources. By adhering to FAIR data principles, the PSD will promote transparency, reproducibility, and cross- disciplinary reuse. All analysis pipelines, code, and data will be released through CyVerse and GitHub to ensure transparency and community accessibility. The project will also generate manuscripts describing both the database resource and the cross-species comparative analysis, contributing to the NCEMS mission of fostering synthesis and discovery through shared data integration. Rationale for a Working Group and NCEMS support This project requires interdisciplinary expertise in proteomics, computational biology, and evolutionary systems analysis that extends beyond any single laboratory. The team brings complementary strengths: Ghaemmaghami and Lau provide expertise in dynamic labeling, quantitative mass spectrometry, and data harmonization; Vogel contributes expertise in large-scale modeling of protein turnover and proteostasis networks as well as expertise in the evolution of protein structure and function; and NCEMS provides the ideal collaborative and computational environment for cross-disciplinary synthesis. Dedicated staff support and NCEMS cyberinfrastructure are essential for metadata curation, ontology development, and large- scale computation. The Working Group model will enable close coordination among institutions, facilitate the creation of community standards, and ensure that all outputs are openly disseminated for future use. By unifying fragmented datasets and creating a scalable comparative framework, this project will directly advance the NCEMS goal of uncovering emergent principles in molecular and cellular systems. Requested Resources All computation will be performed on standard CyVerse CPU and GPU nodes. Preliminarily we anticipate requiring up to 5,000 V100/A100 GPU hours, which will cover architecture comparison, transformer model training, protein embedding constructions, architecture comparisons, and interpretability/retraining; we also anticipate up to 5,000 CPU hours for proteomics data processing, statistical modeling, and database construction tasks; and approximately 15 TB of storage (potentially up to 50 TB depending on the scope of mass spectrometry data re-processing). Personnel support includes one Staff Scientist (33% FTE for 12 months) responsible for data integration, ontology design, and predictive modeling, and one Staff Scientist Assistant (50% FTE for 12 months) for metadata curation and dataset reprocessing. Additional support includes one in-person synthesis meeting for all PIs (Year 1) and open-access publication fees for two manuscripts ($5,000 total) Milestones and Timeline Over the two-year project period, the Working Group will begin with a kick-off meeting to catalog datasets and establish metadata standards (Months 1–3), followed by implementation of the half-life re-fitting pipeline and re-analysis of E. coli and yeast datasets (Months 4–6). The mid-year phase will focus on integrating mouse and human data, developing the ontology, and modeling turnover predictors (Months 7–9), ortholog mapping, and presentation of preliminary findings at NCEMS (Months 10–12). The second year will emphasize cross-species modeling and release of a beta version of the Protein Stability Database (PSD) (Months 13–15), manuscript drafting and model validation (Months 16–18), public release of the analysis pipeline and finalized ontology (Months 19–21), and a synthesis meeting culminating in final manuscripts and a white paper summarizing project outcomes (Months 22–24).

title: Predictive Synthesis Framework for Elucidating Biophysical Cell State from Spatial Transcriptomics and Proteomics
title_norm: predictive synthesis framework for elucidating biophysical cell state from spatial transcriptomics and proteomics
abstract_text: Cell states reflect not only molecular abundance but also where molecules reside. Public spatial omics (Spatch) now provide high-plex RNA (Xenium/CosMx) and protein (CODEX) maps, yet cross-modal synthesis at subcellular scales remain fragmented. We will develop an open, end-to-end synthesis framework that (i) registers adjacent-section spatial RNA-Protein images at subcellular resolution using diffeomorphic alignment (STalign), (ii) harmonizes RNA features into protein-scale rasters (SEraster) to create a one-to-one correspondence of patches to be compared (iii) quantify membrane/nuclear proximity, polarity, local density, and other features (iv) trains RNA-to-protein predictors and learn a unified biophysical fingerprint of cell state. Using the paired Xenium/CosMx-CODEX cancer atlas as a validation set and curated public cohorts as application sets, we will benchmark against abundance-only baselines. Framework performance will be assessed by overall registration quality, verified patch correspondence, and cross-modal predictive accuracy, with appropriate positive and negative controls to rule out leakage and spurious structure. [Full Proposal]
Introduction and Goals: Cells with similar bulk expression can behave very differently because subcellular location—at membranes, along the nuclear periphery, or in polarized domains— shapes function.1,2 In immunity, cancer, and development, this subcellular organization often governs signaling and decision points.3–7 Yet, most spatial omics analyses still treat RNA and protein as separate, abundance-centric snapshots, leaving the predictive role of subcellular organization undermeasured. Progress has been limited due to: (i) scarcity of public datasets that pair spatial transcriptomics with spatial proteomics at subcellular scales; (ii) the technical difficulty of aligning adjacent sections; (iii) standard labels and benchmarks that prioritize abundance over localization; and (iv) the lack of community workflows to compare modalities on matched subcellular patches. A recent benchmarking study introduced Spatch, a large public resource with paired spatial transcriptomics and proteomics from adjacent sections in three human cancers.8 This creates a timely opportunity, but without shared, reproducible methods to compare RNA and protein in the same subcellular context, analyses will remain abundance-centric and incompatible. Our long-term goal is to establish a predictive synthesis framework that treats subcellular organization as a core variable alongside abundance, elucidating biophysical cell state from spatial transcriptomics and proteomics. The objective is to create and test learned biophysical fingerprints—compact, interpretable features that integrate RNA and protein localization—to forecast cell state and fate. We will test two hypotheses: (H1) subcellular RNA and protein organization adds predictive signal for cell state beyond abundance; and (H2) learned biophysical fingerprints precede and predict cell fate and associated protein localization. By learning interpretable fingerprints that link RNA and protein localization to cell state and fate, this work will provide a general framework for connecting molecular maps to emergent behavior and advance the understanding of how cellular systems are organized and regulated. Figure 1. A. Framework flow: Paired spatial RNA(Xenium/CosMx) and protein(CODEX) images are registered (STalign) and aggregated into shared subcellular patches (SEraster), and summarized as biophysically meaningful features. B. Cell state and fate: Hypothesis 1 (left), our multimodal framework will outperform abundance-only models, recovering known types and revealing macrophage sub-states (resting vs activated). Hypothesis 2 (right), analyzing lineage data, the fingerprint separates fates (e.g., neuron vs liver) pre-commitment and predicts branch-specific protein localization from progenitor RNA profiles. Proposed Activities: Activity 1. Develop a unified subcellular synthesis framework. We will construct an open- source pipeline to integrate, annotate, and synthesize paired spatial RNA and protein datasets. It will operate on the paired spatial transcriptomics (Xenium, CosMx) and spatial proteomics (CODEX) data from adjacent serial sections of three human cancers in Spatch. Our pipeline will be configurable and readily extensible to diverse paired spatial RNA and protein datasets across various tissues as they become available. The pipeline proceeds in three distinct steps: (i) register adjacent RNA and protein sections into a common coordinate frame, (ii) harmonize them onto a shared pixel grid to create one-to-one subcellular patches, and (iii) quantify biophysically meaningful features on each matched patch. Subcellular registration (STalign). Adjacent sections may undergo rotations, stretching, and other non-rigid distortions during imaging, making rigid or affine transformations insufficient for image alignment. To address these challenges, we previously developed STalign, which uses large deformation diffeomorphic metric mapping (LDDMM) to align thin 2D sections so that shared tissue structures coincide in a common coordinate framework.9,10 We will apply STalign to register Xenium with CODEX, as well as CosMx with CODEX, to enable comparison of transcriptomic and proteomic expression magnitudes at matched spatial locations. Harmonize to shared patches (SEraster). To evaluate correspondence at matched spatial locations, we will apply our previously developed method SEraster to aggregate molecular expression onto patches on a shared pixel grid, yielding a one-to-one correspondence of patches across modalities to be compared. Quantify biophysical features. For each patch across the registered datasets, we will compute (i) total expression magnitude; (ii) nuclear and cytoplasmic expression integrating DAPI-nuclear staining; (iii) membrane-associated expression; (iv) colocalization; (v) supervised image features such as SIFT scores; and (vi) deep-learning-based extracted features from domain-specific vision foundation models such as SubCell.11 This spatial registration and rasterization will establish the essential framework for subsequent analysis and hypothesis testing. Evaluation. We will quantify registration accuracy by (i) median/RMSD error between manually annotated shared landmarks and (ii) concordance of matched-location molecular signals (Pearson/Spearman or mutual information), plus per-cell centroid error where segmentations exist. Deformation quality will be checked via Jacobian regularity and inverse-consistency. Patch correspondence will be verified by identical shared-grid indices and mask overlap (tissue, nuclei, membrane; Dice/IoU). Controls include (i) RNA-to-RNA alignment (Xenium to CosMx) to provide an upper bound in the absence of cross-modality differences, and (ii) spatial shuffles/label permutations as negative controls to ensure apparent structure requires true spatial correspondence. The Spatch resource supplies paired Xenium/CosMx (RNA) and adjacent- section CODEX (protein) data and documents CODEX to Xenium/CosMx registration, providing an appropriate basis for cross-modal evaluation. Activity 2. Test Hypothesis 1 — Cell state: subcellular RNA–protein organization adds predictive signal beyond abundance. RNA and protein levels often correlate poorly due to post-transcriptional control, yet the predictive contribution of subcellular localization is rarely quantified.12–15 With the Spatch dataset and registered sections, shared subcellular patches, and quantified features from Activity 1, we will (i) learn a multimodal fingerprint (embedding) of cell state and (ii) build spatial RNA-to-protein predictors. Primary Question: biophysical fingerprint (embedding) of cell state. We will train with a contrastive, multimodal embedding that maps RNA and protein from the same cell/region to nearby points, yielding a single numeric fingerprint of cell state. To interpret these fingerprints, we will use a two-step validation and discovery approach. (i) Validation: we will project Spatch’s cell-state labels into the learned embedding and compare against abundance-only embeddings to confirm recovery of known groups and proper RNA-protein pairing. (ii) Discovery: within a single annotated type, we will test whether adding spatial features reveals biophysical sub-states missed by abundance-only clustering and characterize each sub-state by its RNA-protein spatial relationships (e.g, colocalization, mutual exclusion, boundary-restricted patterns), with representative patches for interpretation. For example, for T cells, validation requires that CD4+ and CD8+ classes from distinct neighborhoods and that paired RNA/protein from the same region are nearest neighbors across modalities. For discovery within macrophages, the embedding may separate a resting sub-state with diffuse protein distribution from an active/polarized sub-state with membrane-enriched proteins. We will summarize these patterns with their defining RNA-protein spatial features and patches. Secondary Question: Predictive model. We will train a second model to predict protein- localization maps from spatial RNA features. We will then benchmark it against two baselines: (i) RNA-abundance-only model using per-cell RNA counts aggregated across space (Xenium/CosMx), and (ii) non-spatial model using SEraster patch RNA totals with spatial cues removed. All models will be evaluated against the same CODEX protein localization maps on the shared SEraster grid. We hypothesize that incorporating spatial RNA features will improve protein-location predictions by capturing trafficking and other biophysical processes absent from non-spatial measurements. Activity 3. Test Hypothesis 2 — Cell fate: biophysical fingerprints can predict cell fate decisions. Building on Activity 1 (registered sections, shared subcellular patches, quantified features) and Activity 2 (validated fingerprint and RNA to protein predictor), we will test whether subcellular organization provides early predictive signal of cell fate. Current fate models rely on transcriptomic snapshots, yet transcriptionally similar cells can diverge, implying that determinative information may be carried by spatial molecular organization. We will compute fingerprints to test whether spatial signatures (i) separate lineages before abundance changes and (ii) let progenitor profiles forecast fate-specific protein patterns. Primary Question: Numeric fingerprint model. We will apply the validated fingerprint model to trajectory datasets. We will test whether cells destined for different fates (e.g., progenitor versus differentiated) separate in fingerprint space before detectable changes in bulk gene expression. We will then summarize the dimensions driving early separation as specific RNA-protein spatial relationships (e.g., membrane enrichment, boundary-restricted patterns). Secondary Question: Predictive model. We will apply the validated RNA-to-protein predictor to generate per-cell protein-localization maps. We will track how these predicted protein patterns change along inferred lineages and branches. We will test whether progenitor RNA profiles predict the protein-localization signatures of downstream differentiated states. We will benchmark against predictors that ignore spatial structure and against RNA-abundance-only baselines. Together, these analyses will generate testable hypotheses about how subcellular spatial architecture influences cell fate. Outcomes: Technological advancement. A validated computational and biophysical framework will be produced, together with an open-source toolchain for spatial registration, cross-modal integration, and hypothesis generation. These resources will enable researchers to apply the framework to large, heterogeneous public datasets and to reproduce analyses across labs. Scientific advancement. The work will advance the field toward predictive understanding of cellular function by integrating fragmented datasets to identify biophysical mechanisms that govern cellular organization and cell-state transitions. It will address a recognized gap in linking molecular patterns to measurable phenotypes. Data resources. Harmonized Validation and Application datasets, with associated metadata curated by NCEMS staff, will be released as standardized community resources to support future computational and biophysical studies. Publications. One primary literature article is expected to report the framework and the biological insights from its application, including the Hypothesis Roadmap. Rationale for a working group approach: This project spans four expert domains: computational machine learning, single-molecule biophysics, statistical physics, and cell biology, beyond the scope of any single PI’s lab. Dr. Fan will lead the generative AI framework with biophysical constraints. Dr. Chen will provide the single-molecule models and measurements to inform those constraints. Dr. Presse will contribute statistical-physics methods for uncertainty quantification and correlation validation. This team delivers a framework that is computationally robust, biophysically grounded, statistically validated, and biologically interpretable. Rationale for NCEMS support: This project is a data-synthesis effort aligned with the NCEMS mission, but it is not feasible without infrastructure that our PI team does not possess. Feasibility depends on three NCEMS-supported capabilities: (i) expert data harmonization to integrate two large, heterogeneous sources (the Spatch validation set and an Application set assembled from fragmented public data), a task requiring Staff Scientist effort; (ii) scalable computation to train a generative AI model on terabytes of imaging data, enabled through NCEMS-coordinated CyVerse resources; and (iii) dedicated project management to coordinate a multi-institutional, virtual team and keep milestones on track. With this combination of harmonization, computation, and coordination, the work is executable; without it, the project remains out of reach. Requested resources: IT support. We request access to NCEMS-coordinated CyVerse computation and storage, including scalable capacity for the curated validation and application dataset for Aim 1 (estimated 20 TB) and high-performance, GPU-enabled resources to train and validate the generative AI framework for Aim 2 and 3 (estimated 106 CPU hours and GPU hours). Staff scientist support. We request 8-month support from a staff scientist with expertise in bioinformatics, data harmonization, and management of large public repositories. This role will lead data curation, harmonization, and pipeline management for Aim 1. We request a staff scientist (12-month) with expertise in cloud computing and ML/AI pipeline deployment to support PIs in deploying, debugging, and benchmarking the AI model on CyVerse for Aims 2 and 3. title: A Cross-Crop Data Synthesis of Circadian-Gated Vesicle Trafficking Nodes That Constrain Cytokinesis Under Heat Stress
title_norm: a crosscrop data synthesis of circadiangated vesicle trafficking nodes that constrain cytokinesis under heat stress
abstract_text: Plant cytokinesis depends on the coordinated delivery of Golgi- and trans-Golgi network (TGN)-derived vesicles to the phragmoplast midzone, where they fuse to build the new cell plate. Heat stress destabilizes this process, but it remains unclear whether thermal sensitivity of cytokinesis is a fixed molecular property or is instead modulated by the time of day at which heat occurs—an interaction long documented for other stress-responsive pathways but never examined at the level of membrane trafficking machinery that builds the mesoscale structures underlying cell division. This project will synthesize publicly available transcriptomic, proteomic, and genomic datasets across a phylogenetically diverse panel of species (Arabidopsis, maize, sorghum, wheat, and perennial crops such as apple, pear, and peach for which chromosome-scale genomes already exist) to test whether circadian gating of heat-responsive gene expression converges on a conserved, tractable set of endomembrane trafficking regulators required for cell plate biogenesis. We will assemble a curated compendium of RNA-seq experiments that vary time-of-day and temperature treatment, reprocess them through standardized, reproducible pipelines (e.g., GEMmaker/Nextflow) to generate harmonized gene expression matrices, and construct context-specific gene co-expression networks that explicitly model and remove confounding technical and biological variables. Network modules enriched for known cytokinesis- and TGN/UPS-associated genes (e.g., phragmoplast-associated kinesins, cell plate SNAREs, exocyst components, autophagy machinery implicated in membrane remodeling) will be cross-referenced against circadian clock output genes and heat-shock regulons to identify candidate 'bottleneck' nodes whose expression is simultaneously time-of-day gated and heat-responsive. Comparative analysis across annual (short-cycle, heat-exposed field crops) and perennial (long-lived, chronically stressed orchard) species will test whether these regulatory nodes are evolutionarily conserved or lineage-specific, leveraging existing genome assemblies and orthology maps already generated by consortium members. Publicly deposited live-cell imaging datasets and organelle proteomics repositories will be mined to validate whether predicted trafficking bottleneck genes correspond to known markers of phragmoplast/cell plate maturation, connecting network-level predictions back to organelle-scale phenotypes. This synthesis requires the combined expertise of the team: mechanistic knowledge of phragmoplast dynamics and cell plate trafficking, circadian and thermal stress physiology, endomembrane/UPS biology, and large-scale computational network construction—expertise that individually exists in separate labs but has never been integrated across this many species and data modalities. The project directly targets a mesoscale emergent property (how sub-organellar trafficking coordination scales up to determine whether a cell successfully divides under stress) and cannot be addressed by any single dataset or lab alone. All harmonized expression matrices, network models, and analysis workflows will be released as an open, versioned resource, and the project will train graduate students and postdocs in reproducible multi-species network biology, cross-institution data integration, and comparative genomics, building a template for future mesoscale synthesis efforts linking gene regulatory dynamics to subcellular structural outcomes.

The project directly targets a mesoscale emergent property (how sub-organellar trafficking coordination scales up to determine whether a cell successfully divides under stress) and cannot be addressed by any single dataset or lab alone. All harmonized expression matrices, network models, and analysis workflows will be released as an open, versioned resource, and the project will train graduate students and postdocs in reproducible multi-species network biology, cross-institution data integration, and comparative genomics, building a template for future mesoscale synthesis efforts linking gene regulatory dynamics to subcellular structural outcomes.

[Background and Significance]
Cytokinesis in land plants is executed not by an actomyosin contractile ring but by the phragmoplast, a bipolar microtubule-based scaffold that guides Golgi- and TGN-derived vesicles to a defined equatorial plane, where they fuse to construct a new cell wall in the form of a cell plate. This process is exquisitely sensitive to membrane trafficking fidelity: kinesin motors direct vesicle transport along phragmoplast microtubules, SNARE complexes and exocyst subunits mediate vesicle tethering and fusion, and unconventional/autophagy-related trafficking routes contribute additional membrane material during cell plate maturation and expansion. Disruption at any of these mesoscale nodes—structures intermediate in scale between single biomolecules and whole organelles—can stall or misdirect cytokinesis, with cascading consequences for tissue patterning, organ growth, and, ultimately, agricultural yield. Heat stress is a well-established disruptor of this system, destabilizing microtubule arrays, delaying phragmoplast expansion, and impairing cell plate formation, but nearly all such studies have treated thermal sensitivity as a static, temperature-dependent property. A large and independent body of work on circadian regulation demonstrates that many abiotic stress responses—including transcriptional heat-shock responses—are gated by the time of day, such that identical thermal insults produce markedly different molecular outcomes depending on when they occur relative to the internal clock. This gating phenomenon has never been examined for the endomembrane trafficking machinery that physically builds the cell plate, leaving a fundamental gap: does the circadian clock modulate whether cytokinesis succeeds or fails under heat stress by gating the expression of trafficking regulators themselves? Addressing this question requires reconciling three literatures that have developed largely in isolation—phragmoplast/cell plate cell biology, circadian and thermal stress physiology, and endomembrane trafficking—and doing so across multiple species to distinguish conserved regulatory logic from lineage-specific adaptation. No single dataset captures all the necessary dimensions (time-of-day, temperature, species, and trafficking gene annotation), and no single laboratory possesses the full complement of expertise or infrastructure to integrate them. However, the public data landscape has matured to the point where this integration is feasible: large RNA-seq compendia with time-course and stress designs exist for Arabidopsis, maize, sorghum, and wheat; chromosome-scale, haplotype-resolved genome assemblies now exist for perennial crops such as apple, pear, and peach; and organelle proteomics and live-cell imaging repositories provide independent, orthogonal evidence for trafficking protein localization and dynamics. Synthesizing these resources offers a tractable route to identifying conserved 'bottleneck' genes governing the intersection of circadian timing, thermal stress, and cell-plate trafficking—an emergent mesoscale property with direct relevance to crop resilience under a warming climate, and a question that is significant precisely because it sits at the unexplored interface of three mature but historically disconnected fields.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This project addresses three interlocking questions. First, is the transcriptional sensitivity of cytokinesis-associated trafficking genes to heat stress gated by time of day, analogous to previously documented circadian gating of other stress regulons? We hypothesize that a discrete subset of trafficking genes—particularly those encoding phragmoplast-associated kinesins, cell-plate SNAREs, exocyst components, and autophagy-linked membrane remodeling factors—will show heat-responsiveness that is strongly time-of-day dependent rather than uniform across the diel cycle, mirroring gating patterns previously reported for canonical heat-shock regulons. Second, do these gated trafficking nodes form a conserved regulatory module across phylogenetically distant crop species, or are they lineage-specific outcomes of independent adaptation to distinct thermal regimes? We hypothesize that a core set of trafficking bottleneck genes will be conserved across both annual, short-cycle field crops (Arabidopsis, maize, sorghum, wheat) and perennial, chronically stressed orchard species (apple, pear, peach), reflecting deep conservation of cell-plate biogenesis machinery, while a secondary, lineage-specific layer of gating will reflect differences in life history, exposure duration, and thermal ecology between annual and perennial growth habits. Third, do network-predicted bottleneck genes correspond to independently observed organelle-scale phenotypes—specifically, delayed or aberrant phragmoplast/cell plate maturation—captured in existing live-cell imaging and organelle proteomics datasets? We hypothesize that genes occupying central, highly connected positions in context-specific co-expression modules enriched for trafficking and cytokinesis annotations will disproportionately correspond to proteins already documented, through imaging or proteomic evidence, as spatially or temporally associated with cell plate maturation stages, providing convergent, multi-modal support for their functional importance. Collectively, these hypotheses reframe thermal sensitivity of cytokinesis not as a fixed biochemical property but as an emergent outcome of the interaction between circadian regulatory architecture and trafficking network topology—a property that can only be detected by integrating time-resolved transcriptomic data, cross-species genomic annotation, and orthogonal organelle-scale evidence at a scale no single laboratory's dataset can support. A critical secondary question concerns methodology: can existing network inference approaches, when adapted to explicitly model diel and thermal covariates, reliably distinguish genuine circadian-heat interaction signals from confounding batch, developmental, or tissue-specific variation across heterogeneous public datasets originating from dozens of independent laboratories? We hypothesize that context-specific network construction, incorporating explicit covariate modeling, will substantially reduce spurious co-expression relationships relative to naive aggregation, yielding higher-confidence candidate gene lists suitable for downstream cross-species and cross-modality validation. Together these questions and hypotheses define a tractable, falsifiable synthesis project whose resolution requires exactly the kind of multi-species, multi-omic, cross-disciplinary integration that individual investigators, working within a single species or data type, cannot achieve.

[Methods and Approach]
The project proceeds in four integrated phases. Phase 1 (Data Curation): We will systematically identify and catalog publicly available RNA-seq datasets from NCBI SRA/GEO and species-specific repositories that include explicit time-of-day and/or temperature-treatment metadata for Arabidopsis, maize, sorghum, wheat, apple, pear, and peach, prioritizing studies with paired control and heat-stress conditions sampled across multiple circadian time points. Metadata harmonization will standardize treatment, genotype, tissue, and sampling-time annotations into a unified schema. Phase 2 (Reprocessing and Harmonization): All selected raw sequence data will be reprocessed through a standardized, containerized GEMmaker/Nextflow pipeline to generate reproducible, comparably normalized gene expression matrices for each species, eliminating batch effects introduced by heterogeneous original processing pipelines. Existing chromosome-scale, haplotype-resolved genome assemblies and annotation sets for the perennial crops will anchor expression quantification, while established orthology resources will be used to map trafficking, cytokinesis, and circadian clock gene orthologs across all seven species. Phase 3 (Network Construction and Bottleneck Identification): Using the Knowledge Independent Network Construction framework, we will build context-specific gene co-expression networks (csGCNs) for each species that explicitly incorporate time-of-day and temperature as covariates, statistically testing and removing edges attributable to confounding technical or developmental variables. Within each network, modules will be tested for enrichment of curated gene sets representing phragmoplast microtubule motors, cell-plate SNAREs, exocyst subunits, autophagy-related membrane remodeling factors, circadian clock output genes, and canonical heat-shock regulon members. Candidate bottleneck nodes—genes exhibiting both strong circadian-gated expression and heat-responsiveness within trafficking-enriched modules—will be ranked by network centrality and cross-species conservation of orthologous module membership. Phase 4 (Cross-Modal Validation): Candidate genes will be cross-referenced against publicly deposited organelle proteomics datasets and live-cell imaging repositories documenting phragmoplast and cell-plate marker localization, testing whether network-predicted bottlenecks correspond to proteins with documented spatial or temporal association with cell-plate maturation. Comparative statistical analyses (e.g., module preservation statistics, orthogroup enrichment tests) will formally assess conservation versus divergence between annual and perennial lineages. Throughout, all code, containers, and intermediate data products will be version-controlled and benchmarked against held-out datasets to assess pipeline robustness. This approach requires no new experimental data generation; it depends entirely on the reprocessing, harmonization, and multi-modal integration of existing public resources, executed through workflows whose scale and cross-species scope exceed the capacity of any single contributing laboratory.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This synthesis will deliver a ranked, cross-species catalog of candidate trafficking bottleneck genes linking circadian timing to heat-sensitive cytokinesis, accompanied by harmonized expression matrices and context-specific co-expression networks spanning seven crop species. Scientifically, the project will establish whether circadian gating of thermal stress responses extends to the mesoscale trafficking machinery governing cell division, resolving a previously unexamined intersection between two mature but disconnected research areas and reframing cytokinetic thermal sensitivity as an emergent, time-dependent property rather than a fixed biochemical threshold. Agriculturally, identification of conserved versus lineage-specific bottleneck nodes will inform breeding and management strategies aimed at mitigating heat-induced yield loss in both annual field crops and long-lived perennial orchard systems, an increasingly urgent concern under climate change. Methodologically, the project will produce a validated, reusable framework for detecting circadian-environment interaction signals in heterogeneous public transcriptomic data, generalizable to other stress-response systems beyond cytokinesis. The resulting network models and validated gene lists will directly inform testable hypotheses for future hypothesis-driven experiments, effectively de-risking future mechanistic work by prioritizing candidates with convergent transcriptomic, orthological, and organelle-imaging support. Broader impacts include establishing a template for integrating gene regulatory network synthesis with organelle-scale phenotypic data, applicable across NCEMS's mesoscale research priorities. The project will also generate durable community resources—harmonized expression compendia and annotated network models—that lower the barrier for future researchers studying circadian-stress interactions in crop species lacking dedicated experimental infrastructure, thereby expanding participation from researchers at institutions without access to large-scale sequencing or growth chamber facilities.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
All aspects of this project will adhere to open science principles consistent with NCEMS policy. Raw data sources will be exclusively drawn from public repositories (SRA, GEO, and species-specific genome databases), with full provenance tracking from original accession to final processed output. abstract_original: Plant cytokinesis depends on the coordinated delivery of Golgi- and trans-Golgi network (TGN)-derived vesicles to the phragmoplast midzone, where they fuse to build the new cell plate. Heat stress destabilizes this process, but it remains unclear whether thermal sensitivity of cytokinesis is a fixed molecular property or is instead modulated by the time of day at which heat occurs—an interaction long documented for other stress-responsive pathways but never examined at the level of membrane trafficking machinery that builds the mesoscale structures underlying cell division. This project will synthesize publicly available transcriptomic, proteomic, and genomic datasets across a phylogenetically diverse panel of species (Arabidopsis, maize, sorghum, wheat, and perennial crops such as apple, pear, and peach for which chromosome-scale genomes already exist) to test whether circadian gating of heat-responsive gene expression converges on a conserved, tractable set of endomembrane trafficking regulators required for cell plate biogenesis. title: From Nucleosome Mechanics to Cell-Type Identity: A Multiscale Synthesis of Chromatin Polymer Physics, Condensate Biochemistry, and Single-Cell 3D Genomes to Explain Disease-Relevant Genome Folding in the Human Brain

[Abstract]
A central unsolved puzzle in molecular and cellular biology is how nanometer-scale nucleosome-nucleosome interactions and biomolecular condensate formation give rise to megabase-scale chromatin compartments and loop domains that differ systematically across human cell types—and how these emergent architectures channel genetic risk into cell-type-specific disease phenotypes. This gap sits squarely at the mesoscale NCEMS prioritizes: it cannot be resolved by structural biology, polymer physics, or population genetics alone, but requires their synthesis. This Working Group proposes to integrate four classes of existing public data that have never been jointly modeled: (1) single-cell diploid 3D genome structures (Dip-C/scHi-C) spanning dozens of human and mouse brain cell types; (2) nucleosome- and chromatin-fiber-resolution structural and simulation data (cryo-EM structures of pioneer-factor–nucleosome complexes, mesoscale oligonucleosome models, cohesin-loop Hi-C perturbation datasets); (3) biochemical and structural characterizations of chromatin-associated condensate components (corepressor oligomers, histone-modifying enzyme complexes, RNA-binding proteins undergoing liquid-liquid phase separation); and (4) population-scale functional genomics linking genetic variation to cell-type-specific gene expression and disease risk (brain-wide eQTL atlases, GWAS summary statistics for schizophrenia, multiple sclerosis, and Alzheimer's disease). Our central hypothesis is that cell-type-specific genome folding emerges from a hierarchy of physical rules—entropic and electrostatic steric pressures generated by intrinsically disordered chromatin regulators at the nucleosome scale, cooperative condensate formation by transcriptional corepressor/coactivator complexes at the sub-domain scale, and loop-extrusion/compartmentalization dynamics at the topologically associating domain scale—and that this hierarchy is a mechanistic intermediate between GWAS variants and their cell-type-restricted phenotypic effects. We will build coarse-grained, mechanistically grounded polymer models of chromatin fibers parameterized from structural and biophysical data, validate emergent compartment and loop predictions against single-cell Dip-C structures across neuronal and glial subtypes, and test whether condensate-forming regulatory complexes (e.g., corepressor tetramers, methyltransferase-associated assemblies, RNA-binding phase-separating proteins) quantitatively explain observed heterochromatin/euchromatin partitioning differences between cell types. We will then map disease-associated eQTL and GWAS loci onto these physically resolved chromatin states to ask whether variants disrupting predicted condensate-nucleation or loop-anchor regions preferentially explain the cell-type specificity of psychiatric versus neuroimmune disease associations already reported in public datasets. This effort requires collaboration across structural biophysics, polymer theory, single-cell genomics, and population-scale systems immunology/genetics—expertise that no single lab possesses, but that our team collectively spans. Deliverables include an open, versioned multiscale chromatin simulation framework linked to public single-cell 3D genome and eQTL/GWAS resources, reproducible pipelines for condensate-informed loop-domain prediction, and training modules pairing biophysical modeling with population genomics for graduate students and postdocs across participating institutions. By unifying nucleosome-scale biophysics with population-scale genetics through existing data alone, this project exemplifies community-scale synthesis: resolving how physical emergence at the mesoscale of chromatin organization constrains and explains cellular identity and disease susceptibility in the human brain.

[Background and Significance]
The three-dimensional folding of the human genome is a canonical example of biological emergence: compartments, topologically associating domains, and loop anchors arise from local physical and biochemical rules operating far below the megabase scale at which these structures are conventionally observed. Decades of structural biology have characterized how nucleosomes, linker histones, pioneer transcription factors, and chromatin-modifying enzyme complexes interact at atomic-to-nanometer resolution. In parallel, polymer physics has produced mesoscale models describing how oligonucleosome fibers fold under the influence of steric, electrostatic, and entropic forces, including those generated by intrinsically disordered regions of chromatin-associated proteins. Independently, single-cell 3D genome methods have revealed that compartment and loop architecture differs systematically across human and mouse brain cell types, and population-scale functional genomics has mapped disease-associated genetic variants onto cell-type-specific expression programs implicated in schizophrenia, multiple sclerosis, and Alzheimer's disease. Despite the maturity of each of these literatures, they remain almost entirely disconnected: nucleosome-scale structural and biophysical data have not been used to mechanistically explain cell-type-specific compartment structures observed in single-cell Hi-C-type data, and neither has been connected to the eQTL and GWAS variants whose cell-type-restricted effects they may explain. This disconnect is not a matter of insufficient data; it is a synthesis problem. The relevant datasets already exist in public repositories, but integrating them requires reconciling incompatible resolutions, formats, and theoretical frameworks spanning structural biology, statistical polymer physics, single-cell genomics, and population genetics—a task beyond the scope, tools, or expertise of any single laboratory. This gap is precisely the kind of mesoscale emergence phenomenon that motivates NCEMS: understanding how molecular-scale interactions among nucleosomes and their regulatory partners give rise to nuclear-scale architecture, and how that architecture in turn shapes cell-type-specific phenotypic and disease outcomes. Resolving it has substantial biomedical significance. Psychiatric and neuroimmune diseases show strikingly cell-type-restricted genetic associations—for example, neuronal enrichment for schizophrenia risk contrasted with immune cell enrichment for multiple sclerosis and Alzheimer's disease—yet the mechanistic basis for why the same variant class produces cell-type-restricted effects remains largely unexplained. A physically grounded model connecting nucleosome-scale interactions, condensate formation, and genome folding to these expression and disease patterns would provide a mechanistic bridge currently missing from the field, transforming correlative eQTL/GWAS cell-type enrichment findings into testable structural hypotheses. This proposal directly targets that bridge using only existing, publicly available data, fulfilling the community-scale synthesis mission of integrating disparate large-scale resources that have never been jointly modeled to answer a fundamental question about how molecular-scale physical rules generate cellular-scale identity and disease vulnerability.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This Working Group is organized around three linked research questions that move systematically from nucleosome-scale biophysics to population-scale disease genetics. Research Question 1: Can nucleosome- and fiber-scale structural and biophysical parameters, drawn from cryo-EM structures of pioneer-factor–nucleosome complexes, linker histone perturbation datasets, and biophysical measurements of steric pressure generated by intrinsically disordered chromatin regulators, be used to parameterize coarse-grained polymer models that quantitatively reproduce compartment and loop-domain features observed in single-cell diploid genome structures? We hypothesize that a substantial fraction of the compartment-level heterochromatin/euchromatin partitioning differences observed across brain cell types can be explained by measurable differences in nucleosome-fiber mechanical properties and linker histone occupancy inferred from existing structural and epigenomic datasets, without invoking cell-type-specific novel physical parameters. Research Question 2: Do biomolecular condensates formed by chromatin-associated regulatory complexes—including transcriptional corepressor oligomers, histone methyltransferase-associated assemblies, and RNA-binding proteins undergoing liquid-liquid phase separation—provide a quantitatively necessary intermediate scale between nucleosome-level fiber mechanics and megabase-scale compartmentalization? We hypothesize that condensate-forming regulatory complexes act as nucleation centers whose oligomerization state and local concentration, as characterized in existing structural and biochemical datasets, predict the boundaries and strength of compartment domains observed in single-cell 3D genome data better than fiber mechanics alone, particularly in cell types where these complexes are differentially expressed. Research Question 3: Do disease-associated eQTL and GWAS variants preferentially localize to genomic regions predicted by our integrated model to function as condensate-nucleation sites or loop anchors, and does this localization pattern differ systematically between neuronal cell types implicated in psychiatric disease and immune/glial cell types implicated in neuroimmune and neurodegenerative disease? We hypothesize that psychiatric disease risk variants are disproportionately located within predicted condensate-nucleation regions specific to neuronal chromatin states, whereas multiple sclerosis and Alzheimer's disease risk variants are disproportionately located within loop-anchor or compartment-boundary regions specific to immune and glial chromatin states, reflecting distinct physical mechanisms by which genetic variation is channeled into cell-type-restricted phenotypic effects. Collectively, these hypotheses predict a testable, falsifiable causal chain: nucleosome-scale mechanical and condensate properties determine sub-domain architecture; sub-domain architecture determines compartment and loop structure; and that structure determines which disease-associated variants exert cell-type-specific regulatory effects. Because each hypothesis makes quantitative, data-derivable predictions using structures, simulations, and functional genomics datasets that already exist publicly, none require new experimental data collection. The value of this Working Group lies precisely in its capacity to test these cross-scale hypotheses jointly, which is not achievable using any single existing dataset or disciplinary framework in isolation.

[Methods and Approach]
The project proceeds in three integrated phases, each combining datasets and expertise that no single participating laboratory holds independently. Phase 1 (Nucleosome-to-fiber parameterization): We will compile and harmonize existing cryo-EM structures of nucleosome–pioneer-factor complexes, biophysical measurements of steric pressure generated by intrinsically disordered chromatin regulators, and linker histone perturbation datasets (including chromatin architectural profiling from H1-loss models) to parameterize coarse-grained oligonucleosome polymer models. These models will be implemented within an existing mesoscale chromatin simulation framework, extended to incorporate condensate-forming regulatory complexes as explicit interaction terms rather than as implicit chromatin marks. Phase 2 (Validation against single-cell 3D genomes): Using publicly available Dip-C and related single-cell diploid genome structure datasets spanning multiple human and mouse brain cell types, we will benchmark simulated compartment and loop-domain outputs against empirically observed structures, stratified by neuronal and glial subtype. Validation metrics will include compartment strength, loop-anchor positioning, and radial genome organization, compared using established structural similarity statistics. We will systematically test whether adding condensate-nucleation terms—parameterized from biochemical and structural data on corepressor oligomerization, methyltransferase-associated complex assembly, and RNA-binding protein phase separation—improves model fit relative to fiber-mechanics-only models, using nested model comparison and cross-validation across independent cell-type datasets. Cohesin-loop perturbation Hi-C datasets will serve as an orthogonal validation set, testing whether our model correctly predicts the observed elimination of loop domains with preserved compartment structure under cohesin loss. Phase 3 (Mapping to population genetics): We will overlay our physically resolved chromatin state annotations—condensate-nucleation regions, loop anchors, compartment boundaries—onto existing brain-wide eQTL atlases and GWAS summary statistics for schizophrenia, multiple sclerosis, and Alzheimer's disease. Using stratified functional enrichment methods and colocalization analyses standard in statistical genetics, we will test whether disease- and cell-type-specific variant enrichment patterns align with predicted physical chromatin states, following established frameworks for linking cell-type transcriptomic and epigenomic annotations to genetic risk. All datasets will be accessed through public repositories including but not limited to 4D Nucleome, GEO, the Sequence Read Archive, PDB/EMDB, and publicly deposited GWAS/eQTL summary statistics. The Working Group will meet through structured in-person workshops and virtual sprints, with subteams organized around each phase and cross-cutting integration sessions to reconcile resolution mismatches, coordinate coordinate-system harmonization across datasets from different genome assemblies, and jointly interpret discrepancies between model predictions and empirical structures. Computational pipelines will be developed collaboratively and tested against held-out cell types not used in initial parameterization to assess generalizability.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This Working Group will produce a mechanistic, physically grounded framework connecting nucleosome-scale interactions, condensate formation, and genome-scale architecture to cell-type-specific disease risk—an integrative advance not achievable from any single existing dataset or discipline. Primary outcomes include a validated multiscale chromatin polymer model parameterized entirely from public structural, biophysical, and single-cell genomic data; quantitative evidence for or against condensate-mediated mechanisms of compartment formation across brain cell types; and a map of disease-associated genetic variants stratified by their predicted physical role in chromatin organization. These outcomes will directly address a long-standing puzzle regarding why genetic risk for psychiatric versus neuroimmune diseases localizes to distinct cell types, offering a structural and biophysical explanation to complement existing statistical genetic associations. Scientifically, the project will demonstrate whether mesoscale physical emergence—rather than cell-type-specific novel biochemistry alone—can account for major features of genome architecture, informing broader questions about emergent organization in other chromatin contexts and cell types beyond brain tissue. Methodologically, the resulting simulation framework and variant-mapping pipelines will be reusable by the broader community for other tissues and diseases, extending the impact well beyond the initial brain-focused application. The project will also generate training materials that bridge biophysical modeling and population genomics, disciplines rarely taught together, equipping trainees with cross-disciplinary computational skills increasingly needed in data-intensive molecular and cellular bioscience. By demonstrating that a mechanistic, cross-scale question of this complexity can be resolved entirely through synthesis of existing public data, this project will serve as a template for future NCEMS-supported efforts addressing other mesoscale emergence phenomena, reinforcing the broader case for community-scale data synthesis as a distinct and necessary mode of scientific discovery.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
All work in this Working Group will rely exclusively on publicly available datasets, and all derived resources will be released under open licenses consistent with NCEMS and community open-science standards. Harmonized and reprocessed versions of single-cell 3D genome structures, structural and biophysical parameter sets, and chromatin-state annotations will be deposited in public repositories with full provenance tracking linking back to original data sources. The multiscale chromatin simulation framework will be developed as versioned, openly licensed software with containerized environments to ensure computational reproducibility across institutions and hardware. All analysis code, including model parameterization scripts, validation pipelines, and variant-mapping workflows, will be maintained in public version-controlled repositories with continuous documentation, example datasets, and tutorials enabling independent replication. Intermediate outputs, including simulated chromatin structures and predicted condensate-nucleation and loop-anchor annotations, will be released as queryable public resources rather than static supplementary files, allowing other researchers to build upon them directly. The Working Group will adopt pre-registration of key validation analyses, including model comparison criteria established prior to full dataset integration, to guard against post hoc interpretation. Regular internal reproducibility checks will require that any result be independently regenerated by a second team member using only the public code and data repository before inclusion in outputs. Findings will be disseminated through preprints posted prior to journal submission, with data and code availability statements meeting or exceeding FAIR principles. Training materials developed for graduate students and postdocs will likewise be made publicly available as open educational resources, including annotated notebooks demonstrating the full analytical pipeline from structural data to disease variant mapping, explicitly designed to lower barriers for future researchers entering this cross-disciplinary synthesis space.

[Budget and Resources]
This project requires NCEMS support primarily for personnel, computational infrastructure, and coordination costs rather than data generation, consistent with its synthesis-only design. Budget priorities include partial salary support for a postdoctoral researcher and a graduate student trainee to serve as integration leads across the structural, polymer physics, and population genomics subteams, ensuring continuity of technical work between in-person meetings. Computational resources are needed for large-scale coarse-grained polymer simulations parameterized across dozens of cell types and for genome-wide colocalization analyses linking chromatin-state predictions to eQTL and GWAS summary statistics; cloud or high-performance computing allocation is requested accordingly. Funds are requested for two in-person Working Group workshops per year, bringing together investigators with structural biophysics, chromatin polymer modeling, single-cell genomics, and population genetics expertise, plus supplementary virtual working sessions to maintain momentum between meetings. Modest travel support will enable trainee participation in workshops, ensuring direct training benefit rather than restricting collaborative sessions to senior investigators. Data management costs cover curation, harmonization, and public deposition of integrated datasets and derived resources, including repository maintenance beyond the funding period. No funds are requested for new experimental data generation, consistent with the community-scale synthesis mandate. The distributed nature of required expertise—spanning structural biology, biophysical modeling, single-cell genomics, and functional/population genetics located across multiple institutions—necessitates NCEMS-level coordination and infrastructure support that exceeds what any individual laboratory's existing grants could provide, particularly for sustaining the cross-disciplinary integration meetings essential to reconciling disparate data types and theoretical frameworks into a single coherent multiscale model.

title: Functional Redundancy as a Mesoscale Buffer: Synthesizing Ancient and Modern Metagenomes with Host Proteo-Genomic Atlases to Test the Stability of Microbiome-Host Molecular Modules
title_norm: functional redundancy as a mesoscale buffer synthesizing ancient and modern metagenomes with host proteogenomic atlases to test the stability of microbiomehost molecular modules
abstract_text:
A central puzzle in microbial ecology is why host phenotypes associated with the microbiome often remain stable despite enormous taxonomic turnover in microbial communities across individuals, populations, and evolutionary time. One resolution is that functional modules—conserved sets of microbial genes encoding metabolic pathways such as short-chain fatty acid synthesis, bile acid transformation, and tryptophan/indole metabolism—represent an emergent, mesoscale level of biological organization that buffers taxonomic variability and directly couples to host molecular physiology. This project will synthesize publicly available shotgun metagenomic data spanning contemporary human cohorts (Human Microbiome Project, MetaHIT, curatedMetagenomicData, MiBioGen) and ancient microbiomes (dental calculus, paleofeces, and archived shotgun datasets from Paleolithic through historical periods) with large-scale human proteogenomic and metabolomic resources (UK Biobank Pharma Proteomics Project, plasma cis-pQTL maps, NMR metabolomic panels) to test whether specific microbial functional modules show consistent, genetically anchored associations with host circulating protein and metabolite networks, independent of which taxa or strains carry them, and whether this coupling is stable across evolutionary timescales.

We will reprocess all metagenomes using a standardized DIAMOND+MEGAN-based taxonomic and functional binning pipeline to build a harmonized cross-cohort, cross-era atlas of functional module abundance, explicitly accounting for degradation and contamination artifacts characteristic of low-biomass ancient samples using established authentication and decontamination frameworks.
