All code, intermediate outputs, and harmonized datasets will be deposited under FAIR principles, with structured training modules for graduate students and postdocs spanning computational metagenomics, paleogenomics, and human genetics.

[Background and Significance]
Microbiome science has repeatedly documented a striking paradox: while the taxonomic composition of gut, oral, and skin microbial communities varies enormously between individuals, across populations, and over evolutionary time, many host phenotypes linked to the microbiome—metabolic homeostasis, immune tone, circulating metabolite profiles—remain comparatively stable. This has motivated the hypothesis that functional capacity, rather than taxonomic identity, is the biologically meaningful unit of microbiome-host interaction. Pathways such as short-chain fatty acid production, secondary bile acid transformation, and tryptophan/indole metabolism are frequently encoded by phylogenetically unrelated organisms, suggesting that functional modules constitute an emergent, mesoscale organizational layer sitting between individual microbial genomes and whole-community, whole-host physiology. If true, this reframes microbiome-host coupling as a property of gene-function ecology rather than species ecology, with direct implications for how researchers interpret microbiome-disease associations and prioritize therapeutic targets.

Despite the conceptual appeal of functional redundancy, it has never been rigorously tested at scale against host molecular phenotypes, nor examined across deep evolutionary time. Three barriers have historically prevented this test. First, contemporary metagenomic cohorts (HMP, MetaHIT, curatedMetagenomicData, MiBioGen) have been processed with heterogeneous bioinformatic pipelines, precluding harmonized functional comparison across studies. Second, ancient metagenomic datasets from dental calculus and paleofeces—spanning Paleolithic through historical periods—carry well-documented risks of DNA damage, low biomass, and exogenous contamination that require specialized authentication frameworks before functional inference is credible. Third, linking microbial function to host molecular physiology at genetic resolution requires integration with large human proteogenomic resources such as the UK Biobank Pharma Proteomics Project and plasma cis-pQTL/metabolite-QTL maps, a scale of statistical genetics infrastructure rarely available to microbiome research groups.

No single laboratory possesses the full combination of expertise needed to resolve this problem: high-throughput metagenomic alignment and functional binning algorithm development, ancient DNA decontamination and authentication methodology, phylogenetic network theory for quantifying taxonomic substitutability, and biobank-scale human genetic and proteomic analysis. This is precisely the kind of problem for which community-scale data synthesis is uniquely suited. By reprocessing existing public datasets under a single harmonized framework and linking them for the first time to existing human proteogenomic atlases, this project can test whether functional modules are genuinely emergent, evolutionarily conserved buffers of host physiology, or whether apparent redundancy is an artifact of coarse functional annotation. Resolving this question addresses a fundamental problem in mesoscale biology: how molecular-level compositional variability is filtered and stabilized into consistent higher-order phenotypes, directly aligned with NCEMS's mission to understand emergent properties bridging molecular and cellular scales of organization.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This project is organized around four interlocking research questions, each addressed exclusively through synthesis of existing public data.

RQ1: Do microbial functional modules show greater cross-individual and cross-cohort stability than the taxa that encode them? We hypothesize that functional module abundance profiles, once harmonized across cohorts, will exhibit substantially lower variance and higher cross-cohort correlation than species- or strain-level abundance profiles for the same biological samples, consistent with functional redundancy acting as a buffering mechanism.

RQ2: Are specific functional modules genetically and causally coupled to host circulating protein and metabolite networks, independent of the taxa carrying them? We hypothesize that a subset of modules—particularly those governing short-chain fatty acid synthesis, bile acid transformation, and tryptophan/indole metabolism—will show reproducible associations with host cis-pQTL and metabolite-QTL profiles, and that Mendelian randomization and colocalization analyses will support directional or bidirectional causal relationships between microbial functional capacity and host protein/metabolite levels, rather than these associations being explained by confounding taxonomic composition alone.

RQ3: Can taxonomic substitutability underlying each functional module be quantified, and does this 'redundancy index' predict the strength of host-molecular coupling? We hypothesize that modules with higher redundancy indices (i.e., encoded by a broader, more phylogenetically diverse set of taxa, as revealed through gene-family-level split-decomposition network analysis) will show more stable and reproducible host-molecular associations across cohorts, because taxonomic turnover does not erode the functional signal available for host coupling.

RQ4: Are host-microbiome functional-molecular relationships evolutionarily conserved, or are they recent artifacts of industrialized lifestyles? Using ancient dental calculus and paleofeces metagenomes paired with available ancient human genomic data, we hypothesize that functional modules identified as robustly coupled to host physiology in modern cohorts will also be detectable, at comparable relative abundance and with congruent directionality of association where ancient host genetic data permit, in pre-industrial and pre-agricultural populations—supporting deep evolutionary conservation of these molecular relationships rather than recent lifestyle-driven artifacts.

Collectively, these questions test a specific, falsifiable model: that functional modules constitute a genuine emergent mesoscale layer of biological organization, mechanistically decoupled from taxonomic identity, that mediates a substantial fraction of microbiome-host molecular interaction and has been conserved across major transitions in human diet, sanitation, and lifestyle. An alternative, equally informative outcome—that apparent functional stability is largely an artifact of coarse pathway annotation, or that host-molecular coupling is dominated by strain-specific rather than pathway-level effects—would itself represent a significant advance, refining how the field interprets functional metagenomic signatures in disease biomarker studies. Because this hypothesis can only be tested by integrating heterogeneous, large-scale public datasets spanning modern biobanks, historical and prehistoric metagenomes, and existing GWAS/QTL summary statistics, it exemplifies the type of question requiring coordinated, cross-institutional synthesis rather than single-lab experimentation.

[Methods and Approach]
The working group will execute a four-stage synthesis pipeline built entirely on existing public data.

Stage 1 – Harmonized reprocessing of metagenomes: All contemporary shotgun metagenomic samples (Human Microbiome Project, MetaHIT, curatedMetagenomicData, MiBioGen) and available ancient shotgun datasets (published dental calculus, paleofeces, and archived samples spanning Paleolithic to historical periods) will be reprocessed through a single standardized DIAMOND+MEGAN-based pipeline for taxonomic and functional binning against curated protein reference databases. Ancient samples will additionally be passed through established aDNA authentication workflows, including damage-pattern verification, fragment length distribution analysis, and application of consensus contamination-screening criteria for low-biomass samples, ensuring that functional signal is not confounded by exogenous or modern DNA contamination.

Stage 2 – Redundancy index construction: For each functional module of interest, gene-family sequences across all taxa carrying the pathway will be extracted and subjected to phylogenetic network analysis using NeighborNet and related split-decomposition methods to quantify the breadth and structure of taxonomic diversity underlying the function. This yields a per-module, per-cohort redundancy index that captures the degree of taxonomic substitutability, allowing formal comparison of functional versus taxonomic stability (RQ1, RQ3).

Stage 3 – Host genetic and molecular integration: Harmonized functional module abundances will be tested for association with existing microbiome-host GWAS summary statistics, plasma cis-pQTL maps, and NMR-based metabolomic QTL resources drawn from large biobank proteogenomic studies. Mendelian randomization and genetic colocalization analyses will be applied to distinguish causal, reverse-causal, and confounded relationships between microbial functional capacity and host circulating protein/metabolite levels (RQ2). Sparse modeling approaches will be used to prioritize modules with the most robust and reproducible signals across independent cohorts.

Stage 4 – Deep-time validation: Functional modules identified as robustly host-coupled in Stage 3 will be evaluated in the harmonized ancient metagenome atlas from Stage 1, cross-referenced where possible with available ancient human genomic data, to test whether module abundance patterns and inferred host associations are detectable and directionally consistent across major dietary and lifestyle transitions (RQ4).

Throughout, quality control will include sensitivity analyses excluding low-coverage or high-contamination-risk ancient samples, cross-validation across independent modern cohorts, and explicit reporting of statistical power limitations for ancient samples given smaller effective sample sizes. Team responsibilities map directly onto complementary expertise: metagenomic algorithm development and functional binning infrastructure; ancient DNA authentication, contamination control, and archaeological sample interpretation; and proteogenomic statistical genetics, GWAS/QTL integration, and causal inference modeling. Regular working group meetings will coordinate pipeline validation, cross-check redundancy index calculations against independent taxonomic profiling, and ensure consistent interpretation of colocalization results across data modalities.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This project will produce a versioned, reproducible 'Microbiome Functional-Host Proteome Atlas' integrating harmonized functional module abundances across contemporary and ancient metagenomic datasets alongside host proteogenomic and metabolomic associations. This resource will provide the first systematic, falsifiable test of functional redundancy as a mesoscale buffering mechanism, distinguishing modules with genuine emergent, genetically anchored host coupling from those whose apparent stability reflects annotation artifacts or taxon-specific effects. A quantitative redundancy index framework, generalizable beyond this project, will offer the broader field a reusable metric for evaluating functional versus taxonomic stability in any metagenomic dataset.

Scientifically, results will clarify which microbiome-associated molecular phenotypes represent robust, evolutionarily conserved emergent properties suitable for biomarker or therapeutic target prioritization, versus those likely to be population- or era-specific. This directly informs translational microbiome research, where taxonomic biomarkers have often shown poor replicability across cohorts. Methodologically, the harmonized pipeline and deep-time validation approach establish a template for integrating ancient and modern 'omics data with host genetics—an underused synthesis strategy with broad applicability beyond the microbiome field.

Broader impacts include establishing open, reusable computational infrastructure for cross-era metagenomic harmonization, advancing NCEMS's mesoscale emergence research agenda by providing a concrete, testable case study of how molecular-level compositional variability filters into stable higher-order phenotypes, and training a cohort of graduate students and postdocs in transdisciplinary skills spanning computational metagenomics, ancient DNA methodology, and statistical genetics—skills increasingly essential for the future data-intensive molecular and cellular sciences workforce.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
All aspects of this synthesis project will adhere to FAIR and open science principles. Source metagenomic and proteogenomic datasets used are already publicly available through established repositories (SRA, ENA, curatedMetagenomicData, UK Biobank Pharma Proteomics Project, GWAS Catalog); no new experimental data will be generated. All reprocessing pipelines, including the standardized DIAMOND+MEGAN functional binning workflow, ancient DNA authentication scripts, redundancy index calculation code, and Mendelian randomization/colocalization analysis scripts, will be deposited in version-controlled public repositories (GitHub/Zenodo) with persistent DOIs, containerized for computational reproducibility, and accompanied by detailed documentation enabling independent replication.

Harmonized intermediate outputs—including functional module abundance matrices, redundancy indices per pathway and cohort, and summary statistics from genetic association analyses—will be released as structured, versioned datasets under open licenses, with clear provenance tracking linking each output back to original public accessions. Analysis workflows will be implemented in reproducible pipeline frameworks (e.g., Snakemake or Nextflow) to ensure computational transparency and portability across computing environments.

The working group will follow community-endorsed standards for reporting low-biomass and ancient DNA analyses, including explicit contamination and authentication metrics, to ensure that ancient metagenomic findings meet current field-wide reproducibility expectations. Pre-registration of primary hypotheses and analysis plans will be posted prior to Stage 3 genetic integration analyses to guard against analytic flexibility. All data products, code, and documentation will be made available prior to or concurrent with publication, and results will be disseminated through open-access publications, preprints, and public presentation of the Microbiome Functional-Host Proteome Atlas as a standing community resource, explicitly designed for reuse and extension by independent research groups.

[Budget and Resources]
This proposal requests NCEMS support for personnel, computational infrastructure, and collaborative coordination costs that exceed the capacity of any individual laboratory. Personnel support includes partial salary for two postdoctoral researchers—one focused on metagenomic pipeline harmonization and phylogenetic network analysis, one focused on statistical genetics integration (GWAS/QTL, Mendelian randomization, colocalization)—and one graduate student contributing to ancient DNA authentication and functional annotation quality control, providing direct cross-disciplinary training embedded in the working group's core research activities.

Computational resources are substantial given the scale of reprocessing required: high-performance computing allocation for DIAMOND-based alignment of thousands of contemporary and ancient shotgun metagenomic samples against large protein reference databases, storage for harmonized intermediate outputs and the versioned atlas, and cloud or institutional cluster access for genome-wide Mendelian randomization and colocalization analyses across biobank-scale summary statistics.

Coordination funds will support two in-person working group meetings per year to integrate results across the three core expertise areas, plus regular virtual meetings for pipeline validation and cross-checking of redundancy index and genetic association findings. Modest travel funds will enable postdoc and graduate student participation in relevant scientific conferences to present synthesis outputs and receive community feedback.

No funds are requested for new data generation, laboratory reagents, or sample collection, consistent with the synthesis-only scope of this project. Existing institutional computing infrastructure at team member institutions will be leveraged where possible to minimize costs, with NCEMS support specifically targeted at the incremental computational scale, cross-disciplinary personnel time, and coordination overhead required to integrate ancient metagenomics, modern metagenomics, and human proteogenomics into a single reproducible analytical framework—an integration that no participating laboratory could accomplish independently.

This project will synthesize three classes of public data that have never been jointly analyzed at scale: (1) large bacterial gene-expression compendia spanning thousands of conditions and dozens of species (e.g., PRECISE, COLOMBOS, SRA-derived RNA-seq collections, proteomic abundance databases such as PaxDb), (2) sequence-based biophysical predictors of phase-separation propensity and intrinsic disorder (catGRANULE, PScore, FuzDrop) applied proteome-wide, and (3) curated experimental catalogs of known bacterial condensate components together with comparative genomic and evolution-experiment data (ALEdb, clinical isolate genome collections, long-term evolution lineages) documenting mutations in regulatory circuits such as quorum-sensing systems and efflux pumps.

The working group will first build a cross-species atlas linking condition-specific transcriptional/proteomic states to the predicted phase-separation propensity of the expressed proteome, testing whether physiological transitions (e.g., entry into stationary phase, quorum-sensing activation, envelope stress) are consistently accompanied by co-regulated shifts in the abundance of high-propensity, disorder-rich proteins relative to their low-propensity partners. This addresses a mesoscale question central to NCEMS's mission: does gene-regulatory network architecture function, in part, as a control layer for mesoscale self-organization, translating discrete transcriptional states into emergent, spatially organized biomolecular assemblies? [Background and Significance]
Eukaryotic cells achieve compartmentalization through membrane-bound organelles, but a growing body of work demonstrates that bacteria accomplish analogous functional organization through membraneless, often phase-separated or phase-separation-like mesoscale assemblies. BR-bodies concentrate RNA-degradation machinery, PopZ microdomains scaffold polar signaling complexes, ParB/parS partition complexes organize chromosome segregation, and stress- and cold-shock granules sequester translation machinery under adverse conditions. These structures are increasingly understood through the lens of biomolecular condensate biophysics, in which multivalent, often intrinsically disordered proteins self-assemble via associative interactions that can be tuned by concentration, post-translational modification, and interaction valence. Parallel advances in bacterial systems biology have produced extraordinarily rich, standardized gene-expression compendia (PRECISE for E. coli regulatory states, COLOMBOS and SRA-derived RNA-seq atlases spanning many species, PaxDb proteomic abundance data) that capture how transcriptional and regulatory networks reorganize gene products across thousands of physiological conditions, including growth-phase transitions, quorum-sensing activation, envelope stress, and biofilm commitment. Independently, sequence-based biophysical predictors—catGRANULE, PScore, FuzDrop—now permit proteome-scale estimation of phase-separation propensity and intrinsic disorder without requiring new experimental measurement.

Despite the maturity of each of these resources individually, no existing study has integrated them to ask whether bacterial regulatory logic systematically encodes instructions for mesoscale reorganization. That is, when a cell shifts regulatory state—entering stationary phase, activating quorum sensing, mounting an envelope-stress response—does the expressed proteome shift in a coordinated way toward or away from condensate-forming character, and is this shift conserved across bacterial diversity or lineage-specific? This is a foundational question about emergence at the mesoscale: it asks whether higher-order spatial organization within cells lacking organelles is a predictable, encoded output of lower-level regulatory network architecture, rather than an incidental byproduct of protein biophysics alone.

Answering this question additionally requires evolutionary and comparative genomic context. Extensive experimental evolution datasets (e.g., ALEdb) and clinical/environmental isolate genome collections document recurrent loss-of-function mutations in regulatory circuits, including quorum-sensing regulators and efflux systems, that produce unexpected downstream physiological consequences, including altered virulence and stress phenotypes. Whether such mutations also perturb the expression balance of condensate-forming proteins—and thereby alter mesoscale organization as an unselected consequence of adaptation—has never been examined. Addressing this synthesis-scale question requires simultaneous fluency in regulatory genomics, comparative evolutionary biology, and quantitative polymer/condensate biophysics, a combination that does not exist within any single laboratory and that is precisely the kind of cross-disciplinary, data-intensive integration NCEMS is positioned to enable. The proposed working group will produce the first cross-species, condition-resolved atlas connecting regulatory state to predicted mesoscale organization, establishing a new synthesis framework for understanding organelle-free cellular compartmentalization.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This project addresses three linked research questions, each testable using exclusively existing public data.

Question 1: Is bacterial regulatory network architecture systematically coupled to shifts in the phase-separation propensity of the expressed proteome? We hypothesize that physiological transitions with well-characterized regulatory signatures—entry into stationary phase, quorum-sensing activation, envelope and cold-shock stress, biofilm commitment—are accompanied by conserved, co-regulated shifts in the relative abundance of high-propensity, disorder-rich condensate-forming proteins versus their low-propensity structural or metabolic partners. We further hypothesize that this coupling is strongest for regulons directly controlling known condensate components (e.g., RNase E/BR-body machinery, ParB, PopZ, cold-shock proteins) but extends more broadly to co-regulated operons whose products have not yet been experimentally implicated in phase separation, generating testable predictions for previously unrecognized condensate constituents.

Question 2: Can polymer-physics models of associative condensate assembly translate observed or inferred stoichiometric shifts in expression atlases into quantitative predictions of condensate phase behavior? Building on associative-polymer frameworks that explain multivalent-network stoichiometry, client recruitment, and multiphase architecture in reconstituted systems, we hypothesize that regulatory-state-dependent changes in the relative abundance of scaffold and client proteins predict shifts in condensate phase boundaries, internal demixing, and material properties (e.g., viscosity, multiphase coexistence) in a manner consistent with known behavior of characterized bacterial condensates and generalizable to under-studied species and structures.

Question 3: Do naturally occurring or experimentally evolved regulatory mutations alter the expression balance of condensate-forming proteins as an emergent consequence of adaptation? Motivated by documented cases in which loss-of-function mutations in regulatory circuits—including quorum-sensing regulators and antibiotic efflux systems—produce unanticipated downstream physiological effects, we hypothesize that such mutations, captured in long-term evolution-experiment lineages and clinical/environmental isolate genome collections, systematically shift the balance of high- versus low-propensity proteins in ways that predict altered mesoscale organization, even when condensate phenotypes were not directly selected upon.

Confirmation of systematic coupling (Question 1) combined with quantitative, physics-based translation into condensate predictions (Question 2) would establish a generalizable framework for predicting mesoscale reorganization directly from transcriptomic or proteomic state, applicable across the bacterial kingdom. Evidence for evolutionary modulation of this coupling (Question 3) would reveal mesoscale organization as a previously unrecognized axis along which regulatory mutations exert pleiotropic effects, with implications for understanding stress adaptation, antibiotic resistance evolution, and virulence.

[Methods and Approach]
The project is structured as a three-phase synthesis workflow, entirely reliant on public data integration and computational/statistical analysis, requiring no new experimental generation.

Phase 1 – Cross-species expression-to-propensity atlas. We will assemble condition-annotated transcriptomic datasets from PRECISE, COLOMBOS, and curated SRA RNA-seq collections spanning model and non-model bacterial species, harmonizing metadata for physiological state (growth phase, stress type, quorum-sensing activity, biofilm status) using controlled-vocabulary ontologies. Every annotated proteome will be scored genome-wide for phase-separation propensity and intrinsic disorder using catGRANULE, PScore, and FuzDrop, producing a per-condition, per-species distribution of expressed propensity scores. Statistical models (mixed-effects regression, controlling for species phylogeny and technical batch) will test whether propensity-score distributions shift systematically and reproducibly across defined physiological transitions, both within and across species.

Phase 2 – Biophysical translation via polymer-based condensate modeling. Using associative-polymer modeling frameworks previously applied to explain multivalent network stoichiometry and multiphase architecture in reconstituted systems, we will map condition-specific shifts in scaffold-to-client protein abundance ratios (derived from Phase 1) onto predicted phase diagrams for characterized bacterial condensates (BR-bodies, PopZ, ParB/parS, cold-shock granules). This generates quantitative, falsifiable predictions of condensate assembly propensity, internal demixing, and material properties as functions of regulatory state, benchmarked against existing experimental characterizations of these structures in the literature.

Phase 3 – Evolutionary and comparative genomic integration. Using ALEdb long-term evolution-experiment data and curated clinical/environmental bacterial isolate genome collections, we will identify recurrent mutations in regulatory genes (quorum-sensing regulators, efflux pump components, two-component systems) and determine, via matched or inferred expression data, whether these mutations are associated with predicted shifts in condensate-forming protein balance, using the atlas and models from Phases 1–2 as an interpretive framework.

Bacteria lack membrane-bound organelles, yet an increasing number of proteinaceous mesoscale assemblies—BR-bodies, PopZ microdomains, ParB/parS partition complexes, cold-shock and stress granules—are now recognized as functionally important, phase-separated or phase-separation-like structures. This project will synthesize three classes of public data that have never been jointly analyzed at scale: (1) large bacterial gene-expression compendia spanning thousands of conditions and dozens of species (e.g., PRECISE, COLOMBOS, SRA-derived RNA-seq collections, proteomic abundance databases such as PaxDb), (2) sequence-based biophysical predictors of phase-separation propensity and intrinsic disorder (catGRANULE, PScore, FuzDrop) applied proteome-wide, and (3) curated experimental catalogs of known bacterial condensate components together with comparative genomic and evolution-experiment data (ALEdb, clinical isolate genome collections, long-term evolution lineages) documenting mutations in regulatory circuits such as quorum-sensing systems and efflux pumps.

This synthesis requires integrating expertise in bacterial evolutionary genomics and regulatory network biology with quantitative condensate biophysics and polymer theory, a combination not resident in any single laboratory. abstract_text:
A central puzzle in molecular systems biology is why some mutations that destabilize a protein produce negligible phenotypic consequences while others trigger abrupt, disproportionate loss of cellular function. We propose that this threshold-like behavior is an emergent property of the coupling between a protein's biophysical stability and its position within interaction networks, rather than an intrinsic property of the mutation itself. This working group will synthesize three classes of publicly available data that have never been jointly analyzed at scale: (1) proteome-wide thermodynamic stability measurements from deep mutational scanning and mega-scale stability assays (e.g., MaveDB, ProteinGym, Tsuboyama et al. stability atlas, deep receptor scanning datasets for GPCRs), (2) protein-protein and protein-DNA interaction network data from curated interactomes (BioGRID, STRING, IntAct, the Arabidopsis interactome AtPIN, and plant immune signaling networks), and (3) evolutionary and population-genetic datasets capturing selection on protein variants (gnomAD, ClinVar, dN/dS estimates, experimental evolution fitness landscapes).

Our central hypothesis, motivated by prior observations of threshold-like fitness relationships in antibiotic resistance enzymes and by the differential trafficking behavior of destabilized membrane proteins such as CFTR and GPCRs, is that network connectivity buffers the phenotypic consequences of destabilizing mutations up to a critical free-energy threshold, beyond which interaction networks undergo sharp, nonlinear rewiring or collapse. We predict that highly connected hub proteins exhibit wider stability buffering zones due to redundant or cooperative binding interfaces, while peripheral proteins collapse at smaller perturbations, and that this relationship generalizes across kingdoms despite divergent protein architectures (human membrane-embedded receptors and channels versus plant cytoplasmic immune regulators).

To test this, we will build a unified computational pipeline that maps ΔΔG values from deep mutational scanning onto network centrality metrics (degree, betweenness, clustering coefficient) and models how progressive destabilization propagates through interactome topology using percolation and network robustness frameworks. We will compare human disease-relevant systems (CFTR, GPCRs, KCNQ1-type ion channels) with plant immune signaling hubs (e.g., NPR1-centered networks) to ask whether energetic-topological coupling constitutes a conserved organizing principle of cellular systems or is contingent on compartment-specific biophysics (membrane insertion energetics versus cytosolic folding). Single-cell transcriptomic data will be incorporated to test whether cell-type-specific expression of interaction partners modulates the effective stability threshold in situ.

This project requires integration of expertise that no single lab possesses: membrane protein folding thermodynamics and pharmacological chaperone biophysics, network-based systems biology and plant immune signaling, and evolutionary protein biophysics and fitness landscape modeling. The resulting open-source framework, datasets, and reproducible workflows will be released publicly, and the project will train graduate students and postdocs in cross-disciplinary skills spanning biophysical modeling, network science, and comparative genomics, directly addressing NCEMS's mission to reveal mesoscale emergent principles connecting molecular energetics to cellular network behavior.

The resulting open-source framework, datasets, and reproducible workflows will be released publicly, and the project will train graduate students and postdocs in cross-disciplinary skills spanning biophysical modeling, network science, and comparative genomics, directly addressing NCEMS's mission to reveal mesoscale emergent principles connecting molecular energetics to cellular network behavior.

[Background and Significance]
A long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biology concerns the disconnect between a mutation's biophysical effect on protein stability and its ultimate phenotypic consequence. Many destabilizing substitutions are tolerated with little functional cost, while others of similar or even smaller thermodynamic magnitude precipitate catastrophic loss of function. This nonlinearity has been documented repeatedly in disparate contexts: gain- and loss-of-function ion channel variants whose surface expression depends on subtle shifts in folding efficiency, membrane receptors whose biosynthetic fidelity is exquisitely sensitive to sequence context, antibiotic-resistance enzymes exhibiting threshold-like fitness landscapes under selection, and plant immune regulators whose signaling capacity collapses abruptly when destabilized by pathogen effectors. These observations, generated independently across biomedical, plant biology, and evolutionary biophysics communities, point toward a shared but unarticulated principle: that phenotypic robustness to destabilization is not an intrinsic property of a protein's fold alone but emerges from its embedding within larger interaction networks. A protein's tolerance for destabilizing perturbation may depend fundamentally on whether it occupies a highly buffered, redundantly connected hub or a sparsely connected periphery of the interactome. Despite the intuitive appeal of this idea, it has never been rigorously tested at proteome scale because the datasets required to do so have been generated in isolation by different research communities. Deep mutational scanning and mega-scale stability assays now provide ΔΔG measurements for thousands of variants across hundreds of proteins, spanning cytosolic domains, membrane-embedded receptors, and channels. Simultaneously, curated interactome databases document the topology of protein-protein and protein-DNA interaction networks across humans, plants, and other model systems. Population-genetic and evolutionary datasets independently capture the selective consequences of variation at these same positions. No existing study has integrated these three data classes to ask whether network position quantitatively predicts the stability threshold at which phenotypic collapse occurs, nor whether this relationship is conserved across kingdoms with fundamentally different proteomic architectures. This gap represents precisely the kind of emergent, mesoscale question NCEMS is positioned to address: a phenomenon that arises from the coupling of molecular energetics with network-scale organization, requiring synthesis of biophysical, systems-biology, and evolutionary datasets that individually exist in public repositories but have never been jointly mined. Resolving this question would provide a mechanistic, quantitative foundation for predicting when destabilizing mutations become pathogenic or adaptive, with direct implications for interpreting variant effects in human disease (e.g., cystic fibrosis, channelopathies) and for understanding robustness and evolvability in plant immune signaling networks. The proposed synthesis is significant not only because it addresses a fundamental unresolved question but because it establishes a generalizable analytical framework linking thermodynamic and topological data that can be extended to other biological systems and future datasets as they emerge.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This working group is organized around three interlocking research questions. First, does a protein's position within an interaction network quantitatively determine its tolerance to destabilizing mutation, such that highly connected hub proteins exhibit wider ranges of ΔΔG before functional collapse compared to peripheral proteins? Second, is the transition from buffered to collapsed network states nonlinear and threshold-like, consistent with percolation-type behavior in network science, rather than a gradual, proportional decline in function? Third, is this energetic-topological coupling a conserved organizing principle across kingdoms, or is it contingent on compartment-specific biophysical constraints such as membrane insertion energetics in animal systems versus cytosolic folding and effector-driven destabilization in plant immune networks? Our central hypothesis is that network connectivity acts as a buffering mechanism against destabilizing mutation, with redundant or cooperative binding interfaces at hub proteins absorbing folding defects up to a critical free-energy threshold, beyond which interaction networks undergo abrupt, disproportionate rewiring or collapse. We derive three testable sub-hypotheses. First, we predict a positive correlation between network centrality metrics (degree, betweenness, clustering coefficient) and the magnitude of ΔΔG tolerated before measurable loss of interaction capacity or trafficking efficiency, drawing on precedent from destabilized ion channels and receptors that nonetheless reach the cell surface at functional levels due to compensatory interactions. Second, we predict that the relationship between stability and network collapse is nonlinear and better described by percolation or robustness models with defined critical thresholds than by linear dose-response models, mirroring threshold-like fitness relationships previously observed in antibiotic-resistance enzymes under selection. Third, we predict that while the qualitative form of this relationship (buffering followed by threshold collapse) will generalize across human and plant systems, the quantitative parameters of the threshold will differ systematically according to compartment-specific biophysics, with membrane-embedded proteins showing distinct threshold behavior from cytosolic immune regulators due to differences in folding energetics, quality-control stringency, and interaction geometry. A fourth, more exploratory question addresses whether cell-type-specific expression patterns of interaction partners, captured in single-cell transcriptomic atlases, modulate the effective stability threshold observed in bulk biochemical or population-genetic data, potentially explaining tissue-specific penetrance of destabilizing variants in human disease. Testing these hypotheses requires simultaneous access to and integration of stability, interactome, evolutionary, and expression datasets at a scale and diversity no single laboratory currently possesses, and requires reconciling heterogeneous data structures, normalization conventions, and network annotation standards across human and plant systems. The working group's combined expertise in membrane protein biophysics, plant systems network biology, and evolutionary protein energetics is specifically suited to resolving these methodological and conceptual challenges collaboratively.

[Methods and Approach]
The project is structured around three synthesis phases executed collaboratively across the working group's expertise. Phase one focuses on data harmonization. We will assemble ΔΔG stability measurements from deep mutational scanning repositories (MaveDB, ProteinGym, the Tsuboyama et al. mega-scale stability atlas) and receptor-specific biosynthesis datasets, standardizing thermodynamic units and mutation coordinate systems across proteins with divergent domain architectures, including membrane-embedded receptors and channels and cytosolic plant immune regulators. In parallel, we will curate interaction network data from BioGRID, STRING, IntAct, and the Arabidopsis interactome resource, constructing unified graph representations with consistent confidence-weighting schemes and computing centrality metrics (degree, betweenness, clustering coefficient, k-core) for all proteins with corresponding stability data. Evolutionary and population-genetic annotations from gnomAD, ClinVar, and dN/dS estimates will be mapped onto the same variant coordinates to provide independent readouts of selective consequence. Phase two involves statistical and computational modeling of the coupling between stability and topology. We will fit variant-level models relating ΔΔG to network centrality and to functional or clinical outcome annotations, testing for threshold effects using changepoint detection and percolation-based network robustness simulations that model progressive node or edge removal as a function of destabilization. These models will be applied comparatively to matched sets of human disease-relevant proteins (CFTR, GPCRs, KCNQ1-family channels) and plant immune signaling hubs (NPR1-centered networks and interacting partners), enabling direct cross-kingdom comparison of threshold parameters and buffering capacity. Percolation simulations will be validated against known functional outcomes, such as surface trafficking efficiency for membrane proteins and immune signaling output for plant regulators, to ensure that predicted collapse points align with independently measured phenotypic transitions. Phase three integrates single-cell transcriptomic data to test whether cell-type-specific expression of interaction partners shifts the effective network topology and therefore the predicted stability threshold, using coexpression and regulatory network inference approaches applied to existing single-cell atlases. Throughout, the team will develop a modular, open-source computational pipeline implemented in Python, leveraging established network analysis and machine learning libraries, designed for extensibility to additional proteins, species, and future datasets. Regular working group meetings will coordinate cross-disciplinary quality control, ensuring that biophysical interpretation of ΔΔG values, network-theoretic modeling choices, and evolutionary genetic annotations are jointly validated rather than siloed within individual disciplinary perspectives. Sensitivity analyses will assess robustness of conclusions to interactome curation biases and dataset incompleteness, an essential consideration given known ascertainment differences between human and plant interactome resources.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This synthesis will produce a quantitative, generalizable framework describing how protein network position modulates tolerance to destabilizing mutation, directly addressing a long-standing gap between biophysical and systems-level understanding of genotype-phenotype relationships. Primary deliverables include a validated computational pipeline linking thermodynamic stability data to network robustness models, a cross-kingdom comparative dataset annotating centrality-buffering relationships for hundreds of proteins, and empirically derived threshold parameters distinguishing membrane-embedded from cytosolic systems. These outputs will advance interpretation of variant pathogenicity in human disease contexts such as cystic fibrosis and channelopathies by providing network-informed priors for variant effect prediction, complementing existing clinical variant classification pipelines. In plant biology, the framework will offer new mechanistic insight into robustness and fragility of immune signaling networks under pathogen-driven destabilization, informing future breeding and engineering strategies for disease resistance. More broadly, the project establishes network-position-dependent buffering as a candidate general principle of mesoscale emergence connecting molecular energetics to cellular-scale network behavior, a central conceptual target of NCEMS's mission. The comparative cross-kingdom design will clarify which aspects of this principle are universal versus contingent on compartment-specific biophysics, informing future synthesis efforts extending to additional organisms and protein classes. Methodologically, the project will yield reusable analytical tools applicable beyond the specific systems studied here, lowering the barrier for future researchers to integrate stability and network data. The collaborative structure, spanning membrane protein biophysics, plant systems biology, and evolutionary protein science, will also serve as a template for future interdisciplinary synthesis efforts, while directly training graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in transferable skills bridging biophysical modeling, network science, and comparative genomics.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
All data used in this project derive from existing public repositories, including MaveDB, ProteinGym, the Tsuboyama et al. stability atlas, BioGRID, STRING, IntAct, the Arabidopsis interactome resource, gnomAD, ClinVar, and public single-cell transcriptomic atlases; no new experimental data will be generated. The working group commits to full adherence to FAIR data principles throughout the project. All harmonized datasets, including standardized stability measurements, network centrality annotations, and merged variant-level tables, will be deposited in appropriate public repositories with persistent identifiers and clear provenance documentation linking back to original source datasets. All computational pipelines, including data harmonization scripts, network construction and centrality calculation code, percolation and robustness simulation frameworks, and statistical modeling notebooks, will be developed under version control in a public repository, documented with clear installation and usage instructions, and structured to support reproducibility by external users applying the framework to new proteins or species. We will use containerized computational environments to ensure long-term reproducibility independent of software version drift. Intermediate and final analysis outputs, including derived threshold parameters and comparative cross-kingdom results, will be released alongside publications as structured supplementary datasets rather than static figures alone, enabling reuse and reanalysis by the broader community. The working group will follow community-endorsed open and team science practices, including preregistration of key analytical hypotheses where appropriate, transparent reporting of negative or null results arising from threshold model testing, and regular public sharing of intermediate progress through preprints. All trainees involved will be instructed in reproducible research practices, including literate programming, version control workflows, and open data deposition standards, as a core component of their training experience within the working group.

[Budget and Resources]
The proposed synthesis project requires resources primarily supporting personnel time, computational infrastructure, and collaborative coordination rather than experimental costs, consistent with its exclusive reliance on existing public data. Requested funds will support partial salary or effort for one postdoctoral researcher with expertise in network science and computational biology, and partial support for graduate student trainees at each of the three participating institutions, enabling direct hands-on training in cross-disciplinary synthesis methods. Computational resources will include cloud or institutional high-performance computing allocation sufficient for large-scale network robustness simulations and machine learning model training across proteome-wide datasets, alongside data storage for harmonized public datasets and derived analytical products. Modest travel funds are requested to support in-person working group meetings at least twice during the project period, essential for integrating biophysical, network-theoretic, and evolutionary perspectives and for coordinating cross-institutional trainee mentorship. Additional funds will support publication costs, including open-access fees, ensuring findings and datasets are freely available. NCEMS support is essential because this project's scope, spanning proteome-wide stability data, multi-species interactome integration, and evolutionary genetic annotation, exceeds the analytical and personnel capacity of any single participating laboratory, and no existing collaboration among the three research groups currently possesses the shared computational infrastructure or cross-disciplinary training pipeline required. NCEMS's role in convening working group meetings, providing data science training resources, and supporting reproducible workflow infrastructure will substantially accelerate the pace and rigor of this synthesis relative to what could be achieved through informal collaboration alone. The requested budget is deliberately modest and synthesis-focused, reflecting the project's foundation entirely on existing public data and its emphasis on computational integration, model development, and cross-disciplinary training rather than new data generation.

[Background and Significance]
Membraneless organelles such as stress granules, nucleoli, and paraspeckles are archetypal examples of mesoscale emergence: bulk material properties (viscosity, interfacial tension, multiphase layering, aging kinetics) arise from thousands of weak, multivalent interactions among proteins and RNAs, and these properties are not straightforwardly predictable from the biophysics of any single interacting pair. Over the past decade, the field has made substantial progress explaining condensate formation through the lens of RBP intrinsic disorder, multivalent domain architecture, and motif-level RNA recognition. However, a critical variable has remained comparatively underexplored at scale: the structural ensemble of the RNA itself. RNAs are not passive strings of sequence motifs: they fold into secondary and tertiary structures that can occlude or expose binding sites, create multivalent scaffolding through repeated stem-loops, and alter local flexibility in ways that plausibly shape both which proteins are recruited into a condensate and the emergent material state of the resulting assembly. This structural axis is mechanistically distinct from sequence-composition or motif-density explanations currently dominant in phase-separation prediction, yet it has never been systematically tested at the transcriptome or condensate-atlas scale.

The reason this question remains unanswered is not a lack of data but a lack of integration. Genome-wide RBP-RNA interaction maps (eCLIP across ENCODE, PAR-CLIP repositories, aggregated resources such as POSTAR3 and RNAct) exist independently from RNA structural probing data (SHAPE/DMS reactivity profiles archived in the RNA Mapping Database and GEO) and independently again from condensate-level proteomic, transcriptomic, and biophysical characterization datasets (stress granule and nucleolar proteomic atlases, paraspeckle composition studies, and emerging high-throughput condensate-propensity screens covering thousands of protein and RNA sequences). Each of these data classes was generated by different communities, using incompatible genome builds, annotation standards, and file formats, and each requires distinct domain expertise to interpret correctly: RNA structural modeling and energetics, condensate biology and quantitative proteomics, and large-scale computational data harmonization. No individual laboratory possesses the full complement of expertise and bandwidth to responsibly integrate all three layers, which is precisely why this question has persisted as an open problem despite the availability of relevant public data.

This proposal is directly responsive to NCEMS's mission to catalyze synthesis of publicly available molecular and cellular data to resolve fundamental questions about emergent mesoscale phenomena. By combining RNA structural modeling expertise with condensate biology, proteomics, and phase-separation biophysics, our Working Group is positioned to establish RNA structural ensembles as a new, quantitatively tractable axis of condensate emergence — reframing a long-standing puzzle in mesoscale cell biology and producing a resource of lasting value to the broader community of RNA biologists, condensate biophysicists, and computational structural biologists.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This Working Group is organized around one overarching synthesis question and three tractable sub-questions, each addressable only through integration of existing public datasets spanning RNA structural biology and condensate proteomics.

Overarching question: Does the structural ensemble of an RNA molecule — independent of its sequence-level motif content — systematically influence which RBPs it recruits into biomolecular condensates and what emergent material properties result?

Sub-question 1 (structure and recruitment specificity): Do RNAs enriched within specific condensates (stress granules, nucleoli, paraspeckles) exhibit distinctive secondary structural signatures — such as elevated stem-loop density, characteristic single-stranded region length distributions, or recurring multivalent structured motifs — relative to transcriptome-wide background and relative to one another? We hypothesize that condensate identity correlates with distinguishable structural fingerprints beyond what is explained by RBP motif content alone, reflecting a structure-mediated layer of specificity in RNA partitioning.

Sub-question 2 (structural context at RBP binding sites): Does the local structural context surrounding experimentally mapped RBP binding sites (from eCLIP/PAR-CLIP) differ systematically between RBPs that are core, stable condensate residents versus those that are transient or peripheral components, as defined by existing condensate proteomic atlases? We hypothesize that stable condensate-resident RBPs preferentially bind RNA regions with specific structural accessibility profiles (e.g., moderately structured, dynamically breathing regions rather than either fully rigid duplexes or fully unstructured stretches), consistent with a structural “sweet spot” that supports multivalent, exchangeable interactions.

Sub-question 3 (structure and material properties): Do RNA structural features aggregated at the transcript or condensate-transcriptome level correlate with reported condensate biophysical properties — viscosity, interfacial tension, propensity for multiphase architecture, or aging/hardening kinetics — as documented across the condensate literature and high-throughput condensate-propensity screens? We hypothesize that RNAs with higher densities of stable, multivalent structural elements contribute to increased network connectivity and thus correlate with more viscous or gel-like condensate states, while RNAs dominated by flexible, unstructured regions correlate with more liquid-like states.

These hypotheses are motivated by established biophysical principles of multivalency-driven phase separation, in which network connectivity and interaction valency govern material state, combined with the recognition that RNA secondary structure itself constitutes a source of multivalent, cooperative interaction surfaces (via stem-loops, junctions, and higher-order motifs) that has been comparatively neglected relative to protein-side multivalency. Rosetta-derived energetic modeling of RNA structural stability and flexibility, applied at scale across condensate-associated transcripts, offers a principled way to quantify these structural properties beyond simple secondary-structure diagrams.

Critically, none of these questions can be answered using any single existing dataset. Each requires cross-referencing RBP binding maps, RNA structural probing data, and condensate composition/biophysical annotations that were collected by separate consortia for separate purposes. Answering them constitutes genuine community-scale synthesis: the Working Group will produce, for the first time, a jointly harmonized dataset and analytical framework capable of testing whether RNA structure is a previously underappreciated determinant of condensate emergence, generating hypotheses that can subsequently be tested experimentally by the broader community.

[Methods and Approach]
The project proceeds in four integrated phases, each assigned to the team members whose expertise most directly applies, with shared computational infrastructure ensuring reproducibility across phases.

Phase 1 — Data harmonization: We will assemble and standardize three public data layers onto a common genome build and transcript annotation (GENCODE-based). RBP-RNA interaction data will be drawn from ENCODE eCLIP, additional PAR-CLIP datasets, and pre-aggregated resources (POSTAR3, RNAct), retaining peak coordinates, RBP identity, and binding confidence metrics. RNA structural data will be compiled from SHAPE/DMS chemical probing experiments deposited in the RNA Mapping Database and GEO, supplemented by transcriptome-wide computational structure predictions where experimental probing is unavailable, using established secondary-structure prediction algorithms. Condensate composition and biophysical data will be compiled from published stress granule, nucleolar, and paraspeckle proteomic/transcriptomic atlases, and from recently released high-throughput condensate-propensity screening datasets covering thousands of protein sequences. All datasets will be ingested into a unified relational schema with transcript-level and nucleotide-level resolution.

Phase 2 — Structural feature extraction: For every transcript represented across the harmonized dataset, we will compute a standardized set of structural descriptors: base-pairing probability profiles, stem-loop density and length distributions, single-stranded region statistics, and structural ensemble diversity (Shannon entropy of base-pairing). For a curated subset of condensate-relevant transcripts with especially strong evidence of biological importance, we will apply Rosetta-based energetic modeling to estimate structural stability and conformational flexibility, providing a physically grounded complement to purely statistical secondary-structure descriptors.

Phase 3 — Integrative statistical and machine-learning analysis: Using the harmonized dataset, we will test Sub-questions 1–3 through complementary approaches: (a) enrichment analyses comparing structural feature distributions across condensate-associated versus background transcripts; (b) binding-site-centered analyses comparing local structural context between stably condensate-resident and transient/peripheral RBPs, using existing proteomic stability/enrichment metrics as ground truth; and (c) supervised machine-learning models (gradient-boosted trees and neural architectures suited to structured biological data) trained to predict condensate material-property classifications from RNA structural feature vectors, benchmarked against sequence/motif-only baseline models to isolate the structural contribution.

Phase 4 — Validation and synthesis: Findings will be cross-validated against independent, held-out condensate datasets not used in model training, and against orthogonal structural probing datasets, to assess robustness. Trainees will lead specific sub-analyses (e.g., condensate-specific structural fingerprinting, RBP-binding-site context modeling) under joint mentorship, gaining hands-on experience in cross-domain data integration.

Throughout, working group meetings will reconcile methodological choices (e.g., structure prediction thresholds, RBP confidence cutoffs) via documented, version-controlled decisions, ensuring that all integration steps are transparent, auditable, and reproducible by external users of the resulting RNAstruct-Condensome resource.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The Working Group will deliver: (1) RNAstruct-Condensome, an open, harmonized database linking RNA structural features, RBP binding data, and condensate composition/biophysical annotations at transcript and nucleotide resolution; (2) a reproducible computational pipeline for extracting structural descriptors and Rosetta-based energetic metrics transcriptome-wide; (3) a set of statistically validated structural signatures associated with condensate identity, RBP recruitment stability, and reported material properties; and (4) machine-learning models predicting condensate partner recruitment and material-state tendencies from RNA structural input, benchmarked against existing sequence-only predictors.

Scientifically, this work will establish whether RNA structural ensembles constitute an independent, quantifiable axis of mesoscale emergence in condensate biology — a conceptual advance relevant to stress granule dysfunction in neurodegeneration, nucleolar stress responses, and paraspeckle-mediated gene regulation. By demonstrating (or rigorously constraining) the role of RNA structure, the project will refine mechanistic models of phase separation currently dominated by protein-centric multivalency frameworks.

Methodologically, the harmonization pipeline itself is a reusable community resource: it resolves long-standing incompatibilities between RNA structural probing data, CLIP-based interactome data, and condensate proteomic atlases, lowering the barrier for future synthesis projects in RNA biology and condensate research. Trainees engaged in the project will acquire transferable skills in cross-domain data integration, structural bioinformatics, and machine learning applied to heterogeneous molecular datasets, contributing to NCEMS's workforce-development goals. Broader impact extends to experimentalists who can use predicted structural determinants to design targeted follow-up perturbation experiments, accelerating hypothesis-driven research into RNA-directed condensate assembly and material control.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
All components of this project will be developed and released under open science principles consistent with NCEMS and community standards for reproducible synthesis research. Source data are exclusively drawn from publicly accessible repositories (ENCODE, GEO, RNA Mapping Database, POSTAR3, RNAct, and published condensate atlases), and all harmonization scripts, annotation-mapping tables, and structural feature extraction pipelines will be deposited in version-controlled public repositories (GitHub, with archival snapshots on Zenodo) under permissive open-source licenses.

The integrated RNAstruct-Condensome database will be released with full provenance tracking, documenting the original source, access date, and processing steps applied to every data point, enabling exact reconstruction of derived features. Machine-learning models, including trained weights, hyperparameters, and evaluation code, will be shared alongside standardized benchmark datasets so that external groups can reproduce reported performance metrics or apply the models to new transcripts. Analysis workflows will be containerized to ensure computational environment consistency across collaborating institutions and for future community reuse.

We will adopt FAIR data principles throughout, ensuring findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable outputs, and will register the project's data dictionary and schema early in the project to solicit community feedback before finalizing the resource architecture. Intermediate analysis decisions (e.g., structure-prediction confidence thresholds, RBP peak-calling criteria) will be documented in a public methods log to support transparency and enable alternative reanalysis. Consistent with NCEMS's emphasis on team science, we will hold regular open working-group meetings with notes archived publicly, and will prioritize preprinting all findings to accelerate community access ahead of formal publication, ensuring the resource and its insights are available to the broadest possible audience of RNA biologists, condensate researchers, and computational scientists.

[Budget and Resources]
This proposal requests NCEMS support structured around personnel, computational infrastructure, and collaborative training activities rather than experimental costs, consistent with the project's purely synthesis-based scope. Primary budget allocation will support a postdoctoral researcher or senior graduate trainee with combined computational structural biology and data engineering skills to lead data harmonization and pipeline development, alongside partial support for a second trainee focused on condensate proteomic data integration and machine-learning model development, providing direct cross-disciplinary training experience central to NCEMS's workforce goals.

Computational resources will include cloud or institutional high-performance computing allocation sufficient for transcriptome-wide structure prediction, Rosetta-based energetic modeling of selected transcript sets, and training/validation of machine-learning models across large condensate-associated datasets; storage costs for the harmonized multi-terabyte integrated database and its versioned releases are also requested.

Travel funds are requested to support two in-person working-group meetings per year, bringing together the two co-PI labs and invited domain experts (e.g., proteomics data curators, RNA structural probing specialists) to resolve harmonization decisions, validate emerging findings, and coordinate trainee mentorship — activities that benefit substantially from concentrated in-person collaboration beyond routine virtual meetings.

Modest publication and data-repository fees are requested to support open-access publication and permanent archival deposition (Zenodo/GitHub releases) of code, data, and models. No funds are requested for new experimental data generation, consistent with the project's exclusive reliance on existing public datasets. This budget structure reflects the project's core need: dedicated personnel time and computational capacity to accomplish an integration task that exceeds the bandwidth of either contributing lab operating independently, precisely the gap NCEMS support is intended to fill.

title: Decoding Environmental Selection Pressures on Condensate-Forming Sequence Grammars: A Multiscale Data Synthesis Across the Prokaryotic-to-Eukaryotic Thermal and Salinity Continuum

abstract_text:
Intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) drive biomolecular condensation through sequence-encoded 'sticker-and-spacer' grammars, yet whether these grammars are themselves products of environmental selection remains unknown. Organisms spanning psychrophiles, mesophiles, thermophiles, and halophiles have evolved proteomes under vastly different physicochemical constraints (temperature, ionic strength, crowding), but no systematic effort has linked these environmental gradients to the biophysical 'rules' governing mesoscale self-assembly. This project will synthesize four classes of publicly available data that, to date, have never been integrated at scale: (1) curated proteome and IDR annotation databases (UniProt, MobiDB, DisProt) spanning thousands of species with documented optimal growth temperatures and salinities; (2) condensate-associated protein catalogs (PhaSepDB, CD-CODE, DrLLPS) identifying known or predicted phase-separating proteins and their partners; (3) parameterized coarse-grained simulation frameworks (e.g., Mpipi-class models) that translate sequence composition and patterning into predicted phase diagrams, saturation concentrations, and critical solution temperatures; and (4) structural/ultrastructural datasets from cryo-electron tomography, cryo-EM, and SAXS repositories (EMDB, PDB, EMPIAR) that reveal in vivo or in vitro condensate architecture for a subset of these proteins, particularly in bacterial systems where mesoscale organization has been directly visualized.

We will computationally extract sequence-grammar features (aromatic/cationic sticker density, charge patterning, spacer composition and length, net charge per residue) from IDRs across organisms occupying extreme versus moderate environmental niches, then apply existing coarse-grained simulation engines to predict each sequence's phase behavior (critical temperature, droplet viscoelasticity, salt/temperature sensitivity) without generating new experimental data. These predictions will be statistically correlated with organismal growth conditions to test whether specific grammatical features (e.g., increased spacer flexibility or altered stickers valence) systematically track thermal or osmotic adaptation, analogous to known compensatory strategies in folded-protein stability. Where cryo-ET or structural data exist for homologous condensate-scaffolding proteins (e.g., bacterial polar organizing proteins, RNA-binding stress granule components), we will cross-validate simulation-derived phase behavior against observed ultrastructural features (filament versus droplet morphology, interfacial properties) to determine whether sequence-encoded adaptations manifest as predictable changes in mesoscale architecture.

This synthesis requires integrating expertise in structural/mesoscale bacterial biology, physics-based coarse-grained modeling of condensates, and sequence-to-function mapping of disordered regions—capabilities distributed across our three groups and not achievable within any single lab. The project will produce an open-access, queryable atlas linking environmental parameters, IDR sequence grammar, predicted phase behavior, and (where available) structural ground truth, providing a resource for the community to test hypotheses about evolutionary constraints on emergent mesoscale organization. Findings will illuminate whether phase separation itself is an evolvable, selectable trait shaped by environmental pressure, offering a new framework for understanding how molecular-scale sequence features generate cell-scale adaptive phenotypes. All code, curated datasets, and simulation outputs will be released under FAIR principles, and the working group will train graduate students and postdocs in cross-disciplinary integration of genomics, biophysical simulation, and structural data analysis.

Biomolecular condensates formed through liquid-liquid phase separation represent a fundamental mechanism by which cells organize biochemistry in space and time without membrane boundaries. A growing body of work has established that condensate formation is governed by sequence-encoded 'sticker-and-spacer' grammars within intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), wherein aromatic and charged residues act as adhesive stickers embedded within flexible spacer sequences that modulate valence, density, and interaction strength. Coarse-grained simulation frameworks now allow near-quantitative prediction of phase behavior directly from sequence, and structural techniques including cryo-electron tomography have begun to reveal how these sequence-encoded interactions manifest as higher-order mesoscale architectures inside cells, including filamentous and droplet-like assemblies in bacteria. Organisms have diversified across an extraordinary range of thermal and osmotic environments, from psychrophiles surviving near-freezing temperatures to halophiles thriving in saturated brines, and it is well established that folded protein stability, membrane composition, and metabolic strategies have co-evolved with these environmental constraints. This gap persists not for lack of relevant data, but because the data required to address it are scattered across disconnected resources: proteome and disorder annotation databases, condensate-protein catalogs, biophysical simulation parameterizations, and structural repositories have each matured independently without cross-integration.
