The resulting open, versioned database and analysis pipeline will let the community query any protein for its topological status alongside its translational and proteostasis context, generating testable predictions about chaperone requirements or disease risk for uncharacterized entangled folds. Graduate students and postdocs will be trained across topology algorithms, ribosome-profiling bioinformatics, and network biology, producing a genuinely transdisciplinary dataset and workforce capable of reasoning about how molecular-scale geometric complexity propagates into cellular-scale regulatory demands, directly addressing NCEMS's mesoscale emergence mandate.

[Background and Significance]
Non-trivial chain entanglement—knots, slipknots, lassos, and theta-curves—occurs in a small but reproducible fraction of the known protein universe. Over the past decade, systematic topological surveys of the Protein Data Bank and, more recently, of AlphaFold-predicted proteomes have revealed hundreds of examples spanning bacteria, archaea, and eukaryotes, including newly identified knot types in the human proteome. These findings establish that entanglement is not an artifact of a handful of curiosities but a recurring structural motif with plausible functional and evolutionary significance. Yet the field remains fragmented at the level of mechanism: structural topologists have cataloged where entanglement occurs, biophysicists have characterized how individual knotted proteins fold in vitro and in silico, and separately, the ribosome-profiling and chaperone-interactome communities have generated genome-scale data on translational kinetics and proteostasis machinery without reference to topological complexity. No systematic, cross-scale synthesis has yet asked whether entanglement constitutes a predictable design constraint that cells actively manage through coordinated co-translational and chaperone-assisted mechanisms, rather than an incidental byproduct of protein evolution. This gap is significant for several reasons. First, resolving whether translational pausing near entanglement-forming segments is a general evolved strategy—rather than an anecdotal feature described for individual model proteins—would clarify a fundamental principle linking genetic sequence-level features to protein-level topological outcomes, a quintessential mesoscale phenomenon bridging molecular and cellular regulation. Second, identifying systematic chaperone dependencies of entangled folds would refine our understanding of proteostasis network architecture and its evolutionary conservation across kingdoms with divergent chaperone repertoires (e.g., GroEL/GroES-dominated bacterial systems versus Hsp70/Hsp90-dominated eukaryotic systems). Third, determining whether entanglement cores show distinctive purifying selection and human disease-variant enrichment would provide a topological lens on missense pathogenicity prediction, currently underexplored in variant-effect frameworks. Existing single-domain resources—KnotProt, LassoProt, AlphaKnot, the Genus database, ribosome profiling repositories, BioGRID/HumanNet interactomes, ortholog conservation databases, and ClinVar/gnomAD—each answer part of this puzzle but were never designed for joint interrogation. Assembling them requires reconciling incompatible identifiers, structural coordinate systems, sequence coordinate mappings, and statistical frameworks across data types generated by non-overlapping research communities. This is precisely the kind of large-scale, cross-domain integration that exceeds the scope of any single laboratory and instead demands a working group spanning knot theory, polymer physics, structural bioinformatics, and coevolutionary genomics. By synthesizing these resources, this project will generate the first mechanistic, proteome-wide account of entanglement as an emergent constraint operating across translational, chaperone, and evolutionary scales, directly advancing NCEMS's mission to understand emergent mesoscale properties bridging molecular and cellular biology.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This project is organized around three interconnected research questions, each addressed through synthesis of existing public datasets rather than new experimentation. Research Question 1: Does the local translation-elongation landscape systematically differ near entanglement-forming segments compared to matched non-entangled regions? Hypothesis 1a: Codon usage bias will be measurably reduced, and predicted ribosome dwell times elevated, within and immediately downstream of knot-, slipknot-, and lasso-forming sequence windows, consistent with a co-translational folding-delay mechanism that permits controlled topological threading. Hypothesis 1b: This signature will be strongest for knots and slipknots requiring backtracking or loop-threading folding pathways, and comparatively weaker for lasso motifs stabilized primarily by covalent or disulfide loop closure, reflecting mechanistically distinct folding demands already described for these topological classes. Research Question 2: Do entangled proteins exhibit systematic, class-specific dependencies on particular chaperone systems, and are these dependencies detectable through interactome connectivity patterns rather than case-by-case experimental characterization? Hypothesis 2a: Proteins harboring deeply embedded or high-complexity knots will show disproportionate connectivity to chaperonin-type systems (GroEL/GroES in bacteria; CCT/TRiC in eukaryotes) capable of enclosed-cavity folding assistance, whereas shallow or terminal entanglements will associate more strongly with Hsp70-class holdases. Hypothesis 2b: Chaperone dependency patterns will be conserved across bacterial, archaeal, and eukaryotic orthologs of entangled proteins despite divergence in the specific chaperone machinery available, indicating that entanglement imposes a generalizable proteostasis demand rather than a lineage-specific solution. Research Question 3: Are residues within or adjacent to entanglement cores subject to distinctive evolutionary and disease-relevant selective pressures? Hypothesis 3a: Knot- and lasso-core residues will show significantly reduced dN/dS ratios relative to matched surface-exposed and buried non-entangled residues within the same proteins, reflecting structural intolerance to substitution imposed by topological packing constraints. Hypothesis 3b: Missense variants documented in ClinVar as pathogenic or likely pathogenic will be enriched within entanglement-forming regions relative to gnomAD population-frequency variants, after controlling for solvent accessibility and secondary structure, suggesting that topological complexity constitutes an underappreciated structural determinant of variant pathogenicity. Collectively, these hypotheses test whether entanglement functions as a coordinated, multi-scale design constraint—one visible only when structural, translational, proteostasis, and evolutionary datasets are examined jointly. Each hypothesis is falsifiable using existing public data and statistical comparison against carefully matched control sets, and each requires the combined topological, biophysical, and genomic expertise assembled in this working group to move beyond correlative observation toward mechanistic interpretation grounded in established folding and chaperone biology.

[Methods and Approach]
The project proceeds in four integrated phases, all relying exclusively on publicly available data and previously validated analytical tools. Phase 1 (Topological Mapping): We will consolidate entanglement annotations from KnotProt, LassoProt, AlphaKnot, and the Genus database for biomolecules, applying uniform-closure and statistical knot-detection methods already validated by team members to harmonize knot, slipknot, lasso, and theta-curve calls across experimentally solved PDB structures and high-confidence AlphaFold models (filtered by pLDDT thresholds). This yields a non-redundant, cross-referenced proteome-wide entanglement catalog spanning bacterial, archaeal, viral, and eukaryotic proteins, with precise residue-level coordinates for entangled segments. Phase 2 (Translational Context Integration): Using public ribosome profiling datasets (e.g., GWIPS-viz, Trips-Viz repositories) and codon usage/tRNA adaptation index resources, we will compute local translation elongation rate estimates and codon rarity scores for windows flanking each entangled segment, benchmarked against matched control windows drawn from non-entangled regions of the same proteins and length-matched decoy regions genome-wide. Phase 3 (Proteostasis Network Integration): Chaperone-substrate relationships will be extracted from BioGRID, HumanNet, and chaperone-specific interaction datasets for Hsp70, Hsp90, and GroEL/GroES systems, enabling network-based classification of chaperone dependency profiles for entangled versus non-entangled proteins. Network connectivity metrics (degree, betweenness, module membership) will be computed using standard graph-analytic approaches and compared across topological classes and taxonomic groups. Phase 4 (Evolutionary and Disease-Variant Integration): Ortholog alignments and dN/dS estimates will be drawn from existing comparative genomics databases (e.g., OrthoDB, Ensembl Compara), and pathogenic versus benign variant annotations from ClinVar and gnomAD will be mapped onto entanglement-core coordinates. Statistical enrichment will be assessed via permutation testing and logistic regression models controlling for solvent accessibility, secondary structure, and residue conservation, ensuring that observed effects are attributable to topological status rather than confounding structural features. Throughout, coarse-grained polymer physics models and coevolutionary interaction frameworks developed by team members will guide interpretation of folding pathway plausibility and inter-domain packing constraints. All datasets will be merged into a unified relational schema with standardized protein and residue identifiers (UniProt accession, PDB/AlphaFold coordinates), enabling reproducible cross-database queries. Working group meetings will be structured around iterative hypothesis testing, with trainees leading specific integration modules (translation, network, evolutionary) under joint mentorship from topology, biophysics, and genomics team members, ensuring methodological rigor and cross-training across all analytical domains represented in the project.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This synthesis will produce the first proteome-scale, cross-referenced resource linking protein topological complexity to translational kinetics, chaperone dependency, evolutionary constraint, and disease-variant enrichment. Primary deliverables include a versioned, publicly hosted database and accompanying analysis pipeline enabling any researcher to query a protein of interest for its entanglement status alongside predicted translational pausing, likely chaperone requirements, and evolutionary or clinical variant context. Scientifically, the project will determine whether topological entanglement functions as a generalizable mesoscale design constraint requiring coordinated cellular management, or instead represents evolutionarily neutral structural noise—a distinction with direct implications for protein engineering, synthetic biology design of knotted scaffolds, and interpretation of destabilizing disease variants in entangled proteins. abstract_original: Knotted, lassoed, and slipknotted proteins represent rare but functionally persistent topological outcomes of evolution, yet why certain folds tolerate or exploit such non-trivial entanglement while others avoid it remains unresolved. Existing structural databases (KnotProt, LassoProt, AlphaKnot, the Genus database for biomolecules) now catalog topological complexity across tens of thousands of experimentally solved and AlphaFold-predicted structures, while independent community resources capture the cellular machinery and kinetic context in which these proteins are synthesized and maintained: ribosome profiling datasets reporting codon-level translation elongation rates, genome-wide chaperone-substrate interactome maps (BioGRID, HumanNet, chaperone-specific interactomes for Hsp70/Hsp90/GroEL systems), evolutionary conservation and dN/dS databases, and disease-variant repositories such as ClinVar and gnomAD. title: Nucleolar Condensate Scaling Laws as a Mesoscale Determinant of Ribosome Biogenesis Capacity and Skeletal Muscle Hypertrophy: A Multi-Omic, GPU-Accelerated Synthesis

abstract_text:
A long-standing puzzle in skeletal muscle biology is why increases in ribosome biogenesis capacity—rather than acute changes in mTORC1 signaling alone—best predict the magnitude of mechanical-overload-induced hypertrophy across species and individuals. Ribosome biogenesis is orchestrated within the nucleolus, a biomolecular condensate assembled through liquid-liquid phase separation of rRNA, ribosomal proteins, and assembly factors. The nucleolus is a canonical mesoscale structure: it sits between individual macromolecules (Pol I machinery, ribosomal proteins, rRNA) and the organelle-level output (mature ribosomes), and its size, number, and phase behavior are hypothesized to nonlinearly determine translational capacity and thus cellular growth outcomes. Despite decades of molecular characterization of nucleolar components and separate characterization of hypertrophy transcriptomes/proteomes, no synthesis has quantitatively linked condensate-scale biophysical parameters (droplet size, surface tension proxies, assembly-factor stoichiometry) to tissue-scale hypertrophic outcomes using existing public data. This project unites expertise in skeletal muscle translational control, GPU-accelerated computational biology (sequence alignment, graph neural networks, molecular docking), and free-boundary mathematical modeling to construct and test a cross-scale model of nucleolar emergence.

We will assemble a synthesis dataset from public repositories including: (1) transcriptomic and proteomic time-course data from human and rodent resistance-exercise/mechanical-overload studies (GEO, ArrayExpress, MetaMEx), (2) curated nucleolar proteome atlases and condensate phase-separation propensity scores (e.g., PScore, catGRANULE-derived annotations) for rRNA transcription/processing factors, (3) ribosome profiling datasets quantifying translational output across hypertrophy models, and (4) comparative genomic assemblies spanning human, mouse, and rat rDNA loci and regulatory regions. This effort requires convergent expertise no single lab possesses: quantitative muscle physiology, high-performance computational biology, and multiscale mathematical modeling. Deliverables include an open-access cross-species nucleolar-hypertrophy multi-omic database, reproducible GNN and PDE modeling pipelines, and a generalizable framework for linking biomolecular condensate emergence to organismal phenotypic outcomes, with direct training opportunities for graduate students and postdocs in data integration, GPU computing, and multiscale modeling.

[Background and Significance]
Skeletal muscle hypertrophy following mechanical overload is a foundational model for understanding how cells scale their protein-synthetic machinery to meet increased functional demand. For over two decades, mTORC1 activation has been treated as the principal upstream determinant of this adaptive growth response. Yet a substantial body of literature has established that the magnitude of hypertrophy correlates more consistently with expansions in ribosome biogenesis capacity and satellite cell-supported translational reserve than with transient mTORC1 signaling amplitude. This discrepancy constitutes a long-standing puzzle: acute signaling events are necessary but demonstrably insufficient to explain the interindividual and interspecies variability observed in hypertrophic outcomes. What remains unexplained is the mechanistic link between the sub-organellar architecture that produces ribosomes and the tissue-level phenotype it ultimately supports.

The nucleolus, the site of ribosomal RNA transcription, processing, and pre-ribosome assembly, is increasingly understood not as a static structure but as a biomolecular condensate formed through liquid-liquid phase separation. Its emergent properties—size, number per nucleus, internal sub-compartmentalization, and phase behavior—arise nonlinearly from the concentrations and interaction properties of RNA polymerase I components, ribosomal proteins, and assembly factors. This is a textbook example of mesoscale emergence: individually characterized molecular components combine to produce organelle-level behavior that cannot be predicted by studying any single component in isolation, and this organelle-level behavior in turn constrains cellular and tissue-level growth capacity. Despite this conceptual alignment, no existing study has quantitatively connected condensate-scale biophysical parameters to organismal hypertrophic phenotypes using the wealth of public data already available across these different scales.

The reason this synthesis has not been attempted is structural rather than conceptual. The relevant data are scattered across disconnected domains: skeletal muscle physiology repositories contain transcriptomic and proteomic time courses of hypertrophy but lack condensate-scale biophysical annotation; biophysical and structural biology resources contain phase-separation propensity scores and nucleolar proteome atlases but are never cross-referenced against physiological outcome data; and comparative genomics resources containing rDNA locus architecture across species are computationally expensive to align and are rarely interpreted in a muscle physiology context. Bridging these domains requires simultaneous fluency in quantitative muscle biology, GPU-accelerated sequence and structural computation, and multiscale mathematical modeling of moving boundary problems—an expertise combination that does not exist within any single laboratory.

This project directly targets NCEMS's core scientific mission: understanding the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties at the mesoscale and their influence on higher-order cellular and organismal outcomes. By synthesizing existing multi-omic, genomic, and biophysical datasets into a unified cross-scale model, this work will resolve a genuine, long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biology while establishing a generalizable analytical framework for linking condensate-level emergence to phenotype elsewhere in cell biology.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This project is organized around three interconnected research questions that collectively test whether nucleolar condensate-scale parameters, rather than upstream signaling amplitude alone, are the proximate determinants of ribosome biogenesis capacity and hypertrophic outcome.

Research Question 1: Do condensate-scale biophysical parameters of the nucleolus—inferred from public proteomic stoichiometry and phase-separation propensity data—predict interindividual and interspecies variation in hypertrophic response better than canonical mTORC1 signaling markers? Hypothesis 1a: Assembly-factor stoichiometry and predicted phase-separation propensity of core nucleolar components will correlate more strongly with fiber cross-sectional area gains across public resistance-exercise datasets than phosphorylation-based mTORC1 activity markers. Hypothesis 1b: Species and individuals exhibiting greater hypertrophic ceilings will show nucleolar proteomic signatures consistent with larger predicted condensate size or number, independent of acute signaling amplitude.

Research Question 2: Does conserved versus divergent regulatory architecture at rDNA loci and Pol I transcription units explain cross-species differences in nucleolar growth rate and translational ceiling? Hypothesis 2: GPU-accelerated comparative genomic alignment of human, mouse, and rat rDNA regulatory regions will reveal sequence-level divergence in promoter and enhancer architecture that correlates with known interspecies differences in maximal hypertrophic capacity and ribosomal RNA transcription rate, providing a genomic explanation for phenotypic variability not attributable to signaling differences alone.

Research Question 3: Can a free-boundary mathematical model, parameterized entirely from public multi-omic data, reproduce empirically observed nucleolar size dynamics and predict tissue-level hypertrophy trajectories as an emergent consequence of condensate growth kinetics? Hypothesis 3: A phase-separated droplet-growth model in which boundary dynamics depend on rRNA synthesis flux, ribosomal protein import rate, and assembly-factor concentration gradients—each estimated from integrated omic data—will generate scaling laws that quantitatively reproduce independent public measurements of nucleolar size and hypertrophic trajectory, without requiring case-specific parameter fitting for each dataset.

A unifying hypothesis threads these three questions: hypertrophic capacity is fundamentally constrained by an emergent, mesoscale property of nucleolar condensate assembly, such that variability in translational output across individuals and species is better explained by parameters governing condensate formation and growth than by variability in upstream signaling amplitude. This reframes ribosome biogenesis capacity not as a downstream readout of mTORC1 activity but as an emergent property of a phase-separated organelle whose own assembly dynamics impose the rate-limiting constraint on cellular growth. Confirmation of this hypothesis would resolve the disconnect noted in decades of muscle physiology literature between signaling amplitude and hypertrophic outcome, while a negative or partial result would itself be scientifically valuable, clarifying the boundary conditions under which condensate-scale versus signaling-scale determinants dominate. Because every sub-question requires cross-referencing datasets from physiologically, genomically, and biophysically distinct public repositories that have never been jointly analyzed, none of these hypotheses is testable using data or methods available to any single laboratory in isolation.

[Methods and Approach]
The project proceeds in three integrated work packages executed collaboratively across the team's complementary expertise in muscle physiology, GPU-accelerated computational biology, and mathematical modeling.

Work Package 1 (Data Synthesis and Harmonization): We will systematically curate and harmonize public transcriptomic and proteomic time-course datasets from human and rodent mechanical-overload and resistance-exercise studies (GEO, ArrayExpress, MetaMEx), extracting expression trajectories for Pol I machinery, ribosomal proteins, and nucleolar assembly factors. These will be cross-referenced against curated nucleolar proteome atlases and computed phase-separation propensity scores (e.g., PScore- and catGRANULE-type annotations) to assign condensate-relevant biophysical attributes to each protein. Ribosome profiling datasets will be integrated to provide independent measures of translational output, enabling triangulation between transcript-level, protein-level, and functional translational readouts across hypertrophy models with differing severities and species.

Work Package 2 (GPU-Accelerated Comparative Genomics and Network Integration): Using GPU-enabled pairwise and multiple genome alignment tools with diagonal partitioning strategies, we will align human, mouse, and rat rDNA loci and flanking regulatory regions to identify conserved and divergent promoter architecture, transcription factor binding motifs, and Pol I regulatory elements. These alignments will be computationally intensive given the repetitive, high-copy-number nature of rDNA arrays, necessitating GPU parallelization approaches analogous to those previously applied to divergent genome alignment problems. In parallel, graph neural network models will be trained on integrated multi-layer networks combining transcriptional regulatory relationships, nucleolar protein-protein interaction data, and sequence/structural features relevant to phase separation, with the goal of predicting emergent nucleolar assembly states and identifying stoichiometric bottlenecks that limit ribosomal output. Model architectures will draw on pose-prediction and structure-prediction GNN frameworks previously applied to protein-ligand systems, repurposed here for condensate-relevant protein-protein and protein-RNA interaction prediction.

Work Package 3 (Free-Boundary Mathematical Modeling): We will formulate a multi-compartment free-boundary partial differential equation model representing the nucleolus as a growing phase-separated droplet, adapting a growth-front modeling framework previously developed for arterial wall remodeling and aneurysm progression to the intracellular context. Boundary dynamics will depend on rRNA synthesis flux, ribosomal protein import rate, and assembly-factor concentration gradients, each parameterized directly from Work Package 1 and 2 outputs rather than fitted independently, ensuring the model is a genuine synthesis product rather than an independently calibrated simulation. Model predictions of nucleolar size trajectories and translational capacity will be validated against independent public datasets not used in parameterization, including imaging-derived nucleolar size measurements and fiber-level hypertrophy time courses.

Integration across work packages will occur through iterative joint modeling sessions, with GNN-derived stoichiometric constraints directly informing PDE parameter priors, and PDE-generated scaling law predictions used to guide reanalysis of omic data for testable signatures. All computational pipelines will be containerized for reproducibility and executed on GPU-accelerated high-performance computing resources.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This project will produce a quantitative, testable framework linking nucleolar condensate biophysics to hypertrophic phenotype, directly resolving a longstanding disconnect between mTORC1-centric signaling models and empirically observed ribosome biogenesis-driven predictors of muscle growth. Primary deliverables include: (1) an open-access, harmonized cross-species multi-omic database integrating hypertrophy transcriptomic/proteomic time courses with nucleolar condensate biophysical annotations and comparative rDNA genomic architecture; (2) validated GPU-accelerated alignment and graph neural network pipelines for identifying regulatory divergence and stoichiometric bottlenecks in condensate-forming systems, generalizable to other phase-separated organelles; (3) a parameterized free-boundary mathematical model generating scaling laws relating molecular-scale condensate parameters to organelle and tissue-level growth outcomes; and (4) a set of explicit, falsifiable predictions regarding which condensate parameters should be prioritized in future targeted experimental studies.

Scientifically, this work advances the Center's mesoscale emergence mission by providing one of the first quantitative, data-synthesis-derived demonstrations that organelle-scale condensate behavior—rather than upstream signaling alone—constrains a well-studied organismal phenotype. The analytical framework developed here is not muscle-specific: the coupling of GNN-based stoichiometric inference with free-boundary growth modeling is directly transferable to other condensate systems (stress granules, paraspeckles, transcriptional condensates) and other phenotypic outcomes throughout molecular and cellular biology, offering a template for future synthesis research on emergence phenomena.

Broader impacts include establishing reusable, richly annotated public datasets that lower the barrier for future muscle physiology, condensate biology, and computational biology researchers to pursue related questions, and demonstrating a replicable model for transdisciplinary synthesis collaboration between physiology, computational biology, and applied mathematics.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
All research products from this Working Group will be developed and disseminated in strict accordance with open, team, and reproducible science principles. Because this project uses exclusively existing public data, careful provenance tracking is essential: every dataset drawn from GEO, ArrayExpress, MetaMEx, nucleolar proteome atlases, phase-separation propensity resources, and genomic assemblies will be documented with accession numbers, retrieval dates, and preprocessing decisions in a version-controlled data manifest, ensuring full traceability from raw public source to final integrated dataset.

All code—including GPU-accelerated genome alignment pipelines, graph neural network training and inference scripts, and free-boundary PDE solvers—will be developed in public repositories under permissive open-source licenses, with containerized environments (Docker/Singularity) to guarantee computational reproducibility across hardware configurations. Analysis workflows will be structured as modular, documented pipelines (e.g., using Snakemake or Nextflow) so that each stage, from raw data harmonization through final scaling-law derivation, can be independently rerun and audited by external researchers.

The harmonized multi-omic database itself will be deposited in a public, citable repository with a persistent identifier, accompanied by comprehensive metadata describing variable definitions, harmonization procedures, and known limitations, enabling reuse well beyond this project's immediate hypotheses. Model parameters, fitted values, and validation datasets for the PDE model will similarly be archived to allow independent verification of scaling-law claims.

Within the Working Group, we will adopt team-science best practices including shared electronic lab notebooks, regular cross-disciplinary integration meetings, and pre-registration of primary hypotheses and analysis plans prior to full-scale computational runs, reducing the risk of post hoc rationalization given the exploratory nature of large-scale data synthesis. All findings, including negative or partial results relevant to the stated hypotheses, will be reported transparently in publications and preprint form, consistent with NCEMS community standards for open and reproducible synthesis research.

[Budget and Resources]
This project requires resources characteristic of computational synthesis research rather than wet-laboratory experimentation, and is appropriately scoped for NCEMS support given its reliance on sustained GPU compute access, personnel time for cross-disciplinary integration, and trainee involvement.

Personnel: Support is requested for one postdoctoral researcher with expertise in computational biology and GPU programming to lead pipeline development for genome alignment and graph neural network modeling, and one graduate student co-mentored across the muscle physiology and mathematical modeling groups to lead multi-omic data harmonization and PDE parameterization. Partial summer support for the three co-investigators is requested to enable sustained cross-disciplinary coordination, model integration meetings, and joint manuscript preparation.

Computational Resources: The comparative genomic alignment and graph neural network training components require significant GPU-hour allocations; we request access to NCEMS-supported or partner high-performance computing GPU clusters (multi-GPU nodes, e.g., NVIDIA A100-class hardware), along with cloud storage for the multi-terabyte scale harmonized multi-omic database and intermediate alignment outputs.

Training and Dissemination: Funds are requested to support trainee travel to present integrated findings at cross-disciplinary conferences spanning muscle physiology, computational biology, and mathematical biology, as well as participation in NCEMS-sponsored training and community synthesis events. A modest allocation supports publication costs for open-access dissemination and repository fees for permanent archiving of datasets and code.

This budget explicitly excludes any wet-laboratory experimentation, new data generation, or animal/human subjects costs, consistent with the synthesis-only scope of this proposal. The requested resources directly reflect needs that exceed the capacity of any single participating laboratory—particularly sustained GPU infrastructure and cross-disciplinary personnel time—justifying the necessity of NCEMS-level support for this collaborative synthesis effort.

Graduate students and postdocs will be trained in cross-database curation, phylogenetic comparative statistics, and biophysical parameter modeling, building a pipeline transferable to other mesoscale emergence questions in molecular and cellular biology.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) organize cellular biochemistry without membranes, and their material properties—viscosity, interfacial tension, capacity for multiphase organization, and selective client/scaffold partitioning—are now recognized as functionally consequential emergent properties that arise from collective interactions among intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs). Over the past decade, a 'molecular grammar' framework has emerged wherein features such as charge patterning, aromatic residue valence and spacing, and stickers-and-spacers architecture quantitatively predict single-chain conformational behavior and condensate-scale phase behavior. This framework has been validated for individual model systems using orthogonal biophysical techniques including small-angle X-ray scattering, single-molecule FRET, NMR spectroscopy, and coarse-grained molecular simulation. Yet a fundamental puzzle remains unresolved: IDRs are among the least conserved regions of the proteome at the level of primary sequence, exhibiting extensive residue substitution, insertion, and deletion across orthologs and paralogs, even as the condensates they build maintain remarkably conserved material properties and physiological functions across evolutionarily distant organisms. This apparent contradiction—sequence plasticity coexisting with functional robustness—has been noted anecdotally across many individual IDR systems but has never been tested systematically at proteome or cross-species scale. We hypothesize that natural selection acts on emergent physical parameters rather than on sequence identity per se, meaning that evolution tolerates substantial residue-level drift as long as compaction, patterning, and valence properties that dictate condensate-forming capacity are preserved. This hypothesis has profound implications for interpreting disease-associated variation: many ALS/FTD- and neurodegeneration-linked mutations in TDP-43, tau, α-synuclein, and FUS-family proteins occur in IDRs that fall outside canonical sequence-conservation signatures used by standard variant-effect predictors, potentially explaining why physically disruptive variants are systematically under-prioritized by conservation-based pipelines. Testing this hypothesis requires synthesizing heterogeneous, distributed data types—biophysical measurements, condensate composition catalogs, disorder and ortholog annotations, phylogenetic conservation scores, and clinical variant databases—at a scale and cross-disciplinary depth that no single laboratory currently possesses. No existing resource unifies polymer-physics parameterization with evolutionary comparative genomics for IDR-driven condensate systems. Addressing this gap directly serves NCEMS's mission of understanding emergent mesoscale properties bridging biomolecules and higher-order cellular organization, and it exemplifies the type of large-scale data synthesis puzzle—spanning biophysics, evolutionary biology, structural bioinformatics, and disease genetics—that is intractable without a coordinated, cross-disciplinary working group leveraging publicly available data at scale.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This project is organized around a central overarching hypothesis: selection on IDR sequences that drive condensate formation operates predominantly at the level of emergent physical parameters (compaction, charge patterning, aromatic/proline patterning, and stickers-and-spacers valence) rather than on residue-level sequence identity, and this decoupling explains the coexistence of high sequence divergence with conserved condensate material properties across evolution. From this central hypothesis, we derive four specific, testable research questions. Question 1 asks whether physical parameters computed from ortholog and paralog IDR sequences—spanning model organisms from yeast to human—show significantly higher phylogenetic conservation (lower variance relative to divergence time) than conventional sequence-identity or alignment-based conservation scores. We hypothesize that physical-parameter trajectories will exhibit conservation signatures resembling purifying selection even where sequence alignments show near-random substitution patterns, indicating that the parameters, not the residues, are the unit of selection. Question 2 investigates whether disease-associated variants—curated from ClinVar, ALSoD, and related repositories for TDP-43, tau, α-synuclein, and FUS-family proteins—disproportionately shift physical parameters relative to matched benign polymorphisms, even when both variant classes occur at sequence positions with similarly low classical conservation scores. We hypothesize that pathogenic variants will show significantly larger perturbations in compaction and patterning metrics, and that a parameter-based scoring scheme will outperform sequence-conservation-based predictors in distinguishing pathogenic from benign IDR variants. Question 3 asks whether the degree and direction of physical-parameter conservation can predict which condensate systems are susceptible to pathological intra-condensate demixing—as documented for TDP-43 in stress granules—versus systems whose condensates tolerate substantial sequence divergence while preserving single-phase liquid-like behavior. We hypothesize that proteins whose physical parameters cluster near phase boundaries identified by coarse-grained simulation will show greater propensity for demixing-associated pathology, providing a predictive biophysical signature for disease susceptibility that generalizes beyond TDP-43. Question 4 examines whether design principles derived from synthetic condensate-based gene circuits generalize across the natural parameter space captured in the atlas, asking whether engineered IDR fusions that buffer growth-mediated dilution occupy a parameter regime distinct from, or overlapping with, naturally evolved condensate-forming sequences. We hypothesize that synthetic designs successful at buffering dilution will fall within the same physical-parameter envelope associated with evolutionarily robust natural condensate scaffolds, supporting the generalizability of physics-based design rules. Collectively, these questions test whether a unifying, lower-dimensional physical grammar—rather than sequence conservation—constitutes the conserved substrate of condensate emergent function, with direct implications for variant interpretation, mechanistic disease research, and synthetic biology design.

[Methods and Approach]
This is exclusively a data-synthesis project; no new experimental or simulation data specific to novel sequences will be generated beyond applying previously validated computational transformations to existing sequence records. We will assemble a curated IDR sequence corpus by cross-referencing DisProt and MobiDB disorder annotations with UniProt and OrthoDB ortholog/paralog groupings for proteins central to condensate biology, prioritizing TDP-43, tau, α-synuclein, FUS-family members, and prion-like transcription factor domains, extending coverage from human to model organisms spanning mouse, Drosophila, C. elegans, and S. cerevisiae. Each IDR sequence will be computationally translated into a physical parameter vector using established, previously validated sequence-to-parameter mappings, including radius of gyration and Flory scaling exponent estimates calibrated against SASBDB scattering profiles and published single-molecule FRET transfer efficiencies, charge patterning metrics (kappa, sequence charge decoration), and aromatic/proline patterning and valence descriptors derived from stickers-and-spacers and HPS/Mpipi-type coarse-grained model parameterizations already established by team members. Condensate-relevant material property annotations (viscosity, interfacial tension, partitioning behavior, multiphase status) will be extracted from PhaSepDB, CD-CODE, LLPSDB, and DrLLPS. Evolutionary conservation will be quantified using PhyloP and GERP scores aligned to each IDR position, supplemented by ConSurf-derived structural conservation estimates where applicable. Disease-variant data will be drawn from ClinVar, ALSoD, and dbSNP, with pathogenic and benign variants matched on regional sequence-conservation scores to isolate the marginal contribution of physical-parameter shifts. Analytically, we will apply phylogenetic comparative methods (phylogenetic generalized least squares, ancestral state reconstruction) to test whether physical parameters evolve under stronger purifying constraint than raw sequence identity across the ortholog/paralog trees. Supervised and unsupervised machine learning models (gradient-boosted trees, Gaussian process regression, dimensionality reduction) will be trained to predict pathogenicity, demixing propensity, and material-property class from parameter vectors, benchmarked against conservation-score-only baselines using held-out cross-validation stratified by protein family to avoid data leakage. All statistical models will be validated using permutation testing and bootstrapped confidence intervals. The working group will be organized into three coordinated subteams—biophysical parameterization, evolutionary genomics/statistics, and machine learning/predictive modeling—with structured biweekly integration meetings to reconcile data schemas and cross-validate intermediate outputs, ensuring that expertise distributed across polymer physics, condensate materials science, and evolutionary genomics converges on unified, reproducible analytical pipelines.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This project will deliver an open-access, queryable Physical Grammar Atlas linking IDR sequence, physical parameter vectors, evolutionary conservation metrics, and disease-variant annotations across condensate-forming protein families and species. Primary scientific outcomes include quantitative evidence for or against parameter-level conservation exceeding sequence-level conservation, a validated parameter-based variant pathogenicity score for IDR mutations, and predictive models distinguishing demixing-prone from demixing-resistant condensate systems. These outcomes directly address a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biosciences regarding how emergent mesoscale material properties remain functionally robust despite extensive sequence divergence, advancing NCEMS's core scientific vision of understanding emergent properties at the mesoscale. Practically, the atlas and associated scoring framework will provide immediately actionable tools for prioritizing IDR disease variants that current conservation-based pipelines systematically overlook, informing mechanistic follow-up studies in neurodegenerative disease research. The framework will also generalize to synthetic biology, offering design guidelines for engineering condensate-based genetic circuits with predictable material properties. Beyond specific findings, the project establishes a reusable computational pipeline for cross-database integration of biophysical, evolutionary, and clinical data that can be extended to other IDR-containing protein families and other mesoscale emergence questions, providing a durable community resource. The interdisciplinary working group structure will train graduate students and postdocs in transferable skills spanning database curation, phylogenetic comparative statistics, coarse-grained biophysical modeling, and machine learning, cultivating a data-savvy workforce equipped to tackle synthesis-scale questions in molecular and cellular biology.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
All aspects of this project will adhere to open science principles consistent with NCEMS and community-endorsed FAIR data standards. The curated Physical Grammar Atlas—including raw extracted annotations, computed physical parameter vectors, conservation scores, and variant classifications—will be deposited in a public, version-controlled repository (e.g., Zenodo with DOI minting, mirrored on GitHub) under an open license permitting reuse and extension. All analytical code, including sequence-to-parameter transformation scripts, phylogenetic comparative analysis pipelines, and machine learning training/evaluation workflows, will be developed using containerized, dependency-locked environments (Docker/Conda) and documented with executable notebooks to ensure computational reproducibility. We will adopt standardized metadata schemas compatible with existing resources (UniProt, MobiDB, PhaSepDB) to maximize interoperability and facilitate community contributions and updates as new orthologs, structures, or variant annotations become publicly available. Intermediate data products, including matched pathogenic/benign variant sets and parameter-conservation statistics, will be released alongside preprints prior to formal peer review to accelerate community feedback. Version control will track all pipeline changes, with releases tagged to specific manuscript submissions for full provenance tracking. We will hold data and workflows to community-created reproducible science checklists, including pre-registration of primary hypotheses and analysis plans where feasible, to reduce researcher-degrees-of-freedom in a project reliant on secondary data synthesis. Regular working group meetings will include reproducibility audits, wherein team members not involved in generating a given analysis attempt independent replication using only the deposited code and data. This practice both strengthens scientific rigor and provides direct experiential training for graduate students and postdocs in reproducible, team-based science, aligning with NCEMS's mandate to train a data-savvy scientific workforce grounded in open science norms.

[Budget and Resources]
This synthesis project requires modest but essential resources concentrated on personnel time, computational infrastructure, and collaborative coordination rather than experimental costs, consistent with its exclusive reliance on publicly available data. Primary budget allocation will support partial salary for one postdoctoral researcher with combined expertise in computational biophysics and evolutionary genomics, who will lead cross-database integration and pipeline development, alongside graduate student trainees at each of the three participating institutions who will contribute to parameter computation, phylogenetic analysis, and machine learning model development under PI mentorship. Computational resources will include cloud or institutional high-performance computing allocation for large-scale coarse-grained parameter calculations across thousands of ortholog/paralog sequences and for training and cross-validating machine learning models; these costs are moderate given that no new molecular dynamics simulations will be run beyond applying existing validated parameterization schemes. Funds are requested for data storage and repository hosting to maintain the public atlas and associated version-controlled workflows beyond the funding period. Travel funds will support in-person working group meetings at least twice yearly to coordinate across the three institutions represented by the team, along with participation in one NCEMS-sponsored cross-team synthesis workshop annually to disseminate progress and integrate feedback from the broader NCEMS community. Modest funds are allocated for publication costs, including open-access fees, to ensure all outputs are freely available. This budget explicitly excludes costs associated with new experimental data generation, reflecting the project's design as a pure synthesis effort. The requested resources reflect the genuine need for dedicated, sustained cross-institutional coordination and computational capacity that exceeds what any single participating laboratory could independently support, justifying NCEMS's role in enabling this collaboration.

title: Emergent Mesoscale Regulation of Torpor: A Cross-Species Synthesis of Biomolecular Condensates and Mitochondrial Reorganization in Independently Evolved Hibernators
title_norm: emergent mesoscale regulation of torpor a crossspecies synthesis of biomolecular condensates and mitochondrial reorganization in independently evolved hibernators
abstract_text: Mammalian hibernation has evolved independently across at least eight lineages—including ursids, sciurid rodents, bats, and even a primate (the fat-tailed dwarf lemur)—yet all hibernators achieve strikingly similar phenotypes: reversible suppression of metabolic rate, translation, and mitochondrial oxidative activity at low body temperature, followed by rapid, damage-free rewarming. While comparative genomic scans have identified candidate genes under selection in hibernators, and tissue-level transcriptomic studies (including our own multi-tissue brown bear resource) have characterized pathway-level shifts in gene expression, little is known about whether convergent evolution acts at the mesoscale—the level of protein assemblies, biomolecular condensates, and organelle architecture that sits between individual gene products and organismal physiology. Emerging evidence in non-hibernator systems shows that temperature- and stress-sensitive phase separation of RNA-binding proteins into stress granules, and reorganization of mitochondrial supercomplexes, can rapidly and reversibly reprogram translation and respiration without new transcription. We hypothesize that hibernators have convergently co-opted or tuned these mesoscale mechanisms as a shared molecular strategy for entering and exiting torpor, and that signatures of this convergence are detectable in existing genomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic datasets. This project will synthesize publicly available whole-genome assemblies and orthology databases (NCBI, Ensembl, Zoonomia), multi-tissue and time-series RNA-seq datasets from hibernating and non-hibernating relatives (SRA, GEO), and proteome-wide intrinsic disorder and phase-separation propensity predictions (e.g., catGRANULE, PScore, MobiDB) to build a cross-species map of condensate-forming and mitochondrial-interacting proteins. We will test for convergent molecular signatures—accelerated evolution, shared amino acid substitutions, or parallel shifts in expression timing—in genes encoding stress granule components, RNA-binding proteins, and mitochondrial supercomplex assembly factors across independently evolved hibernating lineages, using phylogenetic comparative methods that explicitly correct for shared ancestry versus convergence. Where available, we will integrate low-temperature in vitro transcriptomic and metabolic data (e.g., cultured fibroblast time-series data) to link predicted condensate/mitochondrial reorganization events to measured shifts in metabolic and circadian gene expression across torpor-arousal cycles. This effort requires expertise spanning comparative and population genomics, hibernation physiology and multi-tissue transcriptomics, and quantitative biophysical modeling of protein phase behavior and mitochondrial dynamics—capacities that exceed any single lab and necessitate a working group uniting evolutionary genomicists, hibernation biologists, and biophysicists studying condensates and organelle-scale emergence. The synthesis directly targets NCEMS's mesoscale mandate by asking how molecular-scale, temperature-sensitive assembly processes give rise to an emergent, organism-level phenotype (reversible hypometabolism) and whether this emergence follows predictable evolutionary rules. All genomic pipelines, orthology assignments, condensate-propensity scores, and comparative statistical frameworks will be released as open, reusable resources, providing a template for future mesoscale evolutionary synthesis studies and training opportunities for postdocs and graduate students at the interface of genomics, physiology, and biophysics.

[Background and Significance]
Hibernation is one of the most dramatic reversible phenotypic transitions in mammalian biology, involving coordinated suppression of metabolic rate, body temperature, translation, and mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, followed by rapid, damage-free arousal. This capacity has arisen independently in at least eight mammalian lineages—ursids, several rodent clades, multiple bat lineages, and the fat-tailed dwarf lemur—representing a striking case of convergent evolution on a complex physiological state. Decades of comparative genomic and transcriptomic work have identified candidate genes and pathways associated with hibernation, including shifts in lipid metabolism, circadian regulation, and stress-response signaling. Multi-tissue and time-series transcriptomic resources, including publicly deposited brown bear datasets spanning active, hibernating, and fed states, have further revealed pathway-level reprogramming during torpor-arousal cycles. However, these studies operate primarily at the level of gene expression and sequence divergence, leaving a critical gap: whether convergent evolution also acts at the mesoscale, the organizational level of protein assemblies, biomolecular condensates, and organelle architecture that mediates rapid, reversible cellular reprogramming without requiring new transcription or translation. Emerging biophysical literature demonstrates that many organisms use temperature- and stress-sensitive liquid-liquid phase separation of RNA-binding proteins into stress granules and related condensates to rapidly halt translation, and that mitochondrial supercomplex reorganization can rapidly modulate respiratory efficiency, both without new gene expression. These mechanisms are mechanistically well-suited to the rapid, reversible, and energy-conservative demands of torpor entry and arousal, yet they remain almost entirely unexplored in the context of hibernation evolution. This represents a significant conceptual gap: existing genomic and transcriptomic datasets, though extensive, have not been synthesized through a mesoscale lens capable of detecting convergent tuning of condensate-forming proteins or mitochondrial assembly factors across independently evolved hibernators. Addressing this gap requires integrating disparate public data types—whole-genome assemblies, orthology databases, multi-tissue and single-cell/time-series transcriptomes, and proteome-wide biophysical predictions—across taxonomically distant lineages, a task that exceeds the scope of any single laboratory's data, tools, or disciplinary expertise. This proposal directly addresses NCEMS's core scientific mandate by asking whether an emergent, organism-level phenotype (reversible hypometabolism) arises from predictable, convergent tuning of molecular-scale assembly processes at the mesoscale. Successfully mapping such convergence would resolve a long-standing puzzle in hibernation biology—why phenotypically similar torpor states arise from divergent genomic backgrounds—while also providing a generalizable framework for detecting mesoscale convergence in other emergent cellular phenotypes, with translational relevance for metabolic disease, organ preservation, and induced hypometabolic states in non-hibernating species, including humans.

First, do genes encoding stress granule components, RNA-binding proteins with high phase-separation propensity, and mitochondrial supercomplex assembly factors show signatures of convergent molecular evolution—accelerated substitution rates, shared amino acid changes, or parallel shifts in selective constraint—across independently evolved hibernating lineages, relative to their non-hibernating sister taxa? We hypothesize that such convergence will be concentrated in intrinsically disordered regions governing condensate assembly and in mitochondrial contact-site proteins, reflecting repeated evolutionary tuning of mesoscale assembly properties rather than convergence at conserved catalytic residues. Second, do publicly available multi-tissue and time-series transcriptomic datasets from hibernators reveal coordinated expression dynamics of condensate-forming and mitochondrial-reorganization genes across the torpor-arousal cycle that are consistent with predicted phase-separation and supercomplex-remodeling behavior? We hypothesize that transcripts encoding high-propensity condensate proteins will show rapid, non-monotonic expression or translation-associated signatures timed to temperature transitions, distinguishing them from genes undergoing purely transcriptional reprogramming, and that this pattern will recur across taxonomically independent hibernators despite differences in tissue sampling and experimental design. Third, where in vitro time-series data are available (e.g., temperature-manipulated cultured fibroblasts), can we link predicted mesoscale reorganization events—condensate formation, mitochondrial supercomplex shifts—to measured changes in metabolic output and circadian gene expression, thereby establishing a mechanistic bridge between molecular-scale assembly and cellular-scale metabolic suppression? We hypothesize that temperature-dependent shifts in condensate-propensity scores will correlate with measured reductions in ATP production and altered circadian transcript timing, supporting a causal role for mesoscale reorganization in hypometabolic phenotypes. Underlying all three questions is an overarching hypothesis: hibernation represents a case in which natural selection has repeatedly and independently converged not on identical genetic solutions, but on shared mesoscale physical strategies—tunable, reversible, temperature-sensitive assembly and disassembly of protein and organelle structures—that provide a more evolutionarily accessible route to the shared phenotype than convergent point mutations in catalytic genes alone. Testing this hypothesis requires explicit phylogenetic comparative methods capable of distinguishing convergence from shared ancestry, applied jointly to sequence, expression, and biophysical prediction data, a synthesis task that no existing single dataset or single-lab analysis has undertaken. Confirming or refuting these hypotheses will directly inform whether mesoscale emergence follows predictable evolutionary rules, a question of central importance to NCEMS's broader effort to understand how molecular-scale organization gives rise to higher-order biological phenotypes across systems beyond hibernation.

[Methods and Approach]
This synthesis project will proceed in four integrated phases, drawing exclusively on publicly available data and analytical tools. Phase 1 will assemble a curated cross-species genomic resource by retrieving whole-genome assemblies and orthology calls for hibernating and non-hibernating sister taxa from NCBI, Ensembl, and the Zoonomia comparative genomics database, spanning ursids, sciurids, bats, and the fat-tailed dwarf lemur alongside closely related non-hibernating outgroups. Orthologous gene sets will be curated for stress granule components, RNA-binding proteins, and mitochondrial supercomplex assembly factors based on established annotation databases and literature curation. Phase 2 will apply proteome-wide biophysical prediction tools, including catGRANULE, PScore, and MobiDB, to score phase-separation propensity and intrinsic disorder for all curated orthologs across species, generating a comparative condensate-propensity matrix. Phase 3 will implement phylogenetic comparative methods, including branch-site models of molecular evolution (e.g., HyPhy, PAML) and convergence-detection frameworks that explicitly model shared ancestry, to test for accelerated evolution, parallel substitutions, or shifts in selective constraint at condensate- and mitochondria-associated loci across independently hibernating branches relative to non-hibernating lineages. Phase 4 will integrate existing multi-tissue and time-series RNA-seq datasets deposited in SRA and GEO, including multi-tissue brown bear expression atlases and time-series in vitro fibroblast datasets under temperature manipulation, to test whether expression dynamics of condensate- and mitochondria-associated transcripts show patterns consistent with mesoscale reorganization across the torpor-arousal cycle. Differential expression, co-expression network, and time-series trajectory analyses will be harmonized across datasets using batch-correction and meta-analytic frameworks suited to heterogeneous public data. Where in vitro metabolic measurements (e.g., ATP production time-series) are available, we will statistically test associations between predicted condensate/mitochondrial reorganization signatures and measured metabolic shifts using mixed-effects and time-series correlation models. Throughout, uncertainty from heterogeneous sequencing depth, assembly quality, and experimental design across public datasets will be explicitly modeled and reported. The working group will meet through structured virtual and in-person synthesis workshops to iteratively refine gene curation lists, computational pipelines, and statistical models, ensuring that evolutionary genomics, transcriptomics, and biophysical modeling expertise are jointly applied at each analytic stage rather than sequentially siloed. This tightly integrated, multi-domain workflow—requiring simultaneous fluency in comparative genomics, hibernation transcriptomics, and quantitative biophysical prediction—is precisely the kind of cross-disciplinary synthesis that exceeds single-lab capacity and motivates the proposed NCEMS-supported working group structure, including regular consultation with NCEMS computational and data science staff to ensure scalable, reproducible implementation.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This project will produce the first cross-species, mesoscale-focused synthesis of hibernation biology, generating a curated comparative dataset of condensate-forming and mitochondrial-interacting orthologs across independently evolved hibernating lineages, together with associated phase-separation propensity scores, molecular evolution statistics, and expression trajectory annotations. A primary scientific outcome will be a rigorous test of whether convergent evolution in hibernators acts preferentially at the mesoscale rather than solely through canonical coding or regulatory changes, directly addressing a long-standing puzzle regarding the mechanistic basis of phenotypic convergence in torpor. If supported, this hypothesis will reframe hibernation as a model system for mesoscale evolutionary innovation, with implications extending to other reversible hypometabolic and stress-adaptive phenotypes across taxa. The resulting resources—curated ortholog sets, condensate-propensity matrices, and comparative evolutionary statistics—will provide a reusable foundation for future studies of induced hypometabolism relevant to therapeutic hypothermia, organ preservation, and metabolic disease research. Methodologically, the project will establish a generalizable analytical template for detecting mesoscale convergence by jointly leveraging genomic, transcriptomic, and biophysical prediction data, offering a model applicable to other emergent cellular phenotypes beyond hibernation. The working group structure will also generate durable interdisciplinary collaborations bridging evolutionary genomics, physiology, and biophysics, fields that rarely intersect methodologically. Trainees involved in the project will gain hands-on experience with comparative genomics pipelines, large-scale transcriptomic meta-analysis, and biophysical prediction tools, developing cross-disciplinary data science skills directly aligned with NCEMS's workforce training goals. Broader impacts include advancing conceptual understanding of how molecular-scale physical processes give rise to emergent organismal phenotypes, a question central to NCEMS's mesoscale research mandate, while providing openly available tools and datasets that will accelerate future synthesis research across the molecular and cellular sciences.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
All aspects of this synthesis project will adhere to open science principles consistent with NCEMS community standards. Raw and processed public datasets used in this project—including genome assemblies, orthology tables, and transcriptomic datasets from NCBI, Ensembl, Zoonomia, SRA, and GEO—will be explicitly cited with persistent accession identifiers, and all derived data products, including curated ortholog lists, condensate-propensity matrices, and molecular evolution statistics, will be deposited in appropriate public repositories (e.g., Dryad, Zenodo) under permissive licenses. All computational pipelines, including genome annotation curation scripts, phylogenetic comparative analysis code, and transcriptomic meta-analysis workflows, will be developed using version-controlled, containerized environments (Git, Docker/Singularity) to ensure exact reproducibility across computing environments. Analysis workflows will be structured using literate programming frameworks (e.g., Jupyter, R Markdown) with full parameterization documented to enable independent replication and extension by outside researchers. Intermediate and final results, including statistical models and visualization code, will be made available through public code repositories with clear documentation and tutorials designed for reuse by future synthesis teams studying convergence or mesoscale phenomena in other systems. The working group will follow FAIR data principles throughout, ensuring findability, accessibility, interoperability, and reusability of all synthesized resources. Regular internal data and code audits will be conducted to verify pipeline reproducibility before public release. Findings will be disseminated through preprints and open-access publications, with preregistration of key comparative hypotheses where appropriate to enhance transparency. Training materials developed for trainees participating in the working group, including workshop materials on comparative genomics and biophysical prediction tools, will also be made publicly available to extend training impact beyond the immediate project team, consistent with NCEMS's mission to cultivate a broader, data-savvy scientific workforce equipped for reproducible, collaborative synthesis research.

[Budget and Resources]
This project requests NCEMS support primarily for personnel time, computational infrastructure, and collaborative working group activities, reflecting its status as a data synthesis effort rather than a data generation project. Budget priorities include partial salary support for a postdoctoral researcher with expertise in comparative genomics and phylogenetic comparative methods, who will lead pipeline development and cross-species evolutionary analyses, and a graduate student trainee focused on transcriptomic meta-analysis and biophysical prediction integration, providing direct training opportunities central to NCEMS's workforce development goals. Modest computational resources are requested for cloud or high-performance computing access to support genome-scale orthology analyses, phylogenetic model fitting, and large-scale transcriptomic meta-analyses across multiple species and datasets. Funds are also requested to support two in-person working group synthesis workshops bringing together the evolutionary genomics, hibernation physiology, and biophysical modeling collaborators to jointly refine analytical frameworks, interpret emerging results, and coordinate manuscript and resource development; virtual meeting support will sustain collaboration between workshops. Additional funds will support open-access publication costs and data repository deposition fees to ensure full compliance with open science requirements. No funds are requested for new experimental data generation, consistent with NCEMS's synthesis-only scope. The project will also benefit from NCEMS-provided computational consultation and data science training resources, which will enhance pipeline scalability and reproducibility. Existing institutional resources at each collaborating institution, including established computing clusters and prior genomic and transcriptomic datasets generated by team members, will be leveraged in-kind to minimize costs. This lean budget structure reflects the project's core identity as a cross-disciplinary synthesis effort whose primary needs are collaborative coordination, computational integration, and trainee support rather than new data collection, aligning directly with NCEMS's funding priorities for community-scale synthesis research.

abstract_original: Mammalian hibernation has evolved independently across at least eight lineages—including ursids, sciurid rodents, bats, and even a primate (the fat-tailed dwarf lemur)—yet all hibernators achieve strikingly similar phenotypes: reversible suppression of metabolic rate, translation, and mitochondrial oxidative activity at low body temperature, followed by rapid, damage-free rewarming. While comparative genomic scans have identified candidate genes under selection in hibernators, and tissue-level transcriptomic studies (including our own multi-tissue brown bear resource) have characterized pathway-level shifts in gene expression, little is known about whether convergent evolution acts at the mesoscale—the level of protein assemblies, biomolecular condensates, and organelle architecture that sits between individual gene products and organismal physiology. Emerging evidence in non-hibernator systems shows that temperature- and stress-sensitive phase separation of RNA-binding proteins into stress granules, and reorganization of mitochondrial supercomplexes, can rapidly and reversibly reprogram translation and respiration without new transcription. We hypothesize that hibernators have convergently co-opted or tuned these mesoscale mechanisms as a shared molecular strategy for entering and exiting torpor, and that signatures of this convergence are detectable in existing genomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic datasets. This project will synthesize publicly available whole-genome assemblies and orthology databases (NCBI, Ensembl, Zoonomia), multi-tissue and time-series RNA-seq datasets from hibernating and non-hibernating relatives (SRA, GEO), and proteome-wide intrinsic disorder and phase-separation propensity predictions (e.g., catGRANULE, PScore, MobiDB) to build a cross-species map of condensate-forming and mitochondrial-interacting proteins. We will test for convergent molecular signatures—accelerated evolution, shared amino acid substitutions, or parallel shifts in expression timing—in genes encoding stress granule components, RNA-binding proteins, and mitochondrial supercomplex assembly factors across independently evolved hibernating lineages, using phylogenetic comparative methods that explicitly correct for shared ancestry versus convergence. Where available, we will integrate low-temperature in vitro transcriptomic and metabolic data (e.g., cultured fibroblast time-series data) to link predicted condensate/mitochondrial reorganization events to measured shifts in metabolic and circadian gene expression across torpor-arousal cycles. This effort requires expertise spanning comparative and population genomics, hibernation physiology and multi-tissue transcriptomics, and quantitative biophysical modeling of protein phase behavior and mitochondrial dynamics—capacities that exceed any single lab and necessitate a working group uniting evolutionary genomicists, hibernation biologists, and biophysicists studying condensates and organelle-scale emergence. The synthesis directly targets NCEMS's mesoscale mandate by asking how molecular-scale, temperature-sensitive assembly processes give rise to an emergent, organism-level phenotype (reversible hypometabolism) and whether this emergence follows predictable evolutionary rules. All genomic pipelines, orthology assignments, condensate-propensity scores, and comparative statistical frameworks will be released as open, reusable resources, providing a template for future mesoscale evolutionary synthesis studies and training opportunities for postdocs and graduate students at the interface of genomics, physiology, and biophysics.

title: From Residue Couplings to Circuit Memory: A Cross-Scale Synthesis Linking Coevolutionary Statistics, Allosteric Dynamics, and Phase-Separation Propensity to Regulatory Network Hysteresis
