abstract_text: A central puzzle in molecular and cellular biology is how local, residue-level physical couplings within individual proteins propagate upward to produce circuit-level emergent behaviors such as bistability, hysteresis, and irreversible switching in gene regulatory networks. Existing work has separately characterized (i) coevolutionary statistical couplings among residues using Potts models and statistical coupling analysis across protein families, (ii) dynamic allosteric pathways and temperature- or ligand-sensitive contact networks extracted from molecular dynamics trajectories, (iii) sequence-encoded propensities for intrinsically disordered regions and biomolecular condensate formation, and (iv) network-level dynamical properties of transcriptional regulatory systems, including memory and irreversibility following perturbation. No study has yet asked whether these layers are mechanistically linked: does the architecture of coevolutionary coupling and conformational dynamics within individual regulatory proteins predict which nodes of a transcriptional network will exhibit hysteretic, switch-like, or irreversible behavior? This project proposes a community-scale synthesis to test that hypothesis by integrating four classes of publicly available data that no single lab currently combines: (1) multiple sequence alignments and derived direct-coupling/statistical-coupling matrices for transcription factors and signaling proteins (Pfam, UniProt); (2) publicly deposited molecular dynamics trajectories and contact-network datasets for homologous or orthologous regulatory and allosteric proteins (e.g., MDDB, GPCRmd, Dynameomics-type repositories); (3) curated intrinsically disordered region and condensate-propensity annotations (DisProt, MobiDB, PhaSepDB) for the same protein families; and (4) reconstructed bacterial regulatory network topologies and previously published perturbation-response datasets characterizing irreversibility and hysteresis in transcriptional circuits (e.g., RegulonDB/EcoCyc-derived networks). Using information-theoretic measures of coupling entropy and coevolutionary sector structure alongside graph-theoretic and machine-learning analyses of MD-derived allosteric pathways (including random-forest classifiers previously validated for predicting channel-gating states), we will quantify whether proteins with strong long-range coevolutionary coupling and multistable dynamic ensembles are disproportionately embedded in network motifs associated with hysteresis and irreversibility, and whether disorder/condensate propensity modulates this relationship by providing an additional slow, cooperative mode of regulatory memory. The synthesis will produce an open, versioned, FAIR-compliant multi-scale dataset and analysis pipeline—a public 'coupling-to-circuit atlas'—linking residue-level statistical physics, protein dynamics, mesoscale assembly propensity, and network dynamics for a curated set of well-characterized regulatory systems. This effort requires collaboration across evolutionary systems biology, coevolutionary sequence statistics, computational biophysics/MD, and data infrastructure expertise, exceeding what any single lab's data or toolset can address, and will generate testable, falsifiable predictions about which molecular architectures give rise to emergent network-level memory. Training modules will teach graduate students and postdocs to integrate sequence-based statistical models, trajectory-based dynamics, and network reconstruction within reproducible open-science workflows, directly advancing NCEMS's mission to understand how mesoscale molecular organization gives rise to cellular-scale emergent properties.
full_text:
[Abstract]
A central puzzle in molecular and cellular biology is how local, residue-level physical couplings within individual proteins propagate upward to produce circuit-level emergent behaviors such as bistability, hysteresis, and irreversible switching in gene regulatory networks. Existing work has separately characterized (i) coevolutionary statistical couplings among residues using Potts models and statistical coupling analysis across protein families, (ii) dynamic allosteric pathways and temperature- or ligand-sensitive contact networks extracted from molecular dynamics trajectories, (iii) sequence-encoded propensities for intrinsically disordered regions and biomolecular condensate formation, and (iv) network-level dynamical properties of transcriptional regulatory systems, including memory and irreversibility following perturbation. No study has yet asked whether these layers are mechanistically linked: does the architecture of coevolutionary coupling and conformational dynamics within individual regulatory proteins predict which nodes of a transcriptional network will exhibit hysteretic, switch-like, or irreversible behavior? This project proposes a community-scale synthesis to test that hypothesis by integrating four classes of publicly available data that no single lab currently combines: (1) multiple sequence alignments and derived direct-coupling/statistical-coupling matrices for transcription factors and signaling proteins (Pfam, UniProt); (2) publicly deposited molecular dynamics trajectories and contact-network datasets for homologous or orthologous regulatory and allosteric proteins (e.g., MDDB, GPCRmd, Dynameomics-type repositories); (3) curated intrinsically disordered region and condensate-propensity annotations (DisProt, MobiDB, PhaSepDB) for the same protein families; and (4) reconstructed bacterial regulatory network topologies and previously published perturbation-response datasets characterizing irreversibility and hysteresis in transcriptional circuits (e.g., RegulonDB/EcoCyc-derived networks). Using information-theoretic measures of coupling entropy and coevolutionary sector structure alongside graph-theoretic and machine-learning analyses of MD-derived allosteric pathways (including random-forest classifiers previously validated for predicting channel-gating states), we will quantify whether proteins with strong long-range coevolutionary coupling and multistable dynamic ensembles are disproportionately embedded in network motifs associated with hysteresis and irreversibility, and whether disorder/condensate propensity modulates this relationship by providing an additional slow, cooperative mode of regulatory memory. The synthesis will produce an open, versioned, FAIR-compliant multi-scale dataset and analysis pipeline—a public 'coupling-to-circuit atlas'—linking residue-level statistical physics, protein dynamics, mesoscale assembly propensity, and network dynamics for a curated set of well-characterized regulatory systems. This effort requires collaboration across evolutionary systems biology, coevolutionary sequence statistics, computational biophysics/MD, and data infrastructure expertise, exceeding what any single lab's data or toolset can address, and will generate testable, falsifiable predictions about which molecular architectures give rise to emergent network-level memory. Training modules will teach graduate students and postdocs to integrate sequence-based statistical models, trajectory-based dynamics, and network reconstruction within reproducible open-science workflows, directly advancing NCEMS's mission to understand how mesoscale molecular organization gives rise to cellular-scale emergent properties.

[Background and Significance]
Emergent behaviors in gene regulatory networks—bistability, hysteresis, and irreversible switching—are among the most consequential mesoscale phenomena in cell biology, underlying processes from bacterial adaptation to developmental commitment. Prior network analyses have established that certain transcriptional circuits, particularly those built around positive-feedback motifs, exhibit memory: once perturbed, they fail to return to their original state even after the perturbing signal is removed. Reconstructed regulatory networks in model organisms such as Escherichia coli have been used to predict which genes, upon transient perturbation, will show such irreversibility, implicating proximity to positive circuits as a key structural determinant. However, this network-level description treats each regulatory protein as a node with fixed logical function, abstracting away the residue-level biophysics that actually implements switching behavior. In parallel, an entirely separate research tradition has used coevolutionary statistical models—Potts-model direct coupling analysis and statistical coupling analysis—to identify collectively evolving residue networks (sectors) within protein families, linking these sectors to allosteric communication, functional constraint, and evolvability. A third tradition, rooted in molecular dynamics simulation, has characterized how temperature-, ligand-, and mutation-sensitive contact networks reconfigure dynamically to produce multistable conformational ensembles, with graph-theoretic and machine-learning approaches now able to classify gating or activation states directly from simulated contact patterns. A fourth body of work has shown that intrinsically disordered regions and condensate-forming sequences confer additional slow, cooperative modes of assembly and disassembly, potentially serving as an independent memory mechanism operating on timescales relevant to cellular decision-making. Despite deep individual maturity, these four literatures remain unconnected. No existing study asks whether the coevolutionary architecture and dynamic multistability of a regulatory protein itself predicts whether the network node it occupies will behave hysteretically. This is a fundamental gap in understanding emergence: circuit-level memory is currently explained structurally (network topology) without reference to the molecular biophysics of the proteins that implement it, while molecular-level multistability is characterized without reference to its systems-level consequences. Bridging these scales requires simultaneous access to curated sequence alignments and coupling matrices, deposited MD trajectories for homologous regulatory proteins, disorder/condensate annotations, and previously published network perturbation-response datasets—resources that are individually public but have never been integrated within a single analytical framework. No single laboratory possesses the combined expertise in coevolutionary statistics, biomolecular simulation analysis, disorder/condensate bioinformatics, and regulatory network reconstruction necessary to perform this synthesis, nor the computational infrastructure to harmonize these heterogeneous, large-scale public datasets. This proposal directly addresses the NCEMS mission by testing whether mesoscale molecular organization—residue coupling architecture, conformational multistability, and condensate propensity—systematically gives rise to a higher-order cellular property, regulatory network memory, using exclusively existing public data through cross-disciplinary, collaborative synthesis.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This project is organized around one overarching question and three linked sub-questions, each addressed through synthesis of existing public datasets rather than new experimentation. Overarching question: Does the residue-level physical and evolutionary architecture of a regulatory protein predict whether the network node it occupies exhibits hysteretic or irreversible behavior following perturbation? Sub-question 1 (Coevolutionary architecture and network position): Are transcription factors and signaling proteins with strong, long-range coevolutionary coupling—indexed by sector size, coupling entropy, and direct-coupling network connectivity derived from Potts models and statistical coupling analysis—preferentially found at nodes embedded in positive-feedback motifs previously associated with irreversibility in reconstructed bacterial regulatory networks? We hypothesize that long-range coevolutionary coupling reflects an evolved capacity for concerted, cooperative conformational transitions, and that this capacity is enriched among proteins occupying hysteretic network positions, because such positions place a premium on robust, switch-like molecular responses. Sub-question 2 (Dynamic multistability and switching behavior): Do molecular dynamics-derived contact-network signatures of multistability—quantified via graph-theoretic descriptors of alternative contact states and validated by machine-learning classifiers previously shown to predict gating states in ion channels—correlate with the degree of hysteresis observed at the corresponding network node? We hypothesize that proteins whose simulated ensembles show clearly separable, temperature- or ligand-sensitive contact states will map onto network nodes with sharper, more bistable perturbation-response curves, because discrete conformational states provide a molecular implementation of discrete regulatory logic states. Sub-question 3 (Disorder/condensate propensity as an additional memory channel): Does the presence of condensate-forming intrinsically disordered regions in a regulatory protein modulate the relationship between coevolutionary/dynamic architecture and network hysteresis, either by amplifying switch-like behavior through cooperative assembly or by providing an independent, structure-decoupled memory mechanism? We hypothesize that disorder/condensate propensity acts as a secondary, slower memory channel, most influential at nodes where folded-domain coupling and dynamics alone predict weak hysteresis, thereby explaining outlier cases in the network dataset. These questions are deliberately falsifiable: a null result—no statistical association between coevolutionary/dynamic signatures and network hysteresis—would itself be highly informative, indicating that circuit-level memory arises predominantly from topological rather than molecular constraints, and redirecting the field's causal model of emergence. Because each sub-question requires integrating data types that are curated and maintained by different scientific communities (sequence databases, simulation repositories, disorder/condensate databases, and regulatory network reconstructions), no single laboratory's existing data holdings are sufficient to test them. The working group is explicitly structured to bring together complementary expertise in molecular evolution and coevolutionary statistics, computational biophysics and MD-based machine learning, phase-separation and condensate biology, and regulatory network dynamics, ensuring that each sub-question is addressed with methodological rigor appropriate to its data type while remaining integrated within a single cross-scale analytical framework.

[Methods and Approach]
The project proceeds in four coordinated phases, each built entirely on curation and reanalysis of existing public resources. Phase 1 – Protein family and dataset curation: We will assemble a curated set of regulatory and allosteric proteins with (a) available multiple sequence alignments in Pfam/UniProt suitable for direct-coupling analysis, (b) at least one publicly deposited MD trajectory or trajectory ensemble for a homologous or orthologous structure, (c) disorder/condensate annotations in DisProt, MobiDB, or PhaSepDB, and (d) a mapped node in a reconstructed bacterial regulatory network (RegulonDB/EcoCyc) with previously published perturbation-response data. Cross-referencing these databases via UniProt identifiers and structural homology mapping will define the tractable intersection dataset, prioritizing transcription factors and sensor/signaling proteins with the richest cross-database coverage. Phase 2 – Coevolutionary and dynamic feature extraction: For each protein family, we will compute Potts-model direct coupling matrices and statistical coupling analysis sectors from existing alignments, deriving quantitative descriptors of coupling range, sector size, and coupling entropy. In parallel, for proteins with deposited MD trajectories, we will apply established multi-ensemble contact-network analysis, graph-theoretic descriptors of alternative contact states, and previously validated random-forest classifiers to quantify conformational multistability and identify allosteric pathways connecting coupled residues to functional sites. Disorder and condensate propensity scores will be extracted directly from curated database annotations without additional computation. Phase 3 – Network hysteresis quantification: Using previously published perturbation-response datasets and reconstructed network topologies, we will quantify, for each mapped node, the degree of irreversibility following transient perturbation, replicating and extending existing network-analysis pipelines that link circuit position (e.g., proximity to positive-feedback loops) to memory behavior. Phase 4 – Cross-scale statistical integration: We will use multivariate regression, information-theoretic association measures, and machine-learning models (trained and validated with cross-validation across protein families to avoid phylogenetic confounds) to test whether coevolutionary coupling descriptors and MD-derived multistability metrics predict network hysteresis scores, and whether disorder/condensate propensity provides additional predictive power or interacts with the other two feature classes. Robustness will be assessed via family-holdout validation, permutation testing against random network rewiring, and sensitivity analyses across alternative coupling-matrix inference methods. All code, intermediate feature matrices, and integrated datasets will be version-controlled and containerized to support exact reproducibility. Data harmonization challenges—differing residue numbering schemes, structural coverage gaps in MD datasets, and inconsistent disorder-annotation granularity—will be addressed through a shared mapping ontology maintained collaboratively by the working group, itself a key deliverable of the synthesis effort.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This synthesis will produce the first cross-scale, empirically grounded dataset and analytical pipeline linking residue-level coevolutionary architecture, protein conformational dynamics, disorder/condensate propensity, and regulatory network memory. The primary scientific deliverable, a public 'coupling-to-circuit atlas,' will provide quantitative, falsifiable evidence for or against the hypothesis that molecular-level coupling architecture predicts circuit-level hysteresis, reframing how emergent network behaviors are explained mechanistically. Regardless of directionality, results will refine causal models of regulatory network dynamics: a positive association would establish molecular biophysical signatures as predictive features for identifying hysteretic nodes in uncharacterized networks, with implications for synthetic biology circuit design and antimicrobial target prioritization; a null or partial association would clarify the relative contribution of topology versus molecular implementation in producing network memory, redirecting future mechanistic studies. The integrated pipeline itself constitutes a durable community resource, enabling other researchers to extend the analysis to additional protein families, organisms, or perturbation datasets without re-deriving the harmonization infrastructure. By explicitly linking statistical genetics, biophysical simulation, and systems biology methodologies, the project advances NCEMS's mesoscale emergence agenda, demonstrating a generalizable template for cross-scale synthesis applicable to other emergent cellular phenomena. The collaborative structure—requiring coordinated expertise unavailable in any single lab—exemplifies the transdisciplinary, data-synthesis model NCEMS seeks to catalyze, while trainee involvement in each analytical layer builds a workforce fluent in integrating sequence, structure, dynamics, and network data.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
All aspects of this synthesis will adhere to FAIR data principles and community-endorsed open, team, and reproducible science practices. Because the project uses exclusively public data, full provenance tracking from original source (Pfam, UniProt, MD trajectory repositories, DisProt/MobiDB/PhaSepDB, RegulonDB/EcoCyc) through each transformation step will be maintained using version-controlled workflows and containerized computational environments to guarantee exact reproducibility across computing platforms. Coevolutionary coupling matrices, extracted MD-derived contact-network features, disorder/condensate annotations, and network hysteresis scores will be deposited as harmonized, versioned datasets in an open repository with persistent identifiers, accompanied by comprehensive metadata describing residue-numbering mappings and structural homology assignments. All analysis code—including coupling-matrix inference scripts, graph-theoretic and machine-learning pipelines, and statistical integration models—will be released under permissive open-source licenses with executable notebooks enabling independent replication of every reported result. Consistent with emerging community standards for biomolecular simulation data management, MD-derived features will be documented following FAIR-compliant simulation metadata conventions to maximize reuse by the broader biophysics community. The working group will hold regular open lab meetings and pre-register key analytical decisions (feature definitions, validation splits, statistical thresholds) prior to full-scale analysis to guard against post hoc bias. Intermediate and final datasets, along with the coupling-to-circuit atlas, will be made publicly available on submission of manuscripts, with preprints posted concurrently. Documentation will be written for reuse by non-specialists, including tutorials suitable for trainees new to any one of the four constituent data modalities, ensuring the resource serves both as a scientific product and as an educational platform.

[Budget and Resources]
The proposed budget supports a distributed working group requiring computational, personnel, and coordination resources beyond individual lab capacity. Personnel costs will fund two postdoctoral researchers (bridging coevolutionary statistics/network biology and computational biophysics/MD analysis, respectively) and two graduate student trainees embedded across partner labs, ensuring cross-training in all four data modalities. Computational resources include allocation on high-performance computing clusters for reprocessing publicly deposited MD trajectories and running graph-theoretic/machine-learning pipelines at scale, plus cloud storage for hosting harmonized intermediate datasets and the final coupling-to-circuit atlas with redundant backup. Modest funds are requested for data engineering support to build and maintain the cross-database identifier mapping and metadata harmonization infrastructure central to this synthesis, a task requiring dedicated effort distinct from domain-specific scientific analysis. Travel funds will support twice-yearly in-person working group meetings to coordinate analytical decisions, resolve cross-database harmonization challenges, and conduct joint trainee workshops, alongside conference travel to disseminate results to evolutionary biology, biophysics, and systems biology communities. A small allocation is dedicated to open-access publication fees and repository deposition costs to ensure all deliverables remain freely available. No funds are requested for new experimental data generation, consistent with the synthesis-only scope of this proposal. The requested resources are proportionate to a multi-institutional, multi-year collaborative effort and reflect genuine infrastructure and personnel needs that exceed what any single participating laboratory currently supports, justifying NCEMS's distinctive role in enabling this cross-disciplinary, data-integrative research program.

abstract_original: A central puzzle in molecular and cellular biology is how local, residue-level physical couplings within individual proteins propagate upward to produce circuit-level emergent behaviors such as bistability, hysteresis, and irreversible switching in gene regulatory networks. Existing work has separately characterized (i) coevolutionary statistical couplings among residues using Potts models and statistical coupling analysis across protein families, (ii) dynamic allosteric pathways and temperature- or ligand-sensitive contact networks extracted from molecular dynamics trajectories, (iii) sequence-encoded propensities for intrinsically disordered regions and biomolecular condensate formation, and (iv) network-level dynamical properties of transcriptional regulatory systems, including memory and irreversibility following perturbation. Beyond resolving a long-standing question about the evolutionary logic of metabolic robustness, the framework offers a predictive tool for metabolic engineering—flagging which reactions are evolutionarily malleable versus constrained—and provides rich training opportunities for graduate students and postdocs to gain dual fluency in systems biology and population genomics, directly building the interdisciplinary, data-savvy workforce NCEMS aims to cultivate.

[Background and Significance]
Metabolic networks constitute a paradigmatic mesoscale system: thousands of individual enzymatic reactions, encoded by distinct genes, are wired into pathways and modules whose emergent flux behavior determines organismal fitness in ways that cannot be predicted from any single gene in isolation. Decades of population genetics have documented striking heterogeneity in selective constraint across metabolic genes—some enzymes are nearly invariant across billions of years of divergence, while paralogous or pathway-adjacent genes accumulate substantial standing variation and repeatedly serve as substrates for local adaptation (e.g., lactase persistence, FADS1/FADS2 desaturase variation in Arctic and other populations, alcohol dehydrogenase variation across human and Drosophila lineages). Parallel advances in systems biology have produced genome-scale metabolic (GSM) reconstructions for hundreds of organisms, enabling precise, mechanistic characterization of network topology, flux coupling, redundancy, and control-coefficient distributions. Despite the obvious complementarity of these two literatures, they have developed almost entirely in isolation: population geneticists rarely incorporate flux-based network architecture into models of selection, and metabolic modelers rarely test whether their computed topological metrics carry evolutionary signal. This disconnect represents both a scientific and an infrastructural gap. Scientifically, we lack a mechanistic account of why metabolic robustness (redundancy, alternate flux routes, low control coefficients) should buffer certain genes from selection while flux-bottleneck reactions—by analogy to network theory in other biological contexts—might be disproportionately exposed to both purifying and positive selection. Infrastructurally, testing this hypothesis requires simultaneously fluent handling of constraint-based modeling formats (SBML, COBRA-compatible reconstructions), population-scale variant call data, and machine learning frameworks trained on coalescent or forward-simulation output—a combination of skills that is essentially never resident in a single laboratory. Our working group is uniquely positioned to close this gap: it combines expertise in genome-scale metabolic reconstruction and constraint-based flux analysis with population genetic inference of selection using both classical statistics and modern simulation-trained deep learning classifiers. This synthesis is explicitly a mesoscale emergence problem in the sense central to NCEMS's mission: the network-level organization of metabolism, an emergent property of thousands of molecular interactions, shapes higher-order evolutionary outcomes at the level of the gene, the pathway, and ultimately the organism's adaptive trajectory. Resolving why certain network positions are evolutionary hotspots while others are frozen would settle a long-debated puzzle in molecular evolution and, simultaneously, generate a predictive framework of direct value to metabolic engineering, agricultural genomics, and precision medicine, where knowing which reactions are evolutionarily malleable versus constrained informs the design of robust synthetic pathways and the interpretation of disease-associated metabolic variants.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This working group will address three interlocking research questions using exclusively existing, publicly available data. RQ1: Does the topological and flux-based position of a gene within a genome-scale metabolic network predict the strength and mode of natural selection acting on that gene, independent of confounders such as expression breadth, essentiality, and gene age? We hypothesize that genes encoding reactions with high flux control coefficients, low structural redundancy, and central positions within tightly coupled modules experience stronger purifying selection, reflected in reduced nucleotide diversity, lower dN/dS, and depleted rare-variant load in population-scale sequencing panels (1000 Genomes, HGDP, gnomAD). Conversely, we hypothesize that genes in peripheral, redundant, or weakly coupled network positions show relaxed constraint and are disproportionately represented among loci bearing signatures of recent positive selection (elevated iHS, extended haplotype homozygosity, or population-differentiation statistics), because such positions permit adaptive exploration without destabilizing core network flux. RQ2: Do recurrent environmental pressures—dietary shifts, thermal stress, nutrient limitation, and immune activation—preferentially target specific, identifiable mesoscale modules (e.g., lipid metabolism, nitrogen assimilation, redox balance) rather than being randomly distributed across the metabolic network? We hypothesize that well-documented adaptive sweeps such as FADS1/FADS2 variation associated with dietary polyunsaturated fatty acid intake in Arctic populations, and the TBX15/WARS2 archaic-introgressed haplotype affecting adipose differentiation, occupy flux-bottleneck reactions or modules with constrained redundancy, and that this pattern generalizes to independently evolved selection signals in maize under nitrogen stress and in microbial genomes under nutrient or host-immune pressure. RQ3: Are 'evolvability hotspots'—network positions disproportionately enriched for adaptive selection—conserved across kingdoms as an intrinsic property of metabolic network architecture, or are they lineage-specific outcomes of differential network rewiring during evolutionary history? We hypothesize a partial conservation model: core, highly connected reactions central to universal pathways (e.g., glycolysis, TCA cycle) will show consistently strong purifying selection across humans, plants, and microbes, whereas peripheral biosynthetic modules subject to lineage-specific environmental pressures (fatty acid desaturation in humans, nitrogen assimilation in maize, biodegradative pathways in bacteria such as Rhodopseudomonas palustris) will show kingdom-specific evolvability signatures shaped by each lineage's ecological history. Each hypothesis is directly testable through synthesis of existing reconstructions and selection-scan datasets, and each requires the combined constraint-based modeling and population-genomic inference expertise assembled in this proposal, satisfying the requirement that the work exceed what any individual laboratory or existing collaboration could accomplish alone.

[Methods and Approach]
The working group will execute a three-phase synthesis pipeline built entirely on existing public resources. Phase 1 (Data Compendium Construction): We will assemble a cross-species compendium pairing curated GSM reconstructions from BiGG, AGORA2, ModelSEED, and KBase (including previously published context-specific human macrophage and maize nitrogen-stress models) with gene-level identifiers harmonized against population-genomic resources including 1000 Genomes, HGDP, gnomAD, adaptation-focused SNP-chip panels (e.g., Greenlandic Inuit cohorts), and diversity panels for yeast, Arabidopsis, and maize. Careful ortholog and gene-identifier mapping (via Ensembl Compara, KEGG orthology, and UniProt cross-references) will ensure that network-derived and population-genomic features refer to the same loci across organisms. Phase 2 (Feature Computation): For each reconstruction, we will compute standardized topological and flux-based metrics using constraint-based modeling tools (COBRApy, flux variability analysis, flux coupling analysis) including reaction centrality, flux control coefficients, module membership (via community detection on flux-coupled reaction graphs), and redundancy/backup pathway counts. In parallel, we will compute or extract population genetic summary statistics (nucleotide diversity, Tajima's D, dN/dS, iHS, cross-population differentiation) from public variant call datasets, and where simulation-trained classifiers are advantageous, we will adapt existing GAN/CNN selection-inference pipelines, retrained on coalescent simulations appropriate to each species' demographic history, to generate probabilistic selection calls at each locus. Phase 3 (Integration and Modeling): We will merge network-derived and evolutionary features into unified per-gene tables and apply interpretable machine learning—gradient-boosted trees and shallow CNNs with SHAP-based feature attribution—to test whether network position predicts selection signal after controlling for known confounders (expression breadth from public transcriptomic atlases, essentiality from knockout/fitness screens, evolutionary rate baselines). We will specifically test enrichment of known adaptive loci (FADS1/FADS2, TBX15/WARS2) within predicted evolvability hotspots, and extend cross-kingdom comparison using matched analyses in maize and microbial systems. All statistical models will include permutation-based null distributions generated from randomized network topologies to guard against structural confounds. Milestones include: compendium release (months 1–6), feature computation and validation (months 6–14), integrative modeling and hypothesis testing (months 14–22), and cross-kingdom comparative synthesis and manuscript preparation (months 22–30). Regular working group meetings (biweekly video, twice-yearly in-person) will ensure iterative cross-disciplinary quality control between metabolic modelers and population geneticists at each phase.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This synthesis will produce four concrete outputs. First, an open, versioned cross-species compendium linking genome-scale metabolic network features to population-genomic selection statistics, structured for reuse by both the systems biology and population genetics communities. Second, a validated, interpretable machine learning framework quantifying the relationship between network architecture and evolutionary constraint, generalizable to newly released reconstructions or selection scans without requiring new experimental data. Third, a set of empirically grounded 'evolvability maps' for human, plant, and microbial metabolism identifying specific modules and reactions as constrained versus malleable, directly informing metabolic engineering strain-design efforts by flagging targets more likely to tolerate genetic intervention without unpredictable fitness costs. Fourth, a resolution—or substantial refinement—of a decades-old puzzle regarding heterogeneous selective pressure across metabolic genes, reframed through the lens of network-level emergent constraint rather than gene-by-gene analysis alone. Scientifically, this reframes metabolic evolution as a mesoscale phenomenon, directly advancing NCEMS's core mission of understanding emergent properties bridging molecular and cellular scales. Practically, the predictive evolvability framework has direct translational relevance to synthetic biology, crop improvement under environmental stress, and interpretation of human disease-associated metabolic variants. The project's cross-disciplinary design—uniting constraint-based modeling and population genomic inference—will also produce a template methodology other synthesis teams can adapt to different molecular subsystems, and will generate publicly documented training materials that lower the barrier for future researchers to work across these traditionally separate fields, fulfilling NCEMS's mandate to cultivate an interdisciplinary, data-fluent research workforce.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
All data used in this project are already public; no new experimental data will be generated. We commit to depositing the full harmonized cross-species compendium, including gene-identifier mapping tables, computed network metrics, and extracted population genetic statistics, in a public, version-controlled repository (Zenodo/GitHub with DOI-minted releases) under permissive open licenses compatible with source data terms. All analysis code—COBRA-based flux analysis scripts, population genetic statistic pipelines, and machine learning training/evaluation code—will be developed in containerized, dependency-pinned environments (Docker/Conda) and released alongside detailed computational notebooks documenting each analytical step, following FAIR and community-endorsed reproducible-science standards. We will adopt a pre-registration approach for the primary hypothesis tests in RQ1–RQ3, specifying confound-control variables and null-model construction prior to full-scale analysis, with any post hoc analyses clearly flagged as exploratory. Intermediate outputs (per-gene feature tables, trained classifier weights, permutation null distributions) will be archived at each project milestone to support independent verification and reanalysis. We will hold data and workflows to community standards emerging from the genomics (GA4GH) and metabolic modeling (COMBINE/SBML) communities, ensuring interoperability with existing public infrastructure such as BiGG, KBase, and public variant repositories. Documentation will be written with training use in mind, including annotated tutorials suitable for graduate coursework, explicitly supporting NCEMS's goal of building a data-savvy workforce capable of working across systems biology and population genetics. A public project website will track compendium releases, code versions, and links to all downstream publications, and we will submit software tools to appropriate community registries (e.g., Bioconda, PyPI) to maximize long-term accessibility and reuse well beyond the funding period.

[Budget and Resources]
This proposal requests support calibrated to a data-synthesis working group rather than a data-generation project, reflecting NCEMS's emphasis on computational and personnel resources over experimental costs. Primary budget categories include: (1) Personnel—partial salary support for one postdoctoral researcher with dual training in constraint-based modeling and population genetics to serve as the integrative lead, and graduate student support at each partner institution to enable direct mentorship and cross-training in both domains; (2) Computational Infrastructure—cloud computing credits or institutional high-performance computing allocations for flux variability/coupling analyses across hundreds of GSM reconstructions and for training/retraining CNN and GAN-based selection classifiers on large population genomic datasets; (3) Working Group Coordination—travel support for two in-person working group meetings per year to enable intensive collaborative integration sessions, plus videoconferencing infrastructure for biweekly virtual meetings; (4) Data and Software Management—modest costs for repository hosting, DOI minting, and long-term archival storage of the compendium and derived datasets beyond standard institutional allocations; (5) Dissemination—support for open-access publication fees and presentation of results at relevant systems biology and population genetics conferences to maximize cross-community visibility. No funds are requested for new experimental data generation, consistent with the synthesis-only scope of this project. NCEMS support is essential because the project requires sustained, structured collaboration across historically separate research communities—constraint-based metabolic modeling and population genomic inference—along with computational resources and coordination infrastructure exceeding what any single laboratory's existing grants provide. The requested resources are scaled to enable full execution of the three-phase pipeline (compendium construction, feature computation, integrative modeling) within a 30-month period, with built-in flexibility to extend cross-kingdom comparative analyses should early results reveal additional promising directions warranting deeper investigation.

title: Mesoscale Coordination of Proteome Turnover: Synthesizing Public Degradation Kinetics with Complex, Condensate, and Disorder Architecture to Discover Emergent Proteostasis Modules
title_norm: mesoscale coordination of proteome turnover synthesizing public degradation kinetics with complex condensate and disorder architecture to discover emergent proteostasis modules
abstract_text: Protein turnover—the balance of synthesis and degradation—has been measured in hundreds of public datasets using SILAC, dynamic SILAC, 15N/heavy-water metabolic labeling, and pulse-chase mass spectrometry across yeast, mouse tissues, human cell lines, and iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes and endothelial cells. These datasets, generated by dozens of independent labs under different physiological conditions (oxidative stress, hypoxia/hyperoxia, aging, cardiovascular disease models), are rarely integrated with structural and interaction data that describe how proteins are organized at the mesoscale—as stable complexes, transient assemblies, or biomolecular condensates. We propose to build a unified, harmonized turnover atlas that cross-references public half-life datasets with complex membership (CORUM, hu.MAP, BioGRID), intrinsic disorder annotations (MobiDB, IUPred-derived scores), liquid-liquid phase separation databases (PhaSepDB, LLPSDB), and tissue/single-cell expression atlases (Human Protein Atlas, GTEx). Our central question is whether mesoscale organization is a primary determinant of emergent proteostatic behavior: do subunits within stable complexes exhibit coordinated (concerted) degradation kinetics that buffer stoichiometric imbalance, while orphan or condensate-resident proteins show discordant, individually regulated turnover? We hypothesize that loss of this coordination—rather than changes in individual protein half-lives—constitutes an emergent signature of proteostatic collapse in aging and disease, distinguishable only when turnover data are analyzed jointly with structural context rather than protein-by-protein. To test this, we will (1) computationally harmonize turnover rate constants across >30 public datasets spanning organisms, tissues, and physiological perturbations (oxygen tension, replicative and organismal aging, ER/oxidative stress, cardiomyopathy models) using batch-correction and Bayesian hierarchical modeling to place disparate experimental designs on a common kinetic scale; (2) quantify turnover concordance within known complexes and condensates versus size-matched control sets of unrelated proteins, testing whether concordance scales with disorder content, complex stoichiometry, and evolutionary conservation; (3) map how concordance is perturbed under stress and aging conditions already profiled in existing datasets, identifying mesoscale modules whose turnover synchrony breaks down first; and (4) validate cross-tissue generalizability using existing in vivo turnover measurements from heart, lung, and brain under varying oxygen tension and cardiovascular disease models. This effort requires expertise spanning classical proteomic turnover measurement and kinetic modeling, translation and stress-response systems biology, structural/disorder bioinformatics, and cardiovascular tissue-specific proteomics—none of which resides in a single lab, and none of which has previously been assembled at this scale. The project will produce an open, versioned turnover-mesoscale database and reproducible analytical pipeline (containerized, deposited on GitHub/Zenodo), enabling the community to query turnover coordination for any complex, condensate, or disease gene set. Graduate students and postdocs will be trained in cross-lab data harmonization, hierarchical Bayesian kinetic modeling, and structural bioinformatics integration, directly building the data-savvy workforce NCEMS aims to cultivate while addressing a fundamental, previously inaccessible question about how molecular-scale turnover gives rise to emergent, mesoscale proteostatic robustness and its breakdown in aging and disease.

Cellular proteostasis depends not merely on the absolute rate at which individual proteins are synthesized and degraded, but on how these rates are coordinated across functionally related sets of proteins. Over the past fifteen years, metabolic labeling approaches—including SILAC, dynamic SILAC, stable isotope (15N) and heavy-water labeling, and pulse-chase mass spectrometry—have generated proteome-wide half-life measurements spanning budding yeast, primary mouse tissues, human cell lines, and increasingly complex model systems such as iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes and endothelial cells. These datasets have accumulated across dozens of independent studies covering diverse physiological states, including oxidative and hypoxic stress, organismal and replicative aging, and disease models relevant to cardiovascular and neurodegenerative pathology. Individually, each dataset has advanced understanding of protein-specific turnover regulation. Collectively, however, they remain an underexploited resource: turnover measurements are rarely placed in a common kinetic framework across studies, and even more rarely cross-referenced with independent structural and organizational annotations describing how proteins physically associate at the mesoscale—as members of stable multiprotein complexes, as transient interaction partners, or as constituents of biomolecular condensates formed through liquid-liquid phase separation. This gap is significant because a growing body of evidence suggests that proteostatic control operates not simply at the level of single polypeptides but at the level of higher-order assemblies, where imbalanced production or degradation of one subunit can destabilize an entire complex, and where intrinsically disordered regions and condensate participation may confer distinct degradation vulnerabilities compared to well-folded, complex-embedded proteins. Whether such organization-dependent turnover coordination is a general, quantifiable property of the proteome—and whether its breakdown constitutes an early, mechanistic signature of proteostatic collapse in aging, oxidative stress, and cardiovascular disease—cannot be answered from any single existing dataset or organism-specific model system. It requires joint reanalysis of turnover kinetics across many independent experimental designs, coupled to structural, disorder, and condensate annotation resources that themselves are distributed across separate community databases (CORUM, hu.MAP, BioGRID, MobiDB, PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, Human Protein Atlas, GTEx). This is precisely the type of previously inaccessible, emergence-oriented question that community-scale data synthesis is positioned to resolve. By harmonizing public turnover measurements with independently curated mesoscale organizational data, this project will test whether coordinated degradation is a fundamental design principle of proteome organization and whether its disruption offers a generalizable, cross-tissue biomarker of proteostatic dysfunction. The resulting synthesis addresses a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biology—how molecular-scale kinetic behavior gives rise to emergent, higher-order cellular robustness—using only data that already exists but has never been assembled or analyzed at this scale or with this structural lens.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This project is organized around one overarching question and three testable sub-hypotheses concerning the relationship between proteome turnover kinetics and mesoscale structural organization. Overarching question: Is coordinated degradation kinetics among physically or functionally associated proteins an emergent property of mesoscale organization, and does its disruption constitute a generalizable signature of proteostatic dysfunction across cell types, tissues, and physiological perturbations? Hypothesis 1 (Complex-level concordance): Subunits of stable, stoichiometric protein complexes exhibit significantly more concordant turnover rates than size-matched sets of functionally unrelated proteins, reflecting co-regulatory mechanisms—such as coupled translation, co-translational assembly, or degradation of unassembled subunits—that buffer against stoichiometric imbalance. We predict that concordance will scale positively with the degree of obligate stoichiometry and evolutionary conservation of the complex, and negatively with the proportion of intrinsically disordered regions among its members, since disordered segments are associated with more autonomous, context-dependent degradation signals. Hypothesis 2 (Condensate discordance): Proteins that participate in biomolecular condensates via liquid-liquid phase separation, in contrast to stable complex members, will show weaker turnover concordance with their interaction partners, consistent with the more dynamic, concentration- and context-dependent exchange kinetics that characterize condensate residency. We further predict that condensate scaffold proteins and client proteins will display distinguishable turnover signatures, reflecting their different roles in maintaining phase-separated assemblies. Hypothesis 3 (Concordance breakdown as an emergent stress/aging signature): Physiological perturbations already profiled in existing public datasets—oxidative stress, altered oxygen tension, replicative and organismal aging, and cardiomyopathy-associated genetic backgrounds—will preferentially disrupt turnover concordance within specific mesoscale modules (e.g., mitochondrial respiratory complexes, nuclear lamina-associated assemblies, cytoskeletal complexes) before changes are detectable in the average half-life of any single constituent protein. This hypothesis directly tests whether emergent, module-level dyscoordination—rather than protein-by-protein half-life shifts—is the more sensitive and mechanistically informative readout of proteostatic decline. A secondary but integral question concerns generalizability: does the complex-versus-condensate concordance pattern observed in yeast and cultured human cells reproduce in vivo, across mouse heart, lung, and brain tissue under varying oxygen tension and in cardiovascular disease models, and in human iPSC-derived cardiomyocyte and endothelial systems? Confirming cross-species and cross-tissue reproducibility is essential to establishing that mesoscale turnover coordination reflects a conserved organizational principle rather than a cell-type-specific artifact. Collectively, these questions cannot be resolved using any single existing dataset, model organism, or structural annotation resource in isolation; they require the systematic cross-referencing and re-analysis of dozens of independently generated turnover datasets against multiple, non-overlapping structural and interaction databases—precisely the scale and diversity of data integration that motivates this proposal.

[Methods and Approach]
The project proceeds in four integrated aims, each relying exclusively on existing, publicly available datasets. Aim 1 – Data harmonization: We will systematically curate turnover datasets from public repositories (PRIDE, MassIVE, GEO, and supplementary data from published metabolic labeling studies) spanning SILAC, dynamic SILAC, 15N/heavy-water labeling, and pulse-chase designs across yeast, mouse tissue, human cell lines, and iPSC-derived cardiovascular cell types. Because these datasets differ in labeling duration, sampling density, and kinetic modeling assumptions, we will re-derive turnover rate constants where raw or intermediate quantification data are available, and apply Bayesian hierarchical models that treat dataset-of-origin as a random effect, allowing borrowing of statistical strength across studies while explicitly modeling batch-specific technical variance. This produces harmonized, uncertainty-quantified half-life estimates on a common kinetic scale for proteins across conditions and species-matched orthology mappings (using established ortholog databases) to enable cross-species comparison. Aim 2 – Mesoscale annotation integration: Harmonized turnover data will be cross-referenced with complex membership from CORUM and hu.MAP, protein-protein interaction data from BioGRID, intrinsic disorder scores from MobiDB and IUPred-based predictions, and condensate participation from PhaSepDB and LLPSDB. Tissue- and cell-type-specific expression context will be layered in using the Human Protein Atlas and GTEx to restrict analyses to biologically plausible co-expression contexts. Aim 3 – Concordance quantification: For each annotated complex, condensate, and interaction module, we will compute a turnover concordance statistic (e.g., coefficient of variation or intraclass correlation of half-lives among members) and compare this against null distributions generated from size- and abundance-matched random protein sets, using permutation-based significance testing. Regression and mixed-effects models will test whether concordance scales with disorder content, stoichiometric constraint, and evolutionary conservation, per Hypotheses 1 and 2. Aim 4 – Perturbation and cross-tissue mapping: Using existing datasets profiling oxidative stress, hypoxia/hyperoxia, aging, and cardiomyopathy models, we will compute condition-specific concordance shifts for each mesoscale module, identifying which modules show early or disproportionate loss of coordination (Hypothesis 3). In vivo heart, lung, and brain turnover data under varying oxygen tension will serve as an independent validation cohort to assess whether concordance patterns and their perturbation-induced breakdown generalize beyond cultured cell systems. All analytical code will be developed collaboratively across sites using version-controlled, containerized workflows to ensure reproducibility and to support iterative refinement as new public datasets become available during the project period.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This project will deliver a versioned, publicly queryable turnover-mesoscale atlas linking harmonized protein half-life estimates to complex, condensate, and disorder annotations across species and physiological states, along with a documented, containerized analytical pipeline for computing turnover concordance for any user-specified gene set. Scientifically, the work will resolve whether coordinated degradation is a general organizing principle of the proteome and establish concordance breakdown as a candidate mechanistic biomarker of proteostatic dysfunction in aging and cardiovascular disease—insights inaccessible from any single dataset or model system. This reframes existing turnover data, much of it originally collected for narrower, condition-specific purposes, as a resource for addressing a fundamental emergence question in cellular organization. The atlas will enable downstream hypothesis generation across the community: researchers studying specific complexes, disease genes, or condensates will be able to query whether turnover coordination is altered in their systems of interest without generating new data. By connecting kinetic, structural, and disease-relevant datasets that have previously remained siloed within separate subfields (classical proteomics, structural bioinformatics, condensate biology, cardiovascular tissue biology), the project models the kind of cross-disciplinary synthesis NCEMS is designed to catalyze, and produces reusable infrastructure with lasting value beyond the funding period.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
All work will adhere to open, reproducible science principles consistent with NCEMS community policies. Harmonized turnover estimates, mesoscale annotation mappings, and concordance statistics will be deposited as versioned releases in a public repository (Zenodo, with DOI minting) alongside raw provenance metadata linking every derived value back to its original public dataset and accession number, ensuring full traceability. Analytical code—including data harmonization scripts, Bayesian hierarchical modeling pipelines, and concordance statistics—will be developed under version control (GitHub) and packaged in containerized environments (Docker/Singularity) to guarantee computational reproducibility across computing environments and institutions. We will adopt standardized data schemas and controlled vocabularies where available (e.g., UniProt identifiers, PSI-MI interaction formats) to maximize interoperability with existing proteomics and interactomics resources. Intermediate and final analysis outputs will be accompanied by detailed documentation and vignettes enabling other researchers to query the atlas for their own protein or complex of interest. Working group meetings, analytical decisions, and pipeline development milestones will be logged in a shared, publicly accessible project wiki to support transparency and enable community contributions during and after the funding period. Trainees will be given explicit responsibility for maintaining documentation standards, reinforcing reproducible practices as a core professional skill. Where underlying datasets carry usage restrictions, we will comply fully with original data-sharing licenses while maximizing openness of all derived, harmonized products consistent with permitted redistribution.

[Budget and Resources]
Given the project's reliance exclusively on publicly available data, the budget centers on personnel, computational infrastructure, and collaborative coordination rather than experimental costs. Requested support includes salary for one postdoctoral researcher with expertise in Bayesian kinetic modeling and one graduate student trainee focused on structural bioinformatics integration, both jointly supervised across participating labs to ensure cross-disciplinary training. Computational resources include cloud or institutional high-performance computing allocation sufficient for hierarchical modeling across >30 large-scale datasets and for hosting containerized pipelines and the versioned atlas database. Funds are requested for data storage and repository deposition fees (Zenodo/GitHub sustained hosting), as well as software licensing where necessary for structural or disorder prediction tools not otherwise freely available. Travel funds will support in-person working group meetings at least twice annually to coordinate cross-lab analytical decisions, resolve harmonization discrepancies, and conduct hands-on training workshops in Bayesian modeling and structural data integration for trainees across sites. Modest funds are allocated for dissemination, including open-access publication fees and presentation of results at relevant scientific meetings spanning proteomics, systems biology, and cardiovascular research communities. This project explicitly requires NCEMS-level support because it demands sustained coordination among investigators with non-overlapping expertise in proteomic kinetic modeling, translation/stress-response systems biology, structural and condensate bioinformatics, and cardiovascular tissue proteomics, together with computational infrastructure and collaborative time investment exceeding what any single laboratory's existing grant support could provide. The requested resources are scoped to be sufficient but modest, prioritizing personnel and computation over any new data generation, consistent with the synthesis-focused mission of this proposal.

[Abstract]
A central unsolved question in cell biology is whether the mesoscale biophysical behavior of a protein complex—its oligomeric stoichiometry, diffusion coefficient, membrane residence time, or reaction kinetics—can be predicted from the transcriptomic and proteomic context of the cell in which it resides. The model will treat measured single-molecule parameters as noisy, condition-specific observations governed by latent biophysical state variables, and will estimate how these latent states depend on local expression levels, co-expression neighborhoods, and spatial cellular context, explicitly propagating measurement uncertainty and cross-study heterogeneity using probabilistic inference methods drawn from single-molecule photon-counting statistics. The framework will be validated by predicting biophysical parameters for cell types and conditions where single-molecule measurements do not yet exist but transcriptomic/spatial data do, generating falsifiable, quantitative predictions (e.g., expected oligomeric state of ATP7A in a specific reactive astrocyte subtype) that can guide future targeted experiments. This effort requires collaboration beyond any single lab: computational expertise in spatial transcriptomic integration and cell-state annotation, deep domain knowledge of copper homeostasis and membrane trafficking biophysics, and Bayesian modeling expertise for heterogeneous, noisy single-molecule data. The resulting open-source pipeline, curated biophysical parameter database, and trained hierarchical models will be released under FAIR data principles, providing a template applicable to other molecular machines beyond copper transport, and offering hands-on training for graduate students and postdocs at the interface of quantitative single-molecule biophysics and computational spatial genomics—directly addressing NCEMS's mission to explain how mesoscale molecular organization emerges from and shapes higher-order cellular states.

[Background and Significance]
The mesoscale—the regime between individual biomolecules and organelles—is where emergent cellular behaviors first become manifest: proteins oligomerize into functional complexes, diffuse through crowded and compartmentalized environments, and engage in transient, kinetically defined interactions that ultimately determine cellular phenotype. Single-molecule biophysics has, over three decades, generated a rich but fragmented body of quantitative knowledge describing these behaviors for specific molecular machines. Copper-handling and membrane trafficking systems—including the importer Ctr1, the P-type ATPases ATP7A and ATP7B, and the cytosolic chaperones Atox1 and CCS—have been characterized in exquisite biophysical detail using single-molecule tracking, fluorescence resonance energy transfer, magnetic tweezers, and photon-counting statistics, yielding parameters such as oligomeric stoichiometry, diffusion coefficients, membrane residence times, and on/off kinetics. However, these measurements are almost always obtained in a small number of engineered cell lines or reconstituted systems under tightly controlled conditions, disconnected from the broader cellular and tissue contexts in which these same machines actually operate.

Simultaneously, single-cell and spatial transcriptomic and proteomic technologies have produced expression and localization atlases spanning hundreds of cell types, developmental stages, and disease states, including brain-wide single-nucleus RNA-seq datasets, spatial transcriptomic maps generated by imaging-based multiplexing, and antibody-based tissue atlases. These resources capture the expression context—transcript abundance, co-expression neighborhoods, and spatial cellular niches—for the very genes encoding the molecular machines studied at the single-molecule level, yet they contain no information about the biophysical behavior of the encoded proteins. The result is two rich, mature, and independently valuable data universes that have never been formally reconciled.

This gap is scientifically consequential because a foundational but untested hypothesis pervades molecular cell biology: that mesoscale biophysical organization—oligomeric state, complex assembly, residence time—is not fixed but instead emerges from, and dynamically reflects, the local molecular composition of the cell. If true, this hypothesis implies that biophysical parameters measured in one cellular context should be predictable, within quantifiable uncertainty, in other cell types and disease states purely from their expression and spatial profiles. Testing this hypothesis requires exactly the kind of large-scale, cross-study data synthesis that individual laboratories are not positioned to perform, since it demands simultaneous fluency in single-molecule kinetic modeling, hierarchical Bayesian statistics for heterogeneous noisy measurements, and computational integration of spatial and single-cell atlases. By formally linking these domains for a well-characterized model system—metal homeostasis and trafficking machinery, with direct relevance to neurodegenerative diseases such as Wilson's, Menkes, and Parkinson's disease—this project will establish whether mesoscale biophysical states are quantitatively predictable from transcriptomic and spatial context, providing a rigorous, generalizable test of a long-standing but implicit assumption in the field, and directly advancing NCEMS's scientific vision of understanding emergent properties at the mesoscale.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This project is organized around one overarching synthesis question and three testable sub-questions, each addressing a distinct layer of the proposed integration between molecular-scale biophysics and cellular-scale expression context.

Overarching question: Can quantitative single-molecule biophysical parameters of trafficking and metal-homeostasis machinery be predicted, with well-calibrated uncertainty, from the transcriptomic and spatial expression context of the cell in which the machinery operates?

Sub-question 1 (Compositional dependence): Does the oligomeric stoichiometry and diffusion behavior of a given trafficking complex (e.g., ATP7A, Ctr1, Atox1-CCS interactions) vary systematically with the expression levels of its direct binding partners and co-regulated chaperones across cell types, rather than remaining an invariant molecular property? We hypothesize that latent biophysical states are structured by local stoichiometric ratios among interacting partners, such that cell types with elevated chaperone-to-transporter expression ratios exhibit measurably shorter membrane residence times or altered oligomeric distributions, reflecting more efficient hand-off kinetics.

Sub-question 2 (Spatial and disease-state modulation): Do spatial transcriptomic neighborhoods—capturing tissue microenvironment and cell-cell contact context—explain additional variance in biophysical parameters beyond what is captured by cell-intrinsic expression alone, particularly in reactive or disease-associated cell states? We hypothesize that disease-associated cell states (e.g., reactive astrocytes in Parkinson's disease models, hepatocytes in Wilson's disease contexts) exhibit shifted latent biophysical states relative to their homeostatic counterparts, detectable as systematic deviations in the hierarchical model's cell-state-specific parameters, consistent with copper dyshomeostasis contributing mechanistically to pathological trafficking behavior.

Sub-question 3 (Cross-study generalizability and prediction): Can a hierarchical Bayesian model trained on existing single-molecule measurements, appropriately accounting for cross-study heterogeneity in imaging modality and experimental condition, generate falsifiable quantitative predictions of biophysical parameters for cell types and conditions that have never been directly measured but for which transcriptomic or spatial proteomic data exist? We hypothesize that such predictions will be quantitatively accurate within experimentally meaningful tolerance for cell types transcriptomically similar to measured reference types, while explicitly flagging low-confidence predictions for transcriptomically divergent or rare cell states, thereby providing a principled uncertainty-aware extrapolation tool rather than an overconfident black-box predictor.

Collectively, these questions test whether mesoscale biophysical organization is a generalizable, context-dependent property of cellular composition rather than a fixed molecular constant, and whether this relationship can be formally modeled using existing public data alone. Confirmation of these hypotheses would establish a new class of testable, quantitative links between gene expression atlases and biophysical function; refutation or partial confirmation would itself be scientifically informative, revealing where mesoscale behavior is decoupled from bulk expression context and motivating new single-molecule experiments targeted at specific discrepant cell states. Either outcome directly advances mechanistic understanding of how molecular-scale composition shapes mesoscale cellular organization, the central scientific focus of this synthesis effort.

[Methods and Approach]
The project proceeds in three integrated phases, each relying exclusively on publicly available data and requiring the combined expertise of the assembled team.

Phase 1 – Curation of single-molecule biophysical parameters: We will systematically extract quantitative biophysical parameters (oligomeric stoichiometry, diffusion coefficients, kon/koff rates, membrane residence times) for Ctr1, ATP7A, ATP7B, Atox1, CCS, and associated trafficking regulators from published single-molecule fluorescence microscopy, FRET, magnetic-tweezer, and photon-counting studies, alongside metadata on cell type, experimental condition, imaging modality, and measurement uncertainty. Parameters will be harmonized into a structured, versioned database with explicit provenance tracking, enabling downstream propagation of study-specific measurement noise and technical heterogeneity.

Phase 2 – Integration of transcriptomic and spatial atlases: For each cell type or condition represented in the curated database, we will extract matched or closely analogous expression profiles from public resources including the Human Protein Atlas, Allen Brain Atlas, HuBMAP, and existing single-nucleus RNA-seq and spatial transcriptomic (e.g., MERFISH-based) datasets covering relevant brain regions and copper-homeostasis-related tissues. Cell-type harmonization across studies and platforms will employ established single-cell integration approaches to project heterogeneous datasets into a shared embedding space, from which local expression levels, co-expression neighborhood statistics, and spatial niche descriptors will be computed for each gene of interest.

Phase 3 – Hierarchical Bayesian latent-variable modeling: We will construct a hierarchical Bayesian model in which observed single-molecule parameters are treated as noisy realizations of latent, cell-type- and condition-specific biophysical states. These latent states will be modeled as functions of local transcriptomic/proteomic covariates (expression levels, co-expression ratios, spatial neighborhood composition), with hierarchical priors pooling information across related cell types and studies to stabilize inference given sparse single-molecule data. Measurement-level uncertainty will be explicitly modeled using likelihood structures informed by photon-counting and localization-based error models established in the single-molecule biophysics literature, allowing heterogeneous experimental precision to be properly weighted. Posterior inference will be performed using Markov chain Monte Carlo and variational approximations as appropriate for model complexity, with rigorous posterior predictive checks against held-out measurements.

Validation will proceed via leave-one-cell-type-out cross-validation: for cell types with existing single-molecule measurements, the model will be retrained excluding that cell type's biophysical data (while retaining its transcriptomic data) and used to predict its biophysical parameters, quantifying predictive accuracy and calibration. The validated model will then generate prospective predictions for cell types and disease states with transcriptomic or spatial data but no existing single-molecule measurements, explicitly reporting posterior uncertainty to distinguish confident extrapolations from those requiring new experimental validation. All curation scripts, integration pipelines, and model code will be version-controlled and containerized to ensure full computational reproducibility across collaborating institutions.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This synthesis project will produce four concrete deliverables. First, a curated, versioned, publicly hosted database of single-molecule biophysical parameters for copper-homeostasis and trafficking machinery, annotated with cell type, condition, and measurement uncertainty metadata, serving as a durable community resource beyond this project's scope. Second, an open-source computational pipeline for harmonizing single-cell and spatial transcriptomic/proteomic atlases with heterogeneous biophysical measurements, generalizable to other molecular machines and complex families. Third, validated hierarchical Bayesian models quantifying the relationship between local expression context and mesoscale biophysical state, including calibrated, falsifiable predictions for previously unmeasured cell types and disease-associated states, such as specific reactive glial populations or hepatocyte subtypes in metal-overload conditions. Fourth, a set of concrete, experimentally testable hypotheses linking transcriptomic cell-state signatures to expected biophysical behavior, directly informing future single-molecule and structural studies.

Scientifically, this work will provide the first rigorous, quantitative test of whether mesoscale biophysical organization is predictable from cellular composition, addressing a foundational and previously untestable assumption in molecular cell biology. Confirmed predictive relationships would establish a new paradigm for using expression atlases to infer biophysical function at scale, dramatically reducing the experimental burden of characterizing rare or difficult-to-access cell types. Identified discrepancies between predicted and expected behavior would highlight cell states where mesoscale organization is decoupled from bulk expression, motivating targeted follow-up experiments and refining mechanistic models of neurodegenerative disease pathogenesis linked to copper dyshomeostasis. Beyond the specific biological system studied, the modeling framework and integration pipeline will serve as a reusable template applicable to other molecular machines, advancing NCEMS's broader mission of understanding emergence at the mesoscale through data synthesis.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
All aspects of this project will adhere to open science principles consistent with NCEMS community standards. The curated single-molecule biophysical parameter database will be deposited in a public, version-controlled repository with a permissive open license, accompanied by structured metadata describing provenance, experimental condition, and measurement uncertainty to enable independent reuse and extension by the broader research community. All data integration, harmonization, and modeling code will be developed openly on a public code repository from project inception, organized as modular, documented, and containerized workflows to ensure computational reproducibility across computing environments and institutions.

Model specifications, prior choices, inference diagnostics, and posterior predictive checks will be fully documented and released alongside trained model objects, allowing independent verification of all reported predictions and uncertainty estimates. Intermediate outputs, including harmonized cell-type embeddings and covariate matrices linking expression context to biophysical parameters, will be archived as reusable data products rather than treated as disposable intermediate files, maximizing downstream value to the community.

The project will follow FAIR data principles throughout: all deliverables will be findable through persistent identifiers, accessible through standard public repositories, interoperable through use of community-standard file formats and metadata schemas for single-cell and spatial data, and reusable through comprehensive documentation and permissive licensing. The primary objective is to determine if single molecule biophysical parameters of metal homeostasis proteins are predictable from spatial expression contexts, which will be achieved by constructing hierarchical Bayesian latent variable models via Markov chain Monte Carlo inference.
