abstract_original: A central unsolved question in cell biology is whether the mesoscale biophysical behavior of a protein complex—its oligomeric stoichiometry, diffusion coefficient, membrane residence time, or reaction kinetics—can be predicted from the transcriptomic and proteomic context of the cell in which it resides. Decades of single-molecule biophysics have produced quantitative measurements of protein oligomerization, diffusion, and binding kinetics for specific molecular machines (e.g., copper transporters, membrane trafficking complexes, transcription factor–DNA interactions) in isolated cell types and controlled conditions, while single-cell and spatial transcriptomic/proteomic atlases now provide expression and localization maps of these same machineries across hundreds of cell types, tissues, and disease states. These two data universes—molecular-scale kinetic/stoichiometric measurements and cellular-scale expression/spatial context—have never been formally integrated, despite an implicit hypothesis in the field that mesoscale organization (clustering, oligomerization, complex assembly) emerges from, and feeds back onto, the local molecular composition of the cell. We propose to build a public, reusable synthesis framework that curates quantitative single-molecule biophysical parameters (stoichiometry, diffusion, kon/koff, residence times) reported in the literature and repositories for a defined set of trafficking-related and metal-homeostasis machineries (Ctr1, ATP7A/B, Atox1, CCS, and associated chaperones/trafficking regulators), and formally links them, via Bayesian hierarchical latent-variable models, to matched single-cell and spatial transcriptomic/proteomic profiles from public atlases (Human Protein Atlas, Allen Brain Atlas, HuBMAP, and existing brain snRNA-seq/spatial MERFISH datasets) spanning the same or comparable cell types, brain regions, and disease states (e.g., Parkinson's disease, Wilson's/Menkes-related neurodegeneration). The model will treat measured single-molecule parameters as noisy, condition-specific observations governed by latent biophysical state variables, and will estimate how these latent states depend on local expression levels, co-expression neighborhoods, and spatial cellular context, explicitly propagating measurement uncertainty and cross-study heterogeneity using probabilistic inference methods drawn from single-molecule photon-counting statistics. The framework will be validated by predicting biophysical parameters for cell types and conditions where single-molecule measurements do not yet exist but transcriptomic/spatial data do, generating falsifiable, quantitative predictions (e.g., expected oligomeric state of ATP7A in a specific reactive astrocyte subtype) that can guide future targeted experiments. This effort requires collaboration beyond any single lab: computational expertise in spatial transcriptomic integration and cell-state annotation, deep domain knowledge of copper homeostasis and membrane trafficking biophysics, and Bayesian modeling expertise for heterogeneous, noisy single-molecule data. The resulting open-source pipeline, curated biophysical parameter database, and trained hierarchical models will be released under FAIR data principles, providing a template applicable to other molecular machines beyond copper transport, and offering hands-on training for graduate students and postdocs at the interface of quantitative single-molecule biophysics and computational spatial genomics—directly addressing NCEMS's mission to explain how mesoscale molecular organization emerges from and shapes higher-order cellular states.

title: From Chemical Marks to Mesoscale Machines: A Multi-Omics and Molecular Dynamics Synthesis of How tRNA Modification Loss Drives Ribosome Collision Condensates and Translational Stress Phenotypes

[Abstract]
A fundamental unsolved question in molecular and cellular biology is how discrete chemical modifications on individual RNA molecules propagate upward to generate emergent, mesoscale ribonucleoprotein (RNP) assemblies that reshape cellular physiology. tRNA modifications (e.g., wobble-position thiolation, dihydrouridine, queuosine) are known to tune translation speed and codon decoding fidelity at the molecular scale, and prior work has shown that loss of these modifications increases ribosome pausing genome-wide. We will use residue-resolution coarse-grained and atomistic molecular dynamics to model how loss of specific tRNA modifications alters codon-anticodon geometry, decoding kinetics, and interface energetics at collided ribosome junctions, generating physically grounded predictions of collision propensity and condensate nucleation likelihood. These structural predictions will be integrated with cross-organism Ribo-seq pausing signatures and condensate proteomic composition using graph-based imputation and similarity-network-fusion clustering to identify conserved “modification–pausing–condensation” axes, and validated against phenotypic outcomes captured in existing multi-omic disease cohorts. This work directly targets NCEMS’ mesoscale mandate: it treats ribosome collision complexes and stress condensates as an intermediate organizational layer between single biomolecule chemistry and cellular/organismal phenotype, an integration no single lab can achieve alone, requiring RNA modification biology, biomolecular simulation, AI-driven multi-omic integration, and clinical proteomic/epigenomic expertise simultaneously. All modeling pipelines, curated datasets, and integrative code will be released as open, reproducible workflows, and the working group will train graduate students and postdocs across wet-lab microbial genetics, computational biophysics, and biomedical data science, producing a new generation of researchers fluent in bridging atomistic simulation with population-scale omics synthesis.

[Background and Significance]
Transfer RNA modifications constitute one of the most ancient and conserved layers of gene expression regulation, decorating anticodon loops and stems with chemical marks—thiolated uridines, dihydrouridine, queuosine, and dozens of others—that fine-tune codon-anticodon pairing geometry, wobble decoding, and translocation kinetics. Decades of biochemical and structural work, spanning bacteria to humans, have established that loss of individual modification enzymes perturbs local translation speed and can produce ribosome pausing at specific codons. More recently, transcriptome-wide ribosome profiling has revealed that these local kinetic perturbations are not isolated events: modification loss can produce genome-wide shifts in pausing landscapes, implicating a broader, systems-level consequence to what was once considered a codon-specific phenomenon. In parallel, an independent research trajectory has established that ribosome collisions—events in which a trailing ribosome physically contacts a stalled leading ribosome—serve as sensing platforms for quality-control machinery, including the E3 ubiquitin ligase ZNF598, the Pelota/Hbs1 rescue complex, and integrated stress response components. Under conditions of persistent stalling, these collision complexes can nucleate larger mesoscale RNP condensates that resemble stress granules, structures whose composition, material properties, and disease relevance have been extensively catalogued in curated condensate databases and multi-omic disease cohorts. Despite the depth of knowledge accumulated independently in tRNA modification biochemistry, ribosome structural biology, and condensate biophysics, these three literatures remain largely disconnected. No existing study has systematically asked whether the biophysical signature of a modification-deficient decoding event—altered anticodon loop geometry, altered dwell time, altered A-site sampling—is quantitatively predictive of collision frequency, and whether collision frequency in turn predicts condensate nucleation propensity and its associated cellular stress phenotypes. This gap represents precisely the kind of mesoscale emergence problem that motivates NCEMS: a molecular-scale chemical perturbation (loss of a single modified nucleoside) propagating through an intermediate structural complex (the collided ribosome) to produce an emergent, higher-order assembly (the RNP condensate) with organismal and disease consequences (proteostasis collapse, neurodegeneration, leukemic proteome remodeling). Addressing this gap requires simultaneous fluency in molecular dynamics of nucleic acid-protein complexes, comparative genomics of modification enzyme conservation, ribosome profiling analytics across three domains of life, structural interpretation of cryo-EM collision complexes, and multi-omic disease cohort analysis—an assembly of expertise that essentially never resides in one laboratory. The public data ecosystem, however, is now sufficiently mature to permit this synthesis without new experiments: MODOMICS and epitranscriptomic atlases catalogue modification sites across organisms; the Sequence Read Archive and GEO host dozens of Ribo-seq datasets under modification-enzyme-deficient conditions; the PDB and EMDB contain a growing set of collided-ribosome and quality-control complex structures; and condensate and cancer/neurodegeneration proteomic databases document downstream phenotypic consequences. This proposal is designed to knit these resources into the first mechanistic, cross-scale framework linking chemical modification loss to mesoscale condensate emergence and disease phenotype.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This working group is organized around three tightly linked research questions, each addressed exclusively through synthesis of existing public data. Research Question 1 asks: does the biophysical signature of a modification-deficient tRNA at the ribosomal A-site—altered codon-anticodon geometry, altered dwell time, altered interface free energy—quantitatively predict the probability of ribosome collision at the corresponding codon? We hypothesize that specific modification losses (e.g., loss of wobble-uridine thiolation or queuosine) generate distinctive, computable signatures of decoding delay whose magnitude, when mapped onto codon usage and mRNA sequence context, will predict collision hotspots identified independently in public Ribo-seq disome/collision datasets across bacteria, yeast, and human cell lines. Research Question 2 asks: do the structural and energetic properties of collided ribosome junctions determine which complexes proceed to recruit quality-control and condensate-nucleating factors, and can this determination be predicted from existing cryo-EM structures of stalled/collided ribosome-factor complexes deposited in the PDB and EMDB? We hypothesize that specific interface geometries at the collided ribosome junction—particularly those altered by non-canonical decoding events—create preferential binding surfaces for ZNF598 and Pelota/Hbs1 recruitment, such that collision complexes arising from modification loss are structurally biased toward productive condensate nucleation rather than resolution. Research Question 3 asks: does the resulting modification-loss-to-condensation axis manifest as detectable, conserved molecular signatures in disease-relevant multi-omic cohorts, and do these signatures correlate with clinically documented proteostasis and stress phenotypes? We hypothesize that tissues and cell states exhibiting reduced tRNA modification enzyme expression or activity (inferred from transcriptomic/proteomic profiling in existing cohorts) will show elevated condensate-associated proteomic signatures and stress-granule marker enrichment, correlating with adverse phenotypic outcomes in datasets spanning acute myeloid leukemia proteomic subtypes and postmortem neurodegenerative brain atlases. Collectively, these hypotheses predict a conserved, cross-organism, cross-scale causal chain: modification loss → altered decoding biophysics → increased collision propensity → structurally favored condensate nucleation → detectable proteomic/transcriptomic stress signature → phenotypic consequence. Testing this chain requires no new experiments; rather, it requires the coordinated reanalysis, harmonization, and structural-computational modeling of data already deposited across at least six distinct public repositories spanning structural biology, functional genomics, and clinical multi-omics. A secondary, methodological question threads through the biological hypotheses: can graph-based imputation and similarity-network-fusion approaches, developed originally for single-cell and multi-omic cancer subtyping, be adapted to integrate structural-simulation-derived features with sequencing-derived pausing scores and proteomic condensate signatures into a single, cross-organism analytical framework? Establishing this methodological bridge is itself a significant contribution, as it would provide a reusable template for connecting atomistic biophysical prediction to population-scale omics synthesis in other mesoscale emergence problems beyond translation.

[Methods and Approach]
The project is organized into four integrated work packages, each built entirely on existing public resources. Work Package 1 (Modification and Enzyme Curation) will assemble a harmonized cross-organism catalogue of tRNA modification sites and their cognate enzymes using MODOMICS, bacterial and eukaryotic epitranscriptomic mapping datasets, and comparative genomic analyses of enzyme conservation and functional redundancy across bacteria, yeast, and human systems, producing a unified reference table linking modification identity, enzyme, organism, and known phenotypic consequences of loss. Work Package 2 (Structural and Biophysical Modeling) will use residue-resolution coarse-grained and atomistic molecular dynamics, parameterized against existing cryo-EM structures of ribosome-tRNA and collided-ribosome-factor complexes from the PDB and EMDB, to simulate decoding at modified versus unmodified anticodon positions, quantifying differences in dwell time, interface free energy, and A-site sampling geometry; separately, structural ensembles of collided ribosome junctions bound to ZNF598 and Pelota/Hbs1 will be analyzed for interface features correlated with productive complex formation versus resolution. Work Package 3 (Cross-Organism Ribo-seq Integration) will reprocess publicly deposited Ribo-seq and disome-profiling datasets from modification-enzyme-deficient and wild-type bacteria, yeast, and human cell lines using standardized pausing-score and collision-detection pipelines, enabling direct comparison of empirically observed pausing/collision hotspots against the biophysical predictions generated in Work Package 2. Work Package 4 (Multi-Omic Disease Phenotype Integration) will mine condensate composition databases (DrLLPS, PhaSepDB) alongside proteomic, single-cell transcriptomic, and single-cell epigenomic datasets from disease cohorts—including proteomic acute myeloid leukemia subtyping data and postmortem brain single-cell epigenomic atlases—to quantify condensate-associated and stress-granule marker signatures, correlating them with inferred modification-enzyme expression/activity levels and clinical/phenotypic annotations. Integration across work packages will employ graph-based feature propagation methods to impute and denoise sparse single-cell and proteomic measurements, followed by similarity-network-fusion clustering to identify conserved modification–pausing–condensation axes across organisms and disease contexts. Structural predictions from Work Package 2 will be encoded as quantitative features (interface energies, geometric descriptors) and fused with sequencing-derived pausing scores and proteomic condensate scores within this unified network, allowing statistical testing of the proposed causal chain via cross-organism concordance analysis and phenotype correlation. All computational workflows will be version-controlled, containerized, and benchmarked against held-out organism/dataset combinations to assess generalizability. Monthly working group meetings will rotate leadership across the structural biophysics, RNA modification genomics, single-cell/proteomic bioinformatics, and clinical data domains to ensure balanced integration and to surface cross-disciplinary methodological conflicts early, with quarterly synthesis retreats devoted to consolidating cross-work-package findings into unified manuscripts and public data products.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This synthesis will produce the first quantitative, cross-scale model linking specific tRNA modification losses to ribosome collision propensity, condensate nucleation likelihood, and disease-relevant proteostasis phenotypes. Primary deliverables include a harmonized public database of modification-enzyme conservation and phenotypic consequence annotations; a structurally validated biophysical scoring function for collision propensity at modification-deficient codons; a cross-organism atlas of Ribo-seq collision hotspots reanalyzed under standardized pipelines; and an integrative similarity-network-fusion framework linking structural, sequencing, and proteomic condensate features to clinical outcomes in leukemia and neurodegeneration cohorts. Scientifically, this work will resolve a long-standing disconnect between RNA modification biochemistry and ribosome quality-control biophysics, establishing whether collision-triggered condensation is a generalizable, conserved consequence of translational fidelity loss rather than an organism- or context-specific curiosity. Methodologically, the project will demonstrate a reusable template for fusing atomistic simulation output with population-scale multi-omic data, a capability broadly transferable to other mesoscale emergence problems in molecular and cellular biology, directly advancing NCEMS's core analytical mission. Translational impact includes identifying candidate biomarkers of modification-loss-driven proteostatic stress in leukemia proteomic subtypes and neurodegenerative epigenomic atlases, potentially informing future biomarker or therapeutic strategies targeting condensate-associated stress pathways. Broader impacts include establishing an open, extensible computational pipeline that other groups can apply to additional modification systems, organisms, or disease cohorts, and generating cross-training experiences that equip early-career scientists with integrated skills spanning wet-lab RNA biology, molecular simulation, and biomedical data science—directly addressing the workforce development goals central to this funding mechanism.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
All data used in this project are drawn exclusively from public repositories, including MODOMICS, NCBI GEO and Sequence Read Archive Ribo-seq datasets, the Protein Data Bank and Electron Microscopy Data Bank, DrLLPS, PhaSepDB, TCGA, ICGC, and publicly deposited single-cell epigenomic brain atlases; no new experimental data will be generated. Consistent with NCEMS open science policy, every curated dataset, harmonized annotation table, simulation input/output file, and analysis script will be deposited in version-controlled public repositories (GitHub for code, Zenodo or OSF for data and simulation trajectories) under permissive open-source licenses, with persistent identifiers assigned to enable citation and reuse. Molecular dynamics simulation protocols, force field parameters, and analysis pipelines will be packaged as containerized, executable workflows (Snakemake/Nextflow) accompanied by comprehensive documentation to ensure independent reproducibility by external groups lacking specialized simulation expertise. Ribo-seq reprocessing and similarity-network-fusion integration code will be structured as modular, well-documented packages with unit tests and example datasets, enabling adaptation to additional organisms or modification systems beyond those studied here. The working group will adopt pre-registration of key hypotheses and analysis plans for the cross-organism concordance tests, and will release intermediate data products (e.g., harmonized pausing scores, structural feature tables) prior to final manuscript submission to maximize community utility. All findings, including negative or null results regarding proposed causal linkages, will be reported transparently in preprints deposited on bioRxiv prior to journal submission. Regular working group calls will include explicit review of data provenance and licensing compliance to ensure all synthesized resources are used and redistributed according to their original terms. This commitment to transparent, modular, and reusable infrastructure ensures that the project's primary scientific product is not only its findings but also a durable, community-usable synthesis platform.

[Budget and Resources]
Requested resources focus on personnel, computational infrastructure, and collaborative coordination rather than experimental costs, reflecting the project's pure synthesis design. Personnel support includes partial salary for a postdoctoral researcher with expertise in molecular dynamics and structural bioinformatics, a graduate student trainee focused on Ribo-seq reprocessing and comparative genomics, and a data scientist trainee specializing in multi-omic integration and similarity-network-fusion methods, providing direct cross-disciplinary training opportunities central to the RFP's workforce development goals. Computational resources include allocation on high-performance computing clusters for coarse-grained and atomistic molecular dynamics simulations of ribosome-tRNA complexes, along with cloud storage and compute credits for large-scale reprocessing of public Ribo-seq and single-cell proteomic/epigenomic datasets. Modest funds are requested for working group coordination, including quarterly in-person or hybrid synthesis retreats to integrate findings across the four work packages, and travel support enabling trainees to present integrative findings at relevant scientific conferences. Software licensing costs are minimized through reliance on open-source simulation (e.g., GROMACS, OpenMM) and analysis (Python/R-based) tools. A small budget line supports data curation efforts, including manual harmonization of modification-enzyme annotations across organisms and quality control of reprocessed sequencing datasets. No funds are requested for new experimental data generation, reagents, or human/animal subject costs, consistent with the synthesis-only scope of this proposal. The requested budget explicitly leverages NCEMS-provided computational infrastructure and collaborative support mechanisms, as the scale of cross-organism, cross-data-type integration proposed here exceeds what any single participating laboratory currently possesses, justifying the requirement for centralized synthesis center support to enable this multidisciplinary, multi-institutional collaboration.

title: Decoding the 'Organelle Signature' Landscape: A Genomic Deconvolution Framework for Discovering Novel Protein- and Lipid-Bounded Compartments Across Bacteria and Archaea
title_norm: decoding the organelle signature landscape a genomic deconvolution framework for discovering novel protein and lipidbounded compartments across bacteria and archaea
abstract_text: Bacterial and archaeal organelles—carboxysomes, encapsulins, magnetosomes, ferrosomes, and their atypical relatives—represent striking cases of mesoscale emergence, where discrete sets of genes assemble into compartments with properties (selective permeability, biomineralization, redox control) absent from their individual protein components. Despite decades of discovery, our catalog of prokaryotic organelles remains almost certainly incomplete: current identification relies on manual inspection of gene neighborhoods and homology to a handful of known shell or membrane systems, an approach poorly suited to the scale of modern genomic and metagenomic databases. This project proposes to reframe organelle discovery as a signature-deconvolution problem, adapting mutational-signature-style matrix factorization methods (as used in large-scale cancer genomics) to genomic co-occurrence data. Instead of decomposing mutation spectra into additive processes, we will decompose gene-cluster architectures—shell/membrane protein paralogs, cargo enzymes, transporters, and regulatory genes—across hundreds of thousands of public bacterial and archaeal genomes and metagenome-assembled genomes (IMG/M, GTDB, JGI, NCBI) into a small number of recurring 'organelle signatures.' [Background and Significance]
Prokaryotic organelles occupy a privileged position in the study of mesoscale emergence: they demonstrate how a bounded set of genes—encoding shell or membrane proteins, cargo enzymes, transporters, and regulators—self-assembles into compartments whose functional properties (selective permeability, biomineralization, redox buffering) cannot be predicted from any single component in isolation. Carboxysomes concentrate CO2 for carbon fixation; encapsulins sequester reactive enzymatic chemistry; magnetosomes template magnetite biomineralization; ferrosomes store iron to counter host nutritional immunity. Each of these systems was discovered through decades of painstaking, largely manual investigation of individual gene clusters, guided by homology to a small number of already-known shell or membrane architectures. This case-by-case discovery paradigm has been productive but is now a bottleneck: public sequence repositories such as IMG/M, GTDB, JGI, and NCBI contain hundreds of thousands of bacterial and archaeal genomes and metagenome-assembled genomes, vastly exceeding what manual curation can survey. Recent comparative-genomic work has already revealed 'atypical' organelle-like loci (e.g., JEEP systems) that retain only a minimal subset of canonical structural genes, suggesting that a much broader, largely uncatalogued space of compartmentalization strategies exists in nature, hidden in plain sight within public sequence data. The core significance of this problem is that prokaryotic organelles are a natural laboratory for studying how emergent subcellular structure arises from combinatorial gene-cluster architecture—a question directly aligned with NCEMS's mesoscale mission. Yet no systematic, quantitative, genome-scale framework currently exists to detect recurring architectural 'signatures' of organelle-forming loci the way mutational-signature analysis has revealed recurring, biologically interpretable patterns within noisy, high-dimensional cancer genomic data. This proposal imports that logic: gene-cluster composition across genomes can be treated as a high-dimensional co-occurrence matrix amenable to non-negative matrix factorization, extracting a small number of additive 'signatures' that represent recurring organelle-genesis programs, including combinations never previously described. This reframing is significant because it converts organelle discovery from an artisanal, homology-dependent search into a scalable, statistically grounded synthesis task built entirely on existing public data. It also creates a template applicable well beyond iron- and carbon-handling organelles, to any mesoscale molecular machine defined by a recurring, non-random gene-cluster grammar. Because the requisite genomic architecture expertise, iron/heme organelle biogenesis knowledge, microcompartment structural biology, and quantitative signature-extraction methodology are each concentrated in different labs, this problem cannot be solved through incremental single-lab effort; it requires the exact kind of cross-disciplinary data synthesis NCEMS is designed to catalyze.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This project addresses three interlocking research questions. First: can recurring, biologically meaningful 'organelle signatures'—additive combinations of shell/membrane paralogs, cargo enzymes, transporters, and regulatory genes—be extracted directly from public genomic co-occurrence data using matrix factorization, without prior assumption of which combinations constitute a functional organelle? We hypothesize that known organelle systems (carboxysome, encapsulin, magnetosome, ferrosome, and atypical JEEP loci) will resolve as distinct, high-loading signatures when the factorization is applied to a sufficiently large and taxonomically diverse genome set, validating the approach against established ground truth. Second: does the residual signature space—components of the factorization not explained by known systems—contain coherent, reproducible architectural patterns consistent with undescribed compartmentalization systems, rather than statistical noise or lineage-specific artifacts? We hypothesize that a subset of residual signatures will show the hallmarks of genuine organelle-forming loci: phylogenetically dispersed but architecturally conserved gene-cluster co-occurrence, enrichment for protein folds associated with oligomeric shell formation or membrane curvature, and physiological gene neighbors (transporters, redox enzymes, biomineralization-associated genes) analogous to those flanking known organelle loci. Third: can structural and functional context inferred purely from public data—AlphaFold/ESMFold structural predictions, proteomic and transcriptomic expression patterns, and metabolomic association—be used to prioritize candidate novel organelle signatures for likely biological function and expression conditions, without new experimentation? We hypothesize that integrating structural fold predictions (shell-like oligomerization propensity, membrane-remodeling curvature motifs) with condition-specific expression data (e.g., iron limitation, anaerobiosis, oxidative stress, cofactor imbalance) will allow us to rank candidate signatures by functional plausibility and predict the physiological niches in which they are deployed, mirroring the way ferrosome and encapsulin functions were originally inferred from genomic context before mechanistic follow-up. A unifying hypothesis underlies all three questions: organelle-forming capacity in prokaryotes is not idiosyncratic to a handful of well-studied systems but is a generalizable, statistically learnable pattern of gene-cluster architecture, such that the same combinatorial logic that produces carboxysomes and magnetosomes recurs, with variation, across a much larger and largely undiscovered space of microbial compartments. Confirming this hypothesis would fundamentally reframe organelle emergence as a predictable outcome of genomic architecture rather than a rare evolutionary accident, with direct implications for understanding how mesoscale structure arises from molecular parts lists more broadly. Disconfirming evidence—for instance, if residual signatures fail to show structural or contextual coherence—would itself be informative, suggesting that known organelle systems occupy a narrower, more constrained region of architectural space than currently assumed, refining the search strategy for future synthesis efforts.

[Methods and Approach]
The project unfolds in four coordinated phases, each built entirely on public data and requiring the combined expertise of the team. Phase 1, Data Assembly and Locus Extraction: we will compile a comprehensive gene-cluster dataset by mining IMG/M, GTDB, JGI, and NCBI genome and metagenome-assembled genome collections, using existing annotation pipelines and profile-HMM searches to identify candidate organelle-associated loci based on presence of shell/membrane protein paralogs, cargo enzyme families, transporters, and regulators. Loci will be represented as feature vectors encoding gene family composition, order, and co-occurrence frequency, generating a large sparse matrix analogous to the mutation-context matrices used in cancer signature analysis. Phase 2, Signature Extraction and Validation: non-negative matrix factorization (and complementary approaches such as Bayesian NMF and topic models) will be applied to decompose this matrix into a minimal set of additive signatures. Known systems—carboxysome, encapsulin, magnetosome, ferrosome, and atypical JEEP loci—already characterized through comparative genomic and structural work by team members, will serve as labeled anchors to tune factorization rank, assess signature stability via bootstrapping, and establish quantitative benchmarks (reconstruction accuracy, signature reproducibility across resampled genome subsets) for distinguishing genuine biological signal from technical artifact. Phase 3, Candidate Prioritization via Structural and Functional Integration: residual signatures not explained by known systems will be extracted as candidate novel organelle architectures. For each candidate, constituent proteins will be cross-referenced against AlphaFold and ESMFold structural databases to assess propensity for shell-like oligomerization or membrane-remodeling folds, using established structural criteria from prior microcompartment shell characterization. Public proteomics, transcriptomics, and metabolomics datasets (e.g., expression atlases, stress-condition transcriptomes) will be mined to infer likely physiological contexts—iron/heme handling, cofactor regeneration, anaerobic or oxidative stress metabolism—by testing for condition-specific co-expression of candidate loci, paralleling the contextual inference previously used to characterize ferrosome and encapsulin function. Phase 4, Synthesis and Ranking: candidates will be scored on a composite index integrating factorization confidence, structural plausibility, phylogenetic breadth, and functional context coherence, producing a ranked, annotated catalog for community follow-up. Throughout, computational workflows will be modularized and version-controlled, with quantitative benchmarking methodology (analogous to composite-index validation approaches used in clinical data synthesis) applied to ensure the ranking metric is interpretable and reproducible. Regular cross-team working sessions will pair genomic/computational analysis with structural and physiological interpretation, ensuring candidates are evaluated against the mechanistic criteria established for known organelle systems.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This synthesis project will produce three primary deliverables. First, an open, versioned organelle-signature database cataloging both validated known-system signatures and newly discovered candidate architectures, annotated with taxonomic distribution, structural predictions, and inferred physiological context. Second, a reproducible, modular computational pipeline for genomic signature extraction, structural cross-referencing, and functional context integration, designed for extension by the broader community to additional organelle classes or genomic feature sets. Third, a ranked, publicly available list of candidate novel bacterial and archaeal organelles, prioritized for experimental follow-up by the wider research community, effectively seeding future hypothesis-driven work well beyond this consortium's own capacity. Scientifically, this project will substantially expand the known diversity of prokaryotic compartmentalization strategies and provide the first quantitative, generalizable framework for treating organelle emergence as a learnable pattern in genomic architecture rather than a series of isolated discoveries. This reframing has direct relevance to NCEMS's mesoscale emergence mission, illustrating how discrete molecular parts combine combinatorially to generate system-level properties absent from individual components. Methodologically, the adaptation of signature-deconvolution approaches from cancer genomics to microbial genomic architecture establishes a transferable template applicable to other classes of mesoscale molecular machines defined by recurring, non-random gene-cluster grammars—condensates, secretion systems, or multi-enzyme metabolic assemblies. Training materials generated from this pipeline will introduce trainees to matrix-factorization methodology in a genomics context, cultivating a workforce fluent in both structural microbiology and quantitative data science, directly advancing NCEMS's talent-development goals while generating durable, reusable community resources.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
All aspects of this project will adhere to open science principles from inception. Source data are drawn exclusively from public repositories (IMG/M, GTDB, JGI, NCBI, AlphaFold/ESMFold databases, and public proteomic, transcriptomic, and metabolomic archives), with no new experimental data generated. All locus-extraction scripts, feature matrices, factorization code, and candidate-scoring pipelines will be developed in version-controlled public repositories (e.g., GitHub, archived via Zenodo for citable, immutable releases), accompanied by containerized environments to ensure computational reproducibility across platforms. The organelle-signature database itself will be released under an open license, structured for programmatic access (API and bulk download), and designed for community extension as new genomes and structural predictions become available. Analytical decisions—factorization rank selection, validation benchmarks, structural and functional scoring thresholds—will be documented in preregistered analysis plans and detailed methods notebooks, allowing independent reproduction of every candidate ranking. Intermediate outputs, including rejected or low-confidence signatures, will be released alongside final candidates to support transparent community evaluation and avoid selective reporting. The project will follow FAIR data principles throughout, ensuring findability, accessibility, interoperability, and reusability of all generated resources. Working group members will coordinate through shared electronic lab notebooks and regular public progress updates, consistent with community-endorsed team-science practices. Preprints will be posted prior to formal publication, and all resulting manuscripts will target open-access venues. By committing to full pipeline transparency and data availability from the outset, this project ensures that its central contribution—the organelle-signature framework—can be independently validated, critiqued, extended, or repurposed by other research groups, maximizing its value as a durable community resource rather than a one-time analysis.

[Budget and Resources]
This project requires computational and personnel resources appropriate to a data-synthesis working group rather than laboratory experimentation. Primary costs include support for a postdoctoral researcher or senior computational trainee with expertise in matrix factorization and genomic data pipelines, who will lead locus extraction, factorization implementation, and pipeline integration under joint mentorship from all four investigators. A graduate student trainee will focus on structural cross-referencing and functional context integration, gaining direct training in both structural bioinformatics and microbial physiology. Computational costs include high-performance computing allocation for processing hundreds of thousands of genomes and metagenome-assembled genomes, storage for intermediate feature matrices and structural prediction datasets, and cloud or institutional cluster access for iterative factorization runs and bootstrapped validation. Modest travel funds will support two in-person working group meetings annually to synchronize genomic, structural, and physiological interpretation across sites, alongside regular virtual coordination. Because the four investigators are distributed across institutions with complementary but non-overlapping infrastructure—large-scale comparative genomics resources, organelle structural biology facilities, and iron/heme physiology expertise—NCEMS support is essential to fund the shared computational infrastructure, data integration personnel, and coordination mechanisms that no single lab's existing grants are structured to provide. NCEMS resources will also support publication costs for open-access dissemination and Zenodo/database hosting fees to guarantee long-term public availability of the organelle-signature database beyond the funding period. No funds are requested for new experimental data generation, consistent with the synthesis-only scope of this proposal; all resources are directed toward personnel, computation, and coordination needed to integrate and reanalyze existing public genomic, structural, and omics datasets at a scale and cross-disciplinary depth unattainable by any individual participating laboratory.

title: Circadian Control of Heat-Sensitive Mesoscale Assembly During Plant Cell Division
title_norm: circadian control of heatsensitive mesoscale assembly during plant cell division
abstract_text:
Plant growth under episodic high temperature depends not only on stress-responsive transcription but also on whether dividing cells can assemble a functional cytokinetic apparatus at the right time. The central question of this synthesis project is: how do time of day and heat stress jointly alter the emergent mesoscale organization of plant cytokinesis, including microtubule arrays, endomembrane trafficking, cell plate formation, and nascent cell wall deposition? We propose that cytokinetic failure under heat is an emergent systems property arising from misalignment among circadian-regulated stress pathways, vesicle sorting capacity, cytoskeletal reorganization, and cell wall biosynthesis, rather than from disruption of any single gene or organelle.

This NCEMS Working Group will use only publicly available datasets to build a cross-scale synthesis of heat-sensitive plant cell division. We will integrate public RNA-seq time courses from Arabidopsis, sorghum, maize, wheat, and other plant systems exposed to temperature perturbations at different times of day; root and shoot single-cell transcriptomic atlases enriched for proliferative tissues; public proteomic, phosphoproteomic, interactome, and subcellular localization resources; and archived fluorescence and electron microscopy datasets containing dividing plant cells, cytoskeletal markers, Golgi/trans-Golgi network markers, cell plate markers, and cell wall biosynthetic reporters. Existing resources such as GEO, SRA, ENA, PRIDE, BioImage Archive, EMPIAR, TAIR, MaizeGDB, Expression Atlas, SUBA, and plant orthology databases will be harmonized into a reproducible analysis framework.

The project has three synthesis aims. First, we will create a shared ontology and data model linking cytokinetic structures, endomembrane compartments, cell wall assembly processes, heat-response regulators, and circadian phase information across plant species and experimental platforms. Second, we will construct confounder-aware, context-specific gene and protein networks that distinguish heat-responsive modules that are constitutive from those gated by time of day, tissue identity, developmental stage, or genotype. These networks will prioritize conserved and lineage-specific modules connecting calcium signaling, heat shock regulation, vesicle trafficking, autophagy-related remodeling, microtubule organization, and polysaccharide deposition. Third, we will apply standardized image-analysis workflows to public microscopy data to extract mesoscale phenotypes such as phragmoplast geometry, cell plate expansion symmetry, vesicle-marker distribution, microtubule array coherence, and spatial relationships among organelles during cytokinesis. Network features will then be linked to image-derived phenotypes to identify candidate molecular configurations that predict robust versus heat-vulnerable cytokinetic assembly.

The expected outcome is an open, community-curated atlas of plant cytokinetic heat sensitivity that connects molecular state, cellular architecture, circadian timing, and species-level variation. This effort requires NCEMS support because it depends on coordination among plant cell biologists, circadian and stress biologists, endomembrane specialists, computational genomicists, image analysts, statisticians, and trainees across institutions. No individual laboratory could assemble, standardize, and interpret these heterogeneous public datasets at the necessary scale. The Working Group will release containerized workflows, harmonized metadata, image-analysis notebooks, network models, and training materials. By synthesizing public molecular and cellular data, the project will reveal how environmental timing reshapes mesoscale cellular organization and will provide a general framework for studying emergent stress sensitivity in eukaryotic cell division.

[Background and Significance]
Plant productivity during heat waves depends on the ability of meristems and developing tissues to continue producing viable cells. Although heat-stress biology has been studied extensively at the level of transcription factors, chaperones, hormones, and membrane stability, a critical unresolved problem is how high temperature affects the mesoscale machinery that physically completes plant cell division. Plant cytokinesis requires coordinated organization of the phragmoplast microtubule array, targeted vesicle trafficking through Golgi and trans-Golgi network compartments, cell plate membrane maturation, callose and cellulose-related wall deposition, and eventual fusion of the new cross wall with the parental wall. These structures are larger than individual macromolecular complexes but smaller than whole organelles or tissues, placing them directly within the NCEMS focus on emergent mesoscale properties.

The proposed Working Group addresses a fundamental question in molecular and cellular biosciences: why do dividing plant cells become heat vulnerable at particular times, in particular tissues, or in particular genotypes? Public data suggest that the answer cannot be reduced to a single heat shock pathway. Temperature responses are gated by the circadian system, and the magnitude and composition of heat-responsive transcriptional programs vary with time of day. Separately, plant cytokinesis depends on temporally ordered interactions among cytoskeletal proteins, vesicle coats, tethering factors, small GTPases, phosphoinositide metabolism, autophagy-related remodeling, and cell wall biosynthetic enzymes. The emergent behavior of this system is successful partitioning of one cell into two daughters. Heat may disrupt that outcome when circadian phase, stress signaling, membrane trafficking capacity, and wall assembly demand become poorly aligned.

This question is now tractable through synthesis research because large, heterogeneous public resources have accumulated across molecular, cellular, and organismal scales. Time-resolved RNA-seq datasets exist for Arabidopsis and several crops under heat and temperature-shift regimes, including experiments that explicitly vary time of day. Single-cell and single-nucleus atlases identify proliferative root and shoot cell populations and allow cytokinesis-relevant gene programs to be placed in tissue and developmental context. Proteomic, phosphoproteomic, interaction, localization, and orthology databases provide complementary evidence for protein modules and conserved cellular functions. Public light microscopy and electron microscopy repositories include images of dividing plant cells, cytoskeletal markers, endomembrane compartments, cell plates, and cell wall reporters, but these data have not been jointly analyzed for heat-sensitive mesoscale phenotypes.

The project is significant because it will transform dispersed datasets into a community resource for explaining how environmental timing influences cellular architecture. It directly meets NCEMS priorities by using only existing public data, requiring a multidisciplinary team, integrating data types beyond the reach of a single laboratory, and targeting emergence across scales from gene regulation to mesoscale cytokinetic organization. The work will also generate reusable methods for confounder-aware network construction, cross-species metadata harmonization, and image-derived phenotype extraction. These outputs will benefit plant biology, cell biology, climate-resilience research, and the broader study of stress-sensitive cell division in eukaryotes.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
The central research question is how circadian phase and heat stress jointly influence the emergent mesoscale organization of plant cytokinesis. We will address this question through three interlocking synthesis questions that connect molecular state, cellular architecture, and evolutionary conservation.

Question 1: Which cytokinesis-associated molecular modules are heat responsive, circadian gated, or both? We hypothesize that heat-responsive regulation of plant cell division is partitioned into at least three classes: constitutive heat-response modules active across time points; circadian-gated modules whose response amplitude or direction depends on time of day; and cell-cycle- or tissue-restricted modules detectable primarily in proliferative cell populations. We expect core heat shock and protein-folding genes to behave more broadly, whereas modules involving vesicle sorting, microtubule remodeling, calcium signaling, callose deposition, and wall-polysaccharide trafficking will show stronger dependence on circadian phase and developmental context.

Question 2: Do heat-vulnerable cytokinetic states arise from misalignment among interacting mesoscale subsystems rather than from failure of a single pathway? We hypothesize that cytokinetic breakdown under heat reflects loss of coordinated timing among cytoskeleton dynamics, endomembrane delivery, membrane remodeling, and nascent cell wall construction. Under this hypothesis, vulnerability will be predicted by network configurations in which heat-stress regulators are activated but trafficking, microtubule-associated, or wall-synthesis modules are delayed, suppressed, or uncoupled from one another. Robust cytokinesis should instead correspond to coordinated activation of stress-protection and assembly modules at compatible circadian phases.

Question 3: Which aspects of heat-sensitive cytokinesis are conserved across plant lineages, and which are species- or genotype-specific? We hypothesize that conserved modules will include calcium-dependent signaling, chaperone-mediated proteostasis, cytoskeletal regulators, vesicle tethering and fusion components, and core cell plate maturation factors. Lineage-specific or genotype-sensitive modules are expected in expanded gene families involved in cell wall biosynthesis, stress-responsive transcription, hormone signaling, and endomembrane specialization. Cross-species synthesis across Arabidopsis, sorghum, maize, wheat, and additional public plant datasets will distinguish broadly conserved principles from crop-specific adaptation.

Question 4: Can image-derived mesoscale phenotypes be predicted from public molecular data? We hypothesize that extracted features such as phragmoplast expansion symmetry, microtubule array coherence, cell plate curvature, vesicle-marker concentration near the division plane, and cell wall reporter distribution will correlate with context-specific network states. For example, reduced coherence of phragmoplast arrays may associate with altered expression or phosphorylation of microtubule regulators and stress-associated kinases, while abnormal cell plate expansion may associate with endomembrane sorting and polysaccharide deposition modules.

Question 5: What metadata standards are necessary to make time-of-day, heat-treatment, cell-cycle, tissue, and imaging information interoperable? We hypothesize that many currently public datasets are scientifically valuable but underused because key contextual variables are recorded inconsistently. A shared ontology linking circadian phase, thermal regime, cytokinetic structures, subcellular compartments, and developmental identity will enable analyses that are not possible using dataset-specific metadata alone.

Together, these questions test the overarching hypothesis that heat sensitivity in dividing plant cells is an emergent property of cross-scale coordination. The project will not seek a single master regulator. Instead, it will define combinations of molecular and mesoscale features that predict when cytokinesis is buffered against heat and when it becomes a bottleneck for growth.

[Methods and Approach]
This Working Group will conduct a synthesis study using only existing publicly available data. No new experimental data will be generated. The work will be organized into three integrated aims supported by shared data governance, reproducible workflows, and recurring cross-disciplinary analysis meetings.

Aim 1 will build a harmonized cytokinesis-heat-circadian data framework. We will identify and curate public datasets from GEO, SRA, ENA, Expression Atlas, PRIDE, BioImage Archive, EMPIAR, TAIR, MaizeGDB, Gramene, PLAZA, OrthoDB, SUBA, BioGRID, IntAct, and related plant resources. Transcriptomic datasets will include bulk RNA-seq time courses under heat, temperature shifts, diel cycles, and constant-condition circadian experiments in Arabidopsis, sorghum, maize, wheat, and other species where metadata are adequate. Single-cell and single-nucleus atlases will be used to annotate proliferative tissues and cell-cycle states. Proteomic, phosphoproteomic, localization, and interaction resources will provide protein-level support. Image datasets will be screened for dividing cells and markers of microtubules, Golgi, trans-Golgi network, cell plate, plasma membrane, callose, cellulose-related processes, and cell wall assembly. We will develop a lightweight ontology and metadata schema covering species, genotype, tissue, developmental stage, thermal regime, Zeitgeber time or circadian phase, assay type, cell-cycle stage, cytokinetic structure, and imaging modality.

Aim 2 will infer context-specific molecular networks. Public RNA-seq reads will be reprocessed where feasible through containerized workflows using consistent quality control, alignment or pseudoalignment, gene quantification, and orthology mapping. Existing count matrices will be incorporated when raw data are impractical, with provenance recorded. We will model heat response while controlling for confounders including species, genotype, tissue, batch, developmental stage, time after treatment, and time of day. Differential expression, rhythmicity analysis, phase-aware regression, and interaction models will identify genes whose heat response depends on circadian context. Co-expression and protein-supported networks will be constructed using confounder-aware methods, with context-specific edges tested for robustness by resampling, dataset holdout, and comparison across species. Network modules will be annotated for cytokinesis, endomembrane trafficking, autophagy-related remodeling, microtubule organization, calcium signaling, heat response, and cell wall biosynthesis.

Aim 3 will extract and integrate mesoscale image phenotypes. Public fluorescence and electron microscopy datasets will be processed using standardized notebooks and open image-analysis tools. When sufficient annotations exist, supervised or semi-supervised segmentation will identify dividing cells, phragmoplasts, cell plates, vesicle-rich zones, and relevant organelle markers. Where image heterogeneity limits automation, curated benchmark subsets will be analyzed with transparent quality scoring. Extracted features will include phragmoplast length and width, expansion symmetry, microtubule orientation coherence, cell plate continuity, marker enrichment at the division plane, spatial proximity among endomembrane compartments, and wall reporter distribution. Metadata will link image phenotypes to species, genotype, tissue, temperature, and sampling time.

Finally, molecular network features and image-derived phenotypes will be integrated using multilevel statistical models and interpretable machine learning. The goal is not black-box prediction, but identification of reproducible molecular configurations associated with robust or disrupted cytokinetic assembly. Regular NCEMS-supported workshops will bring plant cell biologists, circadian specialists, computational genomics experts, image analysts, statisticians, and trainees together to validate assumptions, refine terminology, troubleshoot metadata gaps, and prioritize community-useful outputs.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The primary outcome will be an open atlas of heat-sensitive plant cytokinesis that connects circadian timing, stress-responsive molecular networks, proliferative cell identities, protein localization, and mesoscale image phenotypes. This atlas will provide curated links among genes, proteins, structures, compartments, and phenotypes across Arabidopsis and major crop species, allowing researchers to query which cytokinetic processes are predicted to be heat vulnerable at specific times of day or in particular tissues.

A second outcome will be a set of conserved and lineage-specific network modules associated with robust or vulnerable cytokinetic assembly. These modules will clarify whether heat sensitivity is driven mainly by proteostasis, calcium signaling, vesicle trafficking, cytoskeletal reorganization, wall biosynthesis, or by failures of coordination among these processes. The project will generate prioritized hypotheses for future experimental laboratories, while the Working Group itself will remain entirely within synthesis research.

A third outcome will be reusable methodology. The metadata schema, ontology, confounder-aware network workflow, cross-species orthology framework, and public microscopy analysis notebooks will be applicable to other mesoscale cellular systems. These tools will help the community analyze emergence where cell behavior cannot be inferred from transcript abundance alone.

The broader impact is timely and substantial. Heat waves increasingly threaten plant development and agricultural productivity, yet cellular bottlenecks in dividing tissues remain poorly synthesized across available data. By revealing how environmental timing reshapes cytokinetic organization, the project will advance fundamental molecular and cellular biology and provide a conceptual framework for climate-relevant plant resilience. The Working Group will also train graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in open data synthesis, reproducible computation, network analysis, and quantitative cell biology. Because the work requires integration across data modalities, species, institutions, and disciplinary cultures, NCEMS support will enable discoveries that would be unattainable through isolated laboratory efforts.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
The project will follow open, team-based, and reproducible science practices from inception. All datasets used will be publicly available, and every accession, download date, license condition, processing decision, and quality-control outcome will be recorded in a public data inventory. Because the project synthesizes existing data rather than generating new experiments, transparency of provenance and analysis decisions is central to scientific rigor.

All code will be developed in public version-controlled repositories, with stable releases archived through Zenodo or an equivalent repository. Workflows for RNA-seq processing, metadata harmonization, orthology mapping, network construction, statistical modeling, and image analysis will be containerized using Docker or Apptainer and orchestrated with reproducible workflow systems such as Nextflow or Snakemake. Computational environments will be documented with locked software versions. Analysis notebooks will include executable examples using small test datasets so that users can verify installation and reproduce core steps without specialized infrastructure.

The Working Group will release harmonized metadata tables, derived count matrices where redistribution is permitted, network edge lists, module annotations, image feature tables, ontology files, and documentation under permissive open licenses whenever compatible with source repositories. Large files will be stored through appropriate community repositories rather than informal file sharing. Public microscopy annotations generated during synthesis will be deposited in formats compatible with community image archives.

Reproducibility will be strengthened through preregistered analysis plans for major comparisons, explicit criteria for dataset inclusion and exclusion, sensitivity analyses, and independent code review by team members not responsible for the original implementation. Trainees will participate in reproducibility checks as part of structured training.

Community engagement will include open virtual tutorials, issue-tracking for ontology refinement, and short training modules on circadian metadata, plant cytokinesis terminology, confounder-aware co-expression analysis, and quantitative image analysis. These practices will ensure that the outputs are not merely publications but reusable resources for molecular and cellular synthesis research.

[Budget and Resources]
NCEMS support is essential because the project requires coordinated synthesis across disciplines, data types, and institutions rather than conventional single-laboratory research. Funds will be used to support Working Group convenings, trainee participation, data curation, computational analysis, open-science dissemination, and community training. No funds will be used to generate new experimental data.

The largest resource need is collaborative time. We request support for two in-person NCEMS meetings per year, supplemented by monthly virtual working sessions. In-person meetings will focus on ontology development, dataset triage, cross-disciplinary interpretation of network and image results, and manuscript and resource planning. Travel support will prioritize participation by graduate students, postdoctoral researchers, early-career investigators, and collaborators from institutions with varied research capacity.

A second budget category is personnel effort for synthesis tasks. Partial support for trainees or research staff will enable public dataset discovery, metadata cleaning, accession tracking, quality-control review, orthology table construction, image annotation, documentation, and reproducibility testing. These tasks are labor-intensive and require coordination but are central to the proposed scientific contribution.

A third category is computation and data management. Although much work can use institutional and NCEMS infrastructure, modest cloud or high-performance computing allocations will be needed for reprocessing large RNA-seq collections, storing intermediate files, running network resampling analyses, and processing public microscopy data. Container registries, repository archiving, and persistent identifiers will support long-term accessibility.

A fourth category is training and dissemination. Funds will support open workshops, tutorial preparation, community feedback sessions, and publication or repository costs where needed to ensure public access. NCEMS staff expertise in synthesis facilitation, data science, team science, and reproducible workflows will be as important as direct financial support.

The requested resources are proportionate to a synthesis Working Group. They enable a geographically distributed, multidisciplinary team to produce shared infrastructure, rigorously integrated analyses, and trainee training that no individual laboratory or existing collaboration could achieve at comparable scale.

Plant growth under episodic high temperature depends not only on stress-responsive transcription but also on whether dividing cells can assemble a functional cytokinetic apparatus at the right time. The central question of this synthesis project is: how do time of day and heat stress jointly alter the emergent mesoscale organization of plant cytokinesis, including microtubule arrays, endomembrane trafficking, cell plate formation, and nascent cell wall deposition? We propose that cytokinetic failure under heat is an emergent systems property arising from misalignment among circadian-regulated stress pathways, vesicle sorting capacity, cytoskeletal reorganization, and cell wall biosynthesis, rather than from disruption of any single gene or organelle.

This NCEMS Working Group will use only publicly available datasets to build a cross-scale synthesis of heat-sensitive plant cell division. We will integrate public RNA-seq time courses from Arabidopsis, sorghum, maize, wheat, and other plant systems exposed to temperature perturbations at different times of day; root and shoot single-cell transcriptomic atlases enriched for proliferative tissues; public proteomic, phosphoproteomic, interactome, and subcellular localization resources; and archived fluorescence and electron microscopy datasets containing dividing plant cells, cytoskeletal markers, Golgi/trans-Golgi network markers, cell plate markers, and cell wall biosynthetic reporters. Existing resources such as GEO, SRA, ENA, PRIDE, BioImage Archive, EMPIAR, TAIR, MaizeGDB, Expression Atlas, SUBA, and plant orthology databases will be harmonized into a reproducible analysis framework.

The project has three synthesis aims. First, we will create a shared ontology and data model linking cytokinetic structures, endomembrane compartments, cell wall assembly processes, heat-response regulators, and circadian phase information across plant species and experimental platforms. Second, we will construct confounder-aware, context-specific gene and protein networks that distinguish heat-responsive modules that are constitutive from those gated by time of day, tissue identity, developmental stage, or genotype. These networks will prioritize conserved and lineage-specific modules connecting calcium signaling, heat shock regulation, vesicle trafficking, autophagy-related remodeling, microtubule organization, and polysaccharide deposition. Third, we will apply standardized image-analysis workflows to public microscopy data to extract mesoscale phenotypes such as phragmoplast geometry, cell plate expansion symmetry, vesicle-marker distribution, microtubule array coherence, and spatial relationships among organelles during cytokinesis. Network features will then be linked to image-derived phenotypes to identify candidate molecular configurations that predict robust versus heat-vulnerable cytokinetic assembly.

The expected outcome is an open, community-curated atlas of plant cytokinetic heat sensitivity that connects molecular state, cellular architecture, circadian timing, and species-level variation. This effort requires NCEMS support because it depends on coordination among plant cell biologists, circadian and stress biologists, endomembrane specialists, computational genomicists, image analysts, statisticians, and trainees across institutions. No individual laboratory could assemble, standardize, and interpret these heterogeneous public datasets at the necessary scale. The Working Group will release containerized workflows, harmonized metadata, image-analysis notebooks, network models, and training materials. By synthesizing public molecular and cellular data, the project will reveal how environmental timing reshapes mesoscale cellular organization and will provide a general framework for studying emergent stress sensitivity in eukaryotic cell division.

[Abstract]
A central unsolved problem in molecular and cellular neuroscience is how molecular features of chromatin regulators, transcription factors, histone modifications, and architectural proteins combine to produce mesoscale genome structures that differ across brain cell types and alter cellular phenotypes. We propose a community-scale synthesis project to define the “chromatin microenvironment grammar” of human brain cells: the rules by which local molecular interactions give rise to emergent 3D regulatory neighborhoods, enhancer hubs, and compartmental domains that influence gene expression and psychiatric disease risk.
