Cancer therapy response is often modeled as a function of individual driver mutations, basal gene expression, or pathway activity. These predictors have produced important biomarkers, yet they frequently fail to explain why genetically similar cancer cells exhibit heterogeneous transcriptional states, reversible drug tolerance, and rapid pathway switching. A growing body of public data suggests that these phenotypes arise from mesoscale regulatory organization: focal amplifications and extrachromosomal DNA alter gene dosage; enhancer landscapes are rewired by structural variation and transcription factor redistribution; 3D chromatin contacts place genes in new regulatory neighborhoods; and coding variants change protein activities within dependency networks. The resulting assemblies are larger than single molecules but smaller than whole organelles or cells, making them a natural focus for NCEMS synthesis research on emergent biological properties. Cancer cell lines are uniquely suited for this question because they have been profiled repeatedly across public resources and perturbation platforms. DepMap and CCLE provide harmonized genomes, transcriptomes, copy-number profiles, proteomics, metabolomics, CRISPR dependency maps, and drug sensitivity data for hundreds of lines. Public single-cell RNA-seq and Perturb-seq datasets reveal intraline heterogeneity and adaptive transcriptional responses. ENCODE, 4DN, Roadmap-derived resources, and individual studies provide chromatin accessibility, transcription factor occupancy, histone modification, Hi-C, Micro-C, and promoter-capture datasets in cancer and lineage-matched contexts. TCGA, PCAWG, and AmpliconArchitect-based analyses provide structural variation, focal amplification, and ecDNA annotations that can be mapped onto cell line genomes. Public microscopy-derived measurements of ecDNA, when available, add an orthogonal view of amplified DNA organization. Individually, these datasets answer modality-specific questions. Synthesized across scales, they can reveal how molecular components combine into regulatory structures that generate phenotypes not predictable from any one data layer. The significance of this working group lies in converting a fragmented public data ecosystem into a testable framework for emergence in cancer cells. Drug tolerance is a particularly compelling emergent phenotype because it is dynamic, heterogeneous, and clinically consequential. A cell line may harbor an amplified oncogene, but drug response depends on whether the amplified segment is chromosomally integrated or extrachromosomal, whether relevant enhancers contact the oncogene promoter, whether transcription factor motifs are accessible, whether protein-altering variants modify downstream signaling, and whether a rare single-cell state already expresses a bypass program. These relationships cross conventional boundaries among cancer genomics, 3D genome biology, single-cell biology, protein function, pharmacogenomics, and machine learning. No single laboratory can curate, harmonize, model, and interpret these data at community scale. NCEMS support will enable a collaborative synthesis effort that addresses a fundamental question in molecular and cellular biosciences: how do interacting genomic, regulatory, and protein features self-organize into mesoscale assemblies that produce emergent cell states and drug responses?

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This project is organized around four interlocking scientific questions. First, what mesoscale regulatory assemblies recur across cancer cell lines with focal amplification or ecDNA? We define a regulatory assembly as a connected set of amplified segments, genes, enhancers, transcription factor motifs, chromatin contacts, expressed proteins, pathway components, and single-cell states whose joint configuration is associated with altered expression or dependency. The working hypothesis is that amplified oncogenes do not act as isolated dosage events. Instead, their phenotypic effects depend on the regulatory context created by enhancer availability, 3D proximity, chromatin accessibility, and variant-modified protein interactions. We expect assemblies to be partly lineage-specific, reflecting developmental enhancer landscapes, and partly convergent, reflecting recurrent selection for drug-tolerant programs. Second, can these assemblies explain drug sensitivity, resistance, or adaptive plasticity better than conventional single-modality features? We hypothesize that multimodal mesoscale features will improve prediction of response to targeted therapies, epigenetic drugs, kinase inhibitors, DNA damage agents, and immunomodulatory pathway perturbations relative to models based only on mutations, expression, or copy number. We further hypothesize that certain drugs will be associated with distinct assembly classes: for example, amplified enhancer-rich oncogene neighborhoods may predict sensitivity to transcriptional or chromatin regulators, whereas assemblies involving altered signaling proteins may predict kinase dependency or pathway bypass. Third, do predicted regulatory assemblies correspond to heterogeneous single-cell states rather than simple bulk-average shifts? Bulk profiles can obscure rare or transient states that seed tolerance. We hypothesize that cell lines with ecDNA or complex focal amplification will show increased single-cell variance, multimodal oncogene expression, and subpopulations enriched for stress-response, epithelial-mesenchymal, stem-like, metabolic, or cell-cycle programs. We will test whether graph-inferred assemblies map onto these subpopulations using public single-cell and Perturb-seq data. A key prediction is that some assemblies will manifest as variable gene dosage and enhancer activity across cells, producing fractional populations that are disproportionately associated with resistance signatures. Fourth, how can coding variant effects be separated from regulatory dosage effects in amplified and dependency-associated genes? Many amplified loci contain both regulatory alterations and protein-altering variants. We hypothesize that integrating protein sequence, structural, conservation, and interaction annotations will clarify whether drug response is driven by increased abundance, altered activity, modified binding interfaces, or combinations of these mechanisms. This distinction is essential for interpreting dependencies and designing transferable models across lineages. Together, these questions test the central hypothesis that drug-tolerant cancer cell states emerge from interactions among genome architecture, regulatory rewiring, dosage variation, and protein function. The hypotheses are falsifiable through held-out prediction, cross-lineage replication, ablation of data layers, comparison to baseline models, and assessment of whether inferred assemblies reproduce known biology while also nominating new mechanisms. The project intentionally uses only publicly available data and prioritizes questions that require synthesis across datasets rather than new experimental generation.

[Methods and Approach]
The working group will implement a staged synthesis plan using existing public data. In Phase 1, we will define the study universe by selecting breast, melanoma, glioblastoma, colorectal, and lung cancer cell lines with sufficient overlap among DepMap/CCLE molecular profiles, drug response, dependency screens, public chromatin or 3D genome resources, and available amplification or ecDNA annotations. We will build a transparent data inventory that records source, release version, assay type, genome build, cell line identifiers, treatment status, lineage, and quality metrics. Cell line identity will be reconciled using common identifiers and known aliases, with exclusion or flagging of ambiguous samples. All genomic coordinates will be lifted to a common reference assembly, and feature matrices will be harmonized with documented normalization choices. In Phase 2, we will construct a multilayer biological graph. Nodes will include genes, enhancers, regulatory motifs, copy-number segments, ecDNA or focal amplicons, structural variants, proteins, metabolites, pathways, drugs, and single-cell states. Edges will represent chromatin contacts, enhancer-gene links, motif-to-factor relationships, gene-protein mappings, pathway membership, drug-target annotations, variant effects, co-expression, co-dependency, and shared amplicon membership. Enhancer-gene assignments will combine promoter capture, Hi-C, Micro-C, accessibility-expression correlation, distance-aware priors, and lineage-matched ENCODE or 4DN evidence. Amplicon and ecDNA calls will be mapped to genes and regulatory elements, and confidence labels will capture uncertainty. Protein-coding variants will be annotated using public structure, domain, conservation, interaction, and sequence-function resources. In Phase 3, we will develop interpretable multimodal learning models. Supervised models will predict drug sensitivity and CRISPR dependency where labels are available. Semi-supervised methods will propagate information across graph neighborhoods for sparsely labeled drugs and lineages. Positive-unlabeled learning will be used for ecDNA and drug-tolerant phenotypes because absence of annotation often reflects missing measurement rather than true absence. Graph neural networks, regularized generalized linear models, random forests, matrix factorization, and calibrated ensemble methods will be compared against baseline mutation-only, expression-only, and copy-number-only predictors. Interpretability will be emphasized through feature attribution, subgraph extraction, stability selection, and biological enrichment analysis. In Phase 4, we will test emergence at the single-cell level. Public scRNA-seq and Perturb-seq datasets will be reprocessed or imported from standardized objects, batch-corrected where appropriate, and analyzed for expression heterogeneity, rare states, pathway activity, inferred copy-number variation, and perturbation-responsive programs. Predicted assemblies will be evaluated for association with single-cell variance, state transitions, and drug-response signatures. Rigor will be supported through pre-specified train-test splits by lineage and drug class, external validation in TCGA or PCAWG tumor data where appropriate, sensitivity analyses for batch effects, negative-control features, data-layer ablation, and reproducible workflow execution.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The project will produce four primary deliverables. First, we will release an open atlas of inferred mesoscale regulatory assemblies across well-profiled cancer cell lines. The atlas will link amplified regions, ecDNA annotations, enhancer landscapes, 3D contacts, affected genes, coding variants, protein and pathway features, and observed single-cell states. Each assembly will include evidence scores, lineage context, uncertainty estimates, and associated drug or dependency phenotypes. Second, we will deliver benchmark datasets for multimodal prediction of emergent cancer cell phenotypes. These benchmarks will include standardized feature matrices, documented labels, baseline models, and recommended evaluation splits, enabling the broader community to compare methods fairly. Third, we will provide interpretable predictive models that identify which combinations of genome architecture, regulatory dosage, protein function, and cellular state best explain sensitivity or resistance across drug classes. Fourth, we will publish reusable workflows and tutorials for integrating pharmacogenomic, single-cell, 3D genome, protein annotation, and cancer genomics data. The scientific impact will be to shift analysis of cancer drug response from isolated biomarkers toward mesoscale organization. By identifying regulatory assemblies that are reproducible across public resources, the project will clarify when focal amplification or ecDNA acts through gene dosage alone and when its effects depend on enhancer capture, chromatin topology, or variant-altered protein function. The work will also provide a general synthesis strategy for studying emergence in molecular and cellular systems: define interacting components, represent them in a cross-scale graph, test whether their collective organization predicts phenotypes beyond individual parts, and validate predictions using independent public data. The translational relevance is substantial but appropriately indirect. The project will not make clinical claims; instead, it will generate mechanistic hypotheses, data resources, and computational tools that can guide future experimental studies and improve interpretation of public cancer models.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
The working group will operate under open, team-based, and reproducible science principles from project initiation. All input datasets will be public, and the data inventory will record accession numbers, download dates, licenses, processing decisions, quality filters, and provenance. Derived datasets that can be redistributed will be deposited in public repositories with persistent identifiers. When source licenses restrict redistribution, we will provide scripts, manifests, checksums, and instructions that allow users to reconstruct the processed data from the original public resources. Code will be developed in a public version-controlled repository using issue tracking, pull requests, code review, and tagged releases. Workflows will be implemented with portable workflow systems and containerized software environments to ensure execution across NCEMS, institutional, and cloud computing platforms. Each major analysis will include executable notebooks or scripts, synthetic test data where needed, and continuous-integration checks for key functions. Model training and evaluation will be documented with fixed random seeds, versioned train-test splits, performance metrics, and complete hyperparameter records. We will maintain a living analysis plan that distinguishes pre-specified analyses from exploratory work. Reproducibility reviews will be assigned to working group members who did not conduct the original analysis, with trainees participating as reviewers and maintainers. Open tutorials will introduce harmonization of public cancer multi-omics data, construction of biological knowledge graphs, positive-unlabeled learning for incomplete biological labels, and interpretation of multimodal graph models. Manuscripts, preprints, data descriptors, and software documentation will be released under permissive terms whenever possible. Community engagement will include public webinars, office hours, and mechanisms for external users to report errors, suggest datasets, or contribute improvements. These practices align directly with NCEMS goals of community-scale synthesis, transparent reuse of public data, training of data-savvy scientists, and durable resources that outlast the working group.

[Budget and Resources]
The requested NCEMS support is essential because the project requires coordinated synthesis across multiple data ecosystems, computational methods, and biological domains rather than isolated analysis by one laboratory. Funds and Center resources will be organized around six categories. First, working group meetings will support two in-person synthesis workshops and regular virtual meetings. The first workshop will finalize the data inventory, harmonization standards, modeling plan, trainee roles, and governance structure. The second will focus on model interpretation, reproducibility review, manuscript preparation, and community release. Second, trainee participation will be supported through travel, stipends, and protected time for graduate students and postdoctoral researchers to join cross-institutional data-analysis sprints. Trainees will rotate through biological curation, workflow engineering, model benchmarking, and open tutorial development. Third, computational resources will support storage, standardized reprocessing of public single-cell and 3D genome data where needed, graph construction, model training, and benchmark evaluation. The project will use NCEMS computing infrastructure where available and cloud resources only for analyses that require scalable parallel execution. Fourth, software and data engineering support will be needed to build reliable pipelines, metadata schemas, containerized environments, and public releases. Fifth, open-science dissemination will support repository hosting, documentation, webinar production, and long-term archiving of derived resources with persistent identifiers. Sixth, coordination support will help manage meetings, task tracking, data-use documentation, and community communication. No funds will be used to generate new experimental data, purchase sequencing, run assays, or create non-public datasets. The principal resources are existing public data, complementary expertise in cancer systems biology, 3D genome organization, single-cell genomics, machine learning, protein variant interpretation, and open software development, and NCEMS infrastructure for collaborative synthesis. This budget structure directly advances the RFP goals by enabling multidisciplinary integration, trainee training, reproducible workflows, and public products that exceed the capacity of any single laboratory or pre-existing collaboration.

title: A Public Multimodal Atlas for Predicting Cytoskeletal Control of Cellular Architecture and Ciliary State

abstract_text:
A central unresolved problem in molecular and cellular biosciences is how local cytoskeletal interactions generate cell-scale architectural outcomes such as organelle positioning, polarized surface domains, and the presence, length, or loss of cilia and flagella. These outcomes are emergent: they cannot be inferred from any single filament, motor, or organelle, but arise from mesoscale organization across actin, microtubules, septins, centrioles, membranes, and transport pathways. We propose a community-scale synthesis project that will integrate publicly available whole-cell imaging, ciliary and flagellar imaging, cytoskeletal perturbation datasets, and biophysical simulation outputs to determine whether shared quantitative rules link cytoskeletal organization to cellular architecture across organisms and imaging modalities.

The working group will build an open, analysis-ready atlas from public repositories including the BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, EMPIAR, Cell Image Library, Allen Cell Collection, and published soft X-ray tomography, fluorescence, electron microscopy, and live-cell imaging datasets. We will include mammalian cells with primary cilia or centrosome-associated cytoskeletal structures, Chlamydomonas and related flagellated systems, and non-ciliated model systems such as yeast or dividing animal cells where cytoskeletal networks produce well-defined cellular-scale structures. Rather than treating these systems as separate case studies, we will represent them through common mesoscale features: filament-network anisotropy, cortical versus internal organization, organelle volumes and curvatures, basal body or centrosome position, membrane protrusion geometry, and time-dependent structural transitions.

The project will develop interoperable workflows for segmentation transfer, morphometric feature extraction, and cross-modal comparison. Deep learning models trained on curated volumetric datasets will be adapted to less annotated public images using transfer learning and human-in-the-loop validation. Extracted cellular and subcellular geometries will be represented as meshes, graphs, and time series. We will use optimal-transport-based methods to compare shapes and dynamics across different dimensionalities, sampling rates, and imaging modalities, enabling principled integration of static 3D cellular anatomy with live cytoskeletal dynamics. Agent-based and continuum simulations of actin, microtubule, and motor-driven organization will be incorporated as synthetic reference data, allowing us to ask which physical mechanisms reproduce observed regions of cellular morphospace.

The primary scientific question is whether ciliary state and broader cellular architecture can be predicted from mesoscale cytoskeletal organization. Specifically, we will test whether cells occupy a small number of recurrent architectural regimes defined by cytoskeletal geometry, organelle packing, and centrosome or basal body context; whether transitions among these regimes correspond to events such as ciliogenesis, ciliary shortening, deciliation, cytokinetic ring formation, or large-scale organelle remodeling; and whether perturbations of motors, severing proteins, or cytoskeletal regulators move cells through this shared morphodynamic landscape in predictable ways.

This project requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory can curate, harmonize, and analyze the breadth of public imaging and simulation resources needed to compare mesoscale organization across cell types, organisms, and modalities. The working group will bring together cell biologists, computational modelers, imaging scientists, data curators, applied mathematicians, and trainees. All curated metadata, segmentation workflows, morphometric features, simulation interfaces, and analysis notebooks will be released openly. The outcome will be both a reusable public resource for cell anatomy synthesis and a mechanistic framework for explaining how cytoskeletal organization gives rise to emergent cellular structures.

The working group will bring together cell biologists, computational modelers, imaging scientists, data curators, applied mathematicians, and trainees. All curated metadata, segmentation workflows, morphometric features, simulation interfaces, and analysis notebooks will be released openly. The outcome will be both a reusable public resource for cell anatomy synthesis and a mechanistic framework for explaining how cytoskeletal organization gives rise to emergent cellular structures.

[Background and Significance]
Cells acquire architecture through interactions among many molecular components that are individually well studied but collectively difficult to predict. Actin networks, microtubules, septins, molecular motors, membrane trafficking pathways, centrioles, basal bodies, and organelles interact at the mesoscale to produce cell-scale outcomes: organelle placement, cell polarity, membrane protrusions, contractile rings, and the presence, length, maintenance, or loss of cilia and flagella. These outcomes are emergent because they depend on spatial organization, mechanical coupling, transport, and dynamic feedback across scales rather than on the behavior of any single molecule. Understanding these relationships is a core challenge for molecular and cellular biosciences and directly matches the NCEMS goal of synthesizing public data to discover principles of emergence at the scale between biomolecules and organelles.

Cilia and flagella provide a powerful entry point into this problem. Their assembly and disassembly require coordination between microtubules, membrane domains, basal bodies, cytoplasmic transport, and the broader cytoskeleton. Mammalian primary cilia can appear, elongate, shorten, or be lost through rapid shedding, while motile flagella in unicellular organisms maintain length through transport and tubulin availability. Yet ciliary state is also embedded in whole-cell architecture: centrosome position, cortical organization, organelle crowding, actin structure, and membrane geometry may determine whether a cilium can form or persist. Similar principles may govern non-ciliary systems, including cytokinetic ring formation, actomyosin network reorganization, and organelle remodeling in yeast and animal cells. A synthesis spanning these systems can reveal whether different cellular structures occupy shared morphodynamic regimes.

The opportunity is timely because public imaging resources now contain diverse data suitable for cross-system synthesis. Whole-cell soft X-ray tomography, fluorescence microscopy, electron microscopy, live-cell imaging, and curated cell atlases provide images of cellular anatomy, cytoskeletal organization, organelle morphology, and dynamic transitions. Public repositories such as the BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, EMPIAR, Cell Image Library, and Allen Cell Collection include datasets that were originally generated for separate purposes but can be harmonized around common features. In parallel, public or reproducible biophysical simulations of actin, microtubules, motors, and continuum cell mechanics provide synthetic reference systems for testing mechanistic explanations.

Despite this potential, current analyses remain fragmented by organism, imaging modality, annotation practice, and disciplinary community. Individual laboratories generally lack the capacity to curate many public datasets, standardize metadata, transfer segmentation models across modalities, compare shapes and time series on common mathematical grounds, and connect observations with mechanistic simulations. NCEMS support is therefore essential. This working group will integrate cell biology, imaging science, applied mathematics, machine learning, and biophysical modeling to build a public atlas and test whether cytoskeletal mesoscale organization predicts emergent cellular architecture and ciliary state.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
The central research question is whether cell-scale architecture and ciliary state can be predicted from mesoscale cytoskeletal organization using only existing public data. We will address this question through three linked aims that connect biological mechanism, quantitative representation, and cross-modal synthesis.

Aim 1 asks whether diverse cells occupy a limited set of recurrent architectural regimes. We will test the hypothesis that cells from mammalian, algal, yeast, and dividing animal systems can be mapped into a shared morphospace defined by measurable features including actin and microtubule anisotropy, cortical enrichment, centrosome or basal body position, cell shape, membrane protrusion geometry, organelle volumes, organelle curvature, and intracellular packing. We predict that this morphospace will not be random or organism-specific but will contain recurrent states corresponding to polarized ciliated cells, non-ciliated proliferative cells, compact flagellated cells, remodeling cells, and contractile or cytokinetic cells. This hypothesis treats cellular anatomy as a set of mesoscale patterns that can be compared across biological systems despite differences in molecular details.

Aim 2 asks whether transitions among architectural regimes correspond to known dynamic cellular events. We will test the hypothesis that ciliogenesis, ciliary shortening, whole-cilium shedding, flagellar length changes, cytokinetic ring assembly, and organelle remodeling appear as trajectories through the shared morphospace. Public live-cell imaging and time-resolved perturbation datasets will be represented as time series of shape, cytoskeletal, and organelle features. We predict that different biological events will share transition motifs, such as movement of the centrosome or basal body toward a specialized surface domain, reorganization of cortical actin, redistribution of microtubule orientation, and changes in organelle crowding. We further predict that transition speed and direction will distinguish gradual remodeling from rapid state changes such as deciliation.

Aim 3 asks whether perturbations of cytoskeletal regulators move cells through the morphospace in predictable directions. We will test the hypothesis that motors, severing enzymes, actin regulators, tubulin transport factors, and cell-cycle regulators produce characteristic displacements in cellular architecture. For example, perturbations that alter microtubule severing or tubulin availability may shift cells toward ciliary shortening or shedding states, whereas altered motor activity may shift actin networks between isotropic, bundled, contractile, or polarized configurations. We will compare perturbation signatures across organisms to identify conserved and system-specific responses.

A final integrative question asks which physical mechanisms are sufficient to generate observed architectural regimes. We will use agent-based and continuum simulations as synthetic data to test whether local rules for filament growth, motor binding, severing, transport, and mechanical coupling reproduce observed regions of the empirical morphospace. We hypothesize that a small number of physical control parameters, including filament turnover, motor processivity, cortical anchoring, and transport capacity, can explain many observed transitions. Support for these hypotheses would establish a predictive framework linking molecular-scale cytoskeletal regulation to emergent cellular organization.

[Methods and Approach]
This project will be conducted as a synthesis working group using only existing publicly available data and reusable computational outputs. No new experimental data will be generated. The work will proceed in five coordinated phases.

Phase 1 will identify, prioritize, and curate public datasets. We will survey repositories including the BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, EMPIAR, Cell Image Library, Allen Cell Collection, and published supplementary archives. Candidate datasets will include volumetric soft X-ray tomography of whole cells, fluorescence imaging of cytoskeletal and organelle markers, electron microscopy of cilia, centrioles, and flagella, live-cell imaging of ciliary dynamics, and perturbation studies involving cytoskeletal motors, severing proteins, actin regulators, tubulin transport, or cell-cycle state. Inclusion criteria will require public accessibility, sufficient metadata for biological interpretation, and image quality adequate for quantitative analysis. Each dataset will be annotated with organism, cell type, imaging modality, resolution, labels, perturbation, time sampling, licensing, and provenance.

Phase 2 will create interoperable segmentation and feature-extraction workflows. Existing annotations and segmentations will be reused when available. For unsegmented images, we will adapt public deep learning models through transfer learning, foundation model prompting, and human-in-the-loop validation by domain experts. Segmentation targets will include cell boundaries, nuclei, organelles, cilia or flagella, centrioles or basal bodies when resolvable, membranes, and cytoskeletal structures. Quality control will use benchmark subsets, inter-rater comparison, uncertainty maps, and failure-mode documentation. Outputs will be stored as standardized masks, meshes, point clouds, skeletons, graphs, and tabular features.

Phase 3 will define a common mesoscale feature vocabulary. Static images will yield features describing cell shape, organelle number and volume, organelle curvature, spatial adjacency, polarity axes, basal body or centrosome position, cytoskeletal anisotropy, cortical enrichment, and ciliary or flagellar geometry. Live images will yield trajectories of length, position, velocity, deformation, and structural transitions. Where raw image resolution differs, we will compute features at multiple confidence levels rather than forcing unsupported measurements.

Phase 4 will integrate heterogeneous data mathematically. We will use dimensionality reduction, graph-based embeddings, and optimal-transport methods to compare shapes, meshes, graphs, and time series across modalities and sampling rates. Gromov-Wasserstein and fused optimal-transport distances will allow comparison among objects with different point densities, dimensionalities, and feature annotations. Clustering and supervised prediction will test whether cytoskeletal features predict ciliary state, organelle organization, or transition class. Cross-validation will be stratified by dataset and organism to distinguish generalizable rules from repository-specific artifacts.

Phase 5 will incorporate simulation outputs as mechanistic references. Publicly available or openly reproducible agent-based and continuum simulations of actin, microtubules, motors, and cell geometry will be converted into the same feature space as empirical data. Parameter ensembles will be compared with observed morphospace regions to identify mechanisms that are sufficient, insufficient, or ambiguous. The working group will meet regularly to review curation decisions, validate biological interpretations, train trainees, and release iterative atlas versions.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The project will produce three primary outcomes. First, it will deliver an open, analysis-ready multimodal atlas of cytoskeletal organization, cell architecture, and ciliary or flagellar state assembled from public datasets. The atlas will include harmonized metadata, curated links to original repositories, standardized segmentations where feasible, morphometric feature tables, meshes, graphs, time-series representations, and documented uncertainty. abstract_original:
A central unresolved problem in molecular and cellular biosciences is how local cytoskeletal interactions generate cell-scale architectural outcomes such as organelle positioning, polarized surface domains, and the presence, length, or loss of cilia and flagella. These outcomes are emergent: they cannot be inferred from any single filament, motor, or organelle, but arise from mesoscale organization across actin, microtubules, septins, centrioles, membranes, and transport pathways. We propose a community-scale synthesis project that will integrate publicly available whole-cell imaging, ciliary and flagellar imaging, cytoskeletal perturbation datasets, and biophysical simulation outputs to determine whether shared quantitative rules link cytoskeletal organization to cellular architecture across organisms and imaging modalities.

The working group will build an open, analysis-ready atlas from public repositories including the BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, EMPIAR, Cell Image Library, Allen Cell Collection, and published soft X-ray tomography, fluorescence, electron microscopy, and live-cell imaging datasets. We will include mammalian cells with primary cilia or centrosome-associated cytoskeletal structures, Chlamydomonas and related flagellated systems, and non-ciliated model systems such as yeast or dividing animal cells where cytoskeletal networks produce well-defined cellular-scale structures. Rather than treating these systems as separate case studies, we will represent them through common mesoscale features: filament-network anisotropy, cortical versus internal organization, organelle volumes and curvatures, basal body or centrosome position, membrane protrusion geometry, and time-dependent structural transitions.

The project will develop interoperable workflows for segmentation transfer, morphometric feature extraction, and cross-modal comparison. Deep learning models trained on curated volumetric datasets will be adapted to less annotated public images using transfer learning and human-in-the-loop validation. Extracted cellular and subcellular geometries will be represented as meshes, graphs, and time series. We will use optimal-transport-based methods to compare shapes and dynamics across different dimensionalities, sampling rates, and imaging modalities, enabling principled integration of static 3D cellular anatomy with live cytoskeletal dynamics. Agent-based and continuum simulations of actin, microtubule, and motor-driven organization will be incorporated as synthetic reference data, allowing us to ask which physical mechanisms reproduce observed regions of cellular morphospace.

The primary scientific question is whether ciliary state and broader cellular architecture can be predicted from mesoscale cytoskeletal organization. Specifically, we will test whether cells occupy a small number of recurrent architectural regimes defined by cytoskeletal geometry, organelle packing, and centrosome or basal body context; whether transitions among these regimes correspond to events such as ciliogenesis, ciliary shortening, deciliation, cytokinetic ring formation, or large-scale organelle remodeling; and whether perturbations of motors, severing proteins, or cytoskeletal regulators move cells through this shared morphodynamic landscape in predictable ways.

This project requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory can curate, harmonize, and analyze the breadth of public imaging and simulation resources needed to compare mesoscale organization across cell types, organisms, and modalities. The working group will bring together cell biologists, computational modelers, imaging scientists, data curators, applied mathematicians, and trainees. All curated metadata, segmentation workflows, morphometric features, simulation interfaces, and analysis notebooks will be released openly. The outcome will be both a reusable public resource for cell anatomy synthesis and a mechanistic framework for explaining how cytoskeletal organization gives rise to emergent cellular structures.

abstract_text:
Transposable elements (TEs) have dispersed millions of potential transcription factor binding sites across mammalian genomes, yet only a minority become functional regulatory elements in any given cell type. A central unresolved question is whether TE-derived regulatory activity emerges primarily from individual insertions with favorable sequence features, or from collective mesoscale organization in which families of related repeats create dense, chromatin-compatible neighborhoods that recruit transcription factors, nucleosomes, cofactors, and 3D genome contacts in a coordinated manner. This working group will synthesize public epigenomic, genomic, and chromatin conformation data to test the hypothesis that TE families generate emergent regulatory properties when their sequence grammars, chromatin states, and spatial clustering cross cell-type-specific thresholds.

The project will integrate existing datasets from ENCODE, Roadmap Epigenomics, Cistrome, GEO/SRA, 4D Nucleome, FANTOM, and public single-cell atlases, focusing initially on human and mouse hematopoietic and immune differentiation because these systems provide unusually rich transcription factor ChIP-seq, chromatin accessibility, histone modification, transcriptomic, and 3D genome data. We will annotate TE insertions by family, age, conservation, genomic context, motif content, and orthology, then link them to matched chromatin accessibility, nuclease footprints, transcription factor occupancy, histone states, enhancer RNAs, promoter contacts, and nearby gene expression. Rather than treating repeats as nuisance sequence, the analysis will ask when groups of related insertions produce regulatory behavior that cannot be predicted by isolated motif matches alone.

[Abstract]

The working group will develop a synthesis framework combining epigenome segmentation, high-resolution binding-site modeling, motif grammar analysis, graph-based chromatin neighborhood detection, and domain-adaptive neural networks that explicitly account for species-specific repeat landscapes. These models will separate three contributions to TE regulatory activity: intrinsic sequence affinity, local chromatin permissiveness, and mesoscale neighborhood effects such as enhancer clustering, contact frequency, and co-occupancy by cooperative transcription factors. Cross-species modeling will determine whether similar regulatory outcomes arise through shared ancestral insertions, lineage-specific TE expansions, or convergent sequence grammars embedded in distinct repeat families.

The expected outcome is an open atlas of TE-associated regulatory neighborhoods across cell states and species, along with predictive models that identify which repeat families are poised to seed new enhancers, insulators, or lineage-specific transcriptional programs. This synthesis will directly address emergence by defining how distributed molecular features—motifs, repeat copy number, chromatin accessibility, nucleosome positioning, and 3D proximity—combine to create higher-order regulatory properties at the mesoscale. The project requires NCEMS-scale coordination because no single lab can uniformly integrate the breadth of public datasets, repeat annotations, machine learning models, chromatin-state maps, and biological expertise needed to compare regulatory emergence across species and cell types. All workflows, harmonized metadata, model outputs, and training materials will be released openly through reproducible computational notebooks and containerized pipelines, with graduate students and postdoctoral researchers trained in collaborative genomic data synthesis, interpretable AI, and open-science practices.

[Background and Significance]
Transposable elements are a major source of regulatory sequence innovation in mammalian genomes. They carry transcription factor motifs, nucleosome-positioning signals, splice and polyadenylation signals, noncoding RNA promoters, and sequence features that can be co-opted into enhancers, promoters, insulators, and repressive chromatin domains. Yet the regulatory potential of TEs is highly conditional. Most copies of a repeat family remain inactive in most cell states, while a subset becomes accessible, bound by transcription factors, marked by enhancer-associated histone modifications, transcribed as enhancer RNAs, or connected to promoters through chromatin looping. This discrepancy creates a fundamental problem in molecular and cellular biology: how do widely dispersed molecular sequence features become integrated into cell-type-specific regulatory systems with emergent properties that exceed the contribution of any single insertion? Current models often emphasize either intrinsic sequence affinity, such as the presence of a high-scoring transcription factor motif, or local chromatin permissiveness, such as accessibility or histone modification status. These explanations are necessary but incomplete. Regulatory activity frequently occurs in clusters of enhancers, super-enhancer-like domains, topologically associated regions, and lineage-specific chromatin neighborhoods where transcription factors, cofactors, nucleosomes, RNA polymerase, and 3D contacts interact over tens to hundreds of kilobases. TE families are uniquely suited to create such mesoscale organization because they amplify related sequence grammars throughout the genome, sometimes in lineage-specific bursts, and can distribute coordinated binding potential across regulatory landscapes. This proposal addresses an emergence question at the scale emphasized by NCEMS: when do repeated molecular components give rise to new regulatory properties at the mesoscale between individual DNA motifs and whole-cell phenotypes? Hematopoietic and immune differentiation provide an ideal initial system. Human and mouse blood lineages are among the best-characterized mammalian cellular systems, with extensive public data for transcription factor occupancy, chromatin accessibility, histone modifications, gene expression, enhancer transcription, nucleosome organization, and chromatin conformation across stem, progenitor, and differentiated states. These lineages also depend on combinatorial transcription factor programs involving factors such as GATA, PU.1, CTCF, RUNX, ETS, IRF, NF-kB, STAT, and AP-1, many of which interact with TE-derived motifs. Public repositories now contain sufficient data to move beyond single-dataset analyses and perform a community-scale synthesis across assays, species, repeat families, and cell states. However, the needed integration is beyond the scope of a typical individual laboratory. It requires expertise in repeat annotation, transcription factor biology, epigenome segmentation, high-resolution binding models, chromatin conformation analysis, machine learning, comparative genomics, and open scientific infrastructure. By synthesizing only existing public data, the working group will transform fragmented resources into a coherent framework for understanding how TE-derived regulatory grammar contributes to emergent cell-state-specific gene regulation. The resulting atlas and models will clarify how evolutionary genome expansion is translated into cellular regulatory innovation.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This working group will pursue three linked research questions. First, what distinguishes TE insertions that become active regulatory elements from inactive copies of the same family in matched cell states? We hypothesize that active insertions are not explained solely by the strongest individual motif matches. Instead, activity reflects an interaction among intrinsic sequence grammar, local chromatin accessibility, neighboring regulatory features, and lineage-specific transcription factor availability. Within a repeat family, we expect active copies to show enriched motif syntax, including motif combinations, spacing, orientation, and predicted affinity profiles that support cooperative binding by cell-state-relevant transcription factors. However, we also expect many inactive copies to contain apparently favorable motifs, demonstrating that sequence is necessary but not sufficient. Second, do related TE insertions form emergent regulatory neighborhoods whose collective behavior cannot be predicted from isolated insertions? We hypothesize that TE families generate mesoscale regulatory properties when multiple copies or TE-derived regulatory elements occur within chromatin-compatible genomic regions, share compatible transcription factor grammar, and participate in enhancer clustering or promoter contacts. These neighborhoods may recruit combinations of transcription factors, cofactors, nucleosomes, architectural proteins, and RNA polymerase in ways that produce nonlinear regulatory outcomes, including enhanced occupancy, stronger enhancer RNA signal, increased contact frequency with target promoters, or coordinated activation of nearby lineage genes. We will test whether models that include neighborhood-level features outperform models based only on single-insertion sequence and local chromatin measurements. A positive result would provide operational evidence for emergence: regulatory behavior arising from the organization of multiple components rather than from any component alone. Third, how conserved or convergent are TE-derived regulatory neighborhoods across human and mouse hematopoietic and immune cell states? We hypothesize that similar regulatory outcomes arise through three mechanisms: direct conservation of ancestral insertions, lineage-specific expansion of distinct repeat families that carry comparable motif grammars, and convergent recruitment of different repeat sequences into analogous chromatin contexts. Because repeat landscapes differ substantially between species, cross-species prediction requires methods that separate conserved regulatory logic from species-specific sequence distributions. We expect that domain-adaptive models will identify both shared transcription factor grammars and species-specific repeat effects that confound simpler comparative analyses. The project will also examine whether TE-derived neighborhoods are associated with particular regulatory classes. Some families may preferentially seed enhancers for inflammatory or differentiation-responsive programs; others may contribute CTCF-associated boundary or loop-anchor activity; others may be linked to repressive chromatin transitions. These hypotheses will be evaluated with explicit, falsifiable statistical criteria: predictive improvement from neighborhood features, enrichment of TE families in reproducible chromatin states, evidence of coordinated accessibility or occupancy across nearby elements, association with promoter contacts and gene expression, and cross-species transferability of regulatory predictions. Together, the questions define a synthesis agenda that connects molecular grammar, chromatin state, 3D organization, and cell identity.

[Methods and Approach]
The project will use only publicly available data and will proceed through coordinated synthesis tasks. Task 1 will create a harmonized catalog of TE insertions in human and mouse genomes. We will combine RepeatMasker annotations, Dfam and Repbase-derived family classifications where licensing permits, genome build conversion resources, synteny maps, age estimates based on divergence from consensus, orthology information, conservation scores, genomic context, proximity to genes, and overlap with annotated promoters, enhancers, and insulators. Each insertion will be represented by family, subfamily, length, truncation status, orientation, age proxy, sequence quality, mappability, and local genomic features. Task 2 will assemble matched public functional genomics data across hematopoietic and immune cell states from ENCODE, Roadmap Epigenomics, Cistrome, GEO, SRA, 4D Nucleome, FANTOM, Human Cell Atlas-related resources, and mouse single-cell atlases. We will prioritize datasets with clear metadata, biological replicates, quality metrics, and compatible cell type definitions. Assays will include ChIP-seq and ChIP-exo where available for transcription factors and histone marks, ATAC-seq, DNase-seq, MNase-seq or related nucleosome maps, RNA-seq, CAGE and enhancer RNA resources, Hi-C, Micro-C, promoter capture Hi-C, ChIA-PET, HiChIP, and single-cell chromatin accessibility or expression datasets. Existing processed data will be used when quality is sufficient; otherwise public raw reads will be uniformly reprocessed with documented pipelines. Task 3 will define regulatory features at individual TE insertions. We will compute motif content with curated transcription factor motif collections, model motif grammar through spacing and orientation features, infer high-resolution occupancy from ChIP and footprinting data where feasible, assign chromatin states using segmentation approaches across accessibility and histone marks, and link insertions to expression or enhancer activity using proximity, promoter contacts, and activity-by-contact models. We will explicitly account for mappability and repeat-induced alignment bias. Task 4 will detect mesoscale regulatory neighborhoods. We will construct cell-state-specific graphs in which nodes represent TE insertions and non-TE regulatory elements, and edges represent genomic distance, shared chromatin state, co-accessibility, contact frequency, promoter linkage, transcription factor co-occupancy, or membership in topological domains. Community detection, graph neural features, and statistical null models preserving TE density, GC content, mappability, and gene proximity will identify neighborhoods enriched for coordinated regulatory activity. Task 5 will build predictive and explanatory models. Baseline models will use isolated sequence features; expanded models will add local chromatin; full models will add neighborhood features. Interpretable machine learning, including regularized models, gradient-boosted trees, convolutional sequence models, and domain-adaptive neural networks, will quantify feature contributions and cross-species transfer. Rigorous validation will include held-out chromosomes, held-out cell types, held-out TE families, replicate consistency, permutation tests, and comparison against matched non-TE regulatory elements. The working group will meet in focused sprints to resolve metadata, modeling, biological interpretation, and dissemination.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The primary outcome will be an open atlas of TE-associated regulatory neighborhoods across human and mouse hematopoietic and immune cell states. The atlas will provide harmonized annotations of TE insertions, repeat family enrichments, predicted transcription factor grammar, chromatin states, occupancy evidence, enhancer or insulator classifications, promoter contacts, and links to gene expression programs. It will enable researchers to query which repeat families are associated with particular cell states, transcription factor combinations, chromatin environments, and 3D regulatory contexts. The second outcome will be a set of predictive models that distinguish inactive, locally active, and neighborhood-associated TE insertions. These models will quantify how much regulatory activity is attributable to intrinsic sequence affinity, local chromatin permissiveness, and mesoscale organization. This framework will provide a practical definition of emergent regulatory behavior and a reusable strategy for studying other repetitive, modular, or clustered genomic components. The third outcome will be comparative insight into mammalian regulatory evolution. By modeling human and mouse jointly, the project will identify cases in which conserved regulatory outputs arise from shared ancestral insertions, lineage-specific repeat expansions, or convergent motif grammars embedded in different TE families. The broader impact is conceptual and methodological. The project will shift TEs from being treated primarily as technical complications to being analyzed as distributed molecular components that may organize cell-state-specific regulatory systems. It will provide community resources for repeat-aware epigenomics, promote reproducible AI-assisted synthesis, and train trainees to work across genomics, chromatin biology, data engineering, and evolutionary biology. These outcomes align directly with NCEMS goals by using public data to address emergence at the mesoscale and by requiring a multidisciplinary working group to produce insights unavailable from isolated analyses.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
The project will follow open, reproducible, and team-based science practices from its outset. All public datasets will be tracked in a versioned metadata registry that records accession identifiers, genome builds, cell type labels, assay types, quality metrics, processing status, use restrictions, and provenance. Harmonized metadata tables, derived feature matrices, analysis code, workflow descriptions, model configurations, and documentation will be released through public repositories using persistent identifiers. When redistribution of derived data is constrained by repository or annotation licenses, we will provide scripts and checksums that allow users to recreate the resource from the original public sources. Computational workflows will be implemented using portable workflow managers and containerized software environments. Core analyses will be executable through documented notebooks and command-line pipelines, with automated tests for key steps such as interval overlap, mappability filtering, motif scoring, chromatin-state assignment, graph construction, and model evaluation. Results will be accompanied by data dictionaries, parameter files, audit logs, and benchmark reports. We will use held-out validation strategies and publish negative or ambiguous findings where they clarify limits of inference. The working group will establish community guidelines for naming regulatory neighborhoods, reporting repeat-aware quality controls, and comparing TE-derived with non-TE regulatory elements. Trainees will participate in open-science training modules covering reproducible workflow design, collaborative coding, metadata standards, ethical reuse of public data, interpretable machine learning, and responsible application of AI to genomics. Meetings will include code review sessions, documentation sprints, and cross-disciplinary tutorials so that computational and biological contributors can evaluate assumptions together. Preprints, conference materials, tutorials, and final manuscripts will point to stable releases of the atlas and software. This plan ensures that the synthesis is transparent, reusable, extensible, and valuable to the broader molecular and cellular sciences community.

[Budget and Resources]
NCEMS support is essential because the proposed work requires coordinated synthesis across many data types, species, analytical domains, and institutions rather than a narrow single-laboratory analysis. Funds will support working group meetings, trainee participation, computational infrastructure, data engineering, open-science dissemination, and cross-disciplinary training. We anticipate a two-year working group structure with three in-person synthesis meetings hosted through NCEMS and regular virtual analysis sprints between meetings. Travel funds will enable participation by investigators, postdoctoral researchers, graduate students, and invited experts in repeat biology, transcription factor modeling, chromatin conformation, hematopoiesis, comparative genomics, and machine learning. Resources will also support participation from institutions with different research capacities and from early-career scientists who bring needed technical skills. Computational costs will include cloud or high-performance computing allocations for reprocessing selected public sequencing datasets, storing harmonized intermediate files, training machine learning models, and maintaining public releases. Funds will support data management personnel or trainee effort for metadata harmonization, workflow testing, documentation, and quality control. Additional resources will be used for open-science products, including tutorial development, container registry maintenance, web-accessible atlas prototypes, and community workshops. No funds will be used to generate new experimental data, purchase laboratory reagents, or conduct new sequencing. Existing public datasets are sufficient for the central aims; the challenge is integration, quality control, interpretation, and reproducible distribution. NCEMS resources will provide the neutral collaborative environment, synthesis expertise, open-science infrastructure, and convening capacity needed to transform fragmented public datasets into a community resource. The budget is therefore directly aligned with the call: it supports multidisciplinary collaboration, public-data synthesis, training of data-savvy scientists, and development of reusable analytical strategies for understanding emergent molecular and cellular phenomena.

[Background and Significance]
Cellular behavior is organized by protein assemblies that operate between the molecular and organelle scales. Ribosomes, spliceosomes, cytoskeletal condensates, signaling scaffolds, metabolic channeling assemblies, membrane contact sites, and repair foci all illustrate a common principle: collective function can arise from many contacts that are individually weak, short lived, partially redundant, or dependent on abundance, localization, modification, and pathway state. These mesoscale assemblies are central examples of emergence in molecular and cellular biology because their properties cannot be inferred by cataloging isolated proteins or even by listing pairwise protein associations alone. Understanding how residue-level contacts combine into functional cellular architecture is therefore a fundamental and timely synthesis challenge. Public molecular data now make this challenge tractable. Crosslinking mass spectrometry provides residue-resolved proximity information by identifying pairs of amino acids that were close enough to be covalently linked in a biological sample. Unlike many interaction assays, crosslinking can capture endogenous complexes, transient contacts, heterogeneous conformations, and contacts within large assemblies. However, crosslinking data are dispersed across public repositories, produced by different chemistries and search pipelines, reported using heterogeneous confidence measures, and rarely integrated with tissue proteomics, pathway knowledge, structural models, or human variation. As a result, much of the biological value of these data remains latent. Crosslinks are commonly reduced to protein-level evidence, causing loss of the interface specificity needed to distinguish an allosteric surface from a catalytic site, a constitutive complex interface from a context-specific pathway contact, or a benign variant from a variant disrupting an assembly hub. Existing public interaction resources are indispensable but are often gene-centric. They typically represent proteins as nodes and interactions as edges, with limited ability to trace claims back to spectra, residue coordinates, proteoforms, crosslinker constraints, or sample context. Structural databases and prediction resources provide three-dimensional models, but they do not generally encode whether predicted contacts are observed in cells, in which tissues they are possible, or how pathway state and disease-associated sequence changes affect them. Human genetics resources identify variants associated with Mendelian disease, complex traits, or population diversity, but these variants are rarely evaluated in the context of residue-resolved assembly maps. This proposal addresses these gaps through a community-scale synthesis using only existing public data. It aligns directly with NCEMS priorities by integrating molecular, mesoscale, cellular, and phenotypic information to study emergent properties. The central significance is twofold. Scientifically, the project will test whether higher-order assemblies follow general rules related to interface recurrence, structural compatibility, abundance, pathway colocalization, and perturbation sensitivity. Methodologically, it will produce reusable infrastructure for transparent, uncertainty-aware reanalysis of public crosslinking datasets and for linking spectral evidence to biological conclusions. The work cannot be accomplished by one laboratory because it requires crosslinking mass spectrometry expertise, proteomics standards, structural interpretation, pathway curation, graph modeling, network biology, and genetics. NCEMS support will enable coordinated synthesis across these communities and create a public framework for interpreting mesoscale protein organization.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
The working group will address three linked scientific questions. First, when do residue-level protein contacts observed by crosslinking mass spectrometry represent components of emergent mesoscale assemblies rather than isolated binary interactions or technical coincidences? We hypothesize that assembly-associated contacts will show recurrent support across independent studies, coherent geometry when mapped to structures, enrichment within known or predicted pathway neighborhoods, and nonrandom clustering into multi-protein modules. We further hypothesize that such modules will separate into classes: stable structural complexes with many mutually compatible restraints, transient pathway intermediates with directional or reaction-specific connectivity, and condition-dependent assemblies supported by specific tissues, cellular states, or perturbation contexts. A key outcome will be a quantitative definition of crosslink-supported mesoscale modules that incorporates residue evidence, spectral confidence, structural feasibility, protein abundance, and pathway topology. Second, how does biological availability constrain which physically possible contacts are observed? Many proteins have compatible surfaces in structural models, yet only a subset of possible contacts occur in a given cellular environment. We hypothesize that tissue-specific abundance, pathway co-membership, subcellular context, and proteoform state explain a substantial fraction of observed crosslink patterns beyond structural compatibility alone. Under this hypothesis, a residue pair may be physically plausible in a model but biologically unavailable if the proteins are not co-expressed, participate in separate pathway states, or are regulated by mutually exclusive modifications. Conversely, crosslinks that violate simple static structural expectations may reveal conformational ensembles, flexible regions, mixed proteoforms, or assembly states not captured by single reference structures. This question directly probes emergence because assembly formation depends on the coordinated presence and state of many components rather than on intrinsic binding compatibility alone. Third, do disease-associated sequence variants and post-translational modifications preferentially affect residues that participate in emergent assembly hubs? We hypothesize that pathogenic variants, high-impact common variants, and regulatory modifications will be enriched at crosslink-supported interfaces that connect multiple proteins, pathways, or tissue-specific modules. Such residues may be more informative than protein-level annotations because a single protein can participate in several assemblies through distinct surfaces. A variant on one surface may disrupt a neuronal assembly while leaving a metabolic or housekeeping role intact. Similarly, phosphorylation, acetylation, ubiquitination, or other modifications near crosslinked residues may act as switches that rewire proximity relationships. We will test whether interface-level burden explains disease relevance better than gene degree, protein abundance, or membership in a known complex alone. These questions will be approached with explicit, falsifiable predictions. Recurrent assembly modules should replicate across datasets more often than degree-matched random networks. Tissue-aware models should outperform structure-only models in predicting crosslink observability. Interface-localized variant and modification signals should show stronger associations with pathway perturbation and phenotype annotations than protein-level aggregation. Negative results will also be informative: failure to detect recurrence or tissue effects would identify limitations in current public data and guide community standards for future deposition. Together, these questions define a rigorous synthesis agenda for discovering principles by which local molecular contacts generate higher-order cellular organization.

[Methods and Approach]
The project will proceed through five coordinated work packages, all using existing publicly available data. Work package 1 will assemble and audit public crosslinking mass spectrometry datasets from ProteomeXchange-associated repositories and other community repositories that provide raw spectra, search results, metadata, or published crosslink tables. We will prioritize human and human-relevant mammalian datasets, while retaining selected model-system datasets for conserved assemblies when orthology mapping is robust. Each dataset will be annotated for sample type, organism, crosslinker chemistry, enrichment method, instrument, search engine, database, reported false discovery approach, and availability of spectrum-level evidence. Universal spectrum identifiers or equivalent persistent spectral references will be assigned wherever possible so that every retained residue-pair claim can be traced to source evidence. Work package 2 will harmonize and reanalyze crosslink evidence. Where raw data and sufficient metadata are available, spectra will be processed through containerized open workflows using documented protein sequence databases, decoy strategies, peptide-spectrum match criteria, and crosslink-level error estimation. Where only processed data are available, reported identifications will be normalized to common controlled vocabularies and confidence fields, while preserving provenance and uncertainty. Crosslinks will be mapped to UniProt accessions, isoforms, sequence variants, and residue coordinates using reproducible sequence reconciliation. Ambiguous peptide mappings, paralog conflicts, missing residues, and proteoform uncertainty will be retained rather than silently discarded. The output will be confidence-scored residue-pair evidence with explicit error, provenance, and mapping status. Work package 3 will build the integrated knowledge graph. Nodes will include spectra, peptides, residues, proteins, proteoforms, crosslinks, protein complexes, pathway reactions, tissues, variants, modifications, structures, and phenotypes. Edges will encode evidence relationships, residue proximity, structural mapping, pathway participation, abundance support, genetic association, and modification annotation. Data sources will include public crosslinking datasets, UniProt, experimentally determined structures, AlphaFold models, curated protein interaction and complex resources, Reactome pathways, tissue proteome maps, post-translational modification repositories, ClinVar and other public variant resources, genome-wide association catalogs, and relevant phenotype ontologies. The graph schema will be developed with community input and will support exports in tabular, RDF-compatible, and property-graph formats. Work package 4 will perform synthesis analyses. Module detection will combine multilayer network clustering, residue-interface aggregation, structural-distance filtering, and pathway enrichment. We will compare crosslink-supported modules to known complexes, pathway reaction neighborhoods, and predicted structural assemblies. Tissue-aware observability models will use protein abundance, co-expression, pathway context, subcellular annotation, and structural compatibility to predict whether a residue-pair contact is observed in a given dataset. Variant and modification analyses will test enrichment at interface residues using matched controls for protein length, domain architecture, solvent accessibility, abundance, study intensity, and network degree. Sensitivity analyses will evaluate alternative false discovery thresholds and mapping assumptions. Work package 5 will organize collaborative data jamborees and interpretation sprints. Crosslinking specialists, proteomics informaticians, structural biologists, pathway curators, network scientists, geneticists, and trainees will jointly review benchmark cases and biological findings. No new experimental data will be generated; all outputs will arise from synthesis, reanalysis, integration, and interpretation of public data.

The primary deliverable will be an open residue-resolved atlas of human protein assembly evidence that connects spectra to residue pairs, proteins, structures, pathways, tissues, variants, modifications, and phenotypes. The atlas will provide confidence-scored crosslink tables, provenance-rich metadata, structural mappings, tissue-aware context fields, and graph exports that can be queried by the community. It will transform public crosslinking data from a dispersed collection of study-specific identifications into a reusable synthesis resource for mesoscale biology. These modules will be classified as likely stable complexes, transient pathway intermediates, condition-specific assemblies, or uncertain cases requiring future investigation. The analyses will reveal whether recurring interface patterns align with pathway organization, whether tissue abundance explains assembly observability, and whether disease-associated variants and post-translational modifications concentrate at assembly hubs. The results will generate testable principles for how many local contacts combine to form emergent cellular functions. Methodologically, the project will establish practical standards for public crosslinking reanalysis, persistent spectral traceability, uncertainty-aware interaction scoring, proteoform-resolved residue mapping, and interoperable graph representation. These methods will be broadly applicable to proteomics and systems biology beyond this specific atlas. The impact for NCEMS will be a high-value synthesis project that addresses a fundamental emergent phenomenon at the mesoscale using only public data and multidisciplinary collaboration. The resource will help researchers interpret disease variants, prioritize interfaces for mechanistic studies, compare assemblies across tissues, and evaluate structural predictions in cellular context. It will also create training opportunities for data-savvy trainees who can move between mass spectrometry, structural biology, network analysis, and biological interpretation.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
The project will follow open, team-based, and reproducible science practices from inception. All code, workflow definitions, graph schemas, metadata templates, documentation, issue tracking, and analysis notebooks will be developed in public version-controlled repositories unless temporary privacy is needed for manuscript coordination. Releases will be assigned persistent identifiers through open archival services, and final datasets will be deposited in appropriate community repositories with permissive reuse licenses. The working group will publish a data management and sharing plan at project launch and update it as community feedback is incorporated. Reproducibility will be enforced through containerized workflows, pinned software versions, recorded reference databases, documented parameter files, and continuous integration tests on representative public datasets. Each crosslink assertion in the atlas will include provenance fields linking it to the original dataset, search or reanalysis workflow, confidence score, residue-mapping status, and, where possible, a persistent spectrum identifier. We will distinguish primary observations from derived inferences so users can evaluate uncertainty at the spectrum, peptide, crosslink, protein, module, and pathway levels. Open science will also shape governance. The group will adopt a contributor policy, authorship and credit guidelines, meeting notes where appropriate, and a lightweight decision process for schema changes. Trainees will receive structured instruction in FAIR data principles, proteomics standards, workflow engineering, graph analysis, and responsible biological interpretation. Tutorials, example notebooks, and recorded training materials will enable reuse by researchers who are not crosslinking specialists. Community review will be sought through public workshops, repository issues, and targeted consultation with standards and pathway-resource experts. The goal is not only to release results but to provide auditable evidence chains and reusable practices that raise the reliability of synthesis research in molecular and cellular sciences.

[Budget and Resources]
NCEMS support is essential because the project requires sustained coordination, shared computational infrastructure, cross-disciplinary meetings, trainee participation, and community curation beyond the scope of a single laboratory. Funds will be used only for synthesis activities and will not support generation of new experimental data. The largest budget category will be personnel effort for a project coordinator or data scientist, trainee participants, and partial support for workflow development, metadata harmonization, and knowledge-graph engineering. This support will ensure continuity across laboratories, repositories, and analytical domains. A second category will support collaborative working group activities, including in-person synthesis meetings at NCEMS, virtual work sessions, data jamborees, and focused interpretation sprints. Travel support will prioritize participation by early-career researchers, trainees, investigators from institutions with different research capacities, and experts whose perspectives are needed for crosslinking mass spectrometry, proteomics standards, structural modeling, pathway representation, network biology, and human genetics. Meeting time will be used for schema design, benchmark decisions, biological interpretation, training, and community feedback, not for experimental planning. A third category will cover computational resources for reanalysis of public raw files, storage of intermediate outputs, graph construction, interactive notebooks, and public web-accessible demonstrations. Where possible, workflows will use open-source tools and cloud or institutional resources compatible with NCEMS reproducibility expectations. Modest funds will support software maintenance, documentation, archival deposition, and accessibility of training materials. Existing public repositories, knowledgebases, and standards will provide the core data resources, including proteomics repositories, protein sequence resources, structural databases, pathway knowledgebases, tissue proteome maps, modification resources, and public genetic-variant catalogs. NCEMS will add value by convening the necessary expertise, providing synthesis infrastructure, promoting open science practices, and enabling trainees to learn reproducible, integrative data science in a real community-scale project.

This working group will synthesize these data to ask a central question: which combinations of microbial genetic modules and expressed proteins reproducibly give rise to emergent metabolite classes across host-associated and environmental microbiomes? We will not generate new experimental data. Instead, we will integrate public datasets from GNPS/MassIVE, MetaboLights, PRIDE, MGnify, IMG/M, NCBI SRA, and public isolate genome resources, prioritizing studies with shared samples, related environments, or compatible metadata. The project will develop an open computational framework that links three layers: (1) spectral evidence for metabolite families and diagnostic chemical substructures from untargeted MS/MS, including reusable query patterns for known and unknown molecular motifs; (2) microbial functional potential from metagenomes and isolate genomes, including gene-neighborhood, operon-like, and pathway-fragment organization rather than only single-gene annotations; and (3) protein-level evidence from public metaproteomics and proteomics datasets where available. Instead of discarding unannotated spectra or hypothetical proteins, we will create cross-modal embeddings that identify recurring associations between spectral motifs and microbial sequence modules across independent studies. All workflows, derived feature tables, models, documentation, and negative results will be released openly.
