[Background and Significance]
Microbial chemistry is a central driver of cellular physiology, host-microbe interaction, nutrient cycling, and environmental adaptation. However, many microbial chemical phenotypes are not attributable to a single enzyme, genome, or taxon. They arise when genetic modules, expressed proteins, metabolite intermediates, spatially associated cells, and ecological exchanges combine to produce higher-order biochemical outcomes. This is a classic problem of emergence in the molecular and cellular sciences: mesoscale organization between individual biomolecules and whole-cell or community phenotypes generates properties that are difficult to predict from isolated parts. Examples include multi-step biotransformations distributed across community members, chemically related metabolite families produced by variable pathway fragments, and molecular signatures that appear only when taxa with complementary functions co-occur. Public data now make it possible to study these phenomena at a scale not achievable by individual laboratories. Untargeted tandem mass spectrometry repositories contain enormous numbers of spectra from host-associated and environmental microbiomes. Public metagenomic and isolate genome resources provide information on microbial functional potential, gene neighborhoods, operon-like architectures, and evolutionary conservation. Public proteomics and metaproteomics repositories provide partial but crucial evidence about which proteins are expressed in relevant samples. Yet these resources remain under-integrated. Metabolomics data are often analyzed without genomic context; metagenomes are frequently reduced to single-gene annotations; proteomics is rarely linked to untargeted metabolite families; and unknown spectra and hypothetical proteins are commonly discarded even though they may contain the strongest signals of uncharacterized microbial chemistry. This proposal addresses a long-standing puzzle: why do similar microbiome chemical phenotypes recur across studies and environments even when the exact species composition differs? We hypothesize that recurrent chemical phenotypes are often generated by combinations of conserved gene modules, pathway fragments, and protein expression patterns that can be assembled through multiple taxonomic routes. Detecting such combinations requires synthesis across repositories, data types, and scientific communities. The project aligns directly with NCEMS priorities by using only existing public data, focusing on mesoscale emergence, integrating molecular and cellular scales, advancing analytical strategies, and requiring collaboration among mass spectrometry informatics, microbial genomics, metaproteomics, evolutionary bioinformatics, statistics, and data stewardship. NCEMS support is essential because the central barrier is not a lack of data but a lack of coordinated synthesis: harmonized metadata, reusable feature definitions, interoperable workflows, and community standards for connecting unknown chemical and genetic signals. The resulting framework will enable discovery of reproducible microbial chemical phenotypes, provide benchmark datasets for artificial intelligence methods, and train a new cohort of researchers to work across metabolomics, genomics, proteomics, and open computational science.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
The working group will address one overarching question: which combinations of microbial genetic modules and expressed proteins reproducibly give rise to emergent metabolite classes across host-associated and environmental microbiomes? We will decompose this question into four testable research questions. First, which metabolite families and diagnostic spectral motifs recur across public microbiome-associated untargeted MS/MS datasets after accounting for instrument type, acquisition mode, sample preparation, and metadata heterogeneity? We hypothesize that many recurring motifs represent conserved chemical substructures or transformation series rather than isolated annotated compounds, and that pattern-based spectral querying will recover these signals more robustly than library matching alone. Second, which microbial genomic features best predict these metabolite motifs: individual genes, gene families, gene neighborhoods, operon-like blocks, pathway fragments, taxa, or combinations of these features? We hypothesize that multi-feature representations will outperform single genes or taxonomic profiles, particularly for metabolite families produced by modular biosynthesis, microbial transformation, or distributed metabolism. Third, does protein-level evidence improve the inference of emergent chemical phenotypes? We hypothesize that public metaproteomic and proteomic datasets, although sparser than metagenomic data, will identify a high-confidence subset of associations in which genetic potential is supported by expressed enzymes, transporters, or protein complexes. Fourth, are similar chemical phenotypes generated by shared ancestry, convergent gene-block assembly, or community-level complementation among different organisms? We hypothesize that both lineage-specific and convergent routes exist, and that evolutionary reconstruction of gene neighborhoods combined with cross-study statistical modeling can distinguish these mechanisms. Emergence will be operationally defined and tested quantitatively. A metabolite feature, spectral motif, or metabolite family will be considered a candidate emergent chemical phenotype when its occurrence, abundance, or transformation pattern is predicted significantly better by combinations of genes, taxa, gene neighborhoods, or expressed proteins than by any single component alone. This definition permits explicit comparisons among additive, interactive, and hierarchical models. We will also test whether emergent predictions replicate across independent datasets, environments, and repository sources. A key hypothesis is that unknowns carry essential information. Unannotated spectra may correspond to microbial metabolites absent from reference libraries, while hypothetical proteins may represent uncharacterized enzymes or pathway components. Rather than treating these as missing data, we will represent unknown spectra through spectral motifs, neutral-loss patterns, molecular-network neighborhoods, and learned embeddings, and represent unknown genes through sequence embeddings, genomic context, co-occurrence, and evolutionary conservation. We expect recurring cross-modal associations between unknown chemical and genetic features to reveal candidate biochemical systems that would be invisible to annotation-dependent analysis. These questions are intentionally structured to produce both biological discoveries and reusable methodological advances for community-scale synthesis.

[Methods and Approach]
The project will proceed through coordinated synthesis work packages and will generate no new experimental data. Work package 1 will identify and harmonize public datasets from GNPS/MassIVE, MetaboLights, PRIDE, MGnify, IMG/M, NCBI SRA, public isolate genome collections, and related repositories. We will prioritize studies with shared samples, matched or related environments, microbiome relevance, accessible raw data, and sufficient metadata. A metadata team will map sample descriptors to common vocabularies for environment, host, body site, extraction method, instrument, acquisition parameters, sequencing strategy, and proteomics workflow. Dataset inclusion, exclusion, and quality criteria will be public and versioned. Work package 2 will derive metabolomics features. Public MS/MS data will be standardized, quality controlled, and processed into spectral features, molecular networks, and motif tables. We will use reusable query patterns for diagnostic ions, neutral losses, mass differences, and fragmentation relationships, while allowing discovery of unknown molecular motifs. Feature definitions will include confidence levels distinguishing library matches, analog matches, motif-level evidence, and unannotated recurrent spectra. Work package 3 will derive genomic and metagenomic features. Public metagenomes and isolate genomes will be annotated using reproducible pipelines, but analysis will not depend solely on reference functions. We will extract gene families, pathway fragments, predicted operon-like neighborhoods, co-localized gene blocks, mobile-context indicators, taxonomic profiles, and alignment-free sequence embeddings. Gene-block conservation and rearrangement will be evaluated across isolate genomes and metagenome-assembled genomes when public assemblies are available. Work package 4 will incorporate protein-level evidence from PRIDE and other public proteomics resources. Where matched samples exist, peptide and protein evidence will be linked directly; where only related environments exist, expression evidence will be incorporated as an orthogonal support layer with appropriate uncertainty. Work package 5 will integrate modalities and test emergence. We will construct sample-by-feature matrices and cross-modal embeddings linking spectral motifs, metabolite families, gene modules, taxa, and proteins. Statistical models will include regularized regression, hierarchical Bayesian models, mixed effects models controlling for study and technology, interaction models, and cross-validation across studies. Emergence tests will compare predictive performance of single-component models against combinatorial models and will require replication in held-out datasets. We will evaluate confounding from batch effects, compositionality, uneven sampling, and metadata sparsity through sensitivity analyses, negative controls, permutation tests, and environment-stratified validation. Work package 6 will convene expert curation sprints to review high-ranking associations, refine feature definitions, and identify candidate mechanisms. Trainees will lead focused analyses under mentorship from specialists in mass spectrometry informatics, microbial genomics, metaproteomics, statistics, and software engineering.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The project will produce four major outcomes. First, we will release a public atlas of microbial gene-module-to-metabolite associations spanning host-associated and environmental microbiomes. The atlas will rank associations by reproducibility, effect size, evidence type, support from protein data, and strength of emergence relative to single-component explanations. Second, we will identify candidate emergent chemical phenotypes: metabolite families or spectral motifs whose recurrence is best explained by combinations of microbial genes, gene neighborhoods, taxa, or expressed proteins. These candidates will include both interpretable known chemistry and unknown chemical-genetic associations suitable for future experimental follow-up by the broader community. Third, we will provide reusable analytical assets, including MassQL-style spectral query collections, gene-neighborhood search workflows, cross-modal feature tables, curated metadata mappings, and benchmark datasets for testing artificial intelligence methods in multi-omics integration. Fourth, the working group will generate community guidance for analyzing unknown spectra and hypothetical proteins as informative biological signals rather than disposable artifacts. The broader impact is to shift microbiome molecular analysis from cataloging isolated genes or metabolites toward explaining how distributed molecular components assemble into reproducible cellular and community properties. This will directly advance NCEMS goals by revealing mesoscale emergence across genetic organization, protein expression, and chemical phenotype. The project will also lower barriers for researchers who wish to reuse public metabolomics, metagenomics, and proteomics data but lack expertise across all three domains. Through trainee-led cross-training, open workflows, and collaborative synthesis meetings, the project will help develop a data-savvy workforce capable of working across molecular data types, computational methods, and biological scales.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
All activities will follow open, team-based, and reproducible science practices. The project will use only publicly available data and will maintain a versioned registry of every dataset considered, including accession identifiers, inclusion decisions, metadata completeness, quality-control outcomes, and known limitations. Workflows will be implemented with portable workflow systems and containerized software environments so that analyses can be rerun on institutional, cloud, or NCEMS-supported computing resources. Code will be developed in public repositories with issue tracking, continuous integration tests where feasible, documented releases, and archived versions with persistent identifiers. Derived feature tables, metadata mappings, spectral queries, gene-neighborhood definitions, model outputs, and benchmark splits will be released under permissive licenses consistent with source repository requirements. We will distinguish raw public data, processed intermediate data, and curated analysis products so users can trace each result back to original accessions. Reproducibility will be supported through predefined analysis plans, provenance tracking, parameter files, executable notebooks for figures and tables, and independent reruns of key analyses by trainees from different disciplinary backgrounds. Negative results will be reported, including metabolite classes or environments where no reproducible association is detected, because these outcomes are essential for benchmarking and preventing publication bias. Community engagement will include open virtual tutorials, documentation sprints, and curation workshops to refine feature definitions and metadata mappings. Authorship, contribution tracking, and data-use expectations will be established at project launch. The working group will also create training materials that introduce mass spectrometry pattern querying, microbial gene-neighborhood analysis, metaproteomics integration, and statistical tests for emergence. These materials will remain public after the award and will be designed for reuse in graduate courses, short workshops, and independent study.

[Budget and Resources]
NCEMS resources are requested to support coordination, computation, trainee participation, and community synthesis that exceed the capacity of any single laboratory. The budget will prioritize working group meetings, trainee exchanges, collaborative software development, cloud or high-performance computing time, data stewardship, and open dissemination. Funds will support two in-person synthesis meetings at NCEMS or a comparable host site, supplemented by regular virtual meetings. These meetings will bring together experts in mass spectrometry informatics, microbial genomics, metaproteomics, evolutionary bioinformatics, statistics, machine learning, metadata standards, and microbiome biology, with intentional inclusion of participants from different institution types, career stages, and geographic regions. Trainee support will include travel, short collaborative visits, and stipends for graduate students or postdoctoral researchers who lead cross-modal analysis modules, documentation, and tutorials. Computational resources are needed for large-scale spectral querying, molecular networking, metagenome and genome feature extraction, sequence embedding generation, model fitting, and repeated cross-validation across public datasets. Funds will also support data management activities, including metadata harmonization, repository deposition, persistent identifiers, and long-term documentation. No budget will be used for new experimental data generation, sample collection, sequencing, mass spectrometry acquisition, or proprietary datasets. Existing public repositories will supply all primary data. NCEMS support is uniquely appropriate because the project requires neutral convening infrastructure, shared standards, synthesis-focused project management, and cross-disciplinary training rather than conventional single-lab experimentation. The requested resources will transform fragmented public datasets into reusable community products: curated feature matrices, open workflows, benchmark datasets, and a ranked atlas of emergent microbial chemical phenotypes. Sustainability will be promoted by using established public repositories, permissive software licenses, containerized workflows, and governance practices that allow additional datasets and contributors to be added after the funded period.

abstract_original: Microbial cells and communities routinely produce chemical phenotypes that cannot be inferred from any single gene, genome, or organism in isolation. These phenotypes emerge from mesoscale organization: co-regulated gene neighborhoods, multi-enzyme pathway fragments, protein complexes, metabolite transformations, and ecological sharing of intermediates. Yet the public record contains the ingredients needed to study this emergence at scale: billions of tandem mass spectra from microbiome-associated metabolomics experiments, thousands of public metagenomes and isolate genomes, and growing proteomics repositories. This working group will synthesize these data to ask a central question: which combinations of microbial genetic modules and expressed proteins reproducibly give rise to emergent metabolite classes across host-associated and environmental microbiomes? We will not generate new experimental data. Instead, we will integrate public datasets from GNPS/MassIVE, MetaboLights, PRIDE, MGnify, IMG/M, NCBI SRA, and public isolate genome resources, prioritizing studies with shared samples, related environments, or compatible metadata. The project will develop an open computational framework that links three layers: (1) spectral evidence for metabolite families and diagnostic chemical substructures from untargeted MS/MS, including reusable query patterns for known and unknown molecular motifs; (2) microbial functional potential from metagenomes and isolate genomes, including gene-neighborhood, operon-like, and pathway-fragment organization rather than only single-gene annotations; and (3) protein-level evidence from public metaproteomics and proteomics datasets where available. The synthesis will combine mass spectrometry pattern querying, molecular networking, alignment-free sequence embeddings, gene-block evolutionary reconstruction, and multilevel statistical models that explicitly test for emergence: metabolite features whose occurrence is better predicted by combinations of genes, taxa, or gene neighborhoods than by any component alone. A key innovation is to treat unknown genes and unknown metabolites as first-class signals. Instead of discarding unannotated spectra or hypothetical proteins, we will create cross-modal embeddings that identify recurring associations between spectral motifs and microbial sequence modules across independent studies. We will then evaluate whether these associations are conserved across environments, enriched in particular microbial lineages, or repeatedly assembled through different taxonomic routes. This will distinguish lineage-specific chemistry from convergent community-level biochemical capacity. The expected outcomes are: a public atlas of microbial gene-module-to-metabolite associations; a ranked set of candidate emergent chemical phenotypes, including metabolite families associated with multi-organism or multi-module genetic configurations; reusable MassQL-style spectral queries and gene-neighborhood search workflows; and benchmark datasets for testing future AI methods in metabolomics-metagenomics integration. The working group requires NCEMS support because the problem spans multiple communities that rarely share standards: mass spectrometry informatics, microbial genomics, metaproteomics, evolutionary bioinformatics, statistics, and data stewardship. NCEMS will enable coordinated metadata harmonization, community curation of reusable feature definitions, collaborative software development, and trainee-led cross-training workshops. All workflows, derived feature tables, models, documentation, and negative results will be released openly. By synthesizing existing public data across molecular and cellular scales, this project will reveal how distributed microbial molecular components assemble into reproducible chemical properties of cells and communities.

title: A Public-Data Atlas of Collective Allosteric State Variables Linking Nuclear Receptor Ligands to Transcriptional Phenotypes

abstract_text:
Nuclear receptors provide a powerful system for understanding emergence in molecular and cellular biology: binding of chemically diverse ligands to a buried pocket produces collective conformational shifts, altered coregulator recruitment, chromatin engagement, and cell-type-specific transcriptional outcomes. Yet a long-standing puzzle remains unresolved: why do ligands with similar affinity for the same receptor often produce distinct efficacy, selectivity, and disease-relevant phenotypes? We propose a community-scale synthesis project to identify the collective allosteric state variables that connect residue-level perturbations in nuclear receptor ligand-binding domains to mesoscale receptor-coregulator-DNA assemblies and downstream transcriptional responses.

This project will use only existing public data. We will integrate structural data from the Protein Data Bank, AlphaFold models, NMR and cryo-EM-derived conformational information, public molecular dynamics trajectories where available, ligand chemistry and activity data from ChEMBL, PubChem, BindingDB, and IUPHAR, protein sequence and evolutionary data from UniProt, OrthoDB, and public phylogenomic resources, coregulator interaction data from BioGRID and IntAct, and cell-level functional data from GEO, SRA, ENCODE, ChIP-Atlas, and Expression Atlas. The resulting resource, NR-AlloState, will harmonize ligands, receptor isoforms, orthologs, mutations, post-translational modifications, coregulator motifs, DNA response elements, chromatin context, and transcriptomic outcomes into a reproducible graph-based knowledge base.

The central hypothesis is that ligand-specific transcriptional phenotypes emerge from low-dimensional, evolutionarily constrained patterns of dynamic coupling rather than from individual contacts alone. We will test this by deriving structure-based flexibility and coupling descriptors from public structures and models, comparing apo, ligand-bound, DNA-bound, and coregulator-bound states across the nuclear receptor superfamily. These descriptors will be integrated with ligand chemical features, mutational effects, disease variants, and transcriptional signatures using uncertainty-aware machine learning and interpretable latent-variable models. The models will be evaluated by their ability to predict held-out ligand efficacy classes, receptor subtype selectivity, coregulator recruitment profiles, and transcriptomic responses across cell types.

The synthesis will address three fundamental questions. First, are there conserved dynamic architectures that explain how nuclear receptors convert ligand binding into regulatory output despite sequence divergence? Second, which residues or residue networks act as evolutionary tuners of ligand sensitivity, partial agonism, or antagonism? Third, when do molecular allosteric changes scale up into predictable cellular transcriptional programs, and when are they overridden by chromatin or coregulator context? By combining evolutionary analysis, protein dynamics, chemical informatics, and functional genomics, the working group will reveal when mesoscale regulatory behavior is encoded in the receptor itself and when it emerges from receptor partnerships in the nucleus.

NCEMS support is essential because the required synthesis spans structural biology, molecular simulation, nuclear receptor pharmacology, evolutionary biophysics, machine learning, and genomics, and depends on harmonizing fragmented datasets that no single laboratory could curate or analyze comprehensively. All curated datasets, code, model outputs, uncertainty estimates, and tutorials will be released openly. Trainees will participate in cross-disciplinary data jamborees and reproducible workflow development, producing both a scientific atlas of nuclear receptor allostery and a generalizable framework for linking molecular conformational ensembles to emergent cellular regulation.

By combining evolutionary analysis, protein dynamics, chemical informatics, and functional genomics, the working group will reveal when mesoscale regulatory behavior is encoded in the receptor itself and when it emerges from receptor partnerships in the nucleus.

NCEMS support is essential because the required synthesis spans structural biology, molecular simulation, nuclear receptor pharmacology, evolutionary biophysics, machine learning, and genomics, and depends on harmonizing fragmented datasets that no single laboratory could curate or analyze comprehensively. All curated datasets, code, model outputs, uncertainty estimates, and tutorials will be released openly. Trainees will participate in cross-disciplinary data jamborees and reproducible workflow development, producing both a scientific atlas of nuclear receptor allostery and a generalizable framework for linking molecular conformational ensembles to emergent cellular regulation.

[Background and Significance]
Nuclear receptors are ligand-regulated transcription factors that convert molecular recognition events into genome-scale regulatory programs. Their ligand-binding domains accommodate endogenous metabolites, drugs, environmental chemicals, and synthetic modulators, yet the same receptor can produce agonism, partial agonism, inverse agonism, antagonism, or selective tissue responses depending on ligand identity and cellular context. This makes nuclear receptors an ideal mesoscale system for studying emergence: residue-level interactions in a buried binding pocket reshape conformational ensembles, alter helix positioning and surface dynamics, modulate coregulator recruitment, influence receptor dimerization and DNA engagement, and ultimately affect transcriptional phenotypes in a cell-type-specific chromatin environment. The central unresolved problem is that ligand affinity alone is a poor predictor of biological output. Compounds with similar binding constants can produce sharply different efficacy, receptor subtype selectivity, therapeutic windows, and disease-associated transcriptional signatures. Static structures have revealed many ligand contacts and canonical conformational changes, particularly around activation surfaces, but they do not fully explain how chemically diverse ligands bias dynamic receptor ensembles or why the same ligand can generate different outcomes across tissues. Molecular dynamics, evolutionary analysis, mutational studies, and functional genomics each provide partial views, but these data streams are fragmented across repositories, receptor subfamilies, species, assays, and cell types. A synthesis approach is now timely because public data have reached sufficient scale to connect molecular structure to cellular function. The Protein Data Bank contains numerous nuclear receptor structures in apo, ligand-bound, DNA-bound, dimeric, and coregulator-bound forms. AlphaFold and related public models extend structural coverage to poorly characterized isoforms and orthologs. Public molecular dynamics trajectories, NMR restraints, cryo-EM models, and ensemble descriptions provide additional evidence about conformational heterogeneity. Ligand databases such as ChEMBL, PubChem, BindingDB, and IUPHAR contain chemical structures, affinities, activity annotations, and pharmacological classifications. UniProt, OrthoDB, and phylogenomic resources enable comparison of conserved and variable positions across receptor evolution. Interaction databases capture receptor-coregulator and protein-protein associations, while GEO, SRA, ENCODE, ChIP-Atlas, and Expression Atlas provide transcriptomic, chromatin occupancy, and regulatory context across cell types and perturbations. Integrating these resources can reveal whether nuclear receptor outputs are governed by low-dimensional collective variables: dynamic coupling patterns, flexible hinges, allosteric communication pathways, and evolutionarily tunable residue networks. Such variables would represent emergent order parameters linking atomistic ligand recognition to mesoscale receptor assemblies and cellular phenotypes. This proposal directly addresses NCEMS priorities by using only public data, requiring collaboration across protein dynamics, nuclear receptor biology, evolutionary biophysics, cheminformatics, machine learning, and functional genomics, and producing reusable community resources. The project is beyond the scope of a single laboratory because it requires harmonizing heterogeneous molecular and cellular data, establishing shared ontologies, building reproducible workflows, and interpreting results across multiple biological scales. The resulting NR-AlloState atlas will advance fundamental understanding of allostery as an emergent phenomenon and provide a generalizable framework for linking conformational ensembles to regulatory outcomes.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This working group will address three integrated research questions. Question 1: Are there conserved dynamic architectures that allow nuclear receptors to convert ligand binding into regulatory output despite sequence divergence and ligand chemical diversity? We hypothesize that receptor ligand-binding domains share a limited set of dynamic coupling architectures that connect the ligand pocket, activation function surfaces, dimer interfaces, DNA-binding domain contacts, and coregulator interaction motifs. These architectures will not be captured by individual ligand contacts alone. Instead, they will appear as recurring patterns in flexibility, residue-residue coupling, coevolution, and conformational state shifts across apo, ligand-bound, coregulator-bound, and DNA-bound structures. Question 2: Which residues or residue networks act as evolutionary tuners of ligand sensitivity, selectivity, partial agonism, and antagonism? We hypothesize that functionally important tuning positions are enriched at dynamically coupled hinges, allosteric pathway bottlenecks, and subfamily-specific sequence divergence sites rather than only at directly contacting ligand-pocket residues. These positions may explain how orthologs and paralogs preserve a shared fold while evolving different endogenous ligands, pharmacological profiles, and regulatory programs. We further hypothesize that known disease variants and experimentally reported activity-altering mutations will concentrate in networks that control conformational redistribution rather than simply destabilizing the global structure. Question 3: When do molecular allosteric state variables scale up into predictable transcriptional programs, and when are they overridden by chromatin, coregulator abundance, or cell identity? We hypothesize that ligand-biased receptor states will predict coregulator recruitment and transcriptional signatures most strongly in cellular contexts where the relevant receptor, partner factors, response elements, and chromatin accessibility are present. Conversely, the same molecular state may yield divergent phenotypes when cell-specific cofactors, competing receptors, post-translational modifications, or chromatin states impose alternative regulatory constraints. These questions define a testable model of emergence. At the molecular scale, ligand chemistry perturbs local contacts and pocket hydration, sterics, electrostatics, and shape complementarity. At the protein mesoscale, these perturbations are amplified or buffered by collective conformational networks. At the assembly scale, receptor states determine the probability of coregulator binding, dimer formation, DNA response element engagement, and interaction with chromatin-associated factors. At the cellular scale, these assemblies produce transcriptional changes conditioned by cell type and regulatory context. The central hypothesis is that interpretable, low-dimensional allosteric state variables can bridge these scales. We will test this hypothesis through prediction and explanation. Predictive tests will evaluate whether state variables inferred from public structural, sequence, and ligand data improve prediction of held-out ligand efficacy, receptor subtype selectivity, coregulator recruitment, and transcriptomic response compared with models based only on affinity, ligand fingerprints, or receptor identity. Explanatory tests will assess whether inferred variables recover known mechanisms, identify conserved and subfamily-specific allosteric networks, and distinguish receptor-encoded effects from context-dependent cellular modulation. The project will explicitly represent uncertainty arising from assay heterogeneity, incomplete structures, inconsistent ligand annotations, and cell-type differences, so that conclusions are robust rather than artifacts of uneven public data coverage.

[Methods and Approach]
Aim 1 will construct NR-AlloState, a harmonized public-data knowledge base linking receptors, ligands, structures, dynamics, interactions, genomic context, and functional outcomes. We will include human nuclear receptors and selected orthologs with sufficient public sequence, structural, pharmacological, or functional data. Structures will be obtained from the Protein Data Bank, AlphaFold models, and public ensemble resources, with metadata describing receptor isoform, domain boundaries, ligand identity, oligomeric state, DNA or coregulator binding, mutations, post-translational modifications, resolution, and experimental method. Ligands will be standardized across ChEMBL, PubChem, BindingDB, and IUPHAR using chemical identifiers, protonation-aware structure normalization, activity units, assay type, target mapping, and efficacy labels. Functional genomics data will be curated from GEO, SRA, ENCODE, ChIP-Atlas, and Expression Atlas, emphasizing studies with defined receptor perturbation, ligand exposure, cell type, time point, and readout. Interaction data from BioGRID and IntAct will be mapped to coregulator motifs, receptor domains, and evidence codes. Aim 2 will derive collective allosteric descriptors from public structures and models. We will compute residue-level flexibility, elastic-network and contact-network coupling, solvent exposure, pocket geometry, ligand interaction fingerprints, coevolutionary constraints, conservation scores, and dynamic communication metrics. Where public molecular dynamics trajectories exist, we will extract ensemble-based features such as conformational populations, correlated motions, pocket breathing, and activation-surface variability. For systems without public trajectories, we will use structure-based statistical mechanics and normal-mode methods that require no new simulation data generation beyond reproducible analysis of public coordinates and models. Descriptors will be aligned across the receptor superfamily using domain-aware structural alignment and sequence homology mapping, enabling comparison of equivalent positions and networks. Aim 3 will integrate molecular descriptors with ligand and cellular phenotypes using uncertainty-aware, interpretable models. We will build a graph knowledge base in which nodes represent receptors, isoforms, orthologs, residues, ligands, structures, assays, coregulators, DNA elements, cell types, and transcriptomic signatures; edges encode binding, homology, physical contacts, dynamic coupling, regulatory association, and evidence provenance. Machine learning will include hierarchical Bayesian models, graph neural networks with attribution constraints, matrix factorization, multi-view latent-variable models, and calibrated classifiers. Model evaluation will use receptor-family-aware, ligand-scaffold-aware, and cell-type-aware splits to prevent information leakage. Primary outcomes will include prediction of ligand efficacy class, subtype selectivity, coregulator recruitment, disease-variant impact, and differential expression signatures. Baseline models will use affinity, ligand fingerprints, or receptor identity alone; improvement over these baselines will test the value of collective allosteric variables. Aim 4 will conduct community working sessions for ontology refinement, benchmark creation, trainee training, and interpretation. No new experimental datasets will be generated. All work will synthesize existing public data through transparent curation, reproducible computation, and cross-disciplinary analysis.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The project will deliver three major scientific products. First, NR-AlloState will provide a curated, queryable, graph-based atlas connecting nuclear receptor ligands, receptor isoforms, orthologs, structures, dynamic descriptors, coregulators, chromatin annotations, and transcriptional outcomes. This resource will transform scattered public information into an integrated framework for testing mechanisms of nuclear receptor allostery. Second, the working group will identify conserved and receptor-specific collective allosteric state variables that explain ligand efficacy, selectivity, and context-dependent transcriptional regulation better than affinity or static contact maps alone. These state variables will clarify how local chemical perturbations propagate through receptor conformational networks to alter mesoscale assemblies. Third, the project will produce benchmark datasets and interpretable predictive models for ligand efficacy, receptor subtype selectivity, coregulator recruitment, and transcriptomic response. Scientifically, the results will address a long-standing puzzle in pharmacology and molecular regulation: why similar binding does not imply similar biological effect. The synthesis will reveal when regulatory information is encoded in receptor dynamics and when it emerges from interactions with coregulators, DNA elements, chromatin landscapes, and cell-specific factors. This distinction is central to understanding emergence across molecular and cellular scales. Practically, the atlas will support hypothesis generation for selective receptor modulation, interpretation of disease-associated variants, and prioritization of public data gaps. The broader impact is a reusable, open framework for linking structural ensembles to cellular phenotypes in other allosteric signaling systems. Trainees will gain experience in public-data synthesis, reproducible workflow engineering, uncertainty-aware machine learning, and team science. By bringing together expertise in protein dynamics, nuclear receptor biology, evolutionary analysis, cheminformatics, and functional genomics, the project will create discoveries and training outcomes that are not achievable by isolated laboratories.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
The project will follow open, team-oriented, and reproducible science practices from inception. All input datasets will be public, and each record in NR-AlloState will retain source identifiers, accession numbers, version dates, license information where available, and evidence provenance. Curated metadata, harmonized tables, graph schemas, model-ready benchmark splits, trained model outputs, uncertainty estimates, and documentation will be released through public repositories such as GitHub and Zenodo under permissive licenses consistent with source database terms. Analysis workflows will be implemented as modular pipelines using open-source languages and workflow managers. Computational environments will be captured with containers and lock files so that analyses can be rerun on NCEMS resources, institutional clusters, or cloud platforms. Continuous integration tests will check data validation rules, identifier mapping, unit conversions, ligand standardization, structural alignment consistency, and model reproducibility. Major analyses will be accompanied by executable notebooks and narrative tutorials for users with different backgrounds, including structural biology, genomics, and machine learning. Reproducibility will be strengthened through preregistered benchmark definitions before final model comparison. We will define training, validation, and test splits that account for receptor homology, ligand scaffold similarity, assay source, and cell type to reduce data leakage. Model reports will include calibration, confidence intervals, sensitivity to missing data, and performance stratified by receptor family, ligand class, and functional assay type. Negative or inconclusive results, such as receptor families for which public data are insufficient to infer reliable state variables, will be reported with the same transparency as positive findings. The working group will develop community guidelines for nuclear receptor allostery data integration, including recommended metadata fields for structures, ligand assays, coregulator measurements, and transcriptomic perturbation studies. Trainees will help maintain documentation, lead reproducibility checks, and participate in data jamborees. Publications will be preprinted when appropriate, and final manuscripts will be open access whenever possible.

[Budget and Resources]
NCEMS support is requested to enable a community-scale synthesis effort that exceeds the capacity of any single laboratory or existing bilateral collaboration. Funds and center resources will be used for working group meetings, trainee participation, data curation sprints, computational workflow development, benchmark evaluation, and dissemination. No funds will be used to generate new wet-lab experimental data. The major resource need is coordinated personnel time and shared infrastructure for harmonizing heterogeneous public datasets across structural biology, ligand pharmacology, protein evolution, interaction networks, and functional genomics. abstract_original:
Nuclear receptors provide a powerful system for understanding emergence in molecular and cellular biology: binding of chemically diverse ligands to a buried pocket produces collective conformational shifts, altered coregulator recruitment, chromatin engagement, and cell-type-specific transcriptional outcomes. Yet a long-standing puzzle remains unresolved: why do ligands with similar affinity for the same receptor often produce distinct efficacy, selectivity, and disease-relevant phenotypes? We propose a community-scale synthesis project to identify the collective allosteric state variables that connect residue-level perturbations in nuclear receptor ligand-binding domains to mesoscale receptor-coregulator-DNA assemblies and downstream transcriptional responses.

This project will use only existing public data. We will integrate structural data from the Protein Data Bank, AlphaFold models, NMR and cryo-EM-derived conformational information, public molecular dynamics trajectories where available, ligand chemistry and activity data from ChEMBL, PubChem, BindingDB, and IUPHAR, protein sequence and evolutionary data from UniProt, OrthoDB, and public phylogenomic resources, coregulator interaction data from BioGRID and IntAct, and cell-level functional data from GEO, SRA, ENCODE, ChIP-Atlas, and Expression Atlas. The resulting resource, NR-AlloState, will harmonize ligands, receptor isoforms, orthologs, mutations, post-translational modifications, coregulator motifs, DNA response elements, chromatin context, and transcriptomic outcomes into a reproducible graph-based knowledge base.

The central hypothesis is that ligand-specific transcriptional phenotypes emerge from low-dimensional, evolutionarily constrained patterns of dynamic coupling rather than from individual contacts alone. We will test this by deriving structure-based flexibility and coupling descriptors from public structures and models, comparing apo, ligand-bound, DNA-bound, and coregulator-bound states across the nuclear receptor superfamily. These descriptors will be integrated with ligand chemical features, mutational effects, disease variants, and transcriptional signatures using uncertainty-aware machine learning and interpretable latent-variable models. The models will be evaluated by their ability to predict held-out ligand efficacy classes, receptor subtype selectivity, coregulator recruitment profiles, and transcriptomic responses across cell types.

The synthesis will address three fundamental questions. First, are there conserved dynamic architectures that explain how nuclear receptors convert ligand binding into regulatory output despite sequence divergence? Second, which residues or residue networks act as evolutionary tuners of ligand sensitivity, partial agonism, or antagonism? Third, when do molecular allosteric changes scale up into predictable cellular transcriptional programs, and when are they overridden by chromatin or coregulator context? By combining evolutionary analysis, protein dynamics, chemical informatics, and functional genomics, the working group will reveal when mesoscale regulatory behavior is encoded in the receptor itself and when it emerges from receptor partnerships in the nucleus.

NCEMS support is essential because the required synthesis spans structural biology, molecular simulation, nuclear receptor pharmacology, evolutionary biophysics, machine learning, and genomics, and depends on harmonizing fragmented datasets that no single laboratory could curate or analyze comprehensively. All curated datasets, code, model outputs, uncertainty estimates, and tutorials will be released openly. Trainees will participate in cross-disciplinary data jamborees and reproducible workflow development, producing both a scientific atlas of nuclear receptor allostery and a generalizable framework for linking molecular conformational ensembles to emergent cellular regulation.

title: From Entangled Proteins to Entangled Genomes: A Synthesis Framework Linking Molecular Topology of Chromatin Regulators to Emergent 3D Genome Organization
title_norm: from entangled proteins to entangled genomes a synthesis framework linking molecular topology of chromatin regulators to emergent 3d genome organization
abstract_text:
A central unresolved question in molecular and cellular biology is how molecular-scale constraints imposed by chromatin-associated proteins give rise to mesoscale nuclear properties such as chromatin loops, domains, compartments, and chromosome mechanics. Many proteins that act on DNA and chromatin are not simple globular binders: they form rings, clamps, bridged circuits, coiled-coil assemblies, topological traps, or deep entanglements that can constrain polymer motion. Yet current models of 3D genome organization typically represent these proteins as generic binders or loop extruders, without incorporating their structural topology. This Working Group will synthesize public structural, genomic, and biophysical data to ask: do the topological features of chromatin-regulating proteins predict where, when, and how stable mesoscale genome structures emerge?

We will build an open, cross-scale atlas connecting protein topology to chromatin architecture. First, we will annotate the molecular topology of chromatin regulators across eukaryotes and bacteria using existing structures from the Protein Data Bank, AlphaFold Database, model organism proteomes, UniProt, ComplexPortal, and curated chromatin-factor databases. The atlas will classify knots, slipknots, lassos, theta-like circuits, ring-forming assemblies, disulfide- or metal-stabilized closures, coiled-coil bridges, and confidence-scored predicted entanglements. All annotations, workflows, benchmark datasets, visualization tools, and model outputs will be released openly. By training graduate students and postdoctoral researchers to work across protein structure, genome organization, and mesoscale modeling, the project will create a data-savvy community positioned to explain how molecular entanglement contributes to emergent cellular organization.

[Background and Significance]
Chromosomes are not passive polymers. Their mesoscale organization emerges from interactions among DNA sequence, epigenetic state, transcriptional activity, molecular motors, architectural proteins, and physical constraints. Public Hi-C, Micro-C, ChIA-PET, SPRITE, DamID, single-cell chromatin conformation, DNA-tracing, microscopy-derived distance, and perturbation datasets have revealed loops, topologically associating domains, compartments, mitotic compaction, bacterial chromosome domains, and cell-type-specific structural heterogeneity. Yet a persistent gap remains between the molecular structures of chromatin regulators and the emergent physical behavior of chromosomes. Most genome-organization models encode chromatin-associated proteins as occupancy tracks, binders, barriers, or generic loop-extruding agents. This representation has been productive, but it discards structural features that may be central to function: rings, clamps, coiled-coil arms, bridged circuits, knots, slipknots, lassos, pseudo-closed loops, disulfide-stabilized closures, metal-mediated constraints, and topological traps. These structural motifs can alter polymer threading, residence time, release probability, cooperative assembly, mechanical response, and the ability of a protein complex to constrain DNA segments over time. Molecular topology is therefore a plausible but underused explanatory layer for mesoscale genome organization. Cohesin and condensin illustrate the opportunity. These SMC complexes form extended coiled-coil assemblies with ring-like architectures and dynamic gates that are often modeled as loop extruders. However, different SMC complexes operate in interphase, mitosis, meiosis, and bacteria, producing distinct loop sizes, compaction states, boundary interactions, and mechanical properties. CTCF, topoisomerases, histone chaperones, remodeling complexes, transcription-associated factors, and bacterial nucleoid proteins impose additional constraints whose structural topologies differ widely. Some act as bridges, some modulate DNA supercoiling or strand passage, some remodel nucleosomes, and some organize higher-order assemblies. The field lacks a systematic public synthesis linking these molecular topologies to genomic locations, perturbation outcomes, evolutionary conservation, and polymer-physics models. The timing is ideal for an NCEMS Working Group because the required data already exist but are dispersed across communities. Structural data are available in the Protein Data Bank, AlphaFold Database, model organism proteomes, UniProt, ComplexPortal, domain databases, and curated chromatin-factor resources. Genome-organization data exist across species, cell types, developmental states, cell-cycle stages, mutants, degron perturbations, drug treatments, and imaging platforms. Topological algorithms can classify open-chain entanglement and closed or pseudo-closed circuits, while polymer models can test whether topology-informed constraints improve predictions beyond occupancy and epigenetic covariates. This project addresses NCEMS priorities by using only existing public data, assembling expertise that exceeds any single laboratory, and focusing on emergence across molecular and mesoscale levels. It asks whether the shape and topology of chromatin regulators help explain how local molecular constraints generate stable, dynamic, and mechanically responsive genome architecture.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
The Working Group will address one overarching question: do topological features of chromatin-regulating proteins provide predictive information about emergent three-dimensional genome organization that is not captured by binding location, expression level, domain composition, sequence conservation, or chromatin state alone? We will decompose this question into four linked research questions. First, what topological classes are present among proteins and protein complexes that regulate chromatin and DNA organization across eukaryotes and bacteria? We hypothesize that chromatin regulators are enriched for specific constraint-generating architectures, including ring-like assemblies, coiled-coil bridged circuits, clamp-like domains, strand-passage enzymes, lasso-like motifs, metal-stabilized closures, and deep entanglements, relative to matched nuclear or cytosolic protein sets. Second, are these topological classes associated with distinct mesoscale chromatin features? We hypothesize that ring-forming and gated architectures are preferentially associated with persistent loop structures and mitotic compaction; bridged or theta-like architectures are associated with boundary insulation and long-range contact hubs; topoisomerase and strand-passage topologies correlate with regions exhibiting high reorganization or supercoiling-linked changes; and remodeling or chaperone complexes with complex flexible topologies are enriched at loci showing rapid structural transitions across cell states. Third, does topology improve predictive models of chromatin architecture? We hypothesize that models incorporating topology-informed constraints will better predict loop strength, loop persistence proxies, boundary insulation, compartment segregation, contact decay, and inferred mechanical response than models using only genomic annotations, ChIP-seq intensity, epigenetic marks, gene expression, and protein identity. Improvement will be evaluated through held-out chromosomes, held-out cell types, perturbation prediction, and cross-species transfer. Fourth, when does topology fail to explain genome organization? This question is essential for rigor. We hypothesize that topology contributes most strongly where a protein physically constrains polymer motion for timescales comparable to chromatin relaxation, and contributes weakly where observed patterns are dominated by transcriptional state, phase separation, local chromatin accessibility, copy number, technical platform effects, or transient low-affinity binding. We will explicitly test alternative explanations, including protein abundance, binding affinity proxies, motif density, post-translational regulation, complex stoichiometry, evolutionary conservation, compartment state, replication timing, transcription, and local mappability. These hypotheses frame molecular topology as neither a universal cause nor a decorative structural feature, but as a testable mechanistic variable. The project will also produce methodological hypotheses: that a shared ontology of protein topology can be made interoperable with genome browser tracks and polymer simulation parameters; that confidence-scored AlphaFold and experimentally resolved structures can be integrated without conflating reliable and uncertain entanglements; and that mesoscale emergence can be studied by comparing recurrent outcomes across independent public datasets rather than by relying on a single assay. Success will be measured by reproducible associations, improved predictive performance, interpretable polymer-model parameters, and community adoption of the atlas and workflows.

[Methods and Approach]
This project will be organized as a synthesis-only Working Group with three integrated workstreams. Workstream 1 will construct a public topology atlas of chromatin regulators. We will assemble candidate proteins and complexes from UniProt, Gene Ontology, ComplexPortal, model organism databases, curated chromatin-factor resources, bacterial nucleoid protein catalogs, and literature-derived lists for cohesin, condensin, CTCF, topoisomerases, histone chaperones, remodelers, SMC-associated factors, transcriptional architectural proteins, and bacterial chromosome organizers. Structural inputs will include Protein Data Bank coordinates, AlphaFold Database models, available multimeric complex models, domain annotations, disulfide and metal-binding annotations, and confidence metrics. Topological classification will use established computational approaches for open-chain knot detection, slipknot analysis, lasso and pierced-loop identification, genus and circuit descriptors, theta-like graph representations, coiled-coil bridge detection, and ring or clamp architecture annotation. Each annotation will include provenance, algorithmic parameters, confidence level, structure source, biological assembly state, and uncertainty flags. Workstream 2 will integrate topology annotations with public genome-organization datasets. We will curate interoperable datasets from GEO, SRA, ENCODE, 4DN, modENCODE, organism-specific repositories, and published supplementary resources, prioritizing matched Hi-C, Micro-C, ChIA-PET, HiChIP, SPRITE, DamID, ChIP-seq, CUT&RUN, CUT&Tag, degron or knockout perturbations, single-cell chromatin conformation, DNA tracing, and microscopy-based distance measurements. Harmonization will use existing genome builds, lifted coordinates where appropriate, standardized quality metrics, replicate-aware normalization, and metadata describing cell type, species, cell-cycle state, perturbation, assay, resolution, and batch. Derived mesoscale phenotypes will include loop strength, boundary insulation, compartment eigenvectors, contact probability scaling, chromatin domain persistence, inter-locus distance distributions, mitotic compaction measures, bacterial macrodomains, and perturbation effect sizes. Workstream 3 will test predictive and mechanistic models. Statistical models will evaluate whether topology classes explain variance in mesoscale phenotypes after controlling for occupancy, expression, conservation, domain architecture, chromatin state, transcription, GC content, mappability, and assay platform. Machine-learning models will use nested cross-validation, held-out cell types, held-out species, and perturbation-based tests to estimate generalization. Polymer-physics and maximum-entropy models will translate topology classes into explicit constraints, such as loop-capture probability, residence-time priors, bridge valency, gated passage, compaction strength, and release kinetics. We will compare topology-aware and topology-agnostic models using contact-map likelihoods, distance-distribution accuracy, insulation prediction, and recovery of perturbation phenotypes. NCEMS convenings will support ontology design, benchmark selection, code review, trainee exchanges, and synthesis workshops. No new experimental data will be generated. All work will reuse public data, and any manual curation will be documented as a reproducible scholarly product.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The project will deliver an open cross-scale atlas linking chromatin-regulator molecular topology to emergent genome organization. The atlas will include confidence-scored annotations of knots, slipknots, lassos, theta-like circuits, rings, clamps, coiled-coil bridges, stabilized closures, and complex assemblies for chromatin-associated proteins across selected eukaryotic and bacterial systems. It will be interoperable with genome browsers, structural viewers, and modeling workflows, allowing researchers to ask whether a bound protein is merely present at a locus or is structurally capable of imposing a particular polymer constraint. A second outcome will be benchmark datasets connecting topology annotations with public chromatin conformation, protein occupancy, perturbation, imaging, and cell-state metadata. These benchmarks will support transparent comparison of models for loops, domains, compartments, compaction, and mechanical response. A third outcome will be a reusable computational framework for topology-aware genome modeling. If topology-informed features improve prediction, the project will establish a new mechanistic layer connecting molecular structure to mesoscale nuclear emergence. If improvements are context-dependent or limited, the project will still clarify when occupancy, chromatin state, or other variables dominate, thereby sharpening mechanistic models. The broader impact is conceptual and practical. Conceptually, the project will bridge protein topology, structural biology, chromatin genomics, and polymer physics, showing how constraints embedded in molecular architecture can propagate to mesoscale cellular organization. Practically, the atlas and workflows will help researchers prioritize chromatin regulators for reanalysis, perturbation interpretation, comparative genomics, and protein engineering. The Working Group will train graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in open data synthesis, topological analysis, statistical modeling, and collaborative software development. By producing reusable standards rather than a one-off analysis, the project will build community capacity for studying emergence from molecular constraints to cellular-scale organization.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
The project will follow open, team, and reproducible science practices from inception. All source code, workflow definitions, documentation, issue tracking, and analysis notebooks will be developed in public version-controlled repositories under permissive open-source licenses. Data products will use persistent identifiers, semantic versioning, machine-readable metadata, and clear provenance records linking each annotation or derived phenotype to its original public source. Because the project uses only existing public data, no embargoed experimental datasets or restricted human subject data will be incorporated unless they are already approved for open use under the relevant repository terms. Reproducibility will be supported through containerized software environments, workflow managers, automated tests, continuous integration, and archived releases on public repositories such as Zenodo. We will define benchmark datasets with frozen versions so that topology-aware and topology-agnostic models can be compared consistently over time. Each major result will include executable scripts for data download, preprocessing, model fitting, visualization, and statistical evaluation. Uncertainty will be reported explicitly, especially for predicted protein structures, multimeric assemblies, low-confidence AlphaFold regions, ambiguous knot closure choices, incomplete complexes, and chromatin datasets with variable resolution or replicate quality. The Working Group will establish community guidelines for topology annotation of chromatin regulators, including nomenclature, confidence categories, minimum metadata, and recommended visualizations. Trainees will participate in code review, data-curation sprints, reproducibility audits, and short training modules on structural bioinformatics, chromatin data formats, polymer modeling, and responsible use of AI-assisted analysis. Publications will be submitted as preprints and to peer-reviewed venues, with all figures traceable to public workflows. We will also provide tutorials, example notebooks, and lightweight web-based visualization tools to make the atlas useful to experimentalists, theorists, and data scientists. These practices will ensure that NCEMS support yields durable community infrastructure, not merely static conclusions.

[Budget and Resources]
NCEMS support is essential because this project requires sustained coordination among communities that rarely share data standards or modeling languages. Requested resources will support four categories. First, Working Group convenings will include two in-person synthesis meetings per year and regular virtual meetings for topology ontology development, dataset prioritization, model benchmarking, and manuscript or software sprints. Travel funds will prioritize participation by trainees, early-career researchers, members from diverse institution types, and collaborators with complementary expertise in protein topology, chromatin biology, polymer physics, structural bioinformatics, statistics, and open-source infrastructure. Second, personnel and trainee support will fund graduate student and postdoctoral effort for data harmonization, software engineering, documentation, benchmark construction, and cross-training. Short trainee exchanges will pair structural-topology trainees with chromatin-modeling groups and genome-data trainees with protein-structure groups. Third, computational resources will support public-data processing, contact-map normalization, structural annotation at proteome scale, model comparison, container builds, and web-accessible visualization. These needs include cloud storage, high-performance computing time, continuous integration services, and archival deposition fees where applicable. Fourth, community dissemination funds will support online tutorials, hackathons, documentation, accessibility improvements, and maintenance of the atlas and benchmark releases. No funds will be used to generate new experimental data. The budget is therefore aligned with NCEMS priorities for synthesis, integration, training, and open community products. Existing public resources provide the raw material, but NCEMS infrastructure provides the collaborative environment needed to transform scattered structural, genomic, and biophysical datasets into an interoperable framework. By investing in coordination, reproducible workflows, and trainee development, the project will create reusable capacity for future synthesis efforts on molecular and cellular emergence.

title: Emergent Translational Reserve as a Multiscale Determinant of Skeletal Muscle Growth, Repair, and Inflammatory Failure
title_norm: emergent translational reserve as a multiscale determinant of skeletal muscle growth repair and inflammatory failure
abstract_text:
Skeletal muscle exhibits striking emergent behavior: molecular changes in signaling, chromatin state, ribosome production, autophagy, immune activity, and mechanical response collectively produce higher-order outcomes such as hypertrophy, regeneration, fibrosis, or functional decline. Yet a central unresolved question remains: why do similar anabolic or mechanical cues produce robust growth in some contexts but maladaptive inflammation, impaired repair, or wasting in others? We propose a community-scale synthesis project to define and model an emergent property we call “translational reserve”: the coordinated capacity of muscle cells and their local niche to expand ribosome biogenesis, maintain protein synthesis, buffer proteostatic stress, and support tissue remodeling under mechanical or inflammatory challenge.

This project will use only publicly available datasets to integrate molecular, cellular, and tissue-scale information across human and animal skeletal muscle studies. Data sources will include bulk and single-nucleus RNA-seq from exercise, resistance training, overload, immobilization, aging, muscular disease, rheumatoid arthritis, myositis, and injury models; public proteomics and phosphoproteomics datasets related to mTOR signaling, ribosome assembly, autophagy, and inflammatory pathways; DNA methylation and chromatin accessibility datasets where available; ribosome profiling and translation-associated datasets from muscle and related cell types; and histological or imaging-derived public metadata on fiber size, fiber type, fibrosis, immune infiltration, and functional outcomes. The project will harmonize these heterogeneous resources into a shared cross-species atlas of muscle adaptation states.
