By synthesizing dispersed public data into a mechanistic, predictive framework, this project will address a fundamental question in molecular and cellular emergence: how molecular-scale control of protein production and stress buffering gives rise to cell- and tissue-scale muscle adaptation or failure.

[Background and Significance]
Skeletal muscle is a highly plastic tissue in which molecular, cellular, and niche-level processes combine to produce system-level outcomes that cannot be inferred from any single pathway alone. Mechanical loading, resistance exercise, injury, disuse, aging, inflammatory disease, and metabolic stress can all activate overlapping signaling programs, including mTOR-associated anabolic signaling, ribosome biogenesis, autophagy, inflammatory cytokine networks, extracellular matrix remodeling, and satellite cell responses. Despite these shared components, the tissue response varies widely. One context yields fiber hypertrophy and improved function; another yields fibrosis, immune infiltration, impaired regeneration, or wasting. This divergence represents a fundamental problem in emergence: how do molecular-scale changes in protein production and stress regulation become coordinated, or fail to become coordinated, into adaptive tissue remodeling? A long-standing gap in muscle biology is the lack of an integrative framework linking translational control to tissue-level adaptation across physiological and disease contexts. Ribosome biogenesis and protein synthesis are essential for sustained growth, but their effects depend on energetic state, proteostasis capacity, autophagy, inflammatory milieu, myonuclear transcriptional state, vascular support, and the behavior of fibro-adipogenic progenitors and immune cells. Conversely, inflammation and fibrosis do not simply suppress anabolism; they may reshape the mesoscale organization of muscle, altering cell-cell communication, nutrient flux, extracellular constraints, and translational capacity. Public data now make it possible to examine these relationships at a community scale. Large numbers of bulk RNA-seq, single-cell and single-nucleus RNA-seq, proteomic, phosphoproteomic, epigenomic, ribosome-associated, imaging, and phenotypic datasets have been deposited from human exercise training studies, rodent overload models, immobilization, aging, dystrophy, injury, rheumatoid arthritis, myositis, cachexia, and related perturbations. However, these resources remain fragmented by species, platform, metadata conventions, analytical pipelines, and disease focus. Most analyses ask whether individual genes or pathways change within a study; few synthesize across contexts to determine whether higher-order modules jointly define adaptive capacity. We propose translational reserve as an emergent mesoscale property: the coordinated capacity of muscle fibers and their niche to expand ribosome production, sustain translation, maintain proteostatic balance, and remodel tissue under challenge. Translational reserve is not equivalent to expression of ribosomal genes, mTOR activity, or autophagy markers alone. It is a systems-level state arising from nonlinear interactions among nucleolar activity, translation machinery, protein quality control, immune-fibrotic signaling, chromatin state, and cell composition. Defining this property requires integration of diverse public datasets and expertise spanning muscle physiology, translational control, inflammatory disease, high-performance computing, graph-based artificial intelligence, and mathematical modeling. This proposal is well aligned with NCEMS because it uses only existing public data to address a fundamental question in molecular and cellular emergence at the mesoscale. The work is beyond the scope of any single laboratory: it requires cross-species data harmonization, scalable reanalysis, community metadata standards, interpretable AI, and mechanistic modeling. The resulting atlas and models will transform dispersed studies into a predictive framework for understanding why muscle adapts, repairs, or fails.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This working group will address four linked scientific questions. Question 1: Can translational reserve be operationally defined from public multi-omic and phenotypic data as a reproducible, cross-context state of skeletal muscle? We hypothesize that adaptive hypertrophy and effective regeneration share a conserved multivariate signature characterized by coordinated ribosome biogenesis, translation initiation and elongation capacity, balanced autophagy and proteasome activity, restrained inflammatory signaling, and permissive niche remodeling. This signature will be detectable across human and animal datasets despite differences in species, platform, and perturbation. Question 2: Do inflammatory and degenerative conditions shift muscle into a low-reserve or misallocated-reserve state? We hypothesize that rheumatoid arthritis, myositis, aging, immobilization, cachexia, and dystrophic contexts will not simply show reduced anabolic signaling. Instead, they will display disrupted coupling among ribosome biogenesis, proteostasis, and tissue remodeling. In some cases, translation-associated programs may be activated without adequate autophagic buffering or extracellular support, producing stress, maladaptive immune activation, and impaired growth. In other cases, inflammatory and fibrotic signaling may suppress nucleolar and translational capacity, lowering the threshold for wasting after mechanical or metabolic challenge. Question 3: Which cell types and niche interactions contribute most strongly to translational reserve? We hypothesize that myonuclei encode much of the core ribosome and translation program, but the emergent reserve state depends on coordinated signals from satellite cells, fibro-adipogenic progenitors, macrophages, endothelial cells, and other stromal or immune populations. Single-nucleus and single-cell datasets will reveal whether high-reserve states require specific ligand-receptor networks, extracellular matrix states, vascular-associated signals, or immune phenotypes. We further hypothesize that fibro-inflammatory niche states can predict whether ribosome biogenesis is coupled to productive growth or diverted toward repair failure and fibrosis. Question 4: Can integrated AI and dynamical models identify tipping points that distinguish adaptive hypertrophy from maladaptive remodeling? We hypothesize that muscle adaptation is governed by nonlinear thresholds rather than linear pathway activity. A moderate inflammatory response may support repair, whereas excessive or persistent immune-fibrotic signaling may decouple translational capacity from tissue growth. Similarly, increased ribosome biogenesis may promote hypertrophy only when proteostasis and autophagy remain sufficient to buffer the increased protein production load. The project will test whether graph neural networks and interpretable latent variable models can predict fiber size, fibrosis, immune infiltration, functional status, or disease state better than single-pathway scores. Mathematical dynamical models will then translate these learned relationships into candidate feedback structures, including mTOR-ribosome-autophagy loops, cytokine-mediated suppression of translational capacity, and niche-driven extracellular constraints. Collectively, these hypotheses frame translational reserve as a measurable and predictive emergent property. The goal is not to identify a universal marker, but to determine how molecular and cellular modules combine differently across contexts to produce growth, repair, decline, or inflammatory failure.

[Methods and Approach]
The project will proceed through four integrated workstreams using only publicly available data. Workstream 1 will create a curated cross-species skeletal muscle adaptation atlas. We will identify datasets from repositories including Gene Expression Omnibus, Sequence Read Archive, ArrayExpress, PRIDE, MassIVE, ProteomeXchange, ENCODE, HuBMAP where applicable, and domain-specific resources linked to human exercise, resistance training, overload, immobilization, aging, injury, muscular disease, inflammatory rheumatic disease, myositis, and cachexia. Eligible datasets will include bulk RNA-seq, microarray data where valuable, single-cell and single-nucleus RNA-seq, proteomics, phosphoproteomics, DNA methylation, chromatin accessibility, ribosome profiling or translation-associated assays, and public histological or functional metadata. No new specimens, experiments, or unpublished restricted datasets will be used. Workstream 2 will harmonize data and metadata. We will define a shared schema for species, muscle group, age, sex, perturbation, time point, disease status, training or overload protocol, injury model, assay type, cell type, fiber type, histology, function, and outcome class. Raw sequencing datasets will be reprocessed where feasible through containerized workflows; processed datasets will be incorporated when raw data are unavailable but quality criteria are met. Ortholog mapping will support mouse-rat-human comparisons. Batch effects will be addressed using study-aware normalization, negative-control evaluations, and sensitivity analyses that preserve biological contrasts. Single-cell and single-nucleus studies will be integrated with standardized quality control, cell annotation, and label transfer, while proteomic and phosphoproteomic datasets will be mapped to pathway and protein-complex features. Workstream 3 will build multiscale models of translational reserve. We will compute interpretable module scores for nucleolar and ribosome biogenesis activity, translation initiation and elongation, mTOR and nutrient signaling, autophagy, proteasome activity, unfolded protein response, inflammatory signaling, extracellular matrix remodeling, vascular programs, and immune-cell composition. These features will seed a heterogeneous graph connecting genes, proteins, complexes, pathways, cell states, perturbations, species, studies, and phenotypic outcomes. Graph neural networks will learn cross-context relationships and predict adaptive versus maladaptive outcomes. Interpretable latent variable models will define reserve axes and quantify uncertainty. GPU-accelerated workflows will support scalable alignment, methylation calling where public nanopore data exist, feature extraction, and model training. Workstream 4 will convert statistical associations into dynamic hypotheses. Using learned network structures, we will formulate reduced ordinary differential equation and, where appropriate, partial differential or compartmental models representing interactions among ribosome biogenesis, proteostasis-autophagy buffering, immune-fibrotic signaling, and tissue remodeling. These models will be fit to public time-course data from overload, injury, immobilization, and training studies. Bifurcation and sensitivity analyses will identify candidate thresholds and feedback loops separating hypertrophy, regeneration, fibrosis, and wasting. The working group will meet through NCEMS-supported in-person synthesis sessions and virtual hackathons. Subteams will focus on data curation, muscle biology interpretation, computational infrastructure, graph AI, mathematical modeling, and trainee-led reproducibility audits.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This project will deliver a public, cross-species atlas of skeletal muscle adaptation states spanning growth, repair, disuse, aging, inflammatory disease, and degenerative failure. The atlas will include harmonized metadata, standardized molecular features, cell-type annotations, phenotype mappings, and quality metrics. Its primary scientific output will be a testable definition of translational reserve as an emergent mesoscale property linking ribosome biogenesis, translation, proteostasis, autophagy, inflammation, and tissue remodeling. We expect to identify conserved high-reserve signatures associated with adaptive hypertrophy and regeneration, as well as low-reserve or uncoupled-reserve states associated with fibrosis, immune infiltration, impaired repair, and functional decline. A major impact will be predictive rather than descriptive. The integrated models will determine whether combinations of ribosome biogenesis, autophagy buffering, and immune-fibrotic niche state predict tissue outcomes better than any single pathway. Cross-species comparisons will clarify which mechanisms from rodent overload and injury models translate to human training and disease cohorts. Cell-resolved analyses will indicate how myonuclei, satellite cells, fibro-adipogenic progenitors, endothelial cells, and immune populations jointly shape emergent outcomes. The project will also produce reusable computational tools: graph-based models, interpretable reserve scores, visualization dashboards, and dynamical model templates. These resources will support future synthesis projects in other tissues where translational capacity and proteostatic stress interact with inflammation, such as heart, tendon, and immune-rich epithelial barriers. For NCEMS, the work directly advances the center mission by using existing public data, AI, and mathematical modeling to explain emergence at the molecular-to-cellular-to-tissue interface. For the broader community, it will provide a mechanistic framework for understanding why similar anabolic cues produce growth in some settings and maladaptive remodeling in others.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
The working group will operate under open, team-based, and reproducible science principles from project initiation. All data used will be publicly available, and each dataset will be documented with accession numbers, licensing status, provenance, assay type, inclusion criteria, quality metrics, and processing decisions. We will release a living data catalog and metadata schema early in the project to invite community feedback before final modeling decisions are locked. Analysis workflows will be implemented with version-controlled repositories, containerized software environments, workflow managers, and continuous integration tests for key pipeline components. Code will be deposited on public platforms under permissive open-source licenses, with stable archival releases assigned digital object identifiers. Reprocessed feature matrices, harmonized metadata, model inputs, trained model weights, and non-restricted derived outputs will be shared through appropriate public repositories. When redistribution of processed data is constrained by repository terms, we will provide scripts that regenerate the features from the original accessions. Reproducibility will be strengthened through prespecified analysis plans, blinded outcome prediction tasks where feasible, independent replication across held-out studies, and negative-control analyses. Model performance will be reported with uncertainty estimates, study-level cross-validation, and explicit tests for species, sex, age, disease, and platform bias. Interpretability methods will be used to identify which features drive predictions, but mechanistic claims will be restricted to patterns supported across independent datasets or dynamic model analyses. Trainees will participate in reproducibility rotations in which they attempt to rerun workflows, inspect metadata consistency, and document failure modes. The group will also create user-facing tutorials for muscle biologists, computational scientists, and mathematical modelers. Publications will be submitted as open access whenever possible, and preprints will be posted. Interactive dashboards will allow users to explore reserve signatures, cell states, perturbations, and model predictions without requiring advanced programming skills.

[Budget and Resources]
NCEMS support is requested for the coordination, computational infrastructure, trainee development, and community engagement required for a synthesis project of this scale. Personnel effort will support a project coordinator or data steward to manage dataset inventories, metadata standards, meeting logistics, documentation, and public releases. Funds will also support graduate student and postdoctoral participation from the collaborating groups, with dedicated time for data curation, GPU-enabled workflow development, graph modeling, mathematical analysis, and reproducibility testing. Travel support is essential for two NCEMS-hosted in-person working group meetings per year, supplemented by virtual analysis sprints. In-person sessions will focus on ontology decisions, biological interpretation of model outputs, trainee training, and integration across muscle physiology, inflammatory disease, AI, and dynamical modeling. Computational resources will include cloud or institutional high-performance computing time, GPU access for large-scale reprocessing and model training, secure project storage for public raw and derived data, and web hosting for dashboards and documentation. The project will not budget for new experimental data generation, animal studies, clinical recruitment, sample acquisition, sequencing, imaging, or wet-lab validation. All analyses will reuse public datasets. Additional resources will support software engineering, container maintenance, data archival fees, open-access publication costs, and accessibility of training materials. NCEMS resources are uniquely necessary because the project requires neutral convening, shared infrastructure, community standards, and cross-disciplinary collaboration beyond existing bilateral collaborations. The working group will include expertise in skeletal muscle adaptation, translational control, inflammation and rheumatic disease, public multi-omic data reuse, high-performance computing, graph neural networks, and mathematical modeling. Trainees will receive structured cross-training through workshops on muscle biology, public repository mining, reproducible bioinformatics, GPU-accelerated analysis, network learning, and dynamical systems. Deliverables tied to budget milestones will include the public dataset catalog, harmonized atlas release, baseline reserve scoring pipeline, graph model release, dynamic model notebooks, visualization portal, and final synthesis manuscripts.

abstract_text:
Biomolecular condensates emerge from many weak, multivalent interactions among intrinsically disordered regions, structured domains, nucleic acids, metabolites, and post-translational modifications. Yet the field lacks a synthesis-level answer to a central question: which molecular features determine whether a condensate remains a dynamic cellular compartment, becomes a gel-like regulatory hub, or crosses into aberrant aggregation? We propose a community-scale synthesis project that will integrate public sequence, biophysical, imaging, proteomic, and disease-variant data to build a predictive atlas connecting disordered-region molecular grammar to mesoscale condensate material properties.

The working group will assemble and harmonize existing public data from LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, DisProt, MobiDB, UniProt, AlphaFold confidence profiles, PhosphoSitePlus, PRIDE, BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, ClinVar, gnomAD, and published supplementary datasets reporting phase diagrams, FRAP recovery, droplet fusion, viscosity proxies, SAXS/NMR-derived ensemble parameters, turbidity, microscopy phenotypes, and aggregation outcomes. The project will focus on three biologically important condensate classes that are rarely analyzed together: RNA-binding protein granules linked to neurodegeneration, transcriptional and chromatin-associated condensates, and stress- or metabolite-responsive condensates involving polyamines, phosphorylation, oxidation, or other cellular-state variables.

Our central hypothesis is that condensate material state is not encoded by single features such as net charge or aromatic content alone, but by higher-order patterns: sticker valence and spacing, charge blockiness, transient structure propensity, partner valence, nucleic acid context, post-translational modification state, and cellular concentration regimes. These features jointly produce emergent mesoscale properties that can be inferred only by integrating heterogeneous datasets across proteins, organisms, experimental modalities, and disease contexts.

The synthesis will proceed in four coordinated activities. First, we will create an open condensate-material ontology that standardizes experimental descriptors such as liquid-like exchange, viscoelasticity, aging, demixing, gelation, and irreversible aggregation. Second, we will extract quantitative and semi-quantitative material-state labels from public tables, figures, repositories, and curated literature using reproducible text-mining and human-in-the-loop annotation. Third, we will compute interpretable polymer-physics and sequence-patterning features for disordered regions and combine them with PTM, mutation, abundance, localization, RNA-binding, and interaction-network features. Fourth, we will train benchmarked machine-learning and statistical models to predict condensate state transitions and identify conserved physical rules shared across neurodegenerative proteins, transcription factors, histone tails, and synthetic condensate scaffolds.

This project requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory can curate, normalize, and interpret the dispersed data spanning biophysics, cell biology, neurodegeneration, genomics, image analysis, and polymer theory. The working group will bring together experts in intrinsically disordered proteins, condensate physics, chromatin organization, neurodegenerative disease, proteomics, bioimage informatics, evolutionary analysis, and interpretable AI. Deliverables will include an openly licensed database, FAIR workflows, benchmark datasets, interactive visualization tools, and training modules for graduate students and postdocs in reproducible data synthesis. By transforming scattered public observations into an integrated mesoscale atlas, the project will provide a general framework for predicting how molecular disorder gives rise to emergent cellular organization and when that organization becomes pathological.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates provide a prominent example of mesoscale emergence in molecular and cellular biology. They are not defined by a single molecular bond or a fixed stoichiometric structure, but by collective interactions among proteins, nucleic acids, small molecules, post-translational modifications, and cellular environments. Intrinsically disordered regions are especially important because their sequence patterns encode weak, multivalent contacts that can produce liquid droplets, viscoelastic assemblies, gels, demixed subphases, or aggregates. These material states influence RNA metabolism, transcription, chromatin organization, stress responses, signaling, and proteostasis. However, the field still lacks a general synthesis-level framework that connects molecular grammar to condensate material state across biological contexts.

This gap is scientifically important because condensates can be functional, adaptive, or pathological depending on their emergent physical properties. RNA-binding proteins such as TDP-43, FUS, hnRNPA1, Tau, and alpha-synuclein illustrate how dynamic assemblies can support cellular regulation yet become associated with neurodegenerative disease when aging, mutation, oxidation, altered concentration, or partner composition shifts the material state toward gelation or aggregation. Transcription factors, chromatin regulators, histone tails, and enhancer-associated proteins form condensates that may concentrate regulatory machinery and reorganize nuclear space. Stress-responsive condensates, including assemblies modulated by phosphorylation, oxidation, metabolites, and polyamines, reveal that cellular state can tune phase behavior without changing the underlying primary sequence. These classes are usually studied in separate communities, limiting discovery of conserved principles.

Public data now make synthesis possible. Databases such as LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, DisProt, MobiDB, UniProt, PhosphoSitePlus, PRIDE, ClinVar, gnomAD, BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, and AlphaFold confidence profiles contain complementary information on phase separation, intrinsic disorder, protein domains, post-translational modifications, variants, abundance, localization, structure prediction confidence, imaging, and disease relevance. Published supplementary datasets further report phase diagrams, FRAP recovery, droplet coalescence, turbidity, viscosity proxies, SAXS and NMR ensemble measurements, microscopy phenotypes, and aggregation outcomes. NCEMS support is essential because the required integration exceeds the scope of a single laboratory. The project demands expertise in polymer physics, protein disorder, condensate biology, neurodegeneration, chromatin, proteomics, bioimage analysis, evolutionary genomics, ontology development, and interpretable AI. It also requires community standards for defining material-state labels and uncertainty. By synthesizing only publicly available data, this working group will directly address NCEMS priorities: discovering emergent principles at the mesoscale, building open analytical strategies, training data-savvy trainees, and creating reusable community infrastructure. The proposed atlas will transform isolated observations into a coherent resource for understanding when molecular disorder generates dynamic cellular organization and when the same principles promote pathological transitions.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
The overarching research question is: which combinations of disordered-region sequence features, molecular partners, modifications, and cellular context determine the emergent material state of biomolecular condensates? We will address this question through five linked subquestions designed for synthesis across publicly available data.

Question 1 asks whether condensate material states can be represented by a shared ontology across experimental systems. Current studies use overlapping but inconsistent descriptors, including liquid-like, dynamic, gel-like, aged, solid-like, immobile, demixed, fibrillar, and aggregated. We hypothesize that these descriptors can be mapped onto a multidimensional material-state framework defined by exchange kinetics, coalescence behavior, viscoelasticity, reversibility, internal organization, and aggregation propensity. This framework will allow both quantitative labels, such as FRAP half-time and mobile fraction, and semi-quantitative labels, such as rapid fusion or irreversible puncta, to be used with explicit uncertainty.

Question 2 asks whether higher-order sequence grammar predicts material state more effectively than simple composition. We hypothesize that sticker valence, aromatic and cationic residue spacing, charge patterning, glycine and proline distribution, hydrophobic clustering, transient helical or beta propensity, low-complexity architecture, and domain-disorder boundaries jointly encode the interaction landscape that drives phase behavior. Single variables such as net charge per residue or fraction of aromatic residues will be informative but insufficient.

Question 3 asks how molecular partners reshape the sequence-to-material relationship. Many condensates arise through interactions among disordered regions, structured RNA-binding domains, RNA or DNA, chromatin, folded enzymes, scaffolds, clients, metabolites, and polyamines. We hypothesize that partner valence and chemical type act as context-dependent modifiers: RNA and chromatin can either solubilize or crosslink condensates, polyamines can strengthen electrostatic bridges, and structured domains can nucleate demixing or aggregation when local unfolding exposes additional stickers.

Question 4 asks how post-translational modifications and disease variants alter emergent states. We hypothesize that phosphorylation, acetylation, methylation, oxidation, and disease-associated substitutions shift material state by perturbing charge blocks, sticker accessibility, transient structure, and interaction specificity. Some modifications will dissolve condensates, whereas others will create new crosslinks or alter aging kinetics. Disease variants will be most interpretable when analyzed as perturbations to sequence grammar and partner networks rather than as isolated annotations.

Question 5 asks whether physical rules are conserved across condensate classes. We hypothesize that RNA-binding granules, transcriptional and chromatin condensates, and stress-responsive condensates share general principles but occupy different regions of a common feature space. The working group will test whether models trained on one condensate class transfer to another, whether conserved sequence patterns correlate with similar material states across species, and whether synthetic condensate systems reveal design rules that also explain natural assemblies. Together, these hypotheses frame condensate material state as an emergent mesoscale phenotype arising from molecular grammar plus context.

[Methods and Approach]
This project will use only existing publicly available data and will be organized as a coordinated NCEMS working group with four integrated workstreams. No new experimental measurements will be generated.

Workstream 1 will define the data model and condensate-material ontology. Domain experts will establish controlled vocabularies for molecular components, experimental modality, perturbation type, environmental condition, concentration regime, phase behavior, material-state descriptor, and evidence strength. The ontology will represent liquid-like exchange, coarsening, fusion, aging, viscoelasticity, gelation, demixing, fibrillization, and irreversible aggregation as related but separable observables. Each label will include provenance, uncertainty, and links to the original public source.

Workstream 2 will assemble and harmonize public datasets. We will integrate entries from LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, DisProt, MobiDB, UniProt, AlphaFold predicted confidence profiles, PhosphoSitePlus, PRIDE, BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, ClinVar, gnomAD, STRING, BioGRID, and relevant supplementary tables from published studies. The working group will focus on RNA-binding and neurodegeneration-linked proteins; transcription factors, histone tails, and chromatin regulators; and stress- or metabolite-responsive condensates. Automated pipelines will retrieve sequences, isoforms, domains, disorder annotations, PTMs, abundance estimates, localization, interaction partners, variants, and available image or biophysical metadata. Literature tables and figures reporting phase diagrams, FRAP, droplet fusion, turbidity, SAXS, NMR, microscopy phenotypes, and aggregation outcomes will be extracted through text mining, table parsing, figure digitization, and human-in-the-loop curation.

Workstream 3 will compute interpretable features. Sequence-level features will include net charge, charge patterning, kappa-like metrics, sticker valence, aromatic spacing, arginine and lysine distribution, hydrophobic clustering, glycine and proline content, predicted disorder, low-complexity segmentation, transient structure propensity, prion-like composition, and domain adjacency. Context features will include RNA-binding annotation, nucleic acid type, partner valence, PTM state, disease or population variants, concentration, salt, temperature, crowding, oxidative condition, polyamine or metabolite presence, cellular compartment, species, and experimental modality. Where possible, ensemble descriptors from public SAXS or NMR studies will be linked to sequence features.

Workstream 4 will build benchmark models and visualization tools. We will train baseline statistical models, regularized regression, random forests, gradient-boosted trees, graph-based models, and uncertainty-aware classifiers to predict material-state labels and transitions. Evaluation will use nested cross-validation, protein-family holdouts, condensate-class holdouts, and modality-specific holdouts to test generalization rather than memorization. Model interpretation will emphasize feature effects, interaction terms, counterfactual sequence perturbations, and transferability across condensate classes. Trainees will participate in annotation sprints, reproducible workflow development, model benchmarking, and community tutorials. NCEMS meetings will enable iterative standard setting, conflict resolution, and cross-disciplinary synthesis that cannot be achieved by isolated groups.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The project will produce a publicly accessible condensate-material atlas that links molecular grammar, biological context, and emergent mesoscale material state. The primary deliverables will be an openly licensed harmonized database, an ontology for condensate material descriptors, benchmark datasets for prediction tasks, reproducible feature-generation pipelines, interpretable modeling workflows, and an interactive web interface for exploring proteins, variants, modifications, partners, and predicted state transitions.

Scientifically, the atlas will address a fundamental unresolved problem: why similar classes of disordered proteins can form dynamic compartments in one context, gel-like regulatory assemblies in another, and pathological aggregates under stress or mutation. By comparing RNA-binding granules, transcriptional and chromatin-associated condensates, and stress-responsive condensates in a common framework, the project will reveal whether shared polymer-physics principles govern diverse cellular assemblies. It will also identify where biological specificity enters through RNA, chromatin, structured domains, PTMs, abundance, localization, or disease variants.

The impact will extend beyond cataloging known condensates. The project will generate testable predictions for future experimental studies, including sequence motifs likely to promote aging, PTMs predicted to dissolve or harden condensates, and variants that may shift functional assemblies toward pathological states. The benchmark datasets will support more rigorous development of machine-learning models for intrinsically disordered proteins and condensates. The ontology will improve communication across communities that currently use inconsistent terminology. For NCEMS, the project directly advances synthesis research on mesoscale emergence by converting heterogeneous public observations into reusable, quantitative knowledge. It will also train graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in data integration, reproducible computation, public-resource curation, and cross-disciplinary collaboration.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
The working group will follow open, team-based, and reproducible science practices from project launch. All data products derived from public sources will be released under permissive licenses whenever source licenses allow, with clear attribution and provenance. The atlas will use persistent identifiers for proteins, isoforms, variants, publications, datasets, images, and curated observations. Each record will include source information, extraction method, curator identity or automated pipeline version, evidence type, and uncertainty level.

All code will be developed in public version-controlled repositories using issue tracking, code review, continuous integration, and documented release tags. Computational workflows will be implemented in reproducible workflow systems such as Snakemake or Nextflow, with containerized environments using Docker or Apptainer. Processed data, benchmark splits, model artifacts, and documentation will be deposited in stable repositories such as Zenodo, Figshare, OSF, or institutional archives with DOIs. Interactive notebooks will demonstrate data retrieval, feature calculation, model training, and visualization.

To ensure reliability, the project will implement independent double annotation for a subset of curated material-state labels, adjudication of disagreements, inter-annotator agreement metrics, and versioned updates. Models will be evaluated on pre-specified benchmark tasks with transparent reporting of missingness, class imbalance, uncertainty, and domain limitations. Negative and ambiguous cases will be retained rather than discarded, because they are essential for robust synthesis.

Training will be embedded in open-science practice. Graduate students and postdocs will receive instruction in FAIR data principles, ontology design, reproducible workflows, responsible machine learning, and public documentation. Community tutorials, annotation guides, and recorded workshops will allow external researchers to reuse and extend the resource. The project will not generate new experimental data, but it will generate openly available synthesis products that enable the broader community to ask sharper mechanistic questions.

[Budget and Resources]
NCEMS support is requested to enable the coordination, infrastructure, and trainee engagement required for a community-scale synthesis effort. The largest need is working-group coordination. Funds will support in-person and virtual meetings that bring together experts in intrinsically disordered proteins, condensate physics, chromatin biology, neurodegeneration, proteomics, bioimage informatics, evolutionary analysis, ontology development, and interpretable AI. Meeting support will cover travel, lodging, facilitation, hybrid participation tools, and structured annotation and modeling sprints.

Personnel support will prioritize trainees and essential technical work. Graduate students and postdoctoral researchers will contribute to curation, literature mining, workflow implementation, benchmark construction, model evaluation, and documentation. Limited support for a data scientist or research software engineer will ensure that pipelines, database schemas, APIs, visualization tools, and public releases meet community standards. Trainee participation is central to the project because the atlas requires sustained integration work and provides a practical training environment in modern synthesis biology.

Computational resources will include cloud storage and compute for public dataset retrieval, image metadata processing, feature calculation, model benchmarking, container builds, and web deployment. The project will use open-source software whenever possible and will rely on NCEMS cyberinfrastructure, collaboration platforms, and reproducibility guidance to reduce duplication and increase sustainability.

Additional resources will support open dissemination: DOI-linked data deposition, website hosting, workshop materials, community webinars, and documentation. No funds will be used to generate new experimental data, purchase laboratory reagents, or conduct new wet-lab assays. The budget is therefore tightly aligned with NCEMS goals: synthesizing existing public molecular and cellular data, supporting collaboration beyond any single laboratory, creating reusable open infrastructure, and training a data-savvy workforce capable of studying emergent mesoscale biological phenomena.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates emerge from many weak, multivalent interactions among intrinsically disordered regions, structured domains, nucleic acids, metabolites, and post-translational modifications. Yet the field lacks a synthesis-level answer to a central question: which molecular features determine whether a condensate remains a dynamic cellular compartment, becomes a gel-like regulatory hub, or crosses into aberrant aggregation? We propose a community-scale synthesis project that will integrate public sequence, biophysical, imaging, proteomic, and disease-variant data to build a predictive atlas connecting disordered-region molecular grammar to mesoscale condensate material properties.

The working group will assemble and harmonize existing public data from LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, DisProt, MobiDB, UniProt, AlphaFold confidence profiles, PhosphoSitePlus, PRIDE, BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, ClinVar, gnomAD, and published supplementary datasets reporting phase diagrams, FRAP recovery, droplet fusion, viscosity proxies, SAXS/NMR-derived ensemble parameters, turbidity, microscopy phenotypes, and aggregation outcomes. The project will focus on three biologically important condensate classes that are rarely analyzed together: RNA-binding protein granules linked to neurodegeneration, transcriptional and chromatin-associated condensates, and stress- or metabolite-responsive condensates involving polyamines, phosphorylation, oxidation, or other cellular-state variables.

Our central hypothesis is that condensate material state is not encoded by single features such as net charge or aromatic content alone, but by higher-order patterns: sticker valence and spacing, charge blockiness, transient structure propensity, partner valence, nucleic acid context, post-translational modification state, and cellular concentration regimes. These features jointly produce emergent mesoscale properties that can be inferred only by integrating heterogeneous datasets across proteins, organisms, experimental modalities, and disease contexts.

The synthesis will proceed in four coordinated activities. First, we will create an open condensate-material ontology that standardizes experimental descriptors such as liquid-like exchange, viscoelasticity, aging, demixing, gelation, and irreversible aggregation. Second, we will extract quantitative and semi-quantitative material-state labels from public tables, figures, repositories, and curated literature using reproducible text-mining and human-in-the-loop annotation. Third, we will compute interpretable polymer-physics and sequence-patterning features for disordered regions and combine them with PTM, mutation, abundance, localization, RNA-binding, and interaction-network features. Fourth, we will train benchmarked machine-learning and statistical models to predict condensate state transitions and identify conserved physical rules shared across neurodegenerative proteins, transcription factors, histone tails, and synthetic condensate scaffolds.

This project requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory can curate, normalize, and interpret the dispersed data spanning biophysics, cell biology, neurodegeneration, genomics, image analysis, and polymer theory. The working group will bring together experts in intrinsically disordered proteins, condensate physics, chromatin organization, neurodegenerative disease, proteomics, bioimage informatics, evolutionary analysis, and interpretable AI. Deliverables will include an openly licensed database, FAIR workflows, benchmark datasets, interactive visualization tools, and training modules for graduate students and postdocs in reproducible data synthesis. By transforming scattered public observations into an integrated mesoscale atlas, the project will provide a general framework for predicting how molecular disorder gives rise to emergent cellular organization and when that organization becomes pathological.

Although public transcriptomic, genomic, proteomic, and metabolomic datasets now exist for bears, ground squirrels, bats, hamsters, tenrecs, dwarf lemurs, and laboratory mouse models of torpor, these datasets remain fragmented across species, tissues, seasons, and analytical frameworks. This working group will synthesize existing public data to ask a central question: what conserved and lineage-specific molecular programs allow diverse mammals to reversibly reorganize cellular energy use during hibernation without pathological damage? By mapping orthologous genes and pathways across species and tissues, we will identify modules that repeatedly change during torpor, arousal, winter fasting, and experimentally induced metabolic shifts. We will then test whether these modules show signatures of convergent regulatory architecture across independent hibernating lineages, using comparative genomics, gene regulatory network inference, ancestral-state-aware enrichment analyses, and machine learning approaches that explicitly account for phylogenetic relatedness. A major innovation will be to move beyond lists of differentially expressed genes toward cross-scale synthesis: we will infer how regulatory changes in individual pathways combine into tissue-level and organism-level hibernation states. full_text:
[Abstract]
Mammalian hibernation is an extreme example of biological emergence: coordinated molecular changes across cells and tissues generate organism-level phenotypes that include profound metabolic suppression, altered insulin sensitivity, muscle maintenance, immune modulation, and reversible shifts in body temperature. Although public transcriptomic, genomic, proteomic, and metabolomic datasets now exist for bears, ground squirrels, bats, hamsters, tenrecs, dwarf lemurs, and laboratory mouse models of torpor, these datasets remain fragmented across species, tissues, seasons, and analytical frameworks. We will build an open, comparative atlas integrating publicly available bulk RNA-seq, single-cell and single-nucleus RNA-seq where available, proteomic, metabolomic, genome annotation, and regulatory datasets from hibernating and non-hibernating mammals. The project will focus on emergent mesoscale processes that link molecules to cellular and tissue phenotypes, including mitochondrial remodeling, lipid droplet dynamics, endoplasmic reticulum stress responses, circadian-metabolic coupling, extracellular matrix remodeling, and immune-cell state shifts. By mapping orthologous genes and pathways across species and tissues, we will identify modules that repeatedly change during torpor, arousal, winter fasting, and experimentally induced metabolic shifts. We will then test whether these modules show signatures of convergent regulatory architecture across independent hibernating lineages, using comparative genomics, gene regulatory network inference, ancestral-state-aware enrichment analyses, and machine learning approaches that explicitly account for phylogenetic relatedness. A major innovation will be to move beyond lists of differentially expressed genes toward cross-scale synthesis: we will infer how regulatory changes in individual pathways combine into tissue-level and organism-level hibernation states. For example, we will evaluate whether mitochondrial genes, lipid-handling genes, circadian regulators, and inflammatory mediators form conserved cross-tissue network motifs that predict hibernation state better than any single tissue or pathway. We will also compare natural hibernation datasets with public datasets from fasting, cold exposure, obesity, diabetes, muscle disuse, and aging models to distinguish hibernation-specific protective programs from generic stress responses. The resulting resource will provide a mechanistic framework for understanding how reversible metabolic depression emerges from coordinated molecular and cellular changes across tissues. NCEMS support is essential because the project requires a transdisciplinary working group spanning evolutionary genomics, hibernation physiology, comparative transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, network biology, data harmonization, and phylogenetic statistics. No single laboratory currently has the breadth of expertise or the capacity to curate, standardize, and jointly analyze these diverse public datasets at community scale. Deliverables will include a FAIR hibernation multi-omics atlas, reproducible analysis workflows, orthology-aware gene module annotations, interactive network visualizations, and training materials for graduate students and postdoctoral researchers. By synthesizing existing public data across mammals, this project will reveal how molecular programs combine into emergent cellular and physiological states, while creating a reusable open-science platform for future studies of metabolic resilience.

[Background and Significance]
Hibernation is among the most striking mammalian examples of reversible physiological reorganization. During torpor and seasonal dormancy, animals can suppress metabolic rate, alter fuel use, tolerate prolonged fasting, preserve skeletal muscle and bone, modulate immune activity, and repeatedly transition between low-temperature and euthermic states without the damage typically associated with hypothermia, starvation, insulin resistance, disuse, or ischemia-reperfusion. These organismal phenotypes emerge from coordinated changes across molecular pathways, cell states, tissues, and endocrine axes. Yet the field lacks a unified comparative framework for identifying which molecular programs are conserved across hibernating mammals, which are lineage-specific, and how these programs combine across biological scales to generate resilient metabolic suppression. Public data now make such a synthesis timely and feasible. Transcriptomic resources are available for hibernating and active-season bears, ground squirrels, hamsters, bats, tenrecs, dwarf lemurs, and mouse models of torpor-like states. Several studies include multiple tissues such as liver, skeletal muscle, adipose, heart, brain, and immune-related tissues; some include time-series or experimentally perturbed conditions, including feeding, cold exposure, and in vitro temperature manipulations. Public proteomic, metabolomic, genome annotation, and regulatory datasets add complementary information on protein abundance, energy metabolites, lipid species, gene family evolution, and cis-regulatory landscapes. However, these datasets are dispersed across repositories, generated using distinct library preparation methods and annotation versions, and analyzed with species-specific pipelines. As a result, current knowledge remains fragmented into organism- or tissue-specific findings, limiting the ability to detect shared emergent principles. This project directly addresses NCEMS priorities by synthesizing existing public molecular and cellular data to investigate an emergent mesoscale phenomenon: the transition from molecular regulatory changes to tissue-level and whole-organism metabolic states. The proposed atlas will focus on cellular processes that sit between individual biomolecules and organelles or tissues, including mitochondrial remodeling, lipid droplet dynamics, endoplasmic reticulum stress buffering, circadian-metabolic coupling, extracellular matrix remodeling, immune-cell state changes, and proteostasis. These mesoscale processes are plausible points at which coordinated gene, protein, and metabolite changes generate higher-order hibernation phenotypes. A comparative evolutionary perspective is essential because hibernation and torpor have arisen in multiple mammalian lineages with different body sizes, thermal strategies, diets, and life histories. Convergent molecular patterns across independent lineages would indicate deeply reusable regulatory solutions, whereas lineage-specific patterns may reveal alternative routes to metabolic resilience. Integrating phylogenetic methods with multi-omics network analysis will allow us to separate shared ancestry from repeated evolutionary recruitment of pathways. The proposed working group is beyond the capacity of a single laboratory. It requires expertise in hibernation biology, evolutionary genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, data harmonization, network inference, comparative methods, and open computational infrastructure. NCEMS support will enable a community-scale synthesis that transforms scattered public datasets into a reusable resource and a mechanistic framework for understanding how reversible metabolic suppression emerges from coordinated molecular and cellular processes.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
The central research question is: what conserved and lineage-specific molecular programs enable diverse mammals to reversibly suppress metabolism while avoiding pathological consequences? We will address this question through four integrated aims. Aim 1 asks which genes, proteins, metabolites, pathways, and cellular modules consistently change across torpor, arousal, winter fasting, and active-season states. We hypothesize that conserved hibernation modules will be enriched for mitochondrial substrate switching, fatty acid transport and beta-oxidation, lipid droplet regulation, redox control, circadian timing, unfolded protein response modulation, and anti-inflammatory signaling. We further hypothesize that these modules will be more reproducible at the pathway and network level than at the individual gene level because orthologous genes may be regulated differently while preserving higher-order cellular functions. Aim 2 asks whether hibernation-associated modules are shared across tissues or specialized by tissue context. We hypothesize that liver, adipose, skeletal muscle, heart, brain, and immune-enriched tissues will show distinct implementations of a common seasonal metabolic program. For example, adipose may emphasize lipid mobilization and endocrine signaling, muscle may emphasize proteostasis and contractile maintenance, liver may emphasize ketogenesis and detoxification, and brain may emphasize circadian and neuroendocrine regulation. We predict that cross-tissue network motifs, rather than any single tissue signature, will best classify hibernation state. Aim 3 asks whether repeated hibernation phenotypes across mammals are associated with convergent regulatory architecture. We hypothesize that independent hibernating lineages will show enrichment of regulatory changes near orthologs involved in energy sensing, nuclear receptor signaling, circadian regulation, and stress-response buffering. We will test whether these signals exceed expectations under phylogenetic null models that account for shared ancestry, genome quality, tissue sampling, and study design. This aim distinguishes true convergence from conservation of ancient mammalian stress responses or lineage-specific adaptation. Aim 4 asks which components of hibernation resemble generic responses to fasting, cold, obesity, diabetes, muscle disuse, inflammation, or aging, and which appear specific to protective reversible metabolic suppression. We hypothesize that hibernators share some molecular responses with non-hibernating stress models, such as increased lipid utilization during fasting and altered inflammatory tone during cold exposure. However, we expect hibernation-specific protective programs to include coordinated suppression of damage-associated inflammation, maintenance of insulin signaling flexibility, preservation of muscle structural networks, and reversible remodeling of mitochondrial function without chronic oxidative injury. Across these aims, our overarching hypothesis is that hibernation is not produced by a single master pathway but by a distributed, modular regulatory architecture. Emergent resilience arises when cellular energy handling, circadian timing, stress buffering, immune modulation, and tissue remodeling are synchronized across organs. This proposal will test that hypothesis using only existing public datasets, with explicit attention to uncertainty, batch effects, phylogenetic non-independence, and differences in sampling design among species.

[Methods and Approach]
The working group will build a curated, orthology-aware multi-omics atlas from public datasets. We will identify datasets through NCBI SRA, GEO, ArrayExpress, ENA, PRIDE, MetaboLights, MassIVE, Dryad, Figshare, Zenodo, Ensembl, NCBI RefSeq, UCSC, and published supplementary materials. Eligible datasets will include publicly available bulk RNA-seq, single-cell or single-nucleus RNA-seq, proteomics, metabolomics, genome annotations, regulatory annotations, and relevant metadata from hibernating mammals and non-hibernating comparator models. No new experimental data will be generated. Inclusion criteria will document species, tissue or cell type, season or physiological state, sex and age when available, sampling temperature, fasting status, library or assay type, repository accession, license, and genome annotation version. Aim 1 will harmonize molecular features across species. For transcriptomes, we will process raw reads where feasible using reproducible workflows for quality control, trimming, alignment or quasi-mapping, transcript quantification, and gene-level summarization. When raw data are unavailable, we will incorporate author-provided count matrices with provenance annotations. Orthology will be established using Ensembl Compara, OrthoDB, NCBI orthologs, and reciprocal sequence searches for species with incomplete annotations. Analyses will be conducted at multiple feature resolutions: one-to-one orthologs, gene families, pathways, and data-driven co-expression modules. Proteomic and metabolomic datasets will be mapped to standardized identifiers, including UniProt, KEGG, Reactome, HMDB, LipidMaps, and MetaboLights vocabularies. Aim 2 will identify conserved and tissue-specific hibernation modules. Within each dataset, we will model state-associated changes using appropriate generalized linear or mixed models, controlling for tissue, sex, batch, season, and study-specific covariates when available. Cross-study synthesis will use random-effects meta-analysis, rank-based aggregation, and pathway-level enrichment to reduce dependence on platform-specific effects. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis, multi-omics factor analysis, and graph-based community detection will identify modules associated with torpor, arousal, interbout euthermia, winter fasting, active season, and experimental perturbations. Single-cell data will be reannotated using reference mapping and marker-based approaches, then integrated to test whether hibernation shifts cell-type abundance, within-cell transcriptional states, or both. Aim 3 will incorporate evolutionary models. We will construct or use published mammalian phylogenies and apply phylogenetic generalized least squares, phylogenetic mixed models, ancestral-state-aware enrichment, and permutation tests that preserve clade structure. We will test whether hibernating lineages independently recruit similar pathways or regulatory features while accounting for genome assembly quality and uneven sampling. Regulatory analyses will integrate public ATAC-seq, ChIP-seq, promoter annotations, conserved noncoding elements, transcription factor motif databases, and inferred regulatory networks. Aim 4 will compare natural hibernation with public datasets from fasting, cold exposure, diabetes, obesity, aging, inflammation, hypoxia, and muscle disuse. Machine learning classifiers, including regularized regression, random forests, gradient boosting, and graph neural network approaches where appropriate, will evaluate whether multi-tissue modules predict hibernation state better than single-pathway models. All models will use nested cross-validation, leave-one-species-out testing, and sensitivity analyses to quantify robustness.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This project will produce five major outcomes. First, we will deliver a FAIR comparative hibernation multi-omics atlas that links species, tissues, physiological states, molecular features, orthology relationships, and analysis-ready data matrices. Second, we will identify conserved and lineage-specific modules associated with reversible metabolic suppression, including modules related to mitochondrial remodeling, lipid handling, circadian regulation, immune modulation, extracellular matrix dynamics, and stress-response buffering. Third, we will generate cross-tissue network models that explain how molecular changes combine into higher-order hibernation states. Fourth, we will distinguish hibernation-specific protective programs from generic responses to fasting, cold exposure, metabolic disease, disuse, and aging. Fifth, we will provide reusable workflows, visualizations, and training materials for the broader molecular and cellular biology community. The scientific impact will be substantial. By moving beyond single-species differential expression studies, the project will reveal whether hibernation relies on deeply conserved mammalian pathways, convergent regulatory solutions, or diverse lineage-specific mechanisms. This will advance fundamental understanding of emergence by showing how coordinated molecular processes produce resilient cellular and organismal phenotypes. The atlas will also create a foundation for hypothesis generation in areas relevant to metabolic disease, muscle preservation, inflammation, hypothermia tolerance, and aging biology, while remaining focused on synthesis of existing data rather than translational claims. The broader impact aligns closely with NCEMS goals. The project requires collaboration across evolutionary biology, physiology, molecular biology, computational biology, and data science. It will train graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in public data reuse, reproducible workflows, comparative methods, and team science. By making all outputs open and reusable, the working group will lower barriers for future researchers, including those at institutions without extensive experimental infrastructure, to participate in discovery-oriented synthesis biology.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
The project will follow open, team, and reproducible science principles from initiation. All public dataset accessions, inclusion decisions, metadata fields, processing steps, and quality-control outcomes will be documented in a version-controlled repository. We will use community standards wherever possible, including MIAME and MINSEQE-inspired metadata for transcriptomics, ProteomeXchange conventions for proteomics, metabolomics identifier standards, NCBI Taxonomy, Uberon tissue terms, Cell Ontology cell-type terms, Gene Ontology, KEGG, Reactome, and standardized orthology resources. Derived data products will be released under permissive licenses compatible with source repositories and journal requirements. Computational workflows will be implemented in workflow managers such as Nextflow or Snakemake and distributed with containerized software environments using Docker, Apptainer, Conda, or Bioconda. Analyses will be documented in executable notebooks and scripted reports. Major results will include provenance records linking every figure, table, and model output to input datasets, software versions, parameters, and commit identifiers. We will deposit code on GitHub or GitLab, archive stable releases on Zenodo, and host analysis-ready matrices, metadata, orthology tables, and network objects on repositories suitable for long-term access. Interactive visualizations will be built using open frameworks and will allow users to query species, tissues, states, pathways, and modules. This project will build an integrated comparative multi omics atlas to determine how diverse mammals reversibly reorganize cellular energy use without pathological damage, and will apply machine learning alongside evolutionary models to identify tissue specific hibernation modules. abstract_original: Mammalian hibernation is an extreme example of biological emergence: coordinated molecular changes across cells and tissues generate organism-level phenotypes that include profound metabolic suppression, altered insulin sensitivity, muscle maintenance, immune modulation, and reversible shifts in body temperature. Although public transcriptomic, genomic, proteomic, and metabolomic datasets now exist for bears, ground squirrels, bats, hamsters, tenrecs, dwarf lemurs, and laboratory mouse models of torpor, these datasets remain fragmented across species, tissues, seasons, and analytical frameworks. This working group will synthesize existing public data to ask a central question: what conserved and lineage-specific molecular programs allow diverse mammals to reversibly reorganize cellular energy use during hibernation without pathological damage? We will build an open, comparative atlas integrating publicly available bulk RNA-seq, single-cell and single-nucleus RNA-seq where available, proteomic, metabolomic, genome annotation, and regulatory datasets from hibernating and non-hibernating mammals. The project will focus on emergent mesoscale processes that link molecules to cellular and tissue phenotypes, including mitochondrial remodeling, lipid droplet dynamics, endoplasmic reticulum stress responses, circadian-metabolic coupling, extracellular matrix remodeling, and immune-cell state shifts. By mapping orthologous genes and pathways across species and tissues, we will identify modules that repeatedly change during torpor, arousal, winter fasting, and experimentally induced metabolic shifts. We will then test whether these modules show signatures of convergent regulatory architecture across independent hibernating lineages, using comparative genomics, gene regulatory network inference, ancestral-state-aware enrichment analyses, and machine learning approaches that explicitly account for phylogenetic relatedness. A major innovation will be to move beyond lists of differentially expressed genes toward cross-scale synthesis: we will infer how regulatory changes in individual pathways combine into tissue-level and organism-level hibernation states. For example, we will evaluate whether mitochondrial genes, lipid-handling genes, circadian regulators, and inflammatory mediators form conserved cross-tissue network motifs that predict hibernation state better than any single tissue or pathway. We will also compare natural hibernation datasets with public datasets from fasting, cold exposure, obesity, diabetes, muscle disuse, and aging models to distinguish hibernation-specific protective programs from generic stress responses. The resulting resource will provide a mechanistic framework for understanding how reversible metabolic depression emerges from coordinated molecular and cellular changes across tissues. NCEMS support is essential because the project requires a transdisciplinary working group spanning evolutionary genomics, hibernation physiology, comparative transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, network biology, data harmonization, and phylogenetic statistics. No single laboratory currently has the breadth of expertise or the capacity to curate, standardize, and jointly analyze these diverse public datasets at community scale. Deliverables will include a FAIR hibernation multi-omics atlas, reproducible analysis workflows, orthology-aware gene module annotations, interactive network visualizations, and training materials for graduate students and postdoctoral researchers. By synthesizing existing public data across mammals, this project will reveal how molecular programs combine into emergent cellular and physiological states, while creating a reusable open-science platform for future studies of metabolic resilience.

title: Predicting Condensate-Scale Emergence from Evolutionary and Structural Coupling Networks in Multivalent Proteins

abstract_text:
A central unsolved problem in molecular and cellular biology is how weak, distributed molecular interactions give rise to sharply different mesoscale outcomes, such as liquid-like compartments, gels, aggregates, or dispersed cellular states. We propose a community-scale synthesis project to determine whether emergent biomolecular condensate behavior can be predicted from evolutionarily conserved networks of residue, domain, and motif couplings within multivalent proteins and their interaction partners. The guiding hypothesis is that many condensate-forming systems are regulated by hidden coupling architectures: perturbations at folded domains, intrinsically disordered regions, RNA-binding surfaces, post-translational modification sites, or ion-binding regions propagate through molecular ensembles to alter mesoscale assembly thresholds and material states.

This project will use only existing public data. We will integrate protein family alignments from UniProt, Pfam, MGnify, and model-organism databases; structural models and experimental structures from AlphaFold DB, PDB, SASBDB, and integrative structure repositories; condensate annotations and phase behavior measurements from LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, PhaSePro, and curated literature-derived datasets; public mutational scans and variant-effect datasets from MaveDB, ClinVar, cBioPortal, and organismal resources; proteomic and phosphoproteomic datasets from PRIDE, MassIVE, and ProteomeXchange; RNA-binding and chromatin-associated interaction datasets from ENCODE and related repositories; and reusable molecular simulation trajectories from public simulation archives where available. These heterogeneous resources will be harmonized into a FAIR, versioned knowledge graph linking sequence features, coevolutionary constraints, structural contacts, dynamic ensembles, modification sites, disease or engineered variants, and observed condensate phenotypes.

Analytically, the working group will combine statistical sequence models, direct coupling and sector-like analyses, information-theoretic measures, graph-based structural communication models, and machine learning on experimentally annotated phase behavior. For each protein family, we will infer conserved coupling networks and map them onto folded domains, disordered regions, short linear motifs, RNA-binding interfaces, and multivalent interaction modules. We will then ask whether particular coupling architectures distinguish proteins that form regulated condensates from homologs that do not, and whether these architectures predict sensitivity to temperature, salt, RNA, phosphorylation, disease mutation, or engineered sequence changes. A major methodological outcome will be an open cross-scale framework that converts evolutionary and structural coupling information into testable predictions of mesoscale assembly propensity and state transitions.

The emergent property addressed here is not any single molecular contact, but the appearance of cellular-scale organization from ensembles of many weakly coupled molecular features.
