NCEMS support would enable the coordinated curation standards, shared computational infrastructure, trainee-led cross-training, and community benchmarking necessary to make the results reusable.

The project will deliver an open atlas of coupling networks in condensate-associated protein families, reproducible workflows for integrating evolutionary, structural, simulation, and cellular phenotype data, and prioritized predictions for variants or modification sites likely to shift mesoscale organization. By linking molecular information flow to condensate-level behavior, this synthesis will provide a general strategy for understanding how cellular material states emerge from protein sequence, structure, dynamics, and evolution.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates exemplify emergence in the molecular and cellular sciences: many individually weak and transient molecular interactions collectively produce distinct mesoscale states with cellular consequences. Proteins and nucleic acids that remain dispersed under one condition can form liquid-like droplets, viscoelastic gels, solid-like assemblies, or pathological aggregates under another. These transitions influence transcription, RNA processing, stress responses, signaling, chromatin organization, and proteostasis. Yet the field lacks a general framework for predicting when sequence-encoded molecular features will generate a particular condensate-scale outcome. This gap limits our ability to explain why closely related proteins differ in assembly behavior, why specific mutations or post-translational modifications alter material state, and how evolution tunes cellular organization without relying on stable stoichiometric complexes alone. Current condensate research has produced rich public resources, but they remain fragmented across scales. Sequence databases capture homologous families and evolutionary variation. Structural repositories contain experimental structures, predicted folded domains, and low-resolution ensemble descriptions. Phase separation databases collect reports of condensate localization, in vitro phase diagrams, disease-associated aggregation, and curated functional annotations. Public proteomic, phosphoproteomic, RNA-binding, chromatin-associated, variant-effect, and simulation datasets provide additional information on regulatory context and molecular dynamics. However, these resources are not yet integrated in a way that supports cross-family inference about how molecular coupling networks generate emergent mesoscale states. The proposed working group addresses this opportunity through synthesis research only, using existing public data to build a multiscale picture of condensate-forming proteins and their interaction partners. The central scientific premise is that condensate behavior is shaped not just by aggregate properties such as net charge, aromaticity, or valence, but by conserved networks of coupled residues, motifs, domains, disorder regions, binding surfaces, and regulatory sites. These networks may act analogously to distributed allosteric systems: perturbations at one site can shift conformational ensembles, interaction preferences, multivalent binding patterns, and ultimately phase boundaries or material states. Such coupling architectures may be visible through evolutionary covariation, structural contact maps, dynamic contact fluctuations, conserved short linear motifs, and recurrent modification or disease-variant patterns. This proposal aligns closely with NCEMS priorities because it focuses on emergence at the mesoscale between biomolecules and organelles, uses only publicly available data, and requires a transdisciplinary team. No single laboratory can assemble, standardize, analyze, and benchmark sequence evolution, structural bioinformatics, molecular simulation, condensate phenotyping, proteomics, RNA biology, and knowledge-graph infrastructure at the necessary community scale. NCEMS support will enable shared curation standards, collaborative analysis sprints, trainee cross-training, and open dissemination. The project will convert heterogeneous public resources into a reusable atlas and computational framework that links molecular information flow to cellular material organization. Its significance is both conceptual and practical: it will test whether principles of allosteric coupling and evolutionary constraint can predict emergent condensate states, and it will provide prioritized variants, sites, and protein families for future experimental study by the broader community.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This working group will pursue four integrated research questions. First, do condensate-associated multivalent proteins contain conserved coupling architectures that distinguish them from homologs or paralogs with similar composition but different mesoscale behavior? Many predictors of phase separation rely on local sequence features, including charge patterning, low-complexity content, aromatic residues, sticker-spacer grammar, disorder propensity, and prion-like domains. These features are informative, but they do not fully explain condition-specific assembly, regulated reversibility, or differences among homologous proteins. We hypothesize that condensate-forming proteins are enriched for statistically detectable networks of coevolving residues, domains, motifs, and regulatory sites that coordinate weak interactions across folded and disordered regions. Second, can these coupling networks predict sensitivity to environmental and biochemical regulators? Condensates often respond sharply to temperature, salt, pH, RNA concentration, nucleotide state, phosphorylation, methylation, acetylation, or ion binding. We hypothesize that regulator sensitivity is encoded in the topology and physical placement of coupling networks: sites that connect interaction modules, disorder regions, folded domains, and nucleic acid binding surfaces will be more likely to shift assembly thresholds than isolated sites with similar local chemistry. This hypothesis will be tested by mapping coupling features to public phase behavior annotations, phosphoproteomic datasets, RNA-binding datasets, known ion-binding sites, and available simulation-derived contact ensembles. Third, do disease-associated and engineered variants that alter condensate phenotypes preferentially occur at network control points? Variants in RNA-binding proteins, transcriptional regulators, signaling scaffolds, and chromatin-associated proteins can convert functional condensates into persistent aggregates or disrupt assembly entirely. We hypothesize that variants with strong condensate effects are enriched at evolutionarily constrained positions, interdomain communication paths, motif interfaces, or modification-linked nodes, even when those positions are not obvious from composition-based analysis. This question will integrate public mutational scans, ClinVar, cBioPortal, MaveDB, model-organism variant resources, and curated literature reports. Fourth, can a cross-scale predictive model generalize across protein families and condensate classes? Condensates differ widely in molecular composition and cellular role. Some are dominated by RNA-protein interactions, others by multivalent signaling domains, chromatin contacts, stress granule scaffolds, or amyloid-like transitions. We hypothesize that distinct coupling architectures correspond to recurrent mesoscale outcomes, such as reversible liquid-like assembly, gelation, temperature-triggered condensation, RNA-dependent buffering, phosphorylation-controlled dissolution, or aggregation-prone hardening. The proposed synthesis will therefore evaluate both family-specific models and transferable representations. Success will be measured by retrospective prediction of held-out condensate annotations, variant effects, and condition sensitivities, as well as by the generation of transparent, ranked hypotheses for future community testing. These questions are designed to advance a general theory of emergence: how distributed molecular constraints, acquired through evolution and expressed through structure and dynamics, combine to produce new cellular-scale material properties.

[Methods and Approach]
The project will proceed through coordinated synthesis modules, all using existing public data. Module 1 will define protein families and phenotype sets. We will compile condensate-associated proteins and controls from LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, PhaSePro, UniProt annotations, model-organism databases, and curated literature-derived datasets. Each entry will be assigned evidence codes for in vivo localization, in vitro phase separation, material state, reversibility, stimulus dependence, RNA involvement, disease association, and perturbation evidence. Control sets will include homologs without condensate annotations, proteins with similar composition but different localization, and paralogs with divergent assembly behavior. Module 2 will construct evolutionary and sequence-feature resources. For each family, we will retrieve homologs from UniProt, Pfam, MGnify, and organismal databases, remove redundancy, assess alignment depth, and build multiple sequence alignments suitable for statistical modeling. We will annotate folded domains, intrinsically disordered regions, low-complexity segments, short linear motifs, prion-like regions, charge patterning, aromatic clusters, RNA-binding motifs, and known post-translational modification sites. Module 3 will infer coupling networks. We will apply direct coupling analysis, Potts-type statistical models, sector-like decomposition, mutual information with phylogenetic correction, and conservation-weighted motif covariance. Couplings will be represented at residue, motif, domain, and protein-interaction levels. Network metrics will include centrality, modularity, path structure, community overlap, evolutionary conservation, and enrichment for regulatory or variant sites. Module 4 will map couplings onto structure and dynamics. Experimental structures from PDB, predicted structures from AlphaFold DB, small-angle scattering data from SASBDB, integrative models, and available public simulation trajectories will be used to determine whether inferred couplings correspond to physical contacts, alternative contact modes, domain interfaces, disordered-region docking sites, or dynamic communication paths. Graph-based structural communication models will estimate how perturbations at specific positions could propagate through folded and disordered interaction modules. Where reusable simulations exist, contact probability networks and ensemble heterogeneity will be extracted; where they do not, the project will not generate new simulations but will mark gaps for future work. Module 5 will integrate data in a FAIR knowledge graph. Nodes will include proteins, isoforms, residues, domains, motifs, modifications, structures, variants, interactions, conditions, and condensate phenotypes. Edges will encode evidence provenance, confidence, database source, and version. This graph will support machine learning and transparent querying. Module 6 will build and benchmark predictive models. We will train interpretable classifiers and regression models to predict condensate association, material class, regulator sensitivity, and variant impact from coupling-network, structural, compositional, proteomic, and interaction features. Evaluation will use nested cross-validation, family-level holdouts, negative-control sampling, literature-time splits where possible, and robustness tests for annotation bias. Trainees will participate in cross-lab analysis teams focused on curation, evolutionary inference, structural mapping, and model evaluation. NCEMS working-group meetings will be used for ontology harmonization, code review, benchmark design, and community feedback.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The project will deliver three primary scientific products. First, we will create an open atlas of evolutionary and structural coupling networks for condensate-associated multivalent protein families. The atlas will connect sequence variation, domains, disordered regions, motifs, modification sites, structures, interaction partners, variants, and condensate phenotypes in a form that can be searched, downloaded, and extended. Second, we will produce validated computational workflows that convert public sequence, structure, proteomic, interaction, variant, and phase-behavior data into predictions of mesoscale assembly propensity, material state, regulator sensitivity, and variant impact. Third, we will generate prioritized hypotheses for residues, motifs, domains, and post-translational modification sites that are likely to control condensate transitions. These predictions will be immediately useful to experimental groups studying stress granules, transcriptional condensates, chromatin compartments, RNA-processing bodies, signaling assemblies, and aggregation-linked disease proteins. The broader impact is a shift from cataloging condensate components to explaining emergent material behavior through conserved molecular information flow. By testing whether principles from allostery, molecular evolution, statistical physics, structural bioinformatics, and phase separation can be unified, the project will address a central NCEMS theme: how new biological properties appear across scales of composition, space, time, motion, and information. The synthesis will also establish community standards for representing condensate evidence, condition dependence, and uncertainty. The resulting knowledge graph and benchmarks will provide durable infrastructure for future method development. Training outcomes will include a cohort of graduate students and postdoctoral researchers who gain practical experience in open data integration, reproducible computational biology, molecular evolution, structural analysis, and collaborative team science. Because the project uses only public data and produces reusable outputs, its impact will extend well beyond the working group.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
Open science is central to the project design. All derived datasets, metadata schemas, analysis workflows, model outputs, and documentation will be released under permissive licenses consistent with source-database requirements. The working group will maintain a public project repository containing version-controlled code, workflow definitions, issue tracking, curation guidelines, benchmark specifications, and release notes. Computational workflows will be implemented with reproducible workflow managers and containerized software environments so that analyses can be rerun on NCEMS infrastructure, institutional clusters, or cloud platforms. Each data release will include persistent identifiers, provenance records, database versions, confidence scores, and machine-readable metadata following FAIR principles. We will distinguish primary public data from derived annotations and will preserve links to source records in UniProt, Pfam, MGnify, PDB, AlphaFold DB, SASBDB, LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, PhaSePro, PRIDE, MassIVE, ProteomeXchange, ENCODE, MaveDB, ClinVar, cBioPortal, and related repositories. Reproducibility will be strengthened through benchmark datasets with frozen training and test splits, negative controls, uncertainty estimates, and documented exclusion criteria. Model performance will be reported with family-level holdouts and sensitivity analyses to identify annotation bias, phylogenetic leakage, and overfitting. The project will follow open team-science practices, including shared authorship expectations, transparent decision logs, regular code review, and trainee-accessible onboarding materials. NCEMS meetings will include reproducibility checkpoints where independent subgroup members rerun selected workflows and compare outputs. Educational materials, including tutorials on coupling inference, condensate data curation, structural mapping, and knowledge-graph queries, will be made publicly available. Publications will be submitted as preprints and, where possible, to open-access venues. The final products will include a public web portal, downloadable graph files, documented APIs, and archived software releases.

[Budget and Resources]
NCEMS support is essential because the proposed synthesis requires sustained coordination, shared cyberinfrastructure, and cross-disciplinary training beyond the capacity of a single laboratory or informal collaboration. Requested resources will support working-group meetings, trainee participation, data engineering, computation, and dissemination. Travel and meeting funds will enable two in-person NCEMS workshops per year, supplemented by monthly virtual analysis meetings. Workshops will focus on ontology design, data harmonization, benchmark construction, model review, and manuscript or software release planning. Funds for graduate students and postdoctoral researchers will support trainee-led curation, workflow implementation, structural mapping, and predictive modeling across institutions. These trainees will be organized into cross-lab teams so that each participant gains skills outside their primary discipline. Computational resources are needed for large-scale sequence alignment, statistical coupling inference, structure mapping, graph construction, model training, and web-portal deployment. We will use NCEMS-supported computing and storage where available, complemented by institutional high-performance computing for reproducible workflow execution. No funds will be used to generate new experimental data. Data-management support will cover knowledge-graph development, metadata validation, containerized software environments, persistent archiving, and documentation. Dissemination funds will support open tutorials, community webinars, trainee hackathons, and maintenance of a public project website. The team will leverage existing public repositories, open-source software, and institutional expertise in molecular evolution, computational biophysics, statistical modeling, structural bioinformatics, proteomics, RNA biology, and open science. The budget is therefore concentrated on synthesis-enabling activities: bringing diverse experts together, making heterogeneous data interoperable, training data-savvy scientists, and producing reusable community resources. This allocation directly matches NCEMS goals of catalyzing collaborative synthesis research on mesoscale emergence.

title: Evolutionary Discovery of Metabolic Network Modules that Generate Mesoscale Membrane and Organelle Organization
title_norm: evolutionary discovery of metabolic network modules that generate mesoscale membrane and organelle organization
abstract_text:
A central unresolved problem in molecular and cellular biology is how evolutionary changes in genes and metabolic reactions give rise to emergent mesoscale cellular properties such as membrane composition, lipid droplet abundance, mitochondrial remodeling, peroxisome activity, and stress-dependent organelle organization. These properties are not encoded by single genes; they emerge from coordinated flux through lipid, amino acid, redox, and energy metabolism. Trainees will participate in cross-disciplinary hackathons and reproducible analysis teams, gaining experience in evolutionary genomics, metabolic network modeling, public data integration, and interpretable AI for molecular and cellular emergence.

[Background and Significance]
Cells convert molecular variation into organized mesoscale states: membranes with characteristic lipid composition, organelles with regulated abundance and morphology, and spatially coordinated metabolic compartments that respond to stress. These properties are emergent because they arise from many coupled reactions, transport processes, redox constraints, and regulatory feedbacks rather than from single genes acting independently. Despite extensive knowledge of individual lipid enzymes, mitochondrial proteins, peroxisomal functions, and stress-response pathways, the field lacks a general synthesis explaining why particular metabolic subnetworks repeatedly shape mesoscale organization across species, environments, and evolutionary histories.

This gap is timely and tractable because public data now span the relevant biological scales. Population genomic resources contain signals of recent and ancient adaptation in humans and other organisms. Comparative genomics and orthology databases support mapping of genes and reactions across taxa. Public transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and lipidomic datasets describe cellular responses to temperature, diet, oxygen availability, infection, nutrient limitation, immune activation, and other perturbations. Genome-scale metabolic reconstructions provide mechanistic representations of reaction stoichiometry, compartmentalization, biomass requirements, thermodynamic constraints, and feasible flux states. Public imaging resources, including high-content microscopy and Cell Painting datasets, increasingly quantify mitochondrial structure, lipid droplets, cell shape, organelle texture, and other phenotypes that reflect mesoscale organization.

The central significance of this working group is that these data have rarely been integrated in a shared coordinate system. Evolutionary studies often produce lists of candidate genes or genomic intervals under selection. Metabolic modeling studies often infer reaction-level consequences of environmental or cellular states. Imaging studies often quantify phenotypes without explicit links to evolutionary pressures or biochemical flux. By organizing public data around reactions, metabolites, orthologs, flux modules, and mesoscale phenotypes, this project will make it possible to ask whether evolution recurrently targets the metabolic architecture that generates membrane and organelle states.

The proposal directly addresses the NCEMS mission by focusing on emergent properties at the mesoscale between biomolecules and organelles. It is also inherently synthetic: no new experimental data will be collected. The work requires a collaborative team because the scientific question sits at the intersection of population genetics, interpretable machine learning, genome-scale metabolic modeling, comparative genomics, lipid and redox metabolism, and image-based cell phenotyping. A single laboratory could analyze one data type or one organism, but not construct a cross-species synthesis linking adaptive history, reaction network structure, predicted flux states, and cellular organization.

The project will also address a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biosciences: why similar environmental pressures often produce similar cellular phenotypes through partly different genes. We hypothesize that convergence may occur at the level of flux-controlling modules rather than at the level of individual orthologous genes. Identifying these modules would provide a mechanistic bridge between genotype, metabolism, and mesoscale phenotype, revealing principles by which evolution and environmental response exploit the same biochemical design space.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This working group will address one overarching question: which metabolic network modules are repeatedly shaped by evolution and environmental response because they control emergent mesoscale membrane and organelle organization? We define a module as a connected set of reactions, metabolites, transport steps, and associated genes whose coordinated activity changes a predicted or observed cellular property, such as phospholipid saturation, sterol balance, acyl-chain remodeling, lipid storage, mitochondrial redox coupling, peroxisomal beta-oxidation, or organelle morphology.

Question 1: Do adaptive evolutionary signals concentrate in metabolic modules that control mesoscale organization? Hypothesis 1 is that genomic regions showing evidence of natural selection in humans and other taxa will be enriched for genes mapped to reaction modules controlling lipid remodeling, redox balance, mitochondrial energy coupling, peroxisomal fatty acid processing, and membrane precursor allocation. We further hypothesize that enrichment will be stronger at the reaction-module level than at conventional pathway or gene ontology levels, because mesoscale phenotypes emerge from distributed biochemical functions rather than single annotated pathways.

Question 2: Do similar environmental pressures produce convergent metabolic network solutions across species? Hypothesis 2 is that cold exposure, lipid-rich diet, nutrient limitation, hypoxia, infection, and immune activation will induce recurrent flux reorganizations in homologous or functionally analogous metabolic modules. These changes may involve different genes across bacteria, plants, animals, and immune cell systems, but they will converge on shared reaction-level functions such as fatty acid desaturation, cardiolipin remodeling, NADPH allocation, amino acid catabolism, oxidative phosphorylation, reactive oxygen management, and lipid droplet storage capacity.

Question 3: Are stress-responsive flux modules in cellular datasets the same modules recurrently shaped by evolutionary history? Hypothesis 3 is that modules inferred to change flux under public perturbation datasets will overlap with modules enriched for population-genetic signatures of selection. Such overlap would indicate that short-term physiological plasticity and long-term adaptation act on common metabolic control points. Conversely, modules that respond strongly to perturbation but lack evolutionary signals may represent constrained or essential functions where genetic change is deleterious.

Question 4: Can interpretable machine learning distinguish selection on isolated loci from selection on coordinated metabolic systems? Hypothesis 4 is that deep learning models trained on neutral and selected haplotype simulations, combined with feature attribution and reaction-level aggregation, will reveal whether apparent selection signals are distributed across genes in the same module. This approach will help identify cases where modest signals across multiple genes collectively indicate selection on a mesoscale-generating process.

Question 5: Can public image-derived phenotypes validate predicted metabolic modules? Hypothesis 5 is that modules predicted to affect membrane lipid composition, mitochondrial redox state, peroxisomal activity, or neutral lipid storage will be statistically associated with public microscopy phenotypes such as lipid droplet abundance, mitochondrial branching, organelle texture, cell size, and stress-dependent morphology. This test will connect biochemical network inference to observable cellular organization.

Together, these questions will evaluate whether evolution repeatedly discovers a limited set of metabolic strategies for producing robust mesoscale cellular states.

[Methods and Approach]
The project will be organized as a synthesis working group using only existing publicly available data. Work will proceed in five integrated activities conducted through NCEMS-supported meetings, virtual analysis sprints, and trainee-led reproducible workflows.

Activity 1: Data inventory and harmonization. We will curate public population genomic datasets from humans and selected nonhuman taxa; comparative genome and orthology resources; public transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and lipidomic datasets from environmental and cellular perturbations; genome-scale metabolic reconstructions from BiGG, ModelSEED, Human-GEM, plant databases, and organism-specific models; and public image-derived organelle and cell morphology datasets. Candidate perturbations will include temperature, diet, nutrient limitation, hypoxia, infection, immune activation, oxidative stress, and developmental or metabolic state transitions. All datasets will be selected using predefined criteria: public accessibility, metadata quality, organism annotation, relevance to metabolism or mesoscale organization, and compatibility with reproducible reanalysis.

Activity 2: Reaction-centered knowledge graph construction. We will build a graph linking variants, genes, orthologs, enzymes, reactions, metabolites, lipid classes, compartments, predicted fluxes, omic measurements, selection statistics, and image phenotypes. Gene identifiers will be mapped through Ensembl, UniProt, KEGG, MetaNetX, and orthology resources. Reactions will be standardized across metabolic reconstructions using shared metabolite and reaction identifiers where possible. The graph will allow all evidence to be queried at gene, reaction, module, organism, environment, and phenotype levels.

Activity 3: Evolutionary inference. For population genomic datasets, we will compile established selection statistics and train interpretable machine learning models on simulated neutral and selected haplotypes matched to relevant demographic scenarios. Models will include convolutional and generative approaches that classify deviations from neutrality while enabling interpretation through feature attribution, summary-statistic comparison, and module-level aggregation. The objective is not only to nominate loci, but to detect whether selection signals cluster within reaction modules more strongly than expected under matched genomic and network null models.

Activity 4: Context-specific metabolic modeling. We will reconstruct or adapt genome-scale metabolic models for selected species and cell types using public omic datasets. Context-specific models will be generated with transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and lipidomic constraints when available. Flux balance analysis, flux variability analysis, parsimonious flux inference, thermodynamic constraints where feasible, and sampling-based methods will estimate condition-dependent flux changes. Particular attention will be given to modules controlling fatty acid synthesis and desaturation, phospholipid and sterol metabolism, cardiolipin remodeling, peroxisomal beta-oxidation, mitochondrial redox coupling, amino acid catabolism, and NADPH regeneration.

Activity 5: Cross-scale synthesis and validation. We will test whether selected genes are enriched in flux-controlling modules; whether environmental perturbations induce convergent flux responses across taxa; and whether predicted modules associate with image-derived phenotypes. Statistical analyses will use permutation tests preserving gene length, recombination rate, expression level, pathway size, and network degree; hierarchical models for species and condition effects; and robustness analyses across orthology definitions and model assumptions. Deliverables will include an atlas of evolutionarily sensitive metabolic modules, an interactive knowledge graph, reusable modeling pipelines, and prioritized mechanistic hypotheses for future experimental studies by the broader community.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The primary outcome will be an open atlas of metabolic network modules that link evolutionary history, environmental response, predicted flux organization, and mesoscale cellular phenotypes. Rather than producing disconnected lists of adaptive genes or stress-regulated pathways, the project will identify reaction-centered modules that plausibly generate emergent cellular properties such as membrane saturation state, lipid droplet formation, mitochondrial remodeling, peroxisomal activity, and redox-dependent organelle behavior.

A second outcome will be a generalizable synthesis framework for connecting population genetics with genome-scale metabolic modeling and image-based cell phenotyping. This framework will enable researchers to analyze evolutionary and cellular systems data in a common metabolic coordinate system. It will be reusable for questions beyond the initial focus, including host-pathogen adaptation, plant stress tolerance, immune cell polarization, microbial niche specialization, and metabolic disease susceptibility.

A third outcome will be a set of testable principles about mesoscale emergence. The project will determine whether convergent environmental pressures act on shared flux modules, whether human adaptive loci disproportionately affect membrane and organelle states, and whether physiological plasticity and evolutionary adaptation use common metabolic control points. These findings will provide mechanistic insight into how molecular changes scale up to cellular organization.

The impact for NCEMS will be substantial. The proposal addresses a fundamental question in emergence at the molecular-to-organelle interface, relies entirely on public data synthesis, requires expertise beyond any single lab, and produces open resources for the community. It will also train graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in cross-disciplinary synthesis science, interpretable AI, metabolic modeling, evolutionary inference, and reproducible team-based research. The resulting products will support future experimental prioritization without generating new data under this award.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
All project activities will follow open, team-oriented, and reproducible science practices. The working group will create a public project repository at the start of the award containing governance documents, contribution guidelines, data dictionaries, issue tracking, workflow documentation, and meeting summaries. Code will be released under a permissive open-source license. Harmonized metadata, derived feature tables, model annotations, trained machine learning models, and knowledge graph exports will be deposited in stable public repositories with persistent identifiers.

Because the project uses only public data, reproducibility will focus on transparent provenance and executable workflows. Each dataset will be accompanied by source accession numbers, download dates, license information, inclusion criteria, preprocessing scripts, quality-control metrics, and known limitations. Analyses will be implemented with version-controlled pipelines using containerized software environments. Where computational cost is substantial, we will release lightweight test datasets, cached intermediate products, and documented instructions for reproducing full analyses on institutional or cloud infrastructure.

The knowledge graph will be distributed in interoperable formats suitable for reuse by both computational and experimental researchers. Metabolic models will include clear records of identifier mappings, reaction additions or removals, objective functions, constraints, and assumptions used for context-specific reconstruction. Machine learning models will include architecture descriptions, training simulations, demographic assumptions, evaluation metrics, and interpretability outputs.

The working group will implement internal reproducibility checks before public release. At least one analyst not involved in developing a workflow will rerun key steps from raw public inputs to final figures or tables. Statistical analyses will include predefined null models, sensitivity analyses, and negative controls. Trainees will be integrated into reproducibility teams so that training is embedded in deliverable production. Publications and preprints will link directly to data, code, workflows, and interactive visualizations, enabling community evaluation and extension.

[Budget and Resources]
NCEMS support is essential because this project requires sustained coordination, shared computational infrastructure, and cross-disciplinary training that exceed the scope of an ordinary bilateral collaboration. The requested resources will support working group meetings, trainee participation, collaborative analysis sprints, data-management assistance, computational resources for large-scale synthesis, and dissemination of open products.

Major resource categories include personnel effort for coordination and synthesis, trainee support, travel and meeting costs, computation, and open-science dissemination. Personnel effort will focus on harmonizing public datasets, maintaining the reaction-centered knowledge graph, developing reproducible workflows, and coordinating analyses across evolutionary genomics, metabolic modeling, and image phenotyping subteams. Trainee funds will support graduate students and postdoctoral researchers who will participate in hackathons, lead reproducibility checks, and develop cross-training modules.

Travel and convening funds will enable two in-person working group meetings and regular virtual workshops. The first meeting will finalize data inclusion criteria, graph schema, analysis standards, and team roles. The second will focus on synthesis of results, validation, manuscript planning, and release of community resources. Short virtual analysis sprints will maintain momentum between meetings and allow participation by researchers from diverse institutions and career stages.

Computational resources will be used for population-genetic simulations, deep learning training and interpretation, graph construction, metabolic flux analyses, and large-scale statistical resampling. Cloud or center-supported compute will be used only for reanalysis of public data and generation of derived public resources. No funds will be used to generate new experimental data.

NCEMS resources will also support open dissemination, including repository maintenance, documentation, tutorials, interactive visualization hosting, and community webinars. These investments will ensure that the project produces durable, reusable products: harmonized datasets, metabolic annotations, trained models, executable workflows, and an accessible atlas of evolutionarily sensitive metabolic modules underlying mesoscale cellular organization.

title: Proteome Flux Codes for Emergent Mesoscale Remodeling During Cellular Stress and Disease

abstract_text:
Cells often respond to stress not by changing the abundance of individual molecules alone, but by reorganizing mesoscale protein systems: ribonucleoprotein assemblies, cytoskeletal and nuclear scaffolds, extracellular matrices, metabolic enzyme clusters, and organelle-associated protein communities. A central unsolved question is how molecular flux through the proteome—translation, degradation, post-translational modification, disorder-mediated interaction, and localization—combines to produce these emergent cellular structures and phenotypes. We propose a community-scale synthesis project to define generalizable “proteome flux codes” that predict when changes in protein synthesis and turnover produce mesoscale remodeling across stress, aging, and cardiometabolic disease contexts.

This working group will integrate only publicly available datasets spanning multiple biological scales. Core inputs will include ribosome profiling, RNA-seq, quantitative proteomics, pulse-labeling and protein turnover datasets, phosphoproteomics and other modification maps, protein disorder and structural annotations, subcellular localization resources, protein interaction networks, phase-separation and condensate-associated protein catalogs, and public single-cell or bulk transcriptomic and proteomic datasets from stress models, iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes and endothelial cells, cardiovascular tissues, cancer stress states, and aging-related systems. Rather than treating mRNA, translation, protein abundance, and degradation as separate regulatory layers, we will build harmonized models of protein residence time, production rate, degradation rate, modification state, and mesoscale membership.

The central hypothesis is that emergent mesoscale remodeling is governed by coordinated shifts in proteome flux, especially among proteins with long residence times, intrinsically disordered regions, modification-rich segments, scaffold-like interaction properties, or compartment-specific localization. These features may explain why some cellular responses are rapid and reversible, whereas others become persistent, pathological, or tissue-specific. We will test this through three synthesis aims. First, we will create an interoperable atlas of proteome flux across public datasets, with uncertainty-aware normalization of turnover, translation, and abundance measurements across organisms, cell types, perturbations, and technologies. Second, we will identify recurrent flux signatures associated with mesoscale assemblies, including stress granule-like systems, nuclear lamina and chromatin-associated networks, mitochondrial and metabolic complexes, extracellular matrix remodeling modules, and cytoskeletal or contractile structures. Third, we will develop predictive machine-learning and mechanistic network models that link molecular flux signatures to higher-order cellular outcomes such as stress adaptation, proteostasis collapse, endothelial inflammation, cardiomyocyte dysfunction, and age-associated remodeling.

This project requires NCEMS-scale synthesis because no single laboratory can curate, reconcile, and model the diverse public datasets needed to connect translation dynamics, proteome turnover, structural disorder, post-translational regulation, and disease-relevant cell phenotypes. The working group would bring together experts in proteomics, ribosome profiling, cardiovascular and stem-cell models, structural bioinformatics, stress biology, network science, and open computational infrastructure. Deliverables will include a FAIR public proteome-flux atlas, reproducible workflows, benchmark datasets for turnover inference, interactive visualization tools, and trainee-led tutorials on integrative molecular data synthesis. By focusing on how molecular rates and regulatory layers combine to generate mesoscale biological organization, this project directly addresses NCEMS priorities and offers a new framework for understanding emergent cellular behavior from existing public data.

[Background and Significance]
Cellular stress responses are frequently interpreted through changes in transcript or protein abundance, yet many decisive biological outcomes arise from reorganization at the mesoscale. Stress granules, ribonucleoprotein assemblies, nuclear lamina networks, mitochondrial contact sites, extracellular matrices, contractile cytoskeletal systems, and metabolic enzyme clusters are not single-gene phenomena. They emerge from coordinated molecular rates, molecular interactions, localization constraints, structural disorder, post-translational modification, and protein residence time. Existing public datasets now make it possible to ask whether these mesoscale transitions follow general rules that are conserved across cell types and disease contexts, but the relevant measurements remain fragmented across repositories, technologies, organisms, and analytical conventions. Proteome flux provides a unifying concept for this synthesis. At steady state, protein abundance reflects production and removal, but during stress or disease, the timing of synthesis, degradation, modification, sequestration, and relocalization can diverge. A rapidly translated protein may have little mesoscale effect if it is unstable or excluded from the relevant compartment. Conversely, a long-lived scaffold with intrinsically disordered regions or dense modification sites may stabilize a cellular structure after only modest abundance change. Such rate-dependent behavior is central to emergence: new system properties can arise when molecular turnover and interaction kinetics exceed thresholds that are not obvious from abundance measurements alone. The proposed working group will focus on public data relevant to stress adaptation, aging, cardiometabolic dysfunction, endothelial inflammation, cardiomyocyte remodeling, cancer stress states, proteostasis impairment, and structural organization of the nucleus and cytoplasm. These domains are scientifically connected by recurring questions about translation control, protein degradation, post-transcriptional regulation, proteome stability, scaffold proteins, and disease-associated cellular phenotypes. They also provide diverse perturbations and biological scales for rigorous comparative synthesis, including acute stress responses, chronic remodeling, developmental or differentiation-associated transitions, and tissue-specific disease states. NCEMS support is essential because the project depends on integration that exceeds the scope of a single laboratory. Ribosome profiling, RNA-seq, mass-spectrometry proteomics, pulse-labeling turnover studies, phosphoproteomics, protein interaction networks, localization resources, disorder annotations, condensate catalogs, and single-cell atlases each use distinct identifiers, normalization schemes, noise structures, and biological assumptions. A community-scale working group can establish shared standards, benchmark inference methods, quantify uncertainty, and produce generalizable models rather than dataset-specific observations. The significance is both biological and methodological. Biologically, the project will identify molecular flux patterns that distinguish reversible adaptive remodeling from persistent pathological restructuring. Methodologically, it will transform static omics comparisons into dynamic, interpretable models of protein system behavior. The work directly aligns with NCEMS priorities by using only existing public data, addressing emergence at the mesoscale, building transdisciplinary synthesis capacity, training data-savvy trainees, and delivering open resources for the molecular and cellular sciences community.

We define proteome flux as the integrated behavior of protein production, residence time, degradation, modification, localization, structural interaction potential, and assignment to mesoscale systems. We will use publicly available data to test whether combinations of these features form reproducible codes that predict cellular remodeling more effectively than any single omics layer. Research Question 1 asks whether protein turnover, translation, and abundance can be harmonized across public datasets to reveal conserved flux regimes. We hypothesize that proteins partition into reproducible classes, including fast-response transient regulators, long-residence structural scaffolds, high-production metabolic proteins, stress-inducible short-lived effectors, and stable compartmental anchors. These classes will be detectable across organisms and cell types after accounting for technology, growth state, and annotation uncertainty. Research Question 2 asks whether specific flux regimes are enriched in mesoscale assemblies. We hypothesize that stress granule and ribonucleoprotein systems will show rapid translational and localization shifts in proteins enriched for RNA-binding domains and disordered regions; nuclear lamina and chromatin-associated systems will show long residence times, modification-sensitive remodeling, and disease-linked persistence; mitochondrial and metabolic assemblies will show coordinated production and turnover changes coupled to energy-state perturbations; extracellular matrix and cytoskeletal modules will show slow remodeling and tissue-specific stabilization. These predictions reflect the idea that mesoscale structures are governed by distinct kinetic constraints. Research Question 3 asks which molecular features explain the transition from adaptive remodeling to pathological remodeling. We hypothesize that persistent disease phenotypes arise when long-lived scaffold proteins, proteins with disordered or low-complexity segments, and modification-rich regulators undergo coordinated flux changes that resist reversal after stress removal. This mechanism may help explain chronic endothelial inflammation, cardiomyocyte contractile dysfunction, age-associated extracellular matrix remodeling, proteostasis collapse, and malignant stress adaptation. Research Question 4 asks whether proteome flux models improve prediction of higher-order phenotypes compared with transcriptomic or proteomic abundance models alone. We hypothesize that incorporating translation efficiency, turnover rate, degradation uncertainty, localization, modification state, disorder, and network position will increase predictive accuracy and improve interpretability. We further hypothesize that cross-context models will reveal both universal flux principles and tissue-specific exceptions. Research Question 5 asks which public datasets are most informative for synthesis and where current measurement gaps limit inference. We hypothesize that uncertainty-aware integration will identify robust findings despite heterogeneous data quality, while also defining community benchmark needs for future public datasets. The project will not generate new experimental data; instead, it will use comparative synthesis to formulate testable principles, open computational models, and prioritizable predictions for future investigators. Together, these questions directly address emergence by linking molecular-scale rate processes to mesoscale structures and cellular phenotypes.

[Methods and Approach]
The working group will implement three integrated synthesis aims using only existing publicly available data. Aim 1 will build a FAIR proteome-flux atlas. We will curate datasets from public repositories including GEO, SRA, PRIDE, MassIVE, ProteomeXchange, CPTAC resources, Human Protein Atlas, UniProt, BioGRID, STRING, IntAct, PhosphoSitePlus where licensing permits, DepMap, public single-cell portals, and specialized resources for condensate-associated proteins, protein disorder, localization, domains, and structural predictions. Eligible datasets will include ribosome profiling, RNA-seq, quantitative proteomics, pulse-SILAC and related turnover measurements, dynamic labeling studies, phosphoproteomics and other modification maps, bulk and single-cell stress datasets, iPSC-derived cardiomyocyte and endothelial cell studies, cardiovascular tissue omics, cancer stress datasets, aging systems, and perturbation studies relevant to proteostasis or metabolism. We will record provenance, organism, cell type, perturbation, time scale, technology, identifiers, normalization status, and uncertainty. Orthology and isoform mapping will be performed conservatively, with analyses repeated at protein group, gene, and orthogroup levels as appropriate. Aim 2 will infer standardized flux features and mesoscale membership. For each protein, we will estimate or annotate transcript abundance, translation efficiency, protein abundance, synthesis rate proxies, degradation or residence time, modification burden, dynamic modification change, subcellular localization, interaction degree, complex membership, disorder content, low-complexity regions, RNA-binding status, scaffold potential, and association with condensates, cytoskeleton, extracellular matrix, nuclear lamina, chromatin, mitochondria, metabolic complexes, or other compartments. Turnover and translation measurements will be harmonized using hierarchical Bayesian or mixed-effect models that account for dataset, organism, technology, labeling strategy, time point, and measurement error. Missing features will be treated explicitly rather than imputed indiscriminately; when imputation is used, downstream sensitivity analyses will quantify its influence. Aim 3 will model relationships between flux codes and cellular outcomes. We will use complementary strategies: unsupervised clustering to define recurrent flux states; network propagation to identify coordinated mesoscale modules; supervised machine learning to predict stress adaptation, inflammatory activation, cardiomyocyte dysfunction, proteostasis impairment, disease class, or age-associated remodeling; and mechanistic ordinary differential equation or probabilistic graphical models for selected modules where time-series data support dynamic inference. Predictive models will be evaluated by nested cross-validation, leave-dataset-out validation, leave-cell-type-out validation, and orthogonal validation using datasets not used for model training. Feature importance will be assessed with interpretable methods such as permutation analysis, SHAP-style summaries, stability selection, and network-level enrichment. The working group structure will include domain subteams for data curation, turnover and translation modeling, structural and localization annotation, disease-context interpretation, software engineering, and trainee-led benchmarking. NCEMS meetings will be used for standards development, code sprints, cross-disciplinary interpretation sessions, and community feedback. Feasibility is high because the project synthesizes mature public data types and produces modular deliverables at each stage.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The project will produce five major outcomes. First, we will deliver a public proteome-flux atlas that harmonizes translation, abundance, turnover, modification, localization, structural, and mesoscale membership information across stress and disease-relevant systems. Second, we will identify recurrent flux signatures associated with ribonucleoprotein assemblies, nuclear and chromatin scaffolds, mitochondrial and metabolic modules, extracellular matrix networks, cytoskeletal systems, and contractile structures. Third, we will generate predictive models that test whether integrated flux features outperform transcript or protein abundance alone in explaining emergent cellular phenotypes. Fourth, we will create benchmark datasets and evaluation criteria for protein turnover and translation inference across heterogeneous public resources. Fifth, we will provide open tutorials and visualization tools that enable trainees and external researchers to reuse the resource. The scientific impact will be a shift from static molecular lists toward rate-aware explanations of cellular organization. The project will clarify why some stress responses are transient and reversible, whereas others become persistent, tissue-specific, or pathological. It will also provide a framework for connecting molecular regulation to cardiovascular remodeling, endothelial inflammation, proteostasis failure, cancer stress adaptation, and aging-associated structural change without generating new data. The broader impact is the establishment of a community model for synthesis research in molecular and cellular biology. By bringing together proteomics, translation biology, disease modeling, structural bioinformatics, network science, and computational infrastructure, the working group will create resources that individual laboratories could not assemble alone. The results will support hypothesis generation for future experimental studies, but all funded activities will remain centered on public data synthesis, open analysis, workforce training, and reproducible computational discovery aligned with NCEMS priorities.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
All project outputs will follow open, reproducible, and team-science practices from the start. We will release a living data-management plan describing dataset inclusion criteria, provenance tracking, identifier mapping, licensing, metadata standards, versioning, quality-control metrics, and procedures for community correction. Only publicly available datasets will be used, and each dataset will retain links to its original repository and accession. Processed harmonized tables will include clear documentation of transformations, normalization, uncertainty estimates, and known limitations. Analysis workflows will be developed in public version-controlled repositories. Code will use containerized environments, workflow managers such as Snakemake, Nextflow, or comparable reproducible systems, and continuous integration tests for core functions. Major analyses will be accompanied by executable notebooks, scripted figures, software release tags, and archived computational environments. Data products will be deposited in appropriate open repositories with persistent identifiers, permissive licenses when compatible with source data, and machine-readable metadata. We will distinguish primary curated data, derived features, model-ready matrices, and summary visualizations to support reuse at different expertise levels. Reproducibility will be assessed through internal rerun challenges in which trainees or collaborating laboratories independently regenerate key figures and model outputs from documented workflows. Model evaluation will include preregistered benchmark splits, leave-dataset-out validation, sensitivity analyses for missingness and orthology mapping, and transparent reporting of negative or non-generalizable findings. The working group will also create community-facing tutorials, short courses, and example analyses focused on turnover inference, ribosome profiling integration, proteomics normalization, network modeling, and responsible machine learning for molecular data. Authorship and contribution policies will be established early using transparent contributor roles. Regular open office hours and public milestone reports will invite feedback from the broader NCEMS community. These practices will ensure that the project is not only scientifically rigorous but also reusable, extensible, and educational for the next generation of data-savvy molecular and cellular scientists.

[Budget and Resources]
We request NCEMS support to enable the coordination, computing, training, and open-resource development required for a community-scale synthesis project. The largest resource need is personnel time for data curation, software engineering, trainee participation, and cross-disciplinary integration. Funds will support graduate students or postdoctoral trainees who will curate public datasets, implement reproducible workflows, benchmark turnover and translation models, build visualization tools, and lead tutorials. Partial support for a data scientist or research software engineer is essential to maintain interoperable infrastructure, containerized workflows, documentation, testing, and public releases. NCEMS meeting support is central to feasibility. We propose recurring virtual working sessions and in-person synthesis meetings for data standardization, model review, hackathons, trainee mentoring, and community feedback. Travel funds will prioritize participation across institutions, career stages, and geographic regions, including early-career investigators and trainees from institutions with varied research resources. Funds will also support accessibility needs, hybrid participation, and dissemination through workshops or conference-adjacent training events. Computational resources will be used for storage of harmonized public datasets, model training, workflow execution, web-based visualization, and archival releases. The project will leverage institutional clusters and free public repositories whenever possible, but NCEMS support is needed for shared cloud computing, managed storage, collaborative platforms, and persistent hosting of lightweight interactive tools. No funds will be used to generate new experimental data, purchase experimental reagents, recruit human subjects, or conduct animal studies. The requested budget directly supports NCEMS goals: synthesis of existing data, multidisciplinary collaboration, open infrastructure, and workforce training. Without NCEMS, the necessary coordination across proteomics, ribosome profiling, structural annotation, disease biology, network modeling, and software development would remain fragmented. With NCEMS support, the working group can deliver a durable public atlas, reproducible analytical standards, predictive models, and training materials that benefit the broader molecular and cellular sciences community.

abstract_original:
Cells often respond to stress not by changing the abundance of individual molecules alone, but by reorganizing mesoscale protein systems: ribonucleoprotein assemblies, cytoskeletal and nuclear scaffolds, extracellular matrices, metabolic enzyme clusters, and organelle-associated protein communities. A central unsolved question is how molecular flux through the proteome—translation, degradation, post-translational modification, disorder-mediated interaction, and localization—combines to produce these emergent cellular structures and phenotypes. We propose a community-scale synthesis project to define generalizable “proteome flux codes” that predict when changes in protein synthesis and turnover produce mesoscale remodeling across stress, aging, and cardiometabolic disease contexts.

This working group will integrate only publicly available datasets spanning multiple biological scales. Core inputs will include ribosome profiling, RNA-seq, quantitative proteomics, pulse-labeling and protein turnover datasets, phosphoproteomics and other modification maps, protein disorder and structural annotations, subcellular localization resources, protein interaction networks, phase-separation and condensate-associated protein catalogs, and public single-cell or bulk transcriptomic and proteomic datasets from stress models, iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes and endothelial cells, cardiovascular tissues, cancer stress states, and aging-related systems. Rather than treating mRNA, translation, protein abundance, and degradation as separate regulatory layers, we will build harmonized models of protein residence time, production rate, degradation rate, modification state, and mesoscale membership.

The central hypothesis is that emergent mesoscale remodeling is governed by coordinated shifts in proteome flux, especially among proteins with long residence times, intrinsically disordered regions, modification-rich segments, scaffold-like interaction properties, or compartment-specific localization. These features may explain why some cellular responses are rapid and reversible, whereas others become persistent, pathological, or tissue-specific. We will test this through three synthesis aims. First, we will create an interoperable atlas of proteome flux across public datasets, with uncertainty-aware normalization of turnover, translation, and abundance measurements across organisms, cell types, perturbations, and technologies. Second, we will identify recurrent flux signatures associated with mesoscale assemblies, including stress granule-like systems, nuclear lamina and chromatin-associated networks, mitochondrial and metabolic complexes, extracellular matrix remodeling modules, and cytoskeletal or contractile structures. Third, we will develop predictive machine-learning and mechanistic network models that link molecular flux signatures to higher-order cellular outcomes such as stress adaptation, proteostasis collapse, endothelial inflammation, cardiomyocyte dysfunction, and age-associated remodeling.

This project requires NCEMS-scale synthesis because no single laboratory can curate, reconcile, and model the diverse public datasets needed to connect translation dynamics, proteome turnover, structural disorder, post-translational regulation, and disease-relevant cell phenotypes. The working group would bring together experts in proteomics, ribosome profiling, cardiovascular and stem-cell models, structural bioinformatics, stress biology, network science, and open computational infrastructure. Deliverables will include a FAIR public proteome-flux atlas, reproducible workflows, benchmark datasets for turnover inference, interactive visualization tools, and trainee-led tutorials on integrative molecular data synthesis. By focusing on how molecular rates and regulatory layers combine to generate mesoscale biological organization, this project directly addresses NCEMS priorities and offers a new framework for understanding emergent cellular behavior from existing public data.

title: Inferring Conserved Mesoscale Kinetic Programs from Public Spatial Omics and Fluorescence Microscopy Atlases

abstract_text:
Cell states are usually defined by transcriptional profiles, yet many consequential state transitions emerge from mesoscale organization: RNA compartmentalization, protein clustering, membrane localization, molecular mobility, and organelle-associated trafficking. A macrophage-exposed tumor cell, a differentiating neural progenitor, or a stressed neuron may share little transcriptomic identity, but may converge on similar mesoscale kinetic solutions such as altered nuclear export, enhanced membrane-proximal signaling, or increased residence time of regulatory proteins in subcellular compartments. This working group will test the hypothesis that diverse cellular transitions are governed by a small set of conserved mesoscale kinetic programs that can be inferred by synthesizing existing public spatial omics, proteomics, and fluorescence microscopy data.

We will build an open synthesis framework that links three public data classes that are rarely analyzed together. First, we will harmonize single-cell and spatial transcriptomic datasets from public repositories, including brain development and adult brain atlases, tumor microenvironment datasets, MERFISH/seqFISH-style measurements with subcellular RNA localization, and spatial cancer atlases. Second, we will integrate proteomic and immunofluorescence resources such as the Human Protein Atlas, public CODEX/IMC datasets, and subcellular protein localization maps. Third, we will mine public microscopy repositories such as the Image Data Resource and BioImage Archive for live-cell, single-particle, FRAP/FCS, super-resolution, and organelle-tracking datasets that report protein mobility, clustering, stoichiometry, or trafficking dynamics. No new experimental data will be generated.

The central methodological innovation will be a Bayesian multimodal model that translates heterogeneous public measurements into a shared latent representation of mesoscale kinetic state. Rather than treating images as qualitative annotations, the framework will extract probabilistic features including nuclear-cytoplasmic RNA partitioning, local transcript density, protein puncta size and number, apparent oligomeric state, organelle adjacency, membrane enrichment, and effective mobility or residence-time estimates where time-resolved data exist. These features will be linked to matched or harmonized transcriptomic cell states using batch-aware integration and uncertainty propagation. The model will explicitly account for differences in optical resolution, fluorophore sampling, segmentation quality, and assay modality, enabling principled comparison across datasets and laboratories.

We will apply the framework to three biological transitions with abundant public data and strong mesoscale relevance: neural differentiation and maturation, inflammatory remodeling of tumor cells and immune neighborhoods, and cellular stress states involving mitochondrial and membrane-trafficking pathways. Across these systems, we will ask whether transcriptionally distinct cell types reuse common mesoscale programs; whether spatially localized RNAs predict protein compartmentalization or mobility; and whether emergent cellular phenotypes are better explained by inferred kinetic features than by gene expression alone. Expected products include an open atlas of inferred mesoscale kinetic programs, reusable workflows for extracting biophysical features from public microscopy data, benchmark datasets for spatial omics–image integration, and candidate molecular modules linking transcriptional regulation to mesoscale organization.

This project requires NCEMS support because it exceeds the scope of any single laboratory: it demands expertise in single-cell and spatial data integration, statistical optics, Bayesian inference, single-molecule biophysics, image analysis, cell-state biology, and open data engineering. The working group will include trainees as core contributors through hackathon-style data integration sprints, reproducible workflow development, and cross-training modules on spatial omics, microscopy uncertainty, and probabilistic modeling. All curated data links, derived features, code, model outputs, and documentation will be released openly to support community reuse and future synthesis studies of emergent cellular organization.
