All curated data links, derived features, code, model outputs, and documentation will be released openly to support community reuse and future synthesis studies of emergent cellular organization.

[Background and Significance]
Molecular and cellular biology has entered an era in which public datasets describe the same biological processes from complementary viewpoints: single-cell gene expression, spatial transcript localization, multiplexed protein abundance, subcellular imaging, and time-resolved molecular motion. Yet these data classes remain largely siloed. Cell states are often operationally defined by transcript abundance because single-cell RNA sequencing is broad, scalable, and analytically mature. However, many emergent cellular behaviors arise between molecular interactions and organelle-scale outcomes, where the relevant variables are mesoscale: molecular crowding, local concentration, phase-like clustering, nuclear-cytoplasmic partitioning, protein residence time, membrane recruitment, organelle proximity, and trafficking flux. These properties can create functional states that are not obvious from transcript counts alone.

This gap is particularly important for cellular transitions. During neural differentiation, RNA localization and nuclear export help coordinate maturation programs before stable cell identities are fully established. In tumors, inflammatory and immune cues can reorganize signaling proteins, membrane receptors, and RNA localization in ways that alter plasticity, invasion, and therapy response. Under metabolic or proteotoxic stress, mitochondrial organization, copper and metal handling, vesicular trafficking, and protein mobility can shift rapidly, generating phenotypes that precede or exceed transcriptional remodeling. These examples suggest that apparently unrelated transitions may reuse conserved mesoscale kinetic strategies, even when their gene-expression signatures differ.

Public data now make it possible to test this idea without generating new experimental data. Spatial transcriptomic atlases provide tissue context and, in image-based platforms, direct measurements of subcellular RNA distributions. Single-cell atlases offer harmonized cell-state maps across development, adult tissues, cancer, and perturbation conditions. Protein resources such as immunofluorescence localization maps, multiplexed tissue imaging, and proteomic atlases provide information on abundance, compartment, and cell-neighborhood structure. Public microscopy archives contain live-cell movies, fluorescence recovery measurements, fluctuation spectroscopy, super-resolution images, single-particle tracking datasets, and organelle-tracking experiments that report mobility, clustering, stoichiometry, and trafficking. Individually, these datasets are valuable; synthesized together, they can reveal whether cell states are governed by recurring mesoscale kinetic programs.

The proposed working group addresses a fundamental NCEMS question: how do new system properties emerge at the mesoscale from molecular components? Our premise is that mesoscale organization is not merely a downstream readout of transcription. Instead, it is a partially independent layer of regulation that can integrate gene expression, physical constraints, biochemical interactions, and spatial context into coherent cellular phenotypes. A synthesis approach is essential because no single dataset contains all relevant modalities, and no single laboratory typically combines expertise in spatial omics, statistical optics, single-molecule biophysics, probabilistic modeling, cell-state biology, and open data engineering.

By integrating existing public datasets, this project will transform scattered observations into a reusable framework for asking whether distinct biological systems share common kinetic solutions. The work directly aligns with NCEMS priorities by addressing emergence in molecular and cellular sciences, developing analytical strategies for heterogeneous public data, building a multidisciplinary working group, training data-savvy trainees, and producing open community resources.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
The overarching question is whether diverse cellular transitions are organized by a limited set of conserved mesoscale kinetic programs that can be inferred from public spatial omics, proteomic, and microscopy datasets. We define a mesoscale kinetic program as a coordinated pattern of subcellular organization and dynamics, including RNA compartmentalization, protein clustering, membrane recruitment, molecular mobility, organelle association, and trafficking-related redistribution, that recurs across biological systems and is associated with a reproducible cellular outcome.

Question 1: Do transcriptionally distinct cell states reuse common mesoscale kinetic programs? We will compare neural differentiation and maturation, inflammatory remodeling in tumor-immune microenvironments, and stress-associated mitochondrial or membrane-trafficking states. These systems differ in tissue, lineage, and stimulus, but all involve transitions in which molecular localization and motion are expected to influence phenotype. Hypothesis 1 is that cross-system integration will identify a small number of reusable mesoscale programs, such as nuclear-retained RNA and delayed export, membrane-proximal signaling enrichment, increased protein residence time in regulatory compartments, puncta-associated concentration of signaling or RNA-binding factors, and enhanced organelle adjacency linked to metabolic adaptation. These programs will be more conserved than the identities of individual marker genes.

Question 2: Can spatial RNA features predict protein localization and dynamic behavior? Image-based transcriptomic data can report nuclear-cytoplasmic partitioning, local transcript density, and proximity of RNAs to organelles or membranes. Protein atlases and microscopy datasets can report compartment enrichment, puncta formation, oligomeric state proxies, and mobility. Hypothesis 2 is that spatial RNA organization will improve prediction of protein localization and kinetic behavior beyond total transcript abundance. For example, nuclear-cytoplasmic RNA partitioning may predict delayed protein accumulation or altered regulatory timing, while locally enriched transcripts may predict compartment-specific protein abundance or clustering.

Question 3: Do inferred mesoscale kinetic features explain emergent phenotypes better than gene expression alone? Many outcomes, including cell-cycle progression, differentiation potential, immune activation, mesenchymal-like tumor remodeling, and stress tolerance, arise from the combined effects of molecular abundance, spatial organization, and kinetic constraints. Hypothesis 3 is that multimodal latent variables incorporating mesoscale features will improve prediction of transition stage, neighborhood response, and stress-associated state compared with transcriptomic embeddings alone. This will be evaluated using held-out datasets and phenotypic annotations available in public resources.

Question 4: Which molecular modules link transcriptional regulation to mesoscale organization? Hypothesis 4 is that regulators of RNA processing and export, cytoskeletal transport, membrane trafficking, metal and mitochondrial homeostasis, chromatin-associated residence, and receptor-proximal signaling will repeatedly associate with inferred kinetic programs across systems. The goal is not to claim direct causality from synthesis alone, but to generate ranked, cross-validated candidate modules that explain how molecular components give rise to mesoscale organization.

Question 5: What methodological principles are required to compare heterogeneous public imaging and omics data? Hypothesis 5 is that uncertainty-aware Bayesian integration, explicit optical and sampling metadata, and batch-aware cell-state harmonization will outperform approaches that treat images as categorical annotations. This methodological question is central to feasibility and community reuse, because public data vary in resolution, labeling strategy, segmentation quality, field of view, and experimental design.

[Methods and Approach]
This working group will conduct a synthesis-only project using existing public datasets. No new experimental measurements will be generated. The work will proceed through coordinated data inventory, harmonization, feature extraction, probabilistic modeling, biological analysis, benchmarking, and community release.

Aim 1: Curate and harmonize public datasets. We will assemble three linked data collections. The transcriptomic collection will include public single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing datasets, spatial transcriptomic atlases, and image-based MERFISH or seqFISH-style datasets from developing and adult brain, tumor microenvironments, and stress-relevant cell systems. The protein and tissue-imaging collection will include Human Protein Atlas immunofluorescence, public CODEX and imaging mass cytometry data, and subcellular protein localization resources. The microscopy collection will include datasets from repositories such as the Image Data Resource and BioImage Archive containing live-cell imaging, single-particle tracking, FRAP, FCS, super-resolution localization, organelle tracking, and related measurements. Each dataset will be annotated with modality, species, tissue, cell type, perturbation, imaging resolution, labeling method, temporal sampling, segmentation availability, and licensing.

Aim 2: Extract uncertainty-aware mesoscale features. For spatial RNA data, we will quantify nuclear-cytoplasmic partitioning, transcript dispersion, local density, cell-edge enrichment, neighborhood gradients, and, when possible, organelle-proximal localization. For protein imaging, we will estimate compartment enrichment, puncta number and size, spatial anisotropy, membrane enrichment, cell-to-cell variability, and colocalization or adjacency to organelle markers. For live and time-resolved microscopy, we will extract or re-estimate apparent diffusion, residence time, recovery kinetics, track confinement, cluster lifetime, and trafficking directionality using published raw data where available and published summary statistics where raw data are unavailable. All features will include uncertainty estimates reflecting photon noise, optical resolution, sampling density, segmentation error, batch, and missing metadata.

Aim 3: Build a Bayesian multimodal latent-state model. We will develop a hierarchical model that maps heterogeneous measurements into a shared latent representation of mesoscale kinetic state. Dataset-specific likelihoods will represent count-based transcriptomics, spatial point patterns, fluorescence intensity images, localization data, and time-series measurements. Batch and platform effects will be modeled explicitly rather than removed blindly. Transcriptomic cell states will be harmonized using established batch-aware integration strategies, then linked to imaging-derived features through probabilistic alignment based on cell type, tissue, perturbation, marker genes, and spatial context. The model will propagate uncertainty from feature extraction to latent program assignment and will permit partial observations, allowing datasets with only one or two modalities to contribute.

Aim 4: Identify conserved programs and test predictive value. We will infer recurring mesoscale programs across three transition classes: neural maturation, tumor-immune inflammatory remodeling, and mitochondrial or membrane-trafficking stress states. We will evaluate conservation by cross-dataset replication, leave-one-dataset-out prediction, permutation controls, and comparison to transcript-only baselines. Predictive tasks will include transition-stage classification, inflammatory or stress-state annotation, spatial neighborhood response, and protein localization or mobility prediction from RNA features. Candidate molecular modules will be identified by associating latent programs with gene sets, protein families, regulatory factors, and pathway annotations.

Aim 5: Organize NCEMS-enabled working group activities. Participants will include experts in spatial and single-cell omics, microscopy physics, Bayesian inference, single-molecule dynamics, image analysis, cell biology, and data infrastructure. Trainees will lead reproducible workflow modules during data-integration sprints and receive cross-training in spatial omics, statistical optics, and probabilistic modeling. Milestones include a curated data registry by month 3, feature-extraction workflows by month 6, first integrated model by month 9, biological program atlas by month 12, benchmark release by month 15, and manuscripts and community tutorials by month 18.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This project will deliver four primary products. First, we will create an open atlas of inferred mesoscale kinetic programs across neural maturation, tumor-immune remodeling, and cellular stress states. The atlas will include program scores, uncertainty estimates, associated cell states, dataset provenance, and interpretable features such as RNA partitioning, protein clustering, membrane enrichment, organelle adjacency, and mobility proxies. Second, we will release reusable workflows for extracting biophysical features from public spatial omics and microscopy data. These workflows will support community analysis of images as quantitative measurements rather than qualitative illustrations. Third, we will produce benchmark datasets and evaluation tasks for multimodal integration across transcriptomics, proteomics, and microscopy. Fourth, we will nominate candidate molecular modules linking transcriptional regulation to mesoscale organization.

The scientific impact will be to test whether emergent cell states can be understood as combinations of conserved mesoscale kinetic strategies. If successful, the project will shift interpretation of cell states from transcript abundance alone toward a more physical and spatially grounded view of cellular regulation. This will help explain why different biological systems can produce similar phenotypes through different marker genes, and why some transitions are poorly predicted by expression profiles alone.

The methodological impact will be a generalizable framework for uncertainty-aware synthesis of heterogeneous public data. The project will also provide a model for NCEMS-style community synthesis: no new experiments, broad collaboration, transparent workflows, and trainee-centered data science training. The resulting resources will enable future studies of organelle dynamics, RNA localization, protein mobility, signaling compartmentalization, and emergent cellular organization across many public datasets beyond the initial biological domains.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
All project activities will follow open, team-based, and reproducible science practices. We will use only publicly available datasets with documented access conditions and will maintain a public data registry containing dataset identifiers, repository links, licenses, file formats, metadata completeness, modality descriptions, and processing status. Because raw imaging files can be large and may have repository-specific access requirements, we will not duplicate restricted data unnecessarily. Instead, we will provide persistent links, checksums when available, standardized metadata tables, and derived features that are permissible to redistribute.

Code will be developed in public version-controlled repositories under a permissive open-source license. abstract_original:
Cell states are usually defined by transcriptional profiles, yet many consequential state transitions emerge from mesoscale organization: RNA compartmentalization, protein clustering, membrane localization, molecular mobility, and organelle-associated trafficking. A macrophage-exposed tumor cell, a differentiating neural progenitor, or a stressed neuron may share little transcriptomic identity, but may converge on similar mesoscale kinetic solutions such as altered nuclear export, enhanced membrane-proximal signaling, or increased residence time of regulatory proteins in subcellular compartments. This working group will test the hypothesis that diverse cellular transitions are governed by a small set of conserved mesoscale kinetic programs that can be inferred by synthesizing existing public spatial omics, proteomics, and fluorescence microscopy data.

We will build an open synthesis framework that links three public data classes that are rarely analyzed together. First, we will harmonize single-cell and spatial transcriptomic datasets from public repositories, including brain development and adult brain atlases, tumor microenvironment datasets, MERFISH/seqFISH-style measurements with subcellular RNA localization, and spatial cancer atlases. Second, we will integrate proteomic and immunofluorescence resources such as the Human Protein Atlas, public CODEX/IMC datasets, and subcellular protein localization maps. Third, we will mine public microscopy repositories such as the Image Data Resource and BioImage Archive for live-cell, single-particle, FRAP/FCS, super-resolution, and organelle-tracking datasets that report protein mobility, clustering, stoichiometry, or trafficking dynamics. No new experimental data will be generated.

The central methodological innovation will be a Bayesian multimodal model that translates heterogeneous public measurements into a shared latent representation of mesoscale kinetic state. Rather than treating images as qualitative annotations, the framework will extract probabilistic features including nuclear-cytoplasmic RNA partitioning, local transcript density, protein puncta size and number, apparent oligomeric state, organelle adjacency, membrane enrichment, and effective mobility or residence-time estimates where time-resolved data exist. These features will be linked to matched or harmonized transcriptomic cell states using batch-aware integration and uncertainty propagation. The model will explicitly account for differences in optical resolution, fluorophore sampling, segmentation quality, and assay modality, enabling principled comparison across datasets and laboratories.

We will apply the framework to three biological transitions with abundant public data and strong mesoscale relevance: neural differentiation and maturation, inflammatory remodeling of tumor cells and immune neighborhoods, and cellular stress states involving mitochondrial and membrane-trafficking pathways. Across these systems, we will ask whether transcriptionally distinct cell types reuse common mesoscale programs; whether spatially localized RNAs predict protein compartmentalization or mobility; and whether emergent cellular phenotypes are better explained by inferred kinetic features than by gene expression alone. Expected products include an open atlas of inferred mesoscale kinetic programs, reusable workflows for extracting biophysical features from public microscopy data, benchmark datasets for spatial omics–image integration, and candidate molecular modules linking transcriptional regulation to mesoscale organization.

This project requires NCEMS support because it exceeds the scope of any single laboratory: it demands expertise in single-cell and spatial data integration, statistical optics, Bayesian inference, single-molecule biophysics, image analysis, cell-state biology, and open data engineering. The working group will include trainees as core contributors through hackathon-style data integration sprints, reproducible workflow development, and cross-training modules on spatial omics, microscopy uncertainty, and probabilistic modeling. All curated data links, derived features, code, model outputs, and documentation will be released openly to support community reuse and future synthesis studies of emergent cellular organization.

The project will use only publicly available data and will synthesize information across RNA modification biology, ribosome profiling, proteomics, structural modeling, single-cell genomics, and microbial metabolism.

Graph-based imputation and feature-propagation methods will harmonize sparse single-cell and bulk datasets, while interpretable machine-learning models will identify conserved translation-sensitive modules. Structural and coarse-grained molecular modeling will be used not to create new simulations as primary data, but to contextualize public structures of affected chromatin regulators, RNA-binding proteins, metabolic enzymes, and immune signaling proteins in terms of complex formation, DNA engagement, and mesoscale assembly potential.

The expected outcome is a quantitative map of how nucleotide-scale chemical information propagates to emergent mesoscale organization. We will focus on three synthesis products: first, a conserved catalog of codon- and modification-sensitive translation bottlenecks across organisms; second, a ranked set of chromatin, immune, and metabolic protein complexes whose stoichiometry is predicted to be unusually sensitive to tRNA modification state; and third, a set of cell-state transition models connecting microbial micronutrient availability, host tRNA modification capacity, ribosome pausing, chromatin accessibility, and immune phenotypes. This framework could help explain why similar transcriptional programs diverge into distinct proteomic or epigenomic outcomes, and why microbial metabolites or transporter variation can have unexpectedly broad cellular effects.

NCEMS support is essential because the project requires coordinated expertise in microbial genomics, RNA modification biology, single-cell data integration, proteomics, chromatin biophysics, structural modeling, and AI. The working group will release harmonized datasets, reproducible workflows, interactive network browsers, and training modules for trainees in open, data-intensive molecular synthesis research.

[Background and Significance]
Emergent properties in molecular and cellular systems often arise when many individually modest molecular effects combine to reorganize cellular behavior. tRNA modifications provide an underexplored example of this principle. More than one hundred chemical modifications decorate tRNAs across bacteria, archaea, and eukaryotes, with many concentrated near the anticodon loop where they influence decoding accuracy, codon recognition, frameshifting, and elongation kinetics. Although individual enzymes and modifications have been characterized, the field lacks a synthesis-level understanding of how variation in tRNA modification capacity propagates from codon-specific translation dynamics to proteome remodeling, protein complex stoichiometry, chromatin regulation, and immune or disease-associated cell states. This gap is increasingly tractable because extensive public data now span tRNA modification annotations, ribosome profiling, RNA-seq, proteomics, single-cell transcriptomics and chromatin accessibility, microbial genomes and metagenomes, metabolomics, and predicted protein structures. Transcript abundance alone does not reliably predict protein abundance or cellular phenotype. Codon usage, tRNA availability, modification state, local mRNA context, ribosome traffic, protein stability, and complex assembly all contribute to the final functional proteome. tRNA modifications are especially compelling mesoscale control points because their effects are neither purely molecular nor fully cellular. A modification defect may slow translation at specific codon contexts, alter co-translational folding, bias production of proteins enriched for sensitive codons, and destabilize multi-protein assemblies. If those assemblies include chromatin remodelers, histone modifiers, RNA-binding proteins, metabolic enzymes, or immune signaling complexes, small RNA chemical changes could create large system-level shifts in epigenomic accessibility, inflammatory responses, differentiation, or stress adaptation. Cross-kingdom synthesis is essential. In microbes, tRNA modification pathways are shaped by genome content, temperature, nutrient availability, and metabolic cofactors, and can affect motility, stress responses, translation pausing, and virulence-related phenotypes. In host cells, micronutrients and microbiome-derived metabolites can influence RNA modification substrates and transport, while cancer, neurodegeneration, cardiovascular stress, and immune activation are associated with altered metabolism, chromatin accessibility, and proteome composition. These observations suggest that microbial metabolic capacity and host tRNA modification state may jointly influence translation-sensitive cell-state transitions. However, existing studies are fragmented by organism, assay type, disease context, and analytical framework. NCEMS is uniquely aligned with this challenge because the proposed work focuses on emergence at the mesoscale between biomolecules and organelles: ribosome traffic, protein complex formation, chromatin-regulatory assemblies, and immune-state networks. The project will not generate new data. Instead, it will integrate public datasets using codon-aware statistics, graph-based harmonization, interpretable machine learning, and structural context from public models. The result will be a community resource and conceptual framework for predicting when nucleotide-scale chemical variation becomes a higher-order cellular phenotype.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This working group will address one overarching question: how do tRNA modification states reshape translation dynamics in ways that generate emergent chromatin, immune, metabolic, and stress-response phenotypes across biological systems? We will decompose this question into four linked synthesis questions. First, which tRNA modifications and modifying enzymes are associated with reproducible codon-specific ribosome pausing signatures across bacteria, yeast, and mammalian cells? We hypothesize that loss, depletion, or metabolic limitation of anticodon-adjacent modifications will produce conserved pausing signatures at defined codons and codon neighborhoods, but that the phenotypic impact will depend on organism-specific codon usage, transcript expression, and protein network architecture. Second, which proteins and protein complexes are most vulnerable to tRNA modification-dependent translation changes? We hypothesize that sensitivity will be enriched in proteins whose coding sequences contain clusters of modification-dependent codons, whose abundance must be tightly balanced within complexes, or whose domains require coordinated translation for folding, binding, or assembly. Candidate vulnerable systems include chromatin regulators, histone-modifying enzymes, RNA-binding proteins, mitochondrial and metabolic enzymes, immune receptors, cytokine signaling components, and stress-response regulators. Third, how do translation-sensitive protein modules relate to single-cell chromatin and immune cell states? We hypothesize that tRNA modification-dependent translation bottlenecks create proteomic shifts that are not visible from mRNA abundance alone but become detectable as altered chromatin accessibility, regulatory motif activity, ligand-receptor signaling, immune activation, exhaustion, tissue-resident memory programs, glial states, or metabolic inflammatory states in public single-cell atlases. Fourth, can microbial genome and metagenome features help explain host variation in tRNA modification-linked phenotypes? We hypothesize that microbial pathways affecting queuine, queuosine, sulfur metabolism, folate-related chemistry, flavin-dependent reactions, and other RNA modification cofactors will correlate with host translation-sensitive modules and immune or chromatin states in datasets where microbiome, metabolomic, transcriptomic, or clinical metadata are publicly available. These questions share a central emergence hypothesis: tRNA modifications act as information filters that convert chemical and metabolic conditions into selective translation-rate changes; these changes alter protein stoichiometry and assembly; altered assemblies remodel chromatin and signaling networks; and the resulting cell states can differ sharply even when transcriptomes are similar. The proposal is intentionally falsifiable. We will test whether observed pausing signatures exceed matched codon-usage and expression controls; whether predicted sensitive proteins show discordant RNA-protein behavior in independent datasets; whether sensitive complexes are enriched for known stoichiometric constraints; and whether cell-state associations replicate across tissues, diseases, and species. Alternative outcomes are informative. If sensitivity is highly organism-specific, the atlas will identify the rules governing context dependence. If chromatin and immune modules are not enriched, the project will delimit where tRNA modification control is strongest. The synthesis will therefore produce both mechanistic hypotheses and rigorous negative evidence.

[Methods and Approach]
The project will proceed through four integrated workstreams using only existing public data. Workstream 1 will construct a cross-kingdom tRNA modification knowledge graph. We will curate modification identities, enzyme families, target tRNAs, anticodon positions, cofactor requirements, organismal distributions, and genetic perturbations from MODOMICS, UniProt, KEGG, BioCyc, NCBI genomes, microbial pangenome resources, published tRNA modification maps, and literature-curated datasets. Orthology relationships will be mapped across bacteria, yeast, mouse, and human, with confidence scores for experimentally supported versus inferred annotations. Workstream 2 will quantify codon-aware translation effects. Public ribosome profiling, matched RNA-seq, and proteomics datasets will be reprocessed through standardized workflows for quality control, read periodicity, codon-site assignment, differential ribosome occupancy, translational efficiency, and protein-RNA discordance. We will prioritize datasets with perturbations in tRNA modification enzymes, nutrient or cofactor limitation, stress responses, immune activation, cancer models, neurodegeneration, and metabolic disease. Models will include codon identity, codon pairs, local sequence context, transcript abundance, initiation effects, mRNA structure proxies, and batch covariates. Pausing signatures will be compared with matched null models based on amino acid composition, codon usage, expression, and gene length. Workstream 3 will connect translation sensitivity to proteins, complexes, and mesoscale assemblies. We will integrate protein abundance, phosphoproteomics and other post-translational modification datasets, CORUM and Complex Portal annotations, STRING and BioGRID interaction networks, Reactome pathways, chromatin regulator catalogs, immune signaling databases, and metabolic enzyme networks. Coding sequences will be scored for modification-sensitive codon burden, ribosome pausing evidence, RNA-protein discordance, complex stoichiometry risk, and network centrality. Public PDB and AlphaFold structures will be used to annotate affected domains, interfaces, DNA- or RNA-binding regions, oligomerization sites, and intrinsically disordered segments. Structural and coarse-grained reasoning will contextualize assembly vulnerability but will not generate new experimental data or rely on new simulations as primary evidence. Workstream 4 will infer cell-state consequences. Public single-cell RNA-seq, single-nucleus RNA-seq, single-cell ATAC-seq, and multiome atlases from tumors, immune perturbations, brain disease, cardiovascular and metabolic tissues will be harmonized using graph-based feature propagation, batch-aware integration, label transfer, and probabilistic mapping from bulk proteomic signatures to cell states. We will estimate activity of translation-sensitive modules, chromatin accessibility programs, transcription-factor motifs, cell-cell communication pathways, and immune states. Microbial genome and metagenome datasets will be annotated for RNA modification and micronutrient pathways and linked to host signatures where public paired data exist. The working group will meet through structured NCEMS workshops, hackathons, trainee-led analysis sprints, and cross-disciplinary interpretation sessions. Milestones include a curated atlas in year one, integrated models in year two, and public synthesis products and manuscripts in year three.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The project will deliver three major synthesis products. First, we will release a conserved catalog of tRNA modification-linked translation bottlenecks, including codons, codon contexts, organisms, perturbation types, confidence levels, and supporting ribosome profiling, RNA-seq, and proteomic evidence. This catalog will allow the community to distinguish broadly conserved decoding sensitivities from context-specific effects. Second, we will generate a ranked atlas of protein complexes and pathways predicted to be unusually vulnerable to tRNA modification state. The atlas will highlight chromatin regulators, immune signaling systems, metabolic pathways, RNA-binding proteins, and stress-response assemblies where small translation shifts may alter stoichiometry, assembly, or downstream cell behavior. Third, we will produce cell-state transition models connecting microbial micronutrient capacity, host tRNA modification pathways, ribosome pausing, protein module activity, chromatin accessibility, and immune phenotypes. These models will generate testable predictions for future experimental groups without requiring this working group to produce new data. The impact is conceptual, methodological, and practical. Conceptually, the work will clarify how nucleotide-scale RNA chemistry can become a mesoscale emergent phenotype through ribosome traffic and protein assembly. Methodologically, it will provide reusable codon-aware and graph-based data synthesis workflows for integrating ribosome profiling, proteomics, single-cell genomics, microbial genomics, and structural annotations. Practically, it may help explain why similar transcriptomes produce divergent proteomes, why metabolic or microbial changes can have unexpectedly broad immunological consequences, and why chromatin or immune states may be sensitive to translation dynamics. The project directly advances NCEMS goals by addressing emergence in molecular and cellular biosciences through multidisciplinary synthesis of public data, producing open resources, engaging trainees, and creating analytical strategies that exceed the scope of any single laboratory.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
The working group will follow open, reproducible, and team-based science practices from project initiation through dissemination. All public datasets will be documented in a living data inventory containing accession numbers, source databases, licenses, organism, tissue, assay type, perturbation, processing status, quality metrics, and reuse constraints. No restricted or newly generated experimental data will be used. Derived harmonized datasets, metadata tables, code, model outputs, and visualization files will be deposited in appropriate public repositories such as Zenodo, Figshare, GitHub, OSF, and domain repositories when required by data type. Analysis workflows will be implemented with containerized environments using Docker or Apptainer and reproducible workflow managers such as Nextflow, Snakemake, or WDL. Versioned releases will include software dependencies, parameter files, quality-control reports, and example datasets. Statistical models will include pre-specified evaluation criteria, negative controls, matched null models, and sensitivity analyses. Machine-learning components will emphasize interpretability, uncertainty estimates, transparent feature definitions, and independent validation across organisms or datasets. We will maintain clear separation between training, tuning, and replication datasets wherever possible. Interactive resources will include a web-accessible atlas or network browser enabling users to explore tRNA modification enzymes, codon pausing signatures, sensitive proteins, complexes, pathways, cell types, and microbial metabolic annotations. Documentation will include tutorials for trainees and external users. Authorship, contribution tracking, code review, and decision-making will follow community standards for collaborative science, with contributor roles recorded using CRediT taxonomy. Trainee training will be embedded in the work through workshops on ribosome profiling analysis, single-cell integration, microbial genome annotation, structural interpretation, machine-learning reproducibility, and responsible use of AI. We will invite feedback from external domain experts and potential users before final release. Publications will be submitted as open access when feasible, and preprints will be posted to accelerate community review. These practices will ensure that the project is auditable, reusable, extensible, and aligned with NCEMS expectations for open synthesis research.

[Budget and Resources]
NCEMS support is required because this project depends on sustained coordination among experts in RNA modification biology, microbial genomics, ribosome profiling, proteomics, chromatin biophysics, structural biology, single-cell genomics, immunology, and AI-enabled data integration. The budget will be organized around activities that enable community-scale synthesis rather than new data generation. Major cost categories will include working group meetings, trainee participation, computational resources, open-science infrastructure, and dissemination. We request support for two in-person NCEMS working group meetings per year, supplemented by monthly virtual meetings and focused analysis sprints. Travel funds will prioritize balanced participation across institutions, career stages, and geographic regions, including graduate students, postdoctoral researchers, early-career investigators, and investigators from institutions with varying research capacities. Trainee support will cover short-term analytical fellowships, workshop participation, and protected time for reproducible workflow development and documentation. Computational costs will support cloud or high-performance computing for reprocessing public ribosome profiling, RNA-seq, proteomics, microbial genome, metagenome, and single-cell datasets; storage of harmonized intermediate files; container builds; and hosting of the interactive atlas. Funds for software engineering and data curation will support metadata standardization, workflow hardening, code review, user documentation, and public release. Dissemination funds will support open-access publication fees when needed, public webinars, training materials, and community feedback sessions. No funds will be used for wet-lab experiments, sequencing, animal studies, clinical recruitment, or generation of new primary experimental data. NCEMS resources are essential because the scientific scope exceeds the capacity of a single laboratory: the project requires harmonized standards across data modalities, shared computational infrastructure, cross-disciplinary interpretation, and neutral convening to produce resources useful to the broader molecular and cellular biosciences community. The investment will yield durable public assets, trained data-savvy researchers, and a reusable model for studying emergent mesoscale biology through synthesis of existing data.

abstract_text:

[Background and Significance]
Prokaryotic cells are not compositionally simple reaction vessels. Many bacteria and archaea assemble mesoscale compartments that spatially organize chemistry, create local microenvironments, and generate functions that cannot be inferred from isolated enzymes or membranes. Magnetosomes align magnetic minerals within lipid-bounded vesicles, bacterial microcompartments package metabolic pathways inside protein shells, encapsulins sequester metalloproteins, and recently described iron-storage compartments reveal additional strategies for controlling metal availability. These systems occupy the scale emphasized by NCEMS: between individual biomolecules and whole organelles or cells, where collective assembly produces emergent properties in space, energy flow, information processing, and chemical regulation.

Metal-redox physiology is a particularly powerful setting for synthesis research because metals and electron carriers are both essential and hazardous. Iron, heme, flavins, quinones, iron-sulfur clusters, and nicotinamide cofactors support respiration, carbon fixation, stress responses, virulence, and environmental adaptation. The same chemistry can catalyze oxidative damage, disrupt membranes, or poison enzymes when poorly controlled. Compartmentalization offers a route to concentrate substrates, protect the cytoplasm, tune diffusion, and route electrons across selective barriers. However, the field remains organized around named compartment classes rather than general principles. Magnetosomes, microcompartments, carboxysomes, encapsulins, and iron-storage structures are usually annotated through separate vocabularies, databases, and experimental traditions. As a result, potential convergence among these systems is difficult to detect.

A central unsolved problem is how to decide from public data when a gene cluster encodes a true compartment-forming system rather than an ordinary operon. Many loci contain partial shells, accessory metalloproteins, transporters, regulatory genes, or membrane-associated factors, but lack complete canonical markers. These atypical or hybrid loci are often dismissed, inconsistently annotated, or treated as isolated curiosities. Conversely, remote homologs and environmentally restricted systems may be missed by marker-based searches. The absence of a cross-system synthesis framework limits discovery, comparative evolutionary analysis, and the ability to prioritize future experiments.

The proposed working group will address this gap using only existing public data. The timing is favorable because genome and metagenome repositories now include broad bacterial and archaeal diversity, public transcriptomes and proteomes capture many stress and metabolic conditions, structural prediction resources cover vast protein families, and cryo-electron tomography and electron microscopy archives increasingly document intracellular architecture. No individual laboratory is positioned to integrate these data types across microbial cell biology, metal homeostasis, redox biochemistry, comparative genomics, structural modeling, imaging, ecology, and data science. NCEMS support is therefore essential for convening a community-scale effort.

The significance extends beyond cataloging compartments. By developing a public atlas and quantitative framework for emergent compartment potential, this project will reveal how combinations of genes, physical structures, regulatory programs, and environmental pressures generate new cellular capabilities. The work will transform scattered observations into testable design rules for prokaryotic organelle emergence, clarify evolutionary relationships among independently evolved systems, and provide a durable resource for microbiology, cell biology, bioengineering, pathogenesis, and environmental science.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
The overarching research question is: what publicly observable combinations of genomic organization, protein architecture, regulation, ecological distribution, and stress-associated expression predict the emergence of prokaryotic mesoscale compartments that manage metal and redox chemistry? We will address this question through four linked aims that convert heterogeneous public data into mechanistic hypotheses and community resources.

Question 1 asks which gene-cluster features distinguish compartment-forming loci from ordinary metabolic operons. We hypothesize that bona fide metal-redox compartments are marked by recurrent modular architectures: a boundary-forming module such as a membrane biogenesis system, protein shell, encapsulin shell, or microcompartment shell; a cargo or catalytic module enriched in metalloproteins, redox enzymes, mineralizing proteins, or cofactor-handling enzymes; a transport or permeability module; and a regulation or positioning module. We further hypothesize that incomplete or atypical loci can still represent functional compartments when they preserve key combinations of these modules or recruit missing functions from elsewhere in the genome.

Question 2 asks whether independently evolved compartments converge on shared solutions for metal toxicity, oxidative stress, heme exposure, anaerobic redox balance, and carbon or energy metabolism. We hypothesize that diverse compartment types will share detectable signatures, including enrichment for iron-sulfur proteins, ferritin-like proteins, heme-handling systems, oxidoreductases, redox-active shell pores, membrane remodeling factors, reactive oxygen stress regulators, and environmental associations with fluctuating metal or oxygen availability. These signatures may reveal common mesoscale design principles even when the structural scaffolds differ.

Question 3 asks how physiological and ecological contexts shape compartment emergence. We hypothesize that candidate loci will show nonrandom distributions across habitats and lifestyles, including host-associated pathogens exposed to nutritional immunity and heme stress, anaerobes managing low-potential electron transfer, cyanobacteria and chemoautotrophs requiring concentrated carbon fixation chemistry, desiccation-tolerant organisms requiring protection of sensitive proteins, and sediment or aquatic microorganisms experiencing steep redox and metal gradients. We also hypothesize that public transcriptomic and proteomic datasets will show coordinated induction of compartment loci with iron limitation, iron excess, peroxide or superoxide stress, heme exposure, oxygen shifts, carbon limitation, infection-relevant conditions, or stationary-phase survival.

Question 4 asks whether public structural and imaging data can connect gene clusters to mesoscale architecture. We hypothesize that candidate loci with high emergent compartment potential will encode proteins with compatible oligomerization, curvature, permeability, targeting, cargo-loading, or membrane-remodeling features. Structural predictions and deposited microscopy data will allow us to infer whether a locus is more likely to form a protein shell, lipid-bounded body, mineral-associated structure, or hybrid assembly.

These hypotheses are intentionally integrative and falsifiable. They predict measurable enrichment patterns, co-expression relationships, phylogenetic distributions, and structural compatibilities that can be tested across public datasets. Negative results will also be informative: loci lacking coordinated regulation, modular structure, or ecological association will help define boundaries between compartmentalized and non-compartmentalized metal-redox metabolism. The outcome will be a quantitative, evidence-weighted model rather than a binary annotation scheme, enabling the community to evaluate known systems, ambiguous loci, and newly discovered candidates within a common framework.

[Methods and Approach]
The working group will execute a synthesis-only project using existing public datasets. No new experimental data will be generated. The project will be organized into four coordinated analysis streams with shared standards, quarterly integration meetings, trainee-led coding sprints, and external community feedback.

First, we will construct a reference corpus of known and candidate metal-redox compartment systems. Sources will include NCBI RefSeq and GenBank, GTDB representative genomes, IMG/M, MGnify, public metagenome-assembled and single-cell amplified genome collections, and published supplementary tables for magnetosome, microcompartment, encapsulin, carboxysome, iron-storage, and atypical shell-protein loci. We will build profile hidden Markov models, orthology groups, and rule-based locus definitions for shell proteins, encapsulins, magnetosome-associated proteins, membrane remodeling factors, ferritin-like and other metalloproteins, heme and iron transporters, oxidoreductases, redox cofactor enzymes, cytoskeletal or positioning factors, and regulators. Loci will be annotated in a standardized format that records gene order, strand, intergenic distance, module composition, genomic neighborhood, taxonomy, assembly quality, and habitat metadata.

Second, we will reanalyze public transcriptomic and proteomic datasets to determine regulatory coherence. We will search NCBI SRA, GEO, ENA, PRIDE, MassIVE, and related repositories for bacterial and archaeal datasets involving iron limitation or excess, heme exposure, oxidative stress, desiccation, oxygen transitions, anaerobic metabolism, carbon fixation, host interaction, infection, and stationary-phase or biofilm states. RNA-seq datasets will be processed with documented pipelines for quality control, read mapping or pseudoalignment, normalization, and differential expression. Public proteomics will be reanalyzed where raw files and metadata permit, or harmonized from published protein abundance tables when raw reprocessing is not feasible. Candidate compartment loci will be scored for co-expression, condition responsiveness, regulator association, and alignment with known stress-response signatures.

Third, we will integrate structural and imaging evidence. Protein sequences will be linked to AlphaFold Database models, experimentally determined structures in PDB, domain databases, and predicted oligomeric assemblies when public models are available. We will annotate shell-pore residues, metal-binding motifs, cofactor-binding domains, targeting peptides, curvature-associated surfaces, transmembrane segments, low-complexity regions, and likely cargo-loading interfaces. Public EMDB, EMPIAR, and published cryo-electron tomography annotations will be surveyed for organisms or compartments represented in the genomic atlas. Imaging evidence will not be treated as required for inclusion, but will provide high-confidence anchors and benchmarking examples.

Fourth, we will develop the emergent compartment potential score. Features from genome architecture, phylogenetic profiling, ecological metadata, expression coherence, proteomic support, structural compatibility, and literature-curated evidence will be combined using interpretable machine learning, network community detection, and nonnegative matrix factorization adapted from signature-decomposition approaches. Known experimentally characterized compartments will form positive reference sets, while matched metabolic operons lacking compartment features will form comparison sets. We will use cross-validation across taxonomic groups to reduce overfitting, uncertainty estimates to flag ambiguous cases, and feature-attribution methods to explain each score. The final outputs will include confidence tiers rather than unsupported absolute classifications. All analyses will be reproducible, versioned, and executable through containerized workflows.

The project will deliver three major products. First, we will release an open atlas of prokaryotic metal-redox compartmentalization spanning bacteria and archaea. The atlas will include standardized locus annotations, organism and habitat metadata, candidate compartment class, module composition, taxonomic distribution, evidence links, and confidence tiers. It will unify information that is currently fragmented across genome papers, metagenomic surveys, structural studies, microscopy reports, and stress-response datasets.

Second, we will produce an interpretable emergent compartment potential score for candidate loci. This score will help distinguish well-supported organelle-like systems from ordinary metabolic operons, partial loci, assembly remnants, and ambiguous clusters. Because the score will report the evidence underlying each prediction, users will be able to identify whether a candidate is supported primarily by genomic modularity, co-expression, structural compatibility, ecological association, or public imaging evidence. This will enable rational prioritization of future experimental work without requiring this project to generate new data.

These results will advance NCEMS priorities by explaining how molecular components self-organize into mesoscale structures with emergent cellular functions.

The impact will be broad. Microbial cell biologists will gain candidates for organelle discovery. Evolutionary biologists will gain a framework for comparing independently evolved compartments. Biochemists and structural biologists will gain predicted protein assemblies and redox modules. Synthetic biologists will gain design rules for engineering compartmentalized metabolism. Trainees will gain experience in collaborative synthesis science, public-data stewardship, and reproducible computation.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
The project will follow open, team-based, and reproducible science practices from the start. All nonrestricted outputs will be public, including code, workflow documentation, data dictionaries, intermediate annotation tables, final atlas releases, model parameters, benchmark sets, tutorials, and meeting-derived methodological decisions. Because the project uses only existing public data, we will maintain full provenance for every record, including accession numbers, repository links, download dates, software versions, filtering criteria, and citation metadata.

Analyses will be implemented in version-controlled repositories using transparent issue tracking and pull-request review. Genome-mining, omics-reanalysis, structural-annotation, and scoring workflows will be packaged using portable workflow managers and containers so they can be rerun by external users. Where computational costs are high, we will provide both full workflows and smaller demonstration datasets for teaching and verification. Major atlas releases will be assigned persistent identifiers through an appropriate public archive, and code releases will be archived with versioned digital object identifiers.

Data standards will be developed collaboratively. The working group will define controlled vocabularies for compartment modules, evidence types, confidence tiers, environmental metadata, and structural features. These standards will be documented in a public schema so that community members can submit corrections or additions. We will distinguish primary public data from derived annotations and will clearly flag predictions, literature-supported annotations, and experimentally confirmed examples.

Training will be embedded in the open-science plan. Graduate students and postdoctoral researchers will lead reproducible analysis sprints, co-develop tutorials, and present workflow modules during working group meetings. Tutorials will cover public genome mining, metadata harmonization, transcriptomic reanalysis, structural annotation, interpretable modeling, and responsible reuse of public data. Authorship and contribution policies will be established at project launch, using transparent contribution tracking to recognize data curation, software, analysis, visualization, writing, and mentoring. These practices will make the project reusable, auditable, and inclusive.

[Budget and Resources]
NCEMS support is requested because the project requires sustained coordination across disciplines and institutions rather than isolated analysis by a single laboratory. The primary budget categories are working group convening, trainee participation, computational infrastructure, open-science dissemination, and project coordination.

Convening funds will support two in-person working group meetings at NCEMS and regular virtual meetings among subteams focused on comparative genomics, omics reanalysis, structural modeling, imaging synthesis, metal-redox physiology, microbial ecology, and data science. In-person meetings are essential for harmonizing definitions across compartment fields, resolving annotation disagreements, designing benchmark datasets, and integrating results into a coherent atlas. Funds will also support participation by scientists at different career stages and institution types, including researchers from primarily undergraduate institutions and trainees who would otherwise lack travel support.

Computational resources will support cloud or center-hosted storage, workflow execution, and collaborative development. The project will process large public genome and metagenome collections, public RNA-seq and proteomics datasets, structural models, and metadata tables. Although all primary data are public, integration at this scale requires shared compute, persistent storage, container registries, workflow testing, and web-accessible distribution of derived products. We will avoid duplicating large repositories when stable links are sufficient, but will archive derived annotations and reproducible manifests.

Open-science funds will support website or portal development, digital object identifier deposition, documentation, tutorial preparation, and community webinars. Modest support for a part-time data coordinator or scientific programmer will ensure consistent schemas, accession tracking, release management, and code review. Trainee support will enable graduate students and postdoctoral researchers to participate in analysis sprints and receive mentoring in synthesis research.

No funds will be used for new experiments, sample collection, sequencing, microscopy, proteomics generation, or animal studies. The requested resources directly match NCEMS goals: enabling a transdisciplinary team to synthesize public molecular and cellular data, produce reusable community resources, train data-savvy scientists, and reveal emergent mesoscale principles in microbial cell biology.

title: Decoding Cytokinetic Resilience: Synthesizing Context-Specific Multi-Omic Networks to Understand Mesoscale Emergence Under Thermal Stress

abstract_text: Plant cytokinesis represents a profound example of mesoscale emergence. During this transient developmental window, molecular components—including cytoskeletal microtubule arrays, trans-Golgi network-derived vesicles, and cell wall polysaccharides—spatially and temporally self-organize to construct a novel, higher-order structure: the cell plate. This highly dynamic process acts as a severe architectural bottleneck that is exceptionally vulnerable to environmental perturbations, particularly extreme temperature fluctuations and heat waves. While isolated studies have mapped individual components of the cytokinetic machinery or global plant stress responses, a massive knowledge gap remains: how do diurnal signaling rhythms, temporal organelle dynamics, and redundant spatial mechanisms synergize to buffer mesoscale cell division networks against severe thermal stress? Addressing this complex phenomenon requires a scale of inquiry beyond the capacity of any single laboratory. We propose a community-scale data synthesis project, utilizing strictly publicly available data, to decode the emergent properties of cytokinetic resilience. Leveraging vast public repositories—such as the Sequence Read Archive (SRA), PRIDE, and various open-access bioimage databases—we will integrate spatiotemporal transcriptomes, vesicle proteomics, and cellular imaging across diverse plant systems ranging from key models like Arabidopsis to vital crops such as Zea mays, Sorghum, and Rosaceae species. No new experimental data will be generated. Instead, to manage the immense scale and heterogeneity of these multi-omic data, we will deploy massively scalable, containerized computational workflows to process tens of thousands of raw RNA-seq samples uniformly. By applying advanced, noise-aware network construction toolkits, we will generate context-specific gene co-expression networks (csGCNs). These algorithms will filter out confounding cross-dataset variables to isolate distinct regulatory modules that are activated exclusively at the intersection of specific times-of-day and high-temperature stress. We will bridge these transcriptomic network predictions to mesoscale cellular phenotypes by synthesizing public proteomic and image data, applying shape-based computational modeling to evaluate how environmental stress alters division-plane orientation, phragmoplast navigation, and unconventional protein secretion pathways. This transdisciplinary approach uniquely fuses chronobiology, endomembrane cell biology, and computational genomics. We aim to identify how the circadian clock temporally gates the trafficking of essential cell wall components during heat stress, and whether redundant genetic mechanisms reorganize the 4D temporal organellome to prevent catastrophic cell division failure. Supported by NCEMS, this collaborative Working Group will not only answer fundamental questions about subcellular emergence but also serve as a premier training ground. Trainees will gain cutting-edge expertise at the intersection of biological synthesis, AI-driven network analysis, and scalable cloud computing. In strict adherence to open science principles, all resulting multi-omic matrices, context-specific networks, and reproducible computational pipelines will be made fully accessible to the global scientific community.

[Background and Significance]
Mesoscale emergence in biological systems bridges the gap between individual macromolecules and macroscopic cellular behaviors. One of the most striking examples of this phenomenon in the molecular and cellular biosciences is plant cytokinesis. During this highly coordinated developmental window, distinct molecular components—including trans-Golgi network (TGN) derived vesicles, cytoskeletal microtubule arrays, and cell wall polysaccharides—spatially and temporally self-organize to construct a higher-order structure: the cell plate. Driven by the phragmoplast, this mesoscale assembly process requires rigorous navigation and membrane remodeling to ensure accurate division-plane orientation. Because cell division is an architectural bottleneck, cytokinesis is exceptionally vulnerable to environmental perturbations, particularly thermal stress. With global temperatures rising and heat waves becoming more frequent, catastrophic failures in cytokinesis represent a major threat to plant development and ecosystem stability.

Despite decades of research, our understanding of cytokinetic resilience remains fragmented. Isolated studies have extensively mapped the canonical pathways of cell plate biogenesis, the circadian gating of global abiotic stress responses, and the fundamental dynamics of the plant endomembrane system. However, a significant knowledge gap persists at the intersection of these fields: we lack a systems-level understanding of how diurnal signaling rhythms, temporal organelle dynamics, and redundant spatial mechanisms synergize to buffer mesoscale cell division networks against severe thermal stress. Addressing this compelling scientific question requires synthesizing heterogeneous layers of biological information—ranging from transcriptomics and vesicle proteomics to shape-based morphometrics and chronobiology—at a scale that far exceeds the capacity of any individual research laboratory.

The National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS) is uniquely positioned to catalyze this transdisciplinary investigation. We propose a community-scale synthesis project to decode the emergent properties of cytokinetic resilience using strictly publicly available data. By integrating multi-omic datasets across diverse plant taxa, including key model organisms like Arabidopsis and critical agricultural crops such as Zea mays, Sorghum, and Rosaceae species, this project will unearth the fundamental principles governing mesoscale adaptability. 

This synthesis will reveal how the circadian clock synchronizes endomembrane trafficking to protect the phragmoplast during peak temperature loads. Furthermore, it will illuminate the role of unconventional protein secretion pathways and redundant genetic mechanisms in maintaining division plane fidelity when canonical cellular machineries are thermally compromised. The significance of this project is two-fold. First, it addresses a long-standing puzzle regarding how complex subcellular structures maintain functional emergence under thermodynamic duress. Second, it develops innovative, noise-aware analytical strategies to mine vast public data repositories, extracting context-specific regulatory modules that govern mesoscale resilience. Ultimately, the insights generated by this NCEMS Working Group will redefine our understanding of the temporal organellome while providing the foundational knowledge necessary to engineer heat-tolerant biological systems in an era of unprecedented climate change.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This community-scale synthesis project will address three fundamental, interconnected research questions aimed at decoding mesoscale emergence and resilience during plant cytokinesis under thermal stress. By synthesizing massive public datasets, we will test the following hypotheses:

Research Question 1: How does the circadian clock temporally gate the transcriptomic and proteomic networks governing cell plate assembly to prevent catastrophic failure during heat stress?
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that the circadian clock acts as a temporal master regulator, restricting the transcription and translation of critical cytokinetic network modules—specifically those controlling phragmoplast navigation and microtubule dynamics—to specific times of day. By gating these processes, the clock ensures that the most vulnerable mesoscale assembly phases do not coincide with peak daily thermal loads. Utilizing context-specific gene co-expression networks (csGCNs) derived from publicly available time-course and temperature-stress transcriptomes, we will identify rhythmic regulatory modules that buffer the division machinery against diurnal heat extremes.

Research Question 2: In what ways do temporal organellome dynamics and endomembrane trafficking reorganize at the mesoscale to sustain cell wall deposition during severe temperature fluctuations?
Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that extreme thermal stress triggers an emergent reorganization of the plant endomembrane system, shifting cargo routing from canonical trans-Golgi network (TGN) pathways to unconventional protein secretion (UPS) and autophagy-related pathways. This spatial and temporal rerouting serves as an adaptive mechanism to sustain the delivery of essential polysaccharides and membrane material to the expanding cell plate. By integrating publicly available vesicle proteomics and spatiotemporal transcriptomic data, we will track the shifting gradients of organelle abundance and cargo trafficking, mapping how these unconventional pathways emerge as dominant survival mechanisms when canonical secretion is thermally compromised.

Research Question 3: What redundant spatial and genetic mechanisms preserve division-plane orientation and phragmoplast navigation under heat stress?
Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that plant cells rely on redundant, shape-based constraints and alternative cytoskeletal navigational cues to rescue division-plane fidelity when primary structural networks are disrupted by heat. Utilizing public cellular imaging datasets and shape-based computational models, we will quantify heat-induced division-plane defects across diverse plant species. We will correlate these morphometric changes with genetic redundancies identified through our massive RNA-seq synthesis, revealing a complex fail-safe network that protects the architecture of the dividing cell.

Together, these questions form a cohesive transdisciplinary framework. We aim to understand how temporal pacing (Question 1), molecular supply chains (Question 2), and spatial architecture (Question 3) integrate to yield emergent cytokinetic resilience. Answering these questions requires precisely the type of community-scale, multi-omic data synthesis that NCEMS is designed to support, transforming isolated datasets into a unified understanding of mesoscale biological robustness.

[Methods and Approach]
To decode the emergent properties of cytokinetic resilience, we will conduct a massive community-scale data synthesis using entirely publicly available datasets, generating zero new experimental data. Our methodology relies on advanced computational genomics, multi-omic integration, and shape-based modeling, executed through highly reproducible workflows.

Data Acquisition and Curation: We will harvest public datasets from repositories such as the Sequence Read Archive (SRA), Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO), PRIDE (for proteomics), and the BioImage Archive. The synthesis will span key model organisms (Arabidopsis thaliana) and economically critical crops with diverse genomic architectures (Zea mays, Sorghum bicolor, and Rosaceae species). Data will be strictly filtered for high-quality spatiotemporal, circadian, and heat-stress experimental designs, yielding tens of thousands of individual omics samples.

Massively Scalable Transcriptomic Processing: Analyzing tens of thousands of heterogeneous RNA-seq samples requires robust, reproducible infrastructure. We will deploy highly scalable, containerized computational workflows (e.g., Nextflow-based GEMmaker pipelines) to process massive datasets across heterogeneous cloud and HPC environments. This approach ensures uniform read alignment, transcript quantification, and quality control without exceeding available data storage capacities, generating massive, standardized gene expression matrices.

Noise-Aware, Context-Specific Network Construction: Traditional gene co-expression networks (GCNs) built from massive, heterogeneous datasets suffer from high false-positive rates due to confounding variables. To isolate modules specifically related to heat stress, cytokinesis, and time-of-day, we will utilize advanced, knowledge-independent network construction toolkits. By applying rigorous statistical testing, we will construct context-specific gene co-expression networks (csGCNs). These algorithms will filter out up to 97% of misleading network edges caused by diverse experimental backgrounds, isolating precise transcriptional modules that activate exclusively at the intersection of circadian gating and thermal stress.

Multi-Omic Integration and Proteomic Synthesis: Transcriptomic predictions will be grounded in mesoscale reality by synthesizing public vesicle proteomics and organellomic data. We will map identified csGCN modules onto proteomic profiles of the trans-Golgi network, phragmoplast, and unconventional protein secretion (UPS) pathways. By tracking temporal organellomic gradients and protein abundance shifts in public thermal-stress studies, we will empirically validate the network-predicted rerouting of cell wall machinery.

Shape-Based Morphometric Modeling: To bridge molecular networks to cellular phenotypes, we will synthesize public microscopic imaging datasets of dividing plant cells under stress. We will apply shape-based computational models to these images to quantify altered division-plane orientations and phragmoplast geometries. By correlating morphometric deviations with transcriptomic network states across different species, we will uncover how redundant geometric and genetic mechanisms rescue cellular architecture during heat waves.

Through this transdisciplinary approach—combining highly scalable data processing, advanced noise-aware AI network analytics, and multi-scale modeling—we will synthesize isolated molecular parts into a coherent understanding of mesoscale emergence. The workflows will remain highly modular, allowing the global scientific community to easily update the synthesis as new public data becomes available.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This proposed community-scale synthesis project will yield transformative outcomes that directly align with the NCEMS mission to decode mesoscale emergence. By mathematically formalizing the emergent resilience of plant cytokinesis under thermal stress, we will solve a long-standing puzzle regarding how the circadian clock, temporal organellome, and redundant spatial mechanisms collaborate to protect architectural bottlenecks in cell division. We expect to discover entirely novel, context-specific regulatory modules that govern unconventional protein secretion and phragmoplast navigation exclusively under heat wave conditions.

The scientific impact of this work will span multiple disciplines. For cell biology and chronobiology, we will provide a unified, multi-omic model of how time-of-day dictates cellular susceptibility to stress. For agricultural sciences, translating these fundamental mesoscale principles from Arabidopsis to vital crops like Sorghum, maize, and pear will identify distinct genetic targets for breeding climate-resilient plants capable of surviving increasingly severe temperature fluctuations.

Beyond biological discovery, this project will drive significant methodological impact. We will establish and validate highly scalable, noise-aware computational frameworks capable of filtering massive confounding variables from heterogeneous public datasets to construct highly accurate, context-specific networks. 

Crucially, this NCEMS Working Group will serve as an elite training incubator for the future data-savvy scientific workforce. Postdoctoral researchers and graduate students will be cross-trained in biological synthesis, cloud computing, advanced multi-omics integration, and open science practices. Trainees will not only engage in cutting-edge transdisciplinary research but also learn to manage complex, multi-institutional collaborations. By empowering diverse new talent to answer complex biological questions using existing data, this project will cultivate the next generation of leaders in computational biosciences and systems biology.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
Our Working Group is deeply committed to the highest gold-standard practices in open, team, and reproducible science. Recognizing that the value of community-scale synthesis lies in its accessibility, every aspect of our methodology and output will adhere strictly to FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) data principles.

All computational workflows, including the scalable Nextflow pipelines and noise-aware network construction toolkits, will be developed using containerized software (e.g., Docker and Singularity) to ensure complete computational reproducibility across any local, HPC, or cloud infrastructure. All scripts, algorithms, and shape-based computational models will be maintained in version-controlled, public GitHub repositories under open-source licenses, accompanied by comprehensive, user-friendly documentation and tutorial vignettes.

While no new experimental data will be generated, the massive, highly curated expression matrices, vesicle proteomics mappings, and context-specific gene co-expression networks (csGCNs) represent highly valuable secondary resources. These synthesized data objects will be deposited in permanent, open-access repositories such as Zenodo or Dryad, complete with rich metadata detailing the provenance of the original public datasets. 

To rapidly disseminate findings, we will submit all manuscripts to open-access preprint servers (e.g., bioRxiv) prior to formal peer review in leading open-access journals. Furthermore, we will create an interactive, web-based public portal that allows researchers globally to query our context-specific networks and visualize temporal organellome dynamics without requiring advanced computational expertise. Through this rigorous adherence to open science principles, our synthesis project will not only answer fundamental questions about mesoscale emergence but also provide the broader cellular and molecular biosciences community with robust, reusable tools and integrated data resources.

[Budget and Resources]
To successfully execute this massive, community-scale data synthesis, clear support and resources from NCEMS are required, as the sheer scale and transdisciplinary nature of this project far exceed the capabilities of any single laboratory. 

We request NCEMS funding to support the centralized computational infrastructure necessary for massive data processing. Processing tens of thousands of raw RNA-seq samples and running computationally intensive, noise-aware network algorithms requires substantial allocation of cloud computing credits and high-performance computing (HPC) time. NCEMS support will ensure the required scalability and data storage capacities are met without bottlenecking the research.

Crucially, funding is required for Working Group collaborative activities. We request travel and accommodation support for bi-annual, in-person transdisciplinary synthesis meetings at the NCEMS hub. These meetings are vital for integrating our diverse scientific perspectives—spanning computational genomics, chronobiology, and endomembrane cell biology—and ensuring cohesive progress across the distributed team of investigators. Virtual collaboration infrastructure and project management tools will also be supported to maintain continuous communication between diverse geographical locations.

Finally, a significant portion of the budget will be dedicated to workforce development. We request stipend and tuition support for postdoctoral researchers and graduate students who will execute the core computational workflows and multi-omic integrations. This investment is directly aligned with the NCEMS goal of training the future data-savvy workforce. Trainees will gain unparalleled experience in transdisciplinary synthesis, AI applications, and open science execution. By providing the essential catalytic resources for computational power, team science logistics, and trainee support, NCEMS will enable our transdisciplinary team to transform fragmented public data into profound insights regarding mesoscale emergence and cytokinetic resilience.

title: Decoding Mesoscale Emergence in the 3D Genome: Synthesizing Multi-Omic and Polymer Physics Data to Uncover IDP-Driven Chromatin Reorganization in Neuro-Immune Phenotypes
