(3) How do these mesoscale structural innovations dictate higher-order cellular outcomes, using well-profiled systems like multi-lineage hematopoiesis as our model framework?

This project fully embraces the NCEMS mandate for open science and reproducible synthesis. Our pipelines will be embedded within flexible, web-based bioinformatics management platforms (e.g., Galaxy-integrated environments) to ensure rigorous quality control and full reproducibility across thousands of public datasets. Furthermore, the Working Group will serve as an essential training incubator. By embedding graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in a collaborative, transdisciplinary ecosystem, we will train a diverse, data-savvy workforce. Trainees will gain unparalleled hands-on experience at the intersection of artificial intelligence, high-throughput epigenomics, and evolutionary theory, ultimately equipping the next generation of scientists to decode the emergent properties of the cell.

[Background and Significance]
Emergent properties in biological systems constitute a defining frontier in modern cellular and molecular biosciences. At the core of cellular identity lies the mesoscale architecture of the genome, where singular, localized molecular interactions dynamically cluster to form robust, higher-order regulatory domains. Among the most profoundly consequential yet poorly understood drivers of these emergent mesoscale phenomena are transposable elements (TEs). Historically dismissed as 'junk DNA,' TEs are highly repetitive sequences capable of mobilizing throughout the genome. Recent empirical paradigms postulate that TEs operate as potent, distributed engines of genomic innovation, dispersing ready-to-use transcription factor (TF) binding modules that collectively nucleate novel regulatory hubs. The integration of these elements into functional, higher-order chromatin landscapes underpins the evolutionary emergence of new cell-type-specific transcriptional programs.

Despite the growing consensus regarding the importance of TEs, a fundamental, long-standing puzzle remains unresolved: how do isolated, species-specific transposition events transcend their local sequence constraints to collaboratively rewire chromatin topology at the mesoscale? Unraveling this mystery requires tracking the continuum of TE evolution, from nascent insertions to cooperative nodes fully integrated into complex enhancer clusters. However, achieving this understanding has been obstructed by severe methodological limitations. The inherent repetitiveness of TEs, coupled with rapid evolutionary sequence divergence, critically confounds standard cross-species genomic alignments and predictive modeling. Because TE networks are species-specific, conventional comparative genomics frameworks consistently fail to capture their regulatory contributions, thereby masking the very mechanisms of evolutionary emergence we seek to understand.

Addressing this profound knowledge gap demands an approach that exceeds the capacities of any single laboratory. The exponential proliferation of high-throughput epigenomic assays—including ChIP-seq, ChIP-exo, ATAC-seq, and DNase-seq—has yielded an unprecedented volume of publicly available data. Yet, these data remain heavily fragmented, locked within silos that reflect disparate experimental protocols, distinct mammalian model systems, and varying levels of data resolution. Translating these raw data archives into unified, mesoscale mechanistic insights necessitates community-scale data synthesis.

Our proposed Working Group aligns directly with the foundational mission of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS). We will assemble a transdisciplinary coalition of computational biologists, AI specialists, and evolutionary genomicists to synthesize ultra-high-resolution chromatin and binding data across mammalian lineages. We bypass the limitations of traditional comparative genomics by leveraging cutting-edge machine learning strategies specifically designed to overcome data fragmentation and species-specific domain shifts. By focusing entirely on existing public data repositories, this project avoids the generation of new experimental data and instead channels resources toward sophisticated data integration and advanced algorithmic development. The significance of this synthesis lies not only in answering long-standing questions regarding TE-mediated genomic evolution but also in establishing a new paradigm for cross-species epigenomic imputation. Through this NCEMS-supported synthesis, we will illuminate how decentralized molecular components spontaneously self-organize into emergent regulatory networks that govern higher-order cellular life.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
Our Working Group centers its synthesis efforts on three compelling, interconnected scientific questions that aim to decode the mechanisms by which transposable elements drive the emergence of mesoscale regulatory networks. These questions bridge the gap between individual molecular interactions and higher-order cellular phenotypes.

Question 1: How do coordinated arrays of TEs collectively nucleate emergent mesoscale chromatin structures, such as robust enhancer clusters?
Hypothesis 1: The emergence of complex mesoscale regulatory hubs is not driven by single, high-affinity transposition events, but rather by the synergistic aggregation of multiple, low-affinity TE insertions. We hypothesize that these coordinated arrays collectively overcome energetic and steric barriers, transitioning the chromatin landscape from a restrictive state to an accessible, stable mesoscale domain. By synthesizing high-resolution DNase-seq and ATAC-seq data across multiple species, we will test whether the spatial distribution and density of specific TE families correlate with the de novo formation of broad, multi-kilobase accessible chromatin regions that were absent in ancestral lineages.

Question 2: What are the specific sequence and chromatin determinants that allow a newly transposed element to transition along a continuum—from an isolated molecular binding event to an integrated, cooperative node within a cell-type-specific regulatory network?
Hypothesis 2: We postulate that the functional integration of a TE operates along a two-dimensional continuum dictated by an interplay between intrinsic sequence motif strength and pre-existing local chromatin permissiveness. A TE will evolve into a stable regulatory node either by harboring exceptionally strong, pioneer-like TF binding sequences that actively remodel closed chromatin, or by inserting into a pre-existing favorable chromatin context where weaker motifs are stabilized through cooperative binding with adjacent regulatory elements. Utilizing publicly available ultra-high-resolution ChIP-exo and ChIP-seq datasets, we will synthetically model this continuum, quantifying the precise binding footprints and epigenetic modifications (e.g., histone H3 marks) required for TEs to achieve integrated regulatory status.

Question 3: How do these mesoscale structural innovations dictate higher-order cellular outcomes, using well-profiled systems like multi-lineage hematopoiesis as a model framework?
Hypothesis 3: Emergent mesoscale TE clusters rewire gene regulatory networks to drive phenotypic diversity and lineage specification during cellular differentiation. We hypothesize that lineage-specific differences in hematopoiesis across mammalian species are largely driven by species-specific TE insertions that have co-opted GATA family transcription factors and other master regulators. By applying our synthetic models to highly characterized, publicly available datasets from hematopoietic stem cells, multilineage progenitor cells, and mature blood cells in mice and humans, we will identify how species-divergent TE integrations map to variations in hematopoietic hierarchy and lineage commitment. This framework will validate the broader principle that mesoscale chromatin emergence directly influences higher-order, cell-type-specific outcomes, answering a central puzzle in the cellular sciences.

[Methods and Approach]
To overcome the barriers of cross-species synthesis and repetitive sequence analysis, our working group will utilize entirely publicly available data and deploy state-of-the-art computational and machine learning approaches. Our methodology is structured across three core, interdependent phases focused exclusively on existing datasets from repositories such as ENCODE, the Sequence Read Archive (SRA), and the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO).

Phase 1: High-Resolution Epigenomic Data Harvesting and Harmonization
We will construct a massive, multi-species compendium of ultra-high-resolution regulatory data, incorporating ChIP-exo, ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq, and DNase-seq. The focus will be on key mammalian lineages—primarily human and mouse, extended to primate and rodent outgroups—with a specific emphasis on models of multi-lineage hematopoiesis. This phase will not generate new data but will systematically harmonize thousands of existing datasets. Using standardized data ingestion workflows, we will process reads to identify high-confidence TF binding events, nucleosome positioning, and nuclease accessibility profiles, paying specialized attention to mapping algorithms that effectively resolve multi-mapping reads associated with TEs.

Phase 2: Domain-Adaptive Neural Networks for Cross-Species Prediction
The crux of our methodological innovation lies in addressing the evolutionary domain shifts caused by species-specific repeats. Standard machine learning models trained on one species fail on another due to these repetitive elements. We will develop and deploy advanced domain-adaptive neural network architectures. These deep learning models employ adversarial training strategies to extract sequence features that are invariant across species while simultaneously learning to correct for the domain shift introduced by lineage-specific TEs. By training these models on paired DNA sequence and harmonized TF binding data, we will accurately impute and predict cell-type-specific TF binding landscapes across species, even in highly repetitive regions that traditional comparative genomics cannot resolve.

Phase 3: Mesoscale State Annotation and Network Reconstruction
To conceptualize isolated binding events as emergent mesoscale networks, we will synthesize the outputs of our neural networks using the Integrative and Discriminative Epigenome Annotation System (IDEAS) or analogous multi-track segmentation algorithms. IDEAS excels at integrating diverse epigenetic signals (e.g., CTCF occupancy, histone H3 modifications, accessibility) simultaneously across multiple cell types and chromosomes. We will use this to create a comprehensive registry of emergent regulatory elements, mapping the physical clustering of TE-derived TF binding sites into complex enhancer domains. Finally, by intersecting these mesoscale annotations with publicly available transcriptomic (RNA-seq) data from matched hematopoietic lineages, we will correlate TE-driven chromatin topology with lineage-specific gene expression shifts, thereby closing the loop between molecular events and higher-order cellular outcomes. This multi-layered synthesis pipeline represents a transformative analytical strategy tailored to the precise requirements of the NCEMS framework.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This community-scale synthesis project will deliver transformative outcomes that directly address NCEMS objectives, pushing the boundaries of what is understood about emergent biological phenomena. By elucidating how transposable elements act as distributed engines for the assembly of mesoscale regulatory networks, we will solve a long-standing puzzle regarding the mechanistic origins of genomic innovation. The conceptual shift from viewing TEs as isolated, selfish genetic elements to recognizing them as collective components of emergent cellular architectures will broadly impact evolutionary biology, genetics, and molecular biology.

Methodologically, our project will produce innovative analytical strategies. The development and deployment of domain-adaptive neural networks tailored for cross-species epigenomic prediction will overcome major barriers in computational genomics. These AI models will be released as robust, highly documented tools, empowering the broader scientific community to analyze repetitive and sequence-divergent regions of the genome without being constrained by traditional alignment-based limitations. The resulting comprehensive registry of TE-derived regulatory annotations across mammalian hematopoiesis will serve as an invaluable resource for researchers studying developmental biology and blood disorders.

Beyond scientific discovery, a paramount outcome of this project is its profound impact on workforce development. The Working Group will serve as a premier transdisciplinary training environment. Graduate students and postdoctoral researchers will be deeply embedded within the project, receiving cross-training that spans artificial intelligence, deep learning, computational epigenomics, and evolutionary theory. By uniting experts across different career stages and geographic locations, we will cultivate a new generation of data-savvy scientists. These trainees will emerge equipped with the specialized expertise necessary to leverage massive, publicly available datasets to uncover the emergent properties of biological systems, perfectly aligning with the NCEMS mission to build the future scientific workforce.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
Our Working Group is unequivocally committed to the highest standards of open, reproducible, and team-based science, strictly adhering to the FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) principles. Because our project relies entirely on synthesizing publicly available data, transparently documenting every step of the harmonization and analysis pipeline is essential. To guarantee rigor and reproducibility from data ingestion to publication-ready figures, we will utilize established, flexible management platforms designed for epigenomic research.

All data processing, from raw public read files to final regulatory state annotations, will be managed and tracked using a comprehensive workflow environment, such as the Platform for Epi-Genomic Research (PEGR), integrated seamlessly with the Galaxy platform. This integration ensures that every computational step, software version, and parameter choice is automatically documented and version-controlled. By embedding our pipelines within these web-based infrastructures, we eliminate the 'black box' problem often associated with deep learning and complex bioinformatics workflows.

Furthermore, all code, including the architectures and trained weights for our domain-adaptive neural networks, will be made publicly available under open-source licenses via GitHub and Zenodo. Comprehensive tutorials and Jupyter/Colab notebooks will be provided to ensure the community can independently run, adapt, and validate our models. The synthesized datasets, cross-species binding predictions, and mesoscale IDEAS annotations will be deposited into public repositories (e.g., UCSC Genome Browser track hubs and Zenodo) prior to publication. By establishing an entirely open ecosystem, we not only fulfill the NCEMS mandate for data sharing but also empower independent researchers to leverage our synthetic discoveries to explore new biological questions.

[Budget and Resources]
The proposed budget is meticulously designed to support the collaborative infrastructure, cloud-based computational resources, and trainee development required for a community-scale synthesis project, in strict accordance with NCEMS guidelines. Crucially, no funds are allocated for the generation of new experimental data.

The primary budget categories are:

1. Collaborative Infrastructure and Working Group Meetings: Funds are requested to support bi-annual, in-person Working Group meetings and regular virtual conferences. These meetings are essential for bridging the transdisciplinary gaps between computational AI experts, epigenomic specialists, and evolutionary biologists. The budget covers travel, lodging, and logistical support to ensure equitable participation across diverse geographic locations and institutional tiers.

2. Trainee Support and Workforce Development: A significant portion of the budget is dedicated to the stipends and salaries of postdoctoral fellows and graduate students. These trainees are the operational core of the synthesis project. Funding them ensures they can focus entirely on data integration, machine learning model development, and cross-species analysis, thereby fulfilling the NCEMS mandate to train the next generation of data-savvy biological scientists.

3. Computational Resources and Cloud Infrastructure: Synthesizing thousands of high-resolution epigenomic datasets (ChIP-exo, ATAC-seq, etc.) and training advanced domain-adaptive neural networks requires substantial computational power. Funds are allocated for cloud computing services (e.g., AWS or Google Cloud) and high-performance computing (HPC) storage. This covers the costs of secure data hosting, GPU-accelerated neural network training, and the long-term public hosting of our integrated databases and web-based platforms (e.g., Galaxy/PEGR integration).

4. Open Access and Dissemination: Funds are reserved for open-access publication fees and the costs associated with maintaining open repositories, ensuring that all findings, datasets, and AI models remain freely accessible to the global scientific community without embargo.

title: Mapping Emergent Mesoscale Architectures by Synthesizing the Global Crosslinking Mass Spectrometry and Genetic Interactome Archives
title_norm: mapping emergent mesoscale architectures by synthesizing the global crosslinking mass spectrometry and genetic interactome archives
abstract_text:
The transition from individual biomolecules to functional organelles is governed by emergent mesoscale properties, which are largely driven by dynamic protein-protein interactions (PPIs) and multi-protein assemblies. While traditional systems biology has mapped cellular networks, these models often lack the spatial resolution required to understand the physical constraints and architectural emergence of mesoscale complexes. Over the past decade, Crosslinking Mass Spectrometry (XL-MS) has emerged as a powerful technique to capture direct physical distance constraints within and between proteins in their native cellular environments. Thousands of such datasets currently reside in public repositories. However, these datasets remain severely fragmented, lacking harmonized error estimation, standardized metadata, and integration with broader cellular networks, thereby obscuring our view of mesoscale biology.

We propose a community-scale synthesis project to systematically re-process, harmonize, and integrate the global public archive of XL-MS data to uncover the structural architecture of emergent mesoscale assemblies. By leveraging standardized frameworks such as the Universal Spectrum Identifier (USI) and the Proteomics Standards Initiative Extended FASTA Format (PEFF), our transdisciplinary working group will extract and validate high-confidence, spatially resolved PPIs from billions of mass spectra deposited across global repositories like ProteomeXchange. We will synthesize these structural distance constraints with existing tissue-specific proteomic atlases and curated pathway knowledgebases to build a comprehensive, 3D-informed interactome of the human cell.

This synthesized structural interactome will allow us to address long-standing questions regarding mesoscale emergence: How do localized protein interactions dynamically scale to form stable multimeric complexes and organelle contact sites across different human tissues? To connect these biophysical properties to human health, we will integrate our structural networks with genome-wide association study (GWAS) data. Using network-propagation analysis, we will map how disease-associated and highly pleiotropic genetic variants specifically perturb the physical architecture of these mesoscale assemblies, altering their emergent properties and downstream cellular outcomes.

This project perfectly aligns with the NCEMS mission. It relies entirely on the synthesis of existing, publicly available data, bypassing de novo experimental data generation. The massive computational scale of re-analyzing disparate XL-MS archives, combined with the required cross-disciplinary fusion of biophysics, bioinformatics standardization, and network genetics, makes this endeavor impossible for a single laboratory. By leveraging NCEMS support, we will assemble a diverse team of structural biophysicists, data scientists, and systems biologists. In strict adherence to open science principles, all harmonized datasets, spatial networks, and programmatic pipelines will be disseminated via public REST APIs and integrated into community resources. Furthermore, the project will serve as a premier training ground, equipping early-career researchers with advanced skills in multi-omics integration, structural modeling, and big data harmonization, ultimately training the next generation of data-savvy scientists to explore the frontiers of mesoscale biology.

Thousands of such datasets currently reside in public repositories. However, these datasets remain severely fragmented, lacking harmonized error estimation, standardized metadata, and integration with broader cellular networks, thereby obscuring our view of mesoscale biology.

We propose a community-scale synthesis project to systematically re-process, harmonize, and integrate the global public archive of XL-MS data to uncover the structural architecture of emergent mesoscale assemblies. By leveraging standardized frameworks such as the Universal Spectrum Identifier (USI) and the Proteomics Standards Initiative Extended FASTA Format (PEFF), our transdisciplinary working group will extract and validate high-confidence, spatially resolved PPIs from billions of mass spectra deposited across global repositories like ProteomeXchange. We will synthesize these structural distance constraints with existing tissue-specific proteomic atlases and curated pathway knowledgebases to build a comprehensive, 3D-informed interactome of the human cell.

This synthesized structural interactome will allow us to address long-standing questions regarding mesoscale emergence: How do localized protein interactions dynamically scale to form stable multimeric complexes and organelle contact sites across different human tissues? To connect these biophysical properties to human health, we will integrate our structural networks with genome-wide association study (GWAS) data. Using network-propagation analysis, we will map how disease-associated and highly pleiotropic genetic variants specifically perturb the physical architecture of these mesoscale assemblies, altering their emergent properties and downstream cellular outcomes.

This project perfectly aligns with the NCEMS mission. It relies entirely on the synthesis of existing, publicly available data, bypassing de novo experimental data generation. The massive computational scale of re-analyzing disparate XL-MS archives, combined with the required cross-disciplinary fusion of biophysics, bioinformatics standardization, and network genetics, makes this endeavor impossible for a single laboratory. By leveraging NCEMS support, we will assemble a diverse team of structural biophysicists, data scientists, and systems biologists. In strict adherence to open science principles, all harmonized datasets, spatial networks, and programmatic pipelines will be disseminated via public REST APIs and integrated into community resources. Furthermore, the project will serve as a premier training ground, equipping early-career researchers with advanced skills in multi-omics integration, structural modeling, and big data harmonization, ultimately training the next generation of data-savvy scientists to explore the frontiers of mesoscale biology.

[Background and Significance]
Understanding the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties—emergence—at the mesoscale is one of the most compelling frontiers in modern biosciences. Mesoscale architectures, functioning at dimensions between individual biomolecules and whole organelles, consist of massive multi-protein complexes, dynamic organelle contact sites, and transient signaling hubs. Despite tremendous advances in traditional structural biology and systems-level network mapping, a critical gap persists: systems biology maps often lack physical and spatial constraints, while high-resolution structural methods typically lack the cellular and tissue-level context necessary to observe emergent phenomena. Crosslinking Mass Spectrometry (XL-MS) offers a unique bridge between these domains by providing direct physical distance constraints (typically ~10–30 angstroms) between and within proteins in their native, complex cellular environments. 

Over the past decade, the global research community has deposited vast quantities of XL-MS data into public repositories such as ProteomeXchange. However, synthesizing these resources to extract mesoscale principles remains a severe challenge. The global XL-MS data archive is highly fragmented, plagued by inconsistent false discovery rate (FDR) modeling, non-standardized metadata, and a lack of interoperability with broader multi-omics databases. Consequently, billions of generated mass spectra lie dormant, their embedded structural insights hidden from the broader scientific community. 

This proposal outlines a transdisciplinary effort to rescue, harmonize, and synthesize this untapped well of publicly available data. We will utilize advanced bioinformatics standardization frameworks—such as the Universal Spectrum Identifier (USI) and the Proteomics Standards Initiative Extended FASTA Format (PEFF)—to systemize the disparate XL-MS landscape. By applying robust, community-standardized error estimation models across these archives, we will extract a highly reliable, spatial-distance-constrained map of protein-protein interactions (PPIs). Crucially, this project will integrate these biophysical constraints with tissue-specific proteomic atlases and curated pathway knowledgebases (e.g., Reactome) to generate a three-dimensional, tissue-aware interactome. 

The significance of this work extends beyond basic architectural mapping. We will deploy network-propagation algorithms to overlay genome-wide association study (GWAS) data onto this 3D interactome, probing how highly pleiotropic genetic variants mechanically perturb the spatial integrity of mesoscale complexes. Understanding how structural disruption scales up to alter cellular phenotypes addresses a fundamental mystery in genotype-phenotype relationships. This community-scale synthesis perfectly embodies the NCEMS mandate. It generates no new experimental data, yet it requires a colossal integration of data science, structural biophysics, and human genetics that far exceeds the capabilities of any single laboratory. By leveraging NCEMS support, we will unlock the global XL-MS universe, fundamentally advancing our understanding of emergent mesoscale biology while establishing gold-standard methodologies for multi-omics structural synthesis.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
Our working group will synthesize public multi-omics and structural data to answer three fundamental questions regarding mesoscale biological emergence, each driven by a central hypothesis:

Question 1: How do localized, binary protein interactions structurally coordinate and scale to form stable, tissue-specific multimeric complexes at the mesoscale?
Targeting the architectural rules of mesoscale emergence, we hypothesize that synthesizing global XL-MS distance constraints with tissue-specific proteome abundance data will reveal combinatorial structural motifs that dictate complex assembly. We posit that mesoscale assemblies are not static entities but rather dynamically reorganized entities whose topological properties—such as the formation of specific organelle contact sites—are governed by tissue-specific expression patterns of critical structural nodes. By anchoring our interactome with tissue-specific data, we expect to uncover distinct architectural configurations of the same core complexes across different cell types, explaining how diverse emergent properties arise from shared biomolecular components.

Question 2: Can the systematic, community-wide harmonization of raw crosslinking mass spectral data rescue hidden interactomes and establish a globally reliable spatial network of the human cell?
The current XL-MS landscape suffers from variable pipeline benchmarking and inconsistent false discovery rate (FDR) calculations. We hypothesize that re-processing the fragmented global ProteomeXchange archive using standardized analytical pipelines, Universal Spectrum Identifiers (USI), and extended metadata structures (PEFF) will eliminate prevalent false positives while simultaneously rescuing thousands of high-confidence, spatially informative "orphan" crosslinks. We anticipate that this rigorous re-estimation of error will dramatically expand the known boundaries of the physical interactome, validating previously theoretical protein-protein interactions and providing physical distance constraints for complexes that have evaded traditional structural biology methods.

Question 3: How do disease-associated and highly pleiotropic genetic variants mechanically perturb the physical architecture of mesoscale assemblies to drive pathological cellular outcomes?
Bridging biophysics and human genetics, we seek to understand how small molecular perturbations cascade into systems-level failures. We hypothesize that highly pleiotropic genetic variants—those associated with multiple distinct complex traits in genome-wide association studies (GWAS)—localize to critical, structurally sensitive hubs within mesoscale assemblies. By utilizing network-based expansion and network-propagation analysis on our newly synthesized 3D-informed interactome, we predict that these variants will be shown to disrupt vital inter-protein crosslinks, thereby destabilizing the quaternary structure of mesoscale hubs. Consequently, this destabilization will alter downstream functional networks and cellular phenotypes. Proving this hypothesis would provide a direct, mechanistic explanation for the pleiotropic effects of common human variants, mapping the exact biophysical pathways through which genetic risk is translated into cellular dysfunction.

[Methods and Approach]
Our community-scale synthesis project is strictly computational, relying entirely on existing, publicly available data. The transdisciplinary approach integrates advanced mass spectrometry informatics, structural biophysics, AI-driven modeling, and network genetics. 

1. Data Acquisition, Harmonization, and Standardization:
We will programmatically harvest raw XL-MS datasets from global repositories, primarily via the ProteomeXchange consortium. To overcome severe fragmentation, we will employ the Universal Spectrum Identifier (USI) to create standard, reproducible virtual paths to all mass spectra. Concurrently, we will implement the Proteomics Standards Initiative Extended FASTA Format (PEFF) to encode comprehensive metadata regarding sequence variants and post-translational modifications. By standardizing the search space, we will re-process billions of spectra using state-of-the-art sequence search engines coupled with unified, rigorous False Discovery Rate (FDR) models. This pipeline benchmarking will eliminate platform-specific biases and yield a globally harmonized dataset of high-confidence structural distance constraints. 

2. AI-Assisted Structural Syntheses and 3D Interactome Construction:
The validated crosslinks—representing spatial distance constraints—will be integrated with the Reactome Pathway Knowledgebase and massive tissue-specific protein abundance atlases. To build a continuous 3D-informed interactome, we will fuse our harmonized XL-MS constraints with AI-driven structural predictions using AlphaFold2 Multimer. The empirical distance constraints derived from the XL-MS data will serve as orthogonal physical filters to score and validate AlphaFold2 predictions of mesoscale multimeric assemblies. This synergistic approach will resolve complex topologies that neither XL-MS nor AI can confidently model in isolation, resulting in a spatially resolved, tissue-specific interactome of the human cell. 

3. Network Propagation and GWAS Integration:
To link mesoscale architecture to emergent cellular phenotypes and human health, we will integrate large-scale genomic data, such as GWAS data from the UK Biobank. We will map trait-associated and pleiotropic variants onto the nodes of our synthesized 3D interactome. Using advanced network-propagation algorithms, we will measure the structural impact of these variants across the network. Specifically, we will computationally evaluate how single amino acid substitutions (derived from genetic variants) alter the electrostatic and structural integrity of critical crosslink interfaces, propagating these local disruptions through the ordered networks of molecular transformations defined in our pathway databases. 

4. Multidisciplinary Working Group Dynamics:
Executing this strategy requires expertise beyond a single laboratory. Under the NCEMS umbrella, we will convene biophysicists, computational proteomics experts, and network biologists. We will conduct recurring synthesis working group hackathons, utilizing cloud-based computational environments to collaboratively refine our AI models and analytical strategies. Trainees will be integrated at every stage, receiving cross-disciplinary mentorship in big data harmonization, structural biophysics, and network analysis, directly fulfilling the NCEMS mission to train a data-savvy workforce.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This synthesis project will deliver transformative outcomes that reshape our understanding of mesoscale biology, while fundamentally upgrading the utility of public proteomics archives. 

Firstly, we will produce the first comprehensive, tissue-specific, 3D-informed interactome of the human cell, derived entirely from the harmonization of existing XL-MS data. This structural atlas will uncover previously undetected multi-protein complexes and organelle contact sites, solving long-standing puzzles regarding how individual proteins dynamically assemble to form functional mesoscale architectures. 

Secondly, by mapping genome-wide association study (GWAS) data onto this structural interactome, we will generate predictive mechanistic models explaining how pleiotropic genetic variants disrupt cellular machinery. This outcome will directly impact biomedical research by providing high-confidence, structurally validated targets for drug repurposing and therapeutic intervention, particularly for complex polygenic traits.

Methodologically, our project will establish a new gold standard for multi-omics integration. By demonstrating the vast potential of the Universal Spectrum Identifier (USI) and the Extended FASTA Format (PEFF) at a community scale, we will drive widespread adoption of these standards, ensuring future mass spectrometry data is intrinsically FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable). The harmonized analytical pipelines developed by our working group will be adopted as community benchmarks for XL-MS error estimation. 

Finally, the impact on human capital will be profound. The project will serve as an elite training hub. Graduate students and postdoctoral researchers will be embedded in a deeply transdisciplinary environment, mastering cloud-scale computing, AI-driven structural modeling, and bioinformatics standardization. By leveraging NCEMS resources to forge these collaborative networks, we will produce a new generation of data-savvy scientists uniquely equipped to interrogate biological emergence through the synthesis of disparate, large-scale datasets.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
Our working group is unconditionally committed to the highest standards of open, reproducible, and team-based science, strictly aligning with FAIR principles. Given that this project relies entirely on synthesizing publicly available data, transparent data provenance is our top priority. 

All re-processed mass spectra, validated crosslink constraints, and generated 3D interactome models will be submitted back to public repositories, including the PRIDE database and ProteomeXchange, ensuring they are accessible to the global community. To facilitate seamless programmatic access, all derived datasets will be integrated into the Omics Discovery Index (OmicsDI). We will develop robust REST APIs to allow researchers worldwide to instantly query our structural networks and cross-reference them with external genomic and transcriptomic datasets. 

To guarantee analytical reproducibility, all computational workflows, AI-assisted modeling scripts, and network-propagation algorithms will be developed in the open. Code will be meticulously version-controlled and hosted on public repositories such as GitHub and Zenodo, carrying permissive open-source licenses (e.g., MIT or Apache 2.0). Furthermore, our data processing pipelines will be fully containerized using technologies like Docker and Singularity, and orchestrated via Nextflow. This ensures that any researcher can download and execute our exact computational environment, regardless of their local hardware, replicating our analyses down to the byte. 

Knowledge dissemination will occur exclusively through open-access publications and pre-print servers (e.g., bioRxiv). Additionally, our team will host open, virtual hackathons and community workshops as part of our NCEMS activities, providing tutorials on implementing our standardized XL-MS pipelines and utilizing the USI and PEFF frameworks, thereby democratizing access to complex structural synthesis methodologies.

[Budget and Resources]
To successfully execute this community-scale synthesis project, we request NCEMS support to fund personnel, cloud computational infrastructure, and multidisciplinary working group activities. 

Personnel (Training the Next Generation): The majority of the budget will support postdoctoral researchers and graduate trainees. These early-career scientists will be jointly mentored by our transdisciplinary team of biophysicists, computational proteomics specialists, and network biologists. They will drive the hands-on data harmonization, AI-driven structural modeling, and systems-level network analyses, acquiring vital skills in big data science and multi-omics integration. 

Cloud Computing and Data Storage: Synthesizing and re-processing billions of mass spectra from global archives necessitates significant computational power. Funds are allocated for secure, high-performance cloud computing resources (e.g., AWS or Google Cloud). This infrastructure will support the computationally intensive pipeline benchmarking, the calculation of rigorous FDR models across massive datasets, the deployment of AlphaFold2 for structural multimer predictions, and the storage of large-scale, containerized databases. 

Working Group Logistics and Collaboration: A crucial component of this NCEMS proposal is the facilitation of cross-disciplinary synergy. We budget for semi-annual, in-person working group meetings and periodic virtual hackathons. These funds will cover travel, accommodation, and logistical support to bring together researchers from diverse geographic locations and institutions, ensuring seamless collaboration across domains. 

Open Science and Dissemination: Funds are requested to cover open-access publication fees, ensuring all findings are freely available. Additionally, resources will be dedicated to hosting and maintaining the REST APIs and interactive web portals through which the global community will access the synthesized 3D interactome. 

This project’s massive data-processing requirements and the requisite fusion of diverse scientific perspectives far exceed the capacity of a single laboratory, fundamentally requiring the comprehensive support and community-building resources provided by the NCEMS.

By bridging disparate biological disciplines, this project will reveal the structural and chemical emergence of microbial ecosystems while maximizing the latent value of public omics data.

[Background and Significance]
Microbial communities govern global biogeochemical cycles, shape host health, and drive environmental adaptation through intricate, emergent biochemical dialogues. At the heart of these complex systems is emergence at the mesoscale: the organizational level bridging fundamental molecular sequences to observable cellular and community-level phenotypes. In microbial ecosystems, mesoscale emergence is prominently characterized by the evolution of highly complex operons that encode multi-enzyme protein assemblies. These structural complexes act as modular cellular factories, collaborating to synthesize heavily modified, structurally diverse specialized metabolites—ranging from novel lipid derivatives to complex polyamine conjugates—that mediate microbial interaction and environmental adaptation. Despite the vast amount of publicly available sequencing and metabolomic data generated over the past decade, a profound disconnect remains. Traditional bioinformatics and mass spectrometry data analysis workflows are intrinsically anchored to reference databases. However, these databases represent only a minute fraction of Earth's biological diversity, heavily biased toward a handful of culturable model organisms. Consequently, the vast majority of environmental genetic blueprints and untargeted mass spectrometry (MS/MS) spectra remain unannotated, relegated to the status of biological "dark matter." This reliance on known annotations critically impedes our ability to understand how novel mesoscale multi-protein structures emerge and how they dictate unexplored chemical diversity. Our understanding of microbial emergence is further fragmented by the historical siloing of multi-omic data. Uncultured metagenomic sequences (genomic potential) and untargeted mass spectrometry data (realized chemical output) are typically analyzed in isolation. To solve this long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biosciences, a massive synthesis of these distinct data modalities is urgently required. Advancements in artificial intelligence, specifically alignment-free deep learning architectures like Siamese neural networks, now allow us to detect shared functionality among highly divergent microbial homologs without relying on reference markers. Concurrently, the development of expressive mass spectrometry query languages permits the rapid, pattern-based mining of billions of untargeted mass spectra to find hidden structural motifs, regardless of whether the exact molecule exists in a database. Synthesizing these computational innovations presents an unprecedented opportunity to transcend reference-based limitations. By integrating global metagenomic repositories with massive public MS/MS datasets, we can reconstruct the ancestral evolution of complex operons and directly correlate these emergent multi-enzyme assemblies with uncharacterized biochemical outputs. This community-scale data synthesis will answer fundamental questions about how biochemical complexity arises at the mesoscale. It is highly significant because it shifts the analytical paradigm from piecemeal, database-restricted observations to a holistic, reference-free mapping of the genomic-to-chemical landscape, ultimately unlocking a vast, untapped reservoir of biological dark matter to advance the molecular and cellular sciences.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This synthesis project is structured around three compelling, interrelated research questions aimed at decoding mesoscale emergence through multi-omic data integration. 

Question 1: How do novel multi-enzyme mesoscale assemblies evolve from ancestral operons across highly divergent, uncultured microbial lineages? 
We hypothesize that by utilizing reference-free, deep-learning-based functional classification on global metagenomic data, we can identify convergent evolutionary trajectories wherein standalone functional genes are recruited into complex, multi-component operons. By mapping these unannotated genetic clusters using maximum parsimony frameworks, we predict we will uncover previously unrecognized vertical evolution models demonstrating how simple genetic elements systematically assemble into emergent, higher-order mesoscale protein complexes capable of novel catalytic functions. 

Question 2: What is the cryptic chemical output of these uncharacterized mesoscale multi-enzyme assemblies, and how do variations in operon architecture translate into structural chemical diversity? 
We hypothesize that untargeted MS/MS spectra housed in public repositories contain robust, predictable structural patterns—such as specific ion fragmentation signatures indicating unique lipid conjugations or polyamine modifications—that map directly to the catalytic capacities of uncharacterized operons. We anticipate that by querying over a billion MS/MS spectra using highly expressive pattern-matching languages, we will discover thousands of unrecognized specialized metabolites and structural modifications whose synthesis is dependent upon the specific architectural variations of emergent multi-protein complexes. 

Question 3: Can we mathematically and computationally synthesize independent genomic and mass spectrometry data streams to accurately predict emergent biochemical phenotypes directly from raw environmental sequence data? 
We hypothesize that the co-occurrence of predicted mesoscale operon assemblies in uncultured metagenomes correlates strongly with the presence of distinct, uncharacterized spectral families in paired or environmentally similar meta-metabolomic datasets. By leveraging AI to synthesize these data types, we will construct a unified "Genomic-to-Chemical Mesoscale Graph." We propose that this integrated network will not only establish definitive links between genetic dark matter and chemical dark matter but will also enable predictive modeling of a microbial community's emergent chemical phenotype based solely on its metagenomic profile. 

Collectively, these research questions challenge the current reliance on annotated molecular data and address long-standing mysteries regarding the origins of biochemical diversity. By exploring these hypotheses through the synthesis of strictly pre-existing data, the Working Group will elucidate the fundamental rules of mesoscale structural assembly and its resulting chemical emergence. This approach pushes the boundaries of our understanding of molecular evolution and the vast, unmapped chemical space generated by uncultured microbiomes.

[Methods and Approach]
To answer our proposed research questions, the Working Group will employ a purely data-driven synthesis strategy, exclusively utilizing publicly available datasets and developing a novel, transdisciplinary computational ecosystem. No new experimental data will be generated. 

Data Sources: 
We will harvest terabytes of raw sequence data from environmental and host-associated uncultured metagenomes via the Sequence Read Archive (SRA) and MG-RAST. Concurrently, we will synthesize chemical data by accessing over 1.2 billion untargeted proteomics and metabolomics MS/MS spectra from global community repositories, such as GNPS and PRIDE. 

Phase 1: Reference-Free Genomic Discovery of Mesoscale Assemblies 
To bypass the limitations of heavily biased functional annotations, we will process massive metagenomic datasets using alignment-free deep learning models. Specifically, we will deploy Siamese Neural Networks capable of identifying shared nucleic acid functionalities across divergent homologs by recognizing complex sequence embeddings rather than simple sequence identity. Once novel functional groups are clustered, we will map their genomic neighborhoods to identify putative operons. We will then employ evolutionary reconstruction algorithms utilizing maximum parsimony models to trace the ancestry of these operons, delineating how individual ancestral genes iteratively combined to form emergent mesoscale multi-enzyme complexes across microbial lineages. 

Phase 2: Pattern-Based Mining of the Mass Spectrometry Universe 
Parallel to genomic analysis, we will analyze the colossal corpus of public MS/MS data. We will utilize advanced Python-based data processing frameworks to standardize, clean, and unify the diverse spectral datasets. Crucially, we will implement expressive Mass Spectrometry Query Languages (MassQL) to execute complex, pattern-based searches across the 1.2 billion spectra. Rather than searching for known exact molecular masses, we will query for conserved structural motifs—such as predictable mass shifts associated with novel bile acid modifications or previously undiscovered polyamine conjugations. This approach will group fragmented "chemical dark matter" into cohesive structural families derived from shared enzymatic modifications. 

Phase 3: Multi-Omic Synthesis and Graph Construction 
The crux of the project lies in the synthesis of Phase 1 and Phase 2 outputs. We will perform large-scale co-occurrence analyses, integrating metadata from paired multi-omic studies where both metagenomic sequencing and untargeted metabolomics were performed on the same biological samples. We will utilize machine learning association models to link the evolutionary appearance of specific mesoscale operon structures (Phase 1) with the emergence of distinct uncharacterized spectral families (Phase 2). This integration will populate the "Genomic-to-Chemical Mesoscale Graph," a multi-layered network directly linking previously unannotated genomic features to their corresponding cryptic chemical outputs. 

Validation and Rigor: 
The computational models will be iteratively refined using a subset of highly characterized datasets (e.g., well-documented secondary metabolite biosynthetic gene clusters and their known MS/MS spectra) to validate the precision of the reference-free alignment and query architectures before deploying them on entirely unannotated biological dark matter. All models will incorporate robust statistical bootstrapping to ensure confidence in the synthetic linkages.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This synthesis project will yield transformative outcomes for the molecular and cellular biosciences. First, we will deliver the "Genomic-to-Chemical Mesoscale Graph," an unprecedented public resource that maps the evolutionary trajectories of uncharacterized mesoscale multi-enzyme complexes directly to their emergent chemical outputs. We expect to identify thousands of novel structural linkages, significantly reducing the proportion of data categorized as biological "dark matter."

Second, the project will result in the discovery of entirely new classes of specialized metabolites, such as previously unrecognized lipid-conjugates and complex polyamine modifications. These discoveries will illuminate the hidden biochemical dialogue of uncultured microbiomes, providing novel insights into community-scale resilience, host-microbiome interactions, and potential biotechnological applications.

Third, we will release a suite of innovative, validated AI and pattern-matching software tools. By proving that alignment-free deep learning and expressive MS/MS query languages can successfully bypass the limitations of biased reference databases, we will provide the scientific community with a new blueprint for reference-free multi-omic discovery.

By resolving long-standing puzzles surrounding the emergence of structural and chemical complexity, this work shifts the paradigm of omics research. Furthermore, the collaborative framework of this project will foster deep cross-pollination between evolutionary genomics and computational mass spectrometry. Importantly, this initiative will profoundly impact workforce development. Code and Software Accessibility: 
All computational pipelines—including the alignment-free Siamese Neural Networks, the evolutionary maximum parsimony scripts, and the Python-based MassQL query algorithms—will be developed entirely in the open. Source code will be hosted in version-controlled public GitHub repositories under an open-source license (e.g., MIT or Apache 2.0). We will utilize containerization technologies, such as Docker, to encapsulate the entire data-processing environment, ensuring that any researcher can perfectly reproduce our computing ecosystems irrespective of their local hardware configuration.

Data Availability and Standards: 
Following FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data principles, all intermediate and final outputs, most notably the "Genomic-to-Chemical Mesoscale Graph," will be made publicly available. Annotated spectral networks and newly discovered chemical motifs will be directly integrated into community data repositories like GNPS (Global Natural Products Social Molecular Networking), allowing immediate use by the global mass spectrometry community. Synthesized genomic annotations and operon models will be deposited in platforms such as Zenodo with clear, standardized metadata.

To maximize the utility of our generated tools, we will provide exhaustive documentation, including step-by-step Jupyter Notebook tutorials demonstrating how to apply our reference-free AI models to new datasets. The proposed research requires NCEMS support because synthesizing global metagenomic repositories with over 1.2 billion MS/MS spectra is fundamentally beyond the capabilities, both computational and intellectual, of any single laboratory. This project demands a transdisciplinary merger of microbial evolutionary genomics, high-performance computational proteomics, and advanced deep learning—a convergence only possible through a dedicated, Center-supported Working Group.

The scale of data requires substantial computational resources. Similarly, querying billions of spectra demands significant memory and parallel processing capabilities. We request budget allocations for cloud computing credits (e.g., AWS or GCP) and dedicated storage to house intermediate data structures, ensuring smooth and rapid execution of our deep learning and pattern-matching algorithms. abstract_original: Microbial communities exhibit remarkable emergent properties, orchestrating complex biochemical dialogues that shape host and environmental systems. These behaviors emerge primarily at the mesoscale, where diverse operons dictate the assembly of multi-enzyme protein complexes. These mesoscale structures subsequently synthesize heavily modified, highly diverse specialized metabolites. However, the vast majority of this biochemical repertoire remains hidden as biological "dark matter," largely because traditional analytical approaches rely on heavily biased reference databases. Consequently, our understanding of how novel mesoscale complexes emerge and drive chemical diversity remains fundamentally fragmented. To solve this long-standing puzzle, we propose the Working Group for Multi-Omic Synthesis of Mesoscale Emergence. This project will execute a community-scale synthesis of massive, publicly available but currently siloed datasets: uncultured metagenomic sequences and billions of untargeted mass spectrometry (MS/MS) proteomics and metabolomics spectra. Because this synthesis requires advanced cross-disciplinary data science spanning microbial evolutionary genomics and computational mass spectrometry, it fundamentally necessitates the collaborative environment and computational infrastructure provided by NCEMS. Our working group will pioneer a reference-free computational ecosystem to link the genetic blueprints of uncultured microbiomes to their emergent mesoscale assemblies and resulting chemical outputs. First, we will utilize alignment-free deep learning architectures—such as Siamese neural networks—to analyze global public metagenomes. This will enable the identification of shared functional domains and the evolutionary reconstruction of complex ancestral operons, bypassing the limitations of known functional annotations. Second, we will deploy expressive pattern-matching algorithms and mass spectrometry query languages to mine over a billion public MS/MS spectra. This computational search will identify structural patterns of uncharacterized metabolites and peptide fragments produced by these previously hidden operon-encoded assemblies. By synthesizing these independent multi-omic data streams, the working group will construct a unified "Genomic-to-Chemical Mesoscale Graph." This integrated network will answer fundamental questions regarding how novel multi-protein structures emerge across microbial lineages and how variations in these mesoscale assemblies translate into unappreciated chemical diversity, such as complex lipid or polyamine modifications. This synthesis will directly link primary molecular sequence data to emergent community-level biochemical phenotypes. The working group is entirely committed to open science principles; all unified data structures, predictive neural network models, and MS/MS querying workflows will be published as open-source computational tools. Furthermore, this initiative emphasizes vital workforce development, providing dedicated training for a diverse cohort of postdocs and graduate students at the intersection of computational multi-omics, deep learning, and mesoscale biology. By bridging disparate biological disciplines, this project will reveal the structural and chemical emergence of microbial ecosystems while maximizing the latent value of public omics data.

Third, we will develop machine learning models that link these dynamic coupling architectures directly to publicly available transcriptomic and high-throughput functional assay datasets (e.g., GEO, ChEMBL). This framework will predict how specific mutation- or ligand-induced shifts in allosteric networks cascade into emergent phenotypic states, such as metabolic reprogramming or disease pathologies. This community-scale synthesis relies exclusively on existing, publicly available data, bypassing de novo experimental generation in strict accordance with the NCEMS mandate. By bridging evolutionary protein dynamics, receptor pharmacology, and exascale computational biophysics, this project demands a transdisciplinary collaboration far surpassing the capacity of any single lab. The initiative champions open science by committing to publish all AI models, dynamic network maps, and synthesized phylogenetic trajectories in robust, open-access portals. Furthermore, it addresses the NCEMS mission by providing rich cross-training opportunities for a diverse cohort of graduate students and postdocs, equipping the next generation of researchers with essential skills in data science, generative AI, and multi-scale biological synthesis. Ultimately, this work will solve long-standing puzzles regarding the structural basis of evolution and establish a predictive framework for allosteric emergence in cellular systems.

[Background and Significance]
The unexpected appearance of new biological properties at the mesoscale—the critical interface between individual biomolecules and higher-order cellular organelles—remains one of the most fundamental mysteries in the molecular and cellular biosciences. At this scale, the transmission of information involves highly complex, emergent phenomena, wherein atomic-level perturbations such as ligand binding or point mutations cascade through a protein's architecture to govern the assembly of massive, multimeric signaling complexes. Prototypical examples of this mesoscale emergence include modular signaling hubs, such as nuclear receptors (NRs) and Src-family kinases. These biomolecular machines function as allosteric switches, translating extracellular and metabolic cues into profound transcriptional cascades and cellular responses. Despite their biological importance and therapeutic relevance, the precise physical principles and evolutionary trajectories that dictate how allosteric signals propagate across these modular domains to mediate mesoscale complex formation remain obscured. Over the past two decades, the global scientific community has amassed an unprecedented volume of publicly available data. We now possess deep phylogenomic alignments capturing billions of years of evolutionary history, tens of thousands of static crystallographic and cryo-EM structures in the Protein Data Bank (PDB), petabytes of exascale molecular dynamics (MD) trajectories hosted in distributed computing archives (e.g., Folding@home), and exhaustive transcriptomic and functional datasets residing in repositories like GEO and ChEMBL. However, these massive datasets exist in isolated silos. Evolutionary biologists analyze sequence conservation, biophysicists study localized atomistic dynamics, and systems biologists map transcriptomic outputs. Consequently, a unified theoretical and computational framework connecting evolutionary sequence space to atomistic dynamics, and ultimately to mesoscale emergent phenotypes, has not yet been established. The synthesis of these disparate data streams represents a profound opportunity to solve the long-standing puzzle of protein allostery and mesoscale regulation. We hypothesize that mesoscale signaling complexes are governed by conserved, dynamically coupled 'wiring diagrams' that have been finely sculpted by evolution. By identifying how functionally critical rigid hinges and highly flexible recognition sites migrate and co-evolve over evolutionary time, we can understand the physical basis of how proteins adapt to bind new ligands and recruit novel co-regulators. Aligning with the core mission of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS), our proposed Working Group seeks to execute a community-scale synthesis project utilizing exclusively publicly available data. We will integrate AI and data science with principles of evolutionary biophysics to link deep evolutionary time with exascale molecular dynamics. By synthesizing structural ensembles, simulated trajectories, and transcriptomic data, we aim to map the dynamic order parameters of allostery. This transdisciplinary approach will fundamentally shift the paradigm from viewing proteins as static entities to understanding them as dynamic, evolving networks. The significance of this project lies not only in addressing fundamental questions regarding the physical basis of biological emergence but also in pioneering novel analytical strategies that can be generalized to other complex mesoscale systems, ultimately establishing a predictive engine for synthetic biology, protein engineering, and precision pharmacology.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
Our transdisciplinary synthesis project is driven by three fundamental research questions that bridge evolutionary history, atomistic dynamics, and mesoscale cellular phenotypes. These questions are designed to challenge our current understanding of allostery and modular protein regulation by leveraging the vast expanse of unintegrated, publicly available structural, dynamic, and functional data. 

Research Question 1: How do ancestral allosteric networks evolve to support the emergence of novel mesoscale signaling complexes? Current evolutionary analyses largely focus on sequence conservation, neglecting the physical dynamics that enable function. We hypothesize that the emergence of novel mesoscale interactions—such as the recruitment of distinct multimeric co-regulators by nuclear receptors or the modular autoinhibition mechanisms of Src-family kinases—is driven by the evolutionary migration of critical dynamic 'wiring diagrams.' Specifically, we hypothesize that the spatial distribution of highly rigid hinges and highly flexible active sites is not static; rather, it co-evolves to accommodate new ligand specificities and facilitate altered complex formations. By synthesizing ancestral sequence reconstruction with predicted structural ensembles, we aim to map the evolutionary trajectories of these allosteric networks, testing the hypothesis that dynamic flexibility is a highly evolvable trait crucial for mesoscale adaptation.

Research Question 2: Can emergent mesoscale properties of modular signaling hubs be quantitatively predicted from atomistic dynamic coupling indices derived from exascale datasets? The gap between microsecond atomistic fluctuations and macroscopic cellular function is historically difficult to bridge. We hypothesize that network-based dynamic metrics—specifically the Dynamic Flexibility Index (DFI) and Dynamic Coupling Index (DCI)—extracted from synthesized petabyte-scale molecular dynamics (MD) trajectories can serve as definitive 'order parameters' for large-scale conformational states. By mining open-source exascale MD archives generated via distributed computing (e.g., Folding@home), we hypothesize that these dynamic indices will reveal hidden, long-range allosteric communication channels. We expect to demonstrate that specific patterns of dynamic coupling dictate the thermodynamic probability of adopting active versus inactive mesoscale assemblies, effectively bridging the atomic and mesoscale regimes.

Research Question 3: How do ligand-induced or mutational perturbations in fundamental dynamic wiring diagrams cascade into systems-level phenotypic changes? To connect physical biophysics with biological emergence, it is necessary to link dynamic changes to actual cellular outputs. We hypothesize that machine learning models can be trained to recognize specific DFI/DCI network signatures and accurately predict corresponding transcriptional or functional outcomes. By synthesizing our dynamic network maps with publicly available high-throughput transcriptomic datasets (GEO) and biochemical assay databases (ChEMBL), we predict that specific perturbations (e.g., a disease-associated point mutation or an allosteric ligand) will induce quantifiable shifts in the dynamic coupling index. We hypothesize that these shifts can be mathematically correlated with emergent phenotypic states, such as metabolic reprogramming or altered immune signaling, thus providing a predictive AI framework for mesoscale emergence.

These interconnected questions directly align with the NCEMS mandate by demanding the synthesis of massive, disparate datasets to solve long-standing puzzles in molecular biology, far exceeding the capability of a single laboratory or traditional experimental approach.

[Methods and Approach]
To achieve our objectives, we will construct a robust, AI-driven computational pipeline structured around three integrated specific aims, utilizing exclusively existing, publicly available data in strict adherence to the NCEMS mandate. Our transdisciplinary methodology integrates phylogenomics, exascale molecular dynamics (MD) mining, network theory, and machine learning (ML).

Aim 1: AI-Enabled Reconstruction of Ancestral Structural Ensembles. We will systematically mine phylogenomic databases (e.g., Pfam, UniProt) to extract deep sequence alignments for modular signaling hubs, primarily targeting Nuclear Receptors (NRs) and Src-family kinases. Using established maximum likelihood phylogenetic tools, we will infer the ancestral sequence space of these protein families. Because empirical structures of these ancestral nodes are largely absent, we will employ state-of-the-art AI-based structural prediction algorithms (e.g., AlphaFold2 and RoseTTAFold) coupled with generative conformational sampling. By synthesizing available structural data from the PDB, we will generate robust ensembles of structural models for thousands of modern and ancestral nodes. This synthesis will map the evolutionary drift of three-dimensional topology alongside primary sequence evolution.

Aim 2: Mining Exascale Trajectories to Map Dynamic Coupling Networks. We will pivot from static structures to functional dynamics by tapping into massive, open-access MD repositories, such as those generated by distributed computing platforms (e.g., Folding@home datasets, MoDEL). For trajectories that are unavailable, we will leverage publicly available Markov State Models to sample conformational space. From these petabytes of atomic coordinates, we will compute network-based dynamic metrics—specifically the Dynamic Flexibility Index (DFI) and Dynamic Coupling Index (DCI). DFI quantifies the resilience of individual residues to random force perturbations, acting as a metric for local flexibility, whereas DCI measures the mechanical coupling between distal functional sites. By mapping DFI and DCI values onto the structural ensembles generated in Aim 1, we will construct evolutionary dynamic network graphs. Graph theory analyses will be applied to trace how rigid allosteric hinges and flexible recruitment interfaces have migrated through evolutionary time to support the emergence of novel mesoscale complex assemblies.

Aim 3: Machine Learning Synthesis for Phenotypic Prediction. To connect biophysical dynamics with emergent cellular functions, we will develop deep learning architectures (e.g., Graph Neural Networks, GNNs). We will construct a synthesized database integrating our DFI/DCI network maps with high-throughput functional data extracted from ChEMBL (binding affinities, transcriptional activity assays) and GEO (ligand- and mutation-specific transcriptomic profiles). The GNNs will use the dynamic network graphs as input features to predict transcriptomic signatures and functional activity states. Recognizing the inherent noise in biological datasets, we will employ sophisticated uncertainty quantification techniques—such as evidential deep learning or Bayesian neural networks—to assign confidence intervals to our phenotypic predictions. This rigorous validation step ensures our models provide actionable, high-confidence insights into how atomic-level perturbations cascade through the allosteric network to dictate mesoscale signaling outputs. This methodology relies entirely on the transdisciplinary synthesis of public data, creating a novel analytical strategy for the broader scientific community.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The proposed Working Group will deliver transformative outcomes that directly advance the NCEMS mission to decode mesoscale emergence. By successfully integrating evolutionary biology, exascale biomolecular simulations, and functional genomics through an AI-driven framework, we expect to deliver a unified, multi-scale model of allosteric regulation. 

Scientifically, this project will yield the first comprehensive maps of evolutionary dynamic coupling for critical modular signaling hubs, specifically nuclear receptors and Src-family kinases. These 'wiring diagrams' will resolve long-standing puzzles surrounding how proteins evolve to accommodate new ligands and recruit diverse, massive co-regulator complexes without disrupting their fundamental folds. Furthermore, the development of Graph Neural Networks that predict transcriptomic outputs directly from atomistic Dynamic Coupling Indices (DCI) will establish a groundbreaking predictive paradigm. This will illuminate how specific mutations or pharmacological interventions at the atomic level precipitate complex cellular behaviors, such as metabolic reprogramming and altered gene transcription.

Methodologically, we will create an innovative suite of analytical strategies that synthesize previously siloed data modalities—spanning PDB structures, Folding@home exascale MD trajectories, and GEO/ChEMBL functional databases. This pipeline will be highly generalized, providing the broader scientific community with the tools to investigate mesoscale phenomena in entirely different protein systems.

Broader impacts include a profound contribution to workforce development, directly answering the NCEMS call. The Working Group will fund and cross-train a diverse cohort of postdocs and graduate students. Trainees will gain rare, highly sought-after expertise at the intersection of generative AI, high-performance distributed computing, and multi-scale biological data synthesis. They will become the vanguard of the next-generation, data-savvy workforce capable of navigating petabyte-scale biological problems. Ultimately, the predictive framework generated by this synthesis effort will catalyze future breakthroughs in protein engineering, synthetic biology, and the development of next-generation allosteric modulators for precision medicine.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
Our Working Group is unequivocally committed to the principles of open, team, and reproducible science, adhering to the highest FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data standards. Because this project is entirely computational and synthesizes existing public datasets, ensuring the transparency and reproducibility of our AI models and analytical pipelines is paramount.

All synthesized datasets, including our reconstructed ancestral sequence alignments, predicted structural ensembles, and compiled dynamic indices (DFI/DCI), will be hosted on stable, open-access repositories such as Zenodo and Dryad. To facilitate community access and exploration, we will develop and deploy the 'Mesoscale Dynamics Atlas,' an interactive, web-based portal where researchers can visualize evolutionary dynamic networks and query mutational impacts on allosteric coupling.

All software, machine learning architectures, and data-processing pipelines developed during this project will be open-source. Codebases will be version-controlled via GitHub, extensively documented, and released under a permissive MIT or Apache 2.0 license. To guarantee reproducibility across different computing environments, all computational workflows will be containerized using Docker and Singularity, and orchestration will be managed via Nextflow. This ensures that any researcher worldwide can seamlessly download our containers and reproduce the calculation of DFI/DCI metrics or the training of our transcriptomic prediction models from raw data inputs.

Furthermore, we commit to disseminating our findings rapidly through open-access channels. All manuscripts will be deposited in preprint servers (e.g., bioRxiv) concurrently with journal submission. We will also publish our data curation and processing protocols on platforms like Protocols.io. By embedding these rigorous open science practices into the core of our operations, we will maximize the value of NCEMS funding, ensuring our methodological innovations and biological insights serve as a permanent, accessible resource for the global molecular and cellular biosciences community.

[Budget and Resources]
To successfully execute this ambitious community-scale synthesis project, we request funding tailored to support transdisciplinary collaboration, massive data processing, and intensive personnel training, fully leveraging the NCEMS infrastructure.

Personnel: The majority of the budget is allocated to support a diverse, cross-institutional team of early-career researchers. We request funding for three full-time postdoctoral fellows and three graduate students. These trainees will be co-mentored across the participating labs, ensuring they receive comprehensive cross-training in phylogenomics, exascale molecular dynamics mining, and machine learning. Additionally, a dedicated Working Group Coordinator will be funded to manage workflow integration, organize meetings, and oversee the execution of our open-science data management plan.

Computational Resources: Given the massive scale of data synthesis—spanning petabytes of open-access MD trajectories and deep phylogenomic databases—we request funds for cloud computing infrastructure (e.g., AWS or Google Cloud). These resources will be crucial for training our compute-intensive Graph Neural Networks, deploying AlphaFold2 for ancestral ensemble prediction, and hosting our public-facing 'Mesoscale Dynamics Atlas.' While we will leverage existing open-source data from Folding@home, the storage and high-throughput I/O processing required to compute Dynamic Flexibility and Coupling Indices (DFI/DCI) across millions of frames necessitate dedicated cloud storage and GPU instances.

Collaboration and Travel: Central to the NCEMS model is robust, transdisciplinary team science. We request funding for bi-annual, in-person Working Group meetings to be hosted at the NCEMS facility. These intensive hackathon-style summits will foster deep collaboration, troubleshoot complex analytical bottlenecks, and integrate the disparate data streams. Funds are also requested for trainees to present their synthesized findings at major computational biology and biophysics conferences.

Justification: This transdisciplinary synthesis, merging petabyte-scale atomistic dynamics with evolutionary and functional genomics, far exceeds the computing, personnel, and expertise capabilities of any single R01-funded laboratory. NCEMS support is absolutely critical to catalyze this collaboration and provide the necessary infrastructure to solve these fundamental puzzles of mesoscale emergence.
