[Background and Significance]
The molecular and cellular biosciences are currently undergoing a paradigm shift, transitioning from the study of isolated biomolecules to the investigation of mesoscale assemblies. The mesoscale—the spatial and functional regime spanning nanometers to micrometers—is where fundamental molecular interactions orchestrate the emergence of complex, systems-level biological properties. Among the most striking examples of mesoscale emergence is the three-dimensional organization of the genome. Chromatin architecture dictates gene regulation, cellular differentiation, and mechanical stability, driven by the dynamic action of structural maintenance of chromosomes (SMC) complexes, transcription factors, and phase-separated condensates. Concurrently, structural biology has revealed a previously hidden layer of complexity within individual biomolecules: topological entanglement. Over recent years, structural bioinformatics has demonstrated that a significant portion of the proteome contains deep topological features, including open knots, slipknots, pierced lassos, and theta-curves formed by covalent or ionic linkages. 

Despite an explosion of publicly available data in both genome architecture (e.g., high-resolution Hi-C contact maps, microscopy datasets) and protein structure (e.g., the Protein Data Bank, AlphaFold predictions), these two fields remain profoundly siloed. A critical, unanswered question in cellular biophysics is how the intrinsic topological complexity of individual proteins scales up to influence the mesoscale physical properties of chromatin networks. While polymer physics and data-driven computational models have successfully described chromosomal loop extrusion and chromatin compartment formation, these models typically treat interacting proteins as simple, topologically trivial nodes or generic bridging constraints. Conversely, studies characterizing intricate protein folding pathways, topological stability, and chaperone-dependent knotting rarely consider how these immense structural barriers function when integrated into macro-molecular chromosomal machines under extreme mechanical stress.

This proposal addresses this critical knowledge gap by catalyzing a transdisciplinary synthesis of physical knot theory, structural bioinformatics, AI-driven structure prediction, and polymer physics. Our overarching objective is to synthesize disparate, publicly available datasets to uncover how protein-level topological entanglements dictate the emergent 3D structural and viscoelastic properties of the genome. By integrating the vast repositories of structural data with chromosomal contact maps, we will determine whether knotted and topologically complex proteins are preferentially enriched within genomic scaffolding and whether their intricate folds serve as mechanical ratchets, viscoelastic anchors, or topological roadblocks during loop extrusion.

The significance of this NCEMS-supported synthesis project lies in its potential to entirely redefine our understanding of mesoscale mechanics in the nucleus. By building a unified, multi-scale framework, we will solve long-standing puzzles regarding the structural stability of the genome under axial stress and uncover new evolutionary principles governing protein folding. This community-scale initiative will transcend the capabilities of any single research lab, uniting mathematicians, computer scientists, structural biologists, and genomicists. In doing so, we will not only derive novel biological insights from existing open-access data but also establish innovative analytical strategies and computational pipelines that will train the next generation of researchers to navigate the converging frontiers of AI, topology, and mesoscale biology.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This synthesis project aims to bridge the gap between individual molecular topology and mesoscale genomic architecture through a coordinated, multi-scalar investigation. By synthesizing public structural, genomic, and evolutionary data, our Working Group will address three compelling research questions, each driven by a central hypothesis.

Question 1: What is the topological landscape of the nuclear proteome, and how are complex entanglements distributed within chromatin-interacting networks?
We currently lack a comprehensive understanding of how topological features are distributed among proteins that govern 3D genomic architecture. We will synthesize structural data from the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database and the PDB to systematically catalog knots, slipknots, and theta-curves in nuclear proteins. 
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that chromatin-associated proteins—specifically subunits of SMC-kleisin complexes, DNA-binding response regulators, and hub proteins in phase-separated genomic condensates—exhibit a statistically significant enrichment in complex topological motifs compared to the general proteome. We further predict that these specific entanglements correspond to regions of high coevolutionary coupling, functioning to lock these proteins into extraordinarily stable, long-lived functional states that are strictly dependent on molecular chaperones (e.g., Hsp90) for their initial folding and assembly.

Question 2: How do protein-level topological constraints structurally modulate the dynamics of large-scale chromosomal loop extrusion?
The spatial organization of the genome is actively maintained by loop extrusion mechanisms, yet the physical barriers that control and limit this extrusion remain poorly characterized at the molecular-mechanical level. By integrating topological data with high-resolution Hi-C maps and data-driven polymer physics models, we will simulate loop extrusion across structurally heterogeneous chromatin.
Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that intricately folded proteins and highly constrained topological networks act as specialized mechanical ratchets or architectural 'speed bumps' during DNA loop extrusion. Rather than merely occupying space, the rigid, knotted cores of these proteins possess distinct mechanical resistance properties that stall or redirect condensin and cohesin complexes, thereby deterministically shaping the boundaries of topologically associating domains (TADs) and genomic compartments.

Question 3: In what ways do co-evolved protein topologies dictate the emergent viscoelastic properties of the entire mesoscale chromosome?
Chromosomes behave as viscoelastic solids, altering their stiffness dramatically between interphase and mitosis. The molecular origins of these distinct mechanical states are not fully explained by DNA composition alone. We will synthesize coevolutionary landscape models with large-scale coarse-grained simulations to analyze stress responses across different cell lines.
Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that the mesoscale viscoelasticity of mitotic and interphase chromosomes emerges directly from the collective mechanical integration of topological protein hubs and dynamic chromatin loops. We propose that the exceptional tensile strength and stiffness observed in mitotic chromosomes are structurally dependent on a coordinated network of specific, knot-stabilized anchor proteins. The coevolution of these topological features represents a hidden physical code that ensures chromosomal integrity during the extreme mechanical stress of cellular division.

[Methods and Approach]
To achieve our community-scale synthesis goals, the Working Group will deploy a transdisciplinary methodological framework strictly utilizing existing, publicly available datasets. Our approach integrates machine learning, mathematical knot theory, coevolutionary landscape modeling, and polymer physics through a three-phase computational pipeline.

Phase 1: AI-Driven Topological Cataloging and Structural Synthesis
We will first construct a high-throughput computational pipeline to mine the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database (covering diverse proteomes, including the human and primary model organisms). Utilizing advanced algorithms based on the uniform closure method and genus trace analysis, we will calculate the topological complexity of all nuclear and chromatin-associated proteins. To handle the scale of this data and filter out prediction artifacts, we will modify custom Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)—originally designed for pattern recognition in complex medical imaging—to automatically detect, classify, and validate intricate topologies (knots, slipknots, pierced lassos, and theta-curves) based on structural coordinates and prediction confidence (pLDDT) scores. This phase will yield the foundational dataset of our project: a genome-wide, confidence-weighted map of nuclear protein entanglement.

Phase 2: Coevolutionary and Genomic Data Integration
Once nuclear topological motifs are mapped, we will synthesize these structural insights with vast evolutionary and genomic datasets. By analyzing deep bacterial and eukaryotic sequence alignments, we will build coevolutionary landscape models using maximum entropy approaches. This will allow us to quantify the inter-domain residue interactions and energetic barriers required to stabilize these complex topological nodes. Concurrently, we will cross-reference the genomic loci of these topologically complex proteins with high-resolution Hi-C chromosomal contact maps from multiple distinct human cell lines. We will employ statistical machine learning techniques to correlate the presence of knotted protein hubs with the spatial boundaries of topologically associating domains (TADs) and A/B genomic compartments, identifying statistically significant colocalizations.

Phase 3: Data-Driven Polymer Physics Simulations
To test how these microscopic topologies drive mesoscale emergence, we will incorporate our structural and genomic synthesis into advanced, coarse-grained polymer physics models of the 3D genome (e.g., MiChroM and MEGABASE frameworks). We will assign distinct biophysical parameters—derived from the structural stability and coevolutionary constraints of the knotted motifs identified in Phase 1 and 2—to specific chromatin-interacting nodes within the simulation environment. Through large-scale molecular dynamics and Monte Carlo conformational sampling, we will simulate the process of DNA loop extrusion and apply simulated axial stretching to the modeled chromosomes. This will allow us to quantitatively observe how the topological resistance of specific protein hubs influences the emergent spatial organization, phase separation (hydrophobic-like collapse), and overall viscoelastic stiffness of the chromosome during both interphase and mitosis.

Collaboration and Feasibility:
This methodology inherently requires the collective expertise of knot theorists, AI specialists, computational biologists, and polymer physicists. By operating exclusively in the computational domain using open-access data, the project bypasses experimental bottlenecks, ensuring a high degree of feasibility and directly aligning with NCEMS's mandate to foster synthesis-based discoveries.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The primary outcome of this synthesis project will be the creation of the 'MesoTopo Atlas,' the first comprehensive, AI-driven open-access database that directly maps protein-level topological entanglements onto 3D genomic architecture. This platform will provide the global scientific community with a novel resource to visualize and interrogate how molecular knots, slipknots, and theta-curves correlate with chromosomal looping, TAD boundaries, and gene regulatory networks across multiple species and cell lines.

Scientifically, this project will resolve critical, long-standing puzzles regarding the mechanical stability of the genome. By demonstrating that specific knotted or topologically complex proteins function as critical architectural ratchets and viscoelastic anchors, we will provide a fundamentally new, physics-based paradigm for understanding chromosomal compaction and mesoscale cellular organization. The integration of polymer physics with structural topology will pioneer innovative analytical strategies that can subsequently be applied to other massive mesoscale assemblies, such as the cytoskeleton or biomolecular condensates.

Furthermore, this Working Group will have a profound impact on workforce development. By deeply integrating trainees (postdoctoral scholars and graduate students) into a highly transdisciplinary environment, we will cultivate a new generation of data-savvy biophysicists fluent in both abstract mathematics (knot theory) and high-performance computational genomics. These scientists will be uniquely positioned to lead the future of AI-driven structural biology.

Ultimately, this research will demonstrate how synthesizing disparate layers of publicly available biological data—from atomic coordinates to macroscopic chromosomal contact maps—can uncover the hidden physical rules governing emergent mesoscale phenomena, fully realizing the strategic scientific vision of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
Our Working Group is deeply committed to the principles of Open, Team, and Reproducible Science, strictly adhering to FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) data standards. Because this project relies entirely on synthesizing publicly available data, ensuring complete transparency of our analytical pipelines and computational models is paramount.

All raw inputs synthesized during this project (e.g., specific subsets of the PDB, AlphaFold databases, Hi-C maps, and coevolutionary alignments) will be thoroughly documented with persistent digital object identifiers (DOIs). The 'MesoTopo Atlas' database generated by this project will be hosted on an open-access web server and mirrored on community repositories such as Zenodo or Dryad to ensure long-term accessibility.

To guarantee the absolute reproducibility of our methodological approaches, all custom software, topological algorithms, convolutional neural networks, and coarse-grained polymer physics simulation scripts will be developed openly via GitHub and GitLab under an MIT or GNU General Public License. We will deploy our workflows using containerization technologies such as Docker and Singularity, allowing any researcher globally to download and execute our exact computational environments, effectively eliminating the "works on my machine" barrier.

We will practice rapid dissemination of our findings by submitting all manuscripts to preprint servers (e.g., bioRxiv or arXiv) prior to rigorous peer review, ensuring immediate access for the broader scientific community. All final publications will be released under Open Access (CC-BY) licenses. Furthermore, detailed Jupyter Notebooks detailing our statistical methodologies, machine learning training regimes, and data visualization protocols will be published alongside all manuscripts, ensuring that our innovative analytical strategies are fully transparent and adaptable for future synthesis research.

[Budget and Resources]
The proposed research requires NCEMS support because the scope of multi-scale synthesis—bridging knot theory, structural AI, and polymer physics—far exceeds the computational and financial resources of any single investigator's laboratory. 

Personnel Support: The primary budget allocation will fund two postdoctoral fellows and two graduate research assistants. These trainees will serve as the crucial integrative links between the disparate disciplines of the Working Group. Funds will provide competitive stipends and tuition remission, fulfilling the NCEMS mandate to train the next-generation, data-savvy workforce. Trainees will benefit from dual-mentorship, gaining expertise in both structural topology and genomic modeling.

Computational Resources: A significant portion of the budget is dedicated to securing high-performance computing (HPC) infrastructure. Developing and training convolutional neural networks on vast structural databases, computing topological invariants across entire proteomes, and running large-scale, molecular dynamics and polymer physics simulations require substantial computational power. We request funding for cloud computing credits (e.g., AWS, GCP) and dedicated time on national supercomputing clusters to guarantee rapid processing and data storage for the 'MesoTopo Atlas.'

Working Group Meetings and Dissemination: To stimulate genuine cross-disciplinary collaboration, we require funding for bi-annual, in-person Working Group meetings at the NCEMS headquarters, alongside regular virtual hackathons. These face-to-face interactions are essential for translating mathematical topology concepts into genomic physics parameters. Additionally, the budget includes travel funds for PIs and trainees to present findings at major national and international biophysics and computational biology conferences.

By leveraging existing open-access data, the budget completely eschews costs associated with wet-lab reagents or experimental equipment, ensuring that all NCEMS funds are highly optimized and directly invested into synthesis, computation, and workforce training.

title: Deciphering the Mesoscale Emergence of Skeletal Muscle Adaptation: A GPU-Accelerated Multi-Omic and Mathematical Synthesis of Ribosome Dynamics under Competing Stresses
title_norm: deciphering the mesoscale emergence of skeletal muscle adaptation a gpuaccelerated multiomic and mathematical synthesis of ribosome dynamics under competing stresses
abstract_text:
Skeletal muscle plasticity—specifically its capacity to undergo hypertrophy or atrophy—is an emergent cellular property strictly governed by mesoscale phenomena: the dynamic assembly, biogenesis, and regulatory control of the ribosome. While individual molecular pathways (e.g., mTORC1 signaling) and systemic influences (e.g., inflammatory cytokines) are well documented, a fundamental mystery remains regarding how competing systemic signals—such as mechanical overload from exercise and systemic inflammatory stress from rheumatic conditions—spatiotemporally integrate at the mesoscale translational machinery to drive opposing phenotypic outcomes. Although individual transcriptomic, translatomic (Ribo-seq), and proteomic studies have profiled these states in isolation, the resulting vast repositories of publicly available data remain fragmented. 

To solve this long-standing puzzle, our Working Group proposes a community-scale synthesis project leveraging massive, publicly available human and rodent multi-omic datasets to map the mesoscale emergence of muscle adaptation. We will integrate transcriptomic, Ribo-seq, phosphoproteomic, and structural data across healthy exercise cohorts and patients with inflammatory conditions. Because aligning and synthesizing such divergent, high-dimensional multi-omic datasets is computationally prohibitive for traditional bioinformatics pipelines, we will develop ultra-fast, GPU-accelerated algorithms and Graph Neural Network (GNN) frameworks. These AI-driven tools will efficiently align divergent sequences, reconstruct dynamic translational networks, and predict the interaction structures of mesoscale molecular assemblies in real time.

To bridge the gap from GNN-derived molecular networks to emergent cellular phenotypes, we will couple our AI frameworks with advanced mathematical modeling. We will construct spatiotemporal systems of partial differential equations (PDEs) with free boundaries to model the physical expansion of the muscle fiber cross-sectional area (hypertrophy) as a direct mathematical consequence of mesoscale ribosome biogenesis and translational output. This hybrid AI-mathematical framework will allow us to simulate how localized mechanical stimuli promote ribosomal assembly, and precisely how inflammatory stress acts as a molecular roadblock to dampen this translational capacity.

This transdisciplinary approach perfectly aligns with the NCEMS mission. The project relies entirely on the computational synthesis of existing public repositories, generating no new experimental data. It demands the integration of three distinct scientific domains—high-performance GPU computing, continuous mathematical modeling, and molecular exercise physiology—a synergy fundamentally beyond the capabilities of any single laboratory. All developed GPU-accelerated pipelines, GNN architectures, PDE models, and integrated datasets will be open-sourced, adhering to the highest standards of reproducible team science. Furthermore, our Working Group will cross-train a new generation of data-savvy postdocs and graduate students at the intersection of AI, computational mathematics, and cellular biology. By decoding the mesoscale logic of translational control under competing biological stresses, this synthesis will uncover profound insights into the emergent nature of cellular growth and adaptation.

Although decades of research have charted isolated signaling cascades, such as mTORC1 activation or the role of inflammatory cytokines, a profound knowledge gap persists. Currently, vast repositories of publicly available omics data—spanning transcriptomics, translatomics (Ribo-seq), proteomics, and structural biology—capture these distinct physiological states. First, the computational demand of aligning and analyzing high-dimensional, multi-omic data across diverse cohorts exceeds the capabilities of standard bioinformatics pipelines, requiring novel GPU-accelerated architectures. Second, establishing a causal, predictive bridge from dynamic molecular interactions (mesoscale) to physical cellular expansion (macroscale) requires sophisticated mathematical frameworks capable of accommodating shifting physiological boundaries, a challenge rarely addressed in biological data science.

We introduce a novel synthesis approach that combines GPU-accelerated sequence alignment, advanced Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for structural pose-prediction, and complex mathematical modeling utilizing partial differential equations (PDEs) with free-boundary conditions. 

The significance of this project is threefold. Biologically, it resolves long-standing questions regarding how the translational machinery parses competing anabolic and catabolic signals to modulate muscle cross-sectional area. Computationally, it pioneers the application of advanced AI and GPU acceleration to significantly reduce the time required to reconstruct multi-omic biological networks. Mathematically, it introduces free-boundary PDE models to cellular biology, effectively treating the growing cell membrane as a mathematical boundary driven by mesoscale translational output. Question 2: Can GPU-accelerated Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) accurately and rapidly reconstruct the dynamic structural conformations of the translational machinery from integrated multi-omic data? 
We hypothesize that by coupling ultra-fast diagonal partitioning parallelization strategies on multi-GPU architectures with GNNs, we can predict mesoscale ribosomal interactions and docking structures up to two orders of magnitude faster than conventional simulation approaches. Existing structural docking algorithms are computationally prohibitive for large-scale, multi-omic synthesis. By training GNNs on publicly available structural datasets (e.g., PDB) and contextualizing them with Ribo-seq data, we expect to successfully generate high-throughput, pose-prediction models that capture the transient protein-protein and protein-RNA interactions underlying translational control in both healthy and inflamed muscle states.

Question 3: How does the mathematical translation of mesoscale ribosomal output govern the macroscopic physical boundaries of the muscle cell during hypertrophy or atrophy? 
We hypothesize that a spatiotemporal system of partial differential equations (PDEs) utilizing free-boundary conditions can accurately predict emergent cellular structural changes (e.g., muscle fiber cross-sectional area) by mapping molecular translational rates directly to structural protein accumulation. While AI and GNNs map the molecular networks, they do not inherently capture physical cellular expansion. By utilizing the GNN-derived translational capacities as forcing functions within a PDE framework, we predict that the shifting sarcolemma boundary can be computationally modeled and validated against historically reported, publicly available histological measurements. 

These interconnected questions directly address the NCEMS objective of elucidating emergent properties at the mesoscale. They demand a synthesis strategy where computational predictions of mesoscale molecular structures directly feed into macroscopic mathematical equations, a synthesis impossible to achieve without the collaborative expertise of computer scientists, mathematicians, and molecular physiologists.

[Methods and Approach]
Our methodology is strictly computational and synthetic, relying entirely on publicly available data. The workflow is designed as a collaborative pipeline across three distinct disciplines: molecular exercise physiology, high-performance computing, and continuous mathematical modeling.

Data Curation and Multi-Omic Harmonization: 
We will first comprehensively mine public repositories (e.g., GEO, SRA, PRIDE, PDB) for human and rodent transcriptomic, translatomic (Ribo-seq), phosphoproteomic, and structural datasets. The inclusion criteria will focus on skeletal muscle tissues subjected to mechanical overload (e.g., resistance exercise paradigms) and systemic inflammatory conditions (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, myositis). Curated data will undergo rigorous quality control and normalization to create a unified, multi-omic metadata repository. 

GPU-Accelerated Sequence Alignment and AI-Driven Structural Prediction: 
To overcome the computational bottlenecks inherent in aligning divergent omic datasets, we will develop optimized parallel algorithms utilizing multi-GPU architectures. By employing diagonal partitioning strategies, we will dramatically reduce the computational overhead for pairwise and multiple sequence alignments, maintaining high sensitivity while accelerating throughput by orders of magnitude compared to traditional CPU-bound tools. 
Once harmonized, this data will feed into custom Graph Neural Network (GNN) frameworks. The GNNs will be designed to predict mesoscale macromolecular interactions—specifically, the assembly of the ribosomal complex and its interaction with translational regulators under various stress conditions. By treating biomolecules as nodes and interactions as edges, the pose-prediction models within the GNN will generate dynamic, flexible molecular docking structures in real time, yielding a highly resolved picture of the translational machinery's functional state under mechanical versus inflammatory stress.

Mathematical Modeling of Emergent Phenotypes: 
To transition from mesoscale molecular interactomes to macroscopic cellular outcomes, we will construct a robust mathematical framework. We will design a system of partial differential equations (PDEs) to model the intracellular diffusion and reaction kinetics of newly synthesized structural proteins. Crucially, we will employ free-boundary problems to simulate the physical boundaries of the muscle cell (the sarcolemma). 
The output from the GNNs—representing the effective translational capacity of the ribosome under specific conditions—will serve as the primary forcing function in the PDEs. As structural protein concentrations increase or decrease within the model, the free-boundary condition will dynamically expand (hypertrophy) or contract (atrophy). 

Validation and Retrospective Synthesis: 
The AI-mathematical hybrid model's predictions will be rigorously validated against distinct, held-out historical datasets containing quantitative phenotypic measurements, such as muscle fiber cross-sectional area and type I/type II fiber ratios. This retrospective synthesis ensures that our predictive models are biologically accurate and generalize across multiple independent public cohorts. Through iterative collaboration, the physiologists will biologically contextualize the mathematical outputs, ensuring the synthesis generates novel insights into muscle adaptation.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This project will deliver a comprehensive, multi-scale molecular map of skeletal muscle adaptation, explicitly defining how competing systemic stresses are resolved at the mesoscale translational machinery to drive macroscopic cellular emergence. By identifying the specific mechanisms by which inflammatory signaling dampens mechanical overload-induced ribosome biogenesis, this synthesis will solve a long-standing puzzle in muscle physiology and rheumatology.

Beyond biological discovery, the methodological impact of this Working Group will be transformative for the wider scientific community. We will produce and release novel, ultra-fast GPU-accelerated algorithms capable of processing complex multi-omic data at unprecedented speeds. Our Graph Neural Network (GNN) frameworks will establish a new benchmark for structural interaction prediction, allowing researchers to model dynamic biological assemblies without relying on computationally prohibitive molecular dynamics simulations. Additionally, the development of our free-boundary PDE framework will provide the biomedical community with a scalable mathematical tool for modeling cellular size and structural adaptation across varying tissue types.

Crucially, this project will fulfill the NCEMS mandate to train the next generation of data-savvy scientists. Graduate students and postdoctoral fellows embedded in this Working Group will receive transdisciplinary cross-training. Trainees with backgrounds in biology will learn high-performance GPU computing and AI utilization, while trainees from computational and mathematical backgrounds will gain deep expertise in molecular cell biology and physiological data interpretation. Ultimately, this transdisciplinary synthesis will lower the barrier to entry for community-scale data integration, driving innovative research strategies in molecular and cellular biosciences well beyond the lifespan of this specific funding mechanism.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
Our Working Group is deeply committed to the principles of open, reproducible, and team science. All research outputs—data, AI models, mathematical frameworks, and analytical workflows—will be made publicly available in strict adherence to FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data principles.

The unified multi-omic dataset generated from public repositories will be thoroughly annotated with comprehensive metadata and hosted on open platforms such as Zenodo and specific NCEMS data portals. This will allow researchers globally to independently query our synthesized cohorts of healthy and inflamed tissues. 

All source code developed for GPU-accelerated alignments, Graph Neural Network training architectures, and PDE simulations will be maintained on public GitHub repositories under open-source licenses (e.g., MIT or GNU GPL). To ensure computational reproducibility regardless of local hardware configurations, we will deploy our full analytical pipeline as containerized environments using Docker and Singularity. Jupyter notebooks documenting the step-by-step synthesis—from raw public data ingestion to the final cellular phenotype prediction—will be included in the repositories to serve as educational and reproducible templates.

Furthermore, we commit to pre-registering our major analytical protocols, publishing all findings in open-access journals, and depositing preprints on servers such as bioRxiv prior to formal peer review. By operating with radical transparency and providing comprehensive documentation, our Working Group will ensure that the tools and insights generated can be seamlessly adopted, validated, and expanded upon by the broader molecular and cellular science community.

[Budget and Resources]
To successfully execute this community-scale synthesis project, we request funding to support an integrated, transdisciplinary Working Group in alignment with NCEMS resource guidelines. The primary allocation of the budget will support human capital, specifically the funding of two postdoctoral researchers and two graduate students. These trainees will be intentionally recruited across disciplines to form the core data-science workforce of the project, receiving cross-training in molecular biology, GPU computing, and mathematical modeling.

A critical portion of the budget will be allocated for high-performance computing resources necessary for the project's success. While we will leverage existing institutional infrastructure where possible, we request funds for dedicated cloud computing instances and multi-GPU node access (e.g., NVIDIA A100 architectures) to facilitate the rapid training of the Graph Neural Networks and the high-throughput, GPU-accelerated sequence alignments required by our synthesis pipeline. This computational support goes far beyond the standard capabilities of a single biology laboratory and is essential for realizing our AI-driven objectives.

Finally, we request travel and administrative support to facilitate robust collaborative partnerships. Funds will cover bi-annual in-person meetings at the NCEMS hub, bringing together the diverse expertise of our Working Group spanning physiology, computer science, and mathematics. These intensive synthesis meetings will be supplemented by regular virtual workshops. The budget will also cover open-access publication fees and the costs associated with long-term public data hosting, ensuring full compliance with our open science and reproducible research commitments.

While individual molecular pathways (e.g., mTORC1 signaling) and systemic influences (e.g., inflammatory cytokines) are well documented, a fundamental mystery remains regarding how competing systemic signals—such as mechanical overload from exercise and systemic inflammatory stress from rheumatic conditions—spatiotemporally integrate at the mesoscale translational machinery to drive opposing phenotypic outcomes. We will integrate transcriptomic, Ribo-seq, phosphoproteomic, and structural data across healthy exercise cohorts and patients with inflammatory conditions. Because aligning and synthesizing such divergent, high-dimensional multi-omic datasets is computationally prohibitive for traditional bioinformatics pipelines, we will develop ultra-fast, GPU-accelerated algorithms and Graph Neural Network (GNN) frameworks. These AI-driven tools will efficiently align divergent sequences, reconstruct dynamic translational networks, and predict the interaction structures of mesoscale molecular assemblies in real time.

To bridge the gap from GNN-derived molecular networks to emergent cellular phenotypes, we will couple our AI frameworks with advanced mathematical modeling. We will construct spatiotemporal systems of partial differential equations (PDEs) with free boundaries to model the physical expansion of the muscle fiber cross-sectional area (hypertrophy) as a direct mathematical consequence of mesoscale ribosome biogenesis and translational output. This hybrid AI-mathematical framework will allow us to simulate how localized mechanical stimuli promote ribosomal assembly, and precisely how inflammatory stress acts as a molecular roadblock to dampen this translational capacity.

By decoding the mesoscale logic of translational control under competing biological stresses, this synthesis will uncover profound insights into the emergent nature of cellular growth and adaptation.

[Abstract]
Biomolecular condensates represent a fundamental paradigm of mesoscale emergence in cellular biology, transitioning from individual biomolecular interactions to functional, non-stoichiometric organelles with highly tunable material properties. Central to this liquid-liquid phase separation are the intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) of proteins. Theoretical frameworks rooted in polymer physics—such as the sticker-and-spacer model—have established that the valence and patterning of specific amino acids (e.g., aromatics, charged residues) govern the thermodynamic stability and viscoelasticity of these condensates. This transdisciplinary project strictly utilizes existing data, moving beyond the traditional single-protein focus to uncover universal rules of phase separation. We will integrate and harmonize diverse public data sources, including IDR sequence databases (DisProt, MobiDB), condensate repositories (PhaSepDB, CD-CODE), large-scale biophysical archives containing Small-Angle X-ray Scattering (SAXS) and Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) structural ensembles (SASBDB, BMRB), and comprehensive clinical mutation registries (ClinVar, gnomAD). 

Our primary objective is to develop a physics-informed machine learning framework that bridges the gap between molecular sequence constraints and emergent mesoscale material properties. By synthesizing deep evolutionary sequence alignments with structural and biophysical data, we will map the multidimensional functional constraints placed on IDRs. First, we will train predictive models to decode the universal 'grammar' of conserved disorder, quantifying how specific patterns of hydrophobic clustering, electrostatics, and transient helicity are preserved across millions of years to maintain optimal condensate fluidity. Second, we will project thousands of clinical mutations onto these physical landscapes to predict which uncharacterized variants induce aberrant phase transitions, such as intra-condensate demixing or pathological fibrillization. 

This project requires NCEMS support to facilitate the necessary cross-disciplinary collaboration, bringing together experts in polymer physics, neuro-pathogenesis, computational structural biology, and artificial intelligence. The resulting synthesis will not only answer fundamental biological mysteries but also pioneer innovative analytical strategies by embedding polymer scaling laws directly into machine learning architectures. These insights will have transformative implications across disciplines, from identifying novel therapeutic targets in neurodegeneration to advancing synthetic biology by enabling the rational design of IDRs for engineered gene circuits. 

In strict adherence to Open Science principles, all harmonized databases, physics-informed AI models, and reproducible analysis pipelines will be released publicly through an interactive, open-source web portal. Furthermore, this working group will provide vital training for the next-generation workforce, immersing graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in a highly collaborative environment that bridges statistical mechanics, biophysics, and advanced data science.

[Background and Significance]
Understanding the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties at different scales of composition is the defining challenge of the mesoscale. Biomolecular condensates represent a primary example of this emergence. Formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), these membrane-less organelles bridge the gap between individual molecular interactions and higher-order cellular compartmentalization. Condensates dynamically concentrate specific macromolecules while excluding others, acting as biochemical crucibles that tune reaction rates, buffer gene expression, and sequester stress-induced toxins. The structural engine driving this emergent phenomenon primarily resides within intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) of proteins. Lacking a stable three-dimensional fold, IDRs possess an exquisite flexibility that allows them to undergo multivalent, weak, and transient interactions. 

Polymer physics theories, particularly the 'sticker-and-spacer' framework, have been instrumental in explaining how these regions mediate mesoscale emergence. In this model, 'stickers' (e.g., aromatic or complementary charged residues) provide the cohesive interactions driving condensation, while 'spacers' (e.g., polar or highly flexible residues) govern chain solvation and modulate the viscoelastic material properties of the resulting dense phase. Despite these theoretical advances, a fundamental mystery persists: how do evolutionary pressures sculpt the 'grammar' of highly flexible, highly mutating IDR sequences to preserve optimal emergent properties? Unlike folded proteins, where structural conservation mandates strict sequence homology, IDRs often exhibit low primary sequence conservation. Yet, their ability to form fluid, functional condensates remains highly conserved across diverse species. 

Furthermore, when this delicate grammatical balance is perturbed by missense mutations or post-translational modifications, the consequences are severe. Aberrant transitions—such as intra-condensate demixing and accelerated fibrillization—are root causes of devastating neurodegenerative disorders, including ALS, Alzheimer's, and Parkinson's disease. Currently, our understanding of these phenomena is restricted to a handful of heavily studied model proteins analyzed in isolated experimental setups. The field lacks a unified, community-scale understanding of the universal biophysical rules governing IDR-driven emergence. 

This proposal addresses these critical knowledge gaps by synthesizing an unprecedented volume of publicly available data. Over the past decade, a wealth of fragmented datasets has emerged, including detailed IDR registries, condensate databases, clinical mutation records, and rich structural ensembles derived from Small-Angle X-ray Scattering (SAXS) and Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy. However, these vital data streams remain dangerously siloed. By integrating evolutionary genomics, structural biophysics, and clinical pathology through the lens of polymer physics and artificial intelligence, this project will execute a transdisciplinary synthesis beyond the capability of any single laboratory. Uncovering the universal language of conserved disorder will not only resolve long-standing puzzles regarding the evolutionary origins of biomolecular condensates but will also unlock rational design frameworks for synthetic biology and yield actionable predictions for neurodegenerative disease therapeutics.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
To uncover the fundamental principles linking molecular sequence grammar to mesoscale emergent properties, our NCEMS Working Group will synthesize disparate data streams to address three compelling scientific questions. 

Question 1: What constitutes the universal 'grammar' of intrinsically disordered regions that ensures the evolutionary conservation of optimal biomolecular condensate fluidity? 
Rather than strict sequence identity, we hypothesize that evolutionary pressures constrain the physical and polymeric attributes of IDRs. We predict that natural selection meticulously preserves specific sticker-to-spacer ratios, the patterning of charged and hydrophobic residues, and the overall polymer scaling exponents (reflecting sequence compaction) across millions of years of evolution. We hypothesize that synthesizing thousands of structural datasets (SAXS and NMR) with deep evolutionary alignments will reveal that divergent sequences often encode convergent emergent properties, maintaining the delicate thermodynamic balance required for liquid-like mesoscale behavior. 

Question 2: How do specific classes of clinical and somatic mutations disrupt this conserved grammar to trigger aberrant phase transitions, such as intra-condensate demixing and pathological fibrillization? 
Biomolecular condensates are exquisitely sensitive to changes in valency and interaction strength. We hypothesize that pathogenic missense mutations—such as those found in the low-complexity domains of neurodegeneration-associated proteins (e.g., TDP-43, Tau, ApoE)—act by subtly altering the polymer physics of the IDR. Specifically, we hypothesize that disease-causing variants will consistently map onto topological disruptions in our sequence grammar models, such as the induction of transient helical subregions that hyper-stabilize sticker interactions, or shifts in the net charge per residue that promote aberrant hydrophobic collapse and transition the condensate from a functional liquid to a pathological hydrogel or solid state. 

Question 3: Can a physics-informed machine learning (PIML) framework, synthesizing both structural ensembles and evolutionary data, predict the emergent material properties of uncharacterized IDRs and engineered synthetic variants from sequence alone? 
Traditional deep learning models applied to biological sequences often fail on IDRs because they lack spatial and physical intuition. We hypothesize that embedding fundamental polymer physics scaling laws and statistical mechanics principles directly into the architecture of a deep learning model—and training this model on a synthesis of diverse, publicly available biophysical and genomic datasets—will yield highly accurate predictions of condensate phase behavior. We predict this approach will vastly outperform current purely data-driven algorithms, allowing us to predict viscosity, critical concentrations, and the impact of missense mutations without generating de novo experimental data. 

By rigorously testing these hypotheses, the working group will transition the field from descriptive single-gene studies to a predictive, universal understanding of mesoscale biological emergence. Answering these questions requires exactly the type of multidimensional data synthesis and cross-disciplinary collaboration that NCEMS is designed to support.

[Methods and Approach]
To achieve our objectives, we will execute a community-scale synthesis of publicly available data without generating new experimental results. Our methodology is structured around data harmonization, physics-informed machine learning, and predictive pathological mapping. 

Phase 1: Multi-Omic and Biophysical Data Harmonization 
The foundation of this project requires linking sequence evolution with biophysical reality. We will extract well-annotated IDR sequences from DisProt and MobiDB and cross-reference them with verified liquid-liquid phase separation behavior cataloged in PhaSepDB and CD-CODE. To capture evolutionary constraints, we will utilize profile Hidden Markov Models (HMMER) and the Pfam database to generate deep multiple sequence alignments for thousands of IDR families, quantifying the conservation of polymer metrics (e.g., net charge per residue, sequence hydropathy, and spatial patterning of aromatic 'stickers') rather than exact amino acid identity. Crucially, we will anchor this sequence data to physical reality by mining the Small Angle X-ray Scattering (SASBDB) and Biological Magnetic Resonance Data Bank (BMRB) repositories. We will extract radius of gyration measurements, maximum particle dimensions, and transient secondary structure propensities to build a comprehensive dataset of IDR conformational ensembles. Finally, we will extract hundreds of thousands of missense mutations from ClinVar and gnomAD to overlay clinical variants onto these biological sequences. 

Phase 2: Physics-Informed Machine Learning (PIML) Framework 
Standard AI algorithms struggle with highly flexible proteins. To solve this, we will develop a PIML architecture that explicitly embeds polymer physics principles. The model's loss function will be regularized using the Flory scaling theory for polymer chains and the analytical sticker-and-spacer mathematical framework. By synthesizing the aligned evolutionary sequences with the SAXS/NMR structural ensembles, we will train the PIML to learn the 'grammar' of emergence. The network will use unsupervised representation learning (e.g., masked language modeling modified for physical properties) to predict the ensemble dimensions and interaction propensities of an IDR directly from its sequence. The embedded physics constraints will ensure that the model remains physically plausible, correctly identifying how subtle changes in amino acid spacing modulate the driving forces of biomolecular condensation. 

Phase 3: Predicting Aberrant Transitions and Synthetic Design 
Once the universal grammar is decoded, we will project the harmonized clinical mutation datasets through the PIML framework. The AI will evaluate how specific ALS or Alzheimer's-associated mutations perturb the physical landscape of the IDR, computing shifts in local helicity or sticker interaction energy. We will classify mutations by their predicted impact on mesoscale emergence, identifying variants likely to cause intra-condensate demixing or pathological rigidification. Furthermore, to demonstrate the applicability of this strategy, we will apply the trained model to in silico design libraries to predict optimized IDR sequences capable of buffering growth-mediated dilution in synthetic gene circuits. 

This robust, multi-stage synthesis demands the combined expertise of polymer physicists, computational structural biologists, and data scientists, embodying the collaborative mandate of the NCEMS funding mechanism.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This community-scale synthesis project will produce outcomes with profound implications for molecular biology, disease pathology, and biotechnology. By mapping the multidimensional evolutionary constraints placed on intrinsically disordered regions, we will deliver the first universal, multiscale sequence grammar governing biomolecular condensates. This represents a paradigm shift, transitioning the field from phenomenological observations of individual proteins to a rigorous, predictive physical framework of mesoscale emergence. 

The primary deliverable will be our Physics-Informed Machine Learning (PIML) model. By embedding polymer scaling laws into deep learning architectures, we will provide a revolutionary analytical strategy capable of forecasting the material properties of phase-separated condensates directly from primary sequence data. This tool will solve the long-standing puzzle of how structurally unconstrained protein sequences can maintain precise, fluid-like functional states across millions of years of evolution. 

The broader impacts of this synthesis are multifaceted. Medically, our approach will illuminate the mechanistic origins of neurodegenerative diseases. By projecting thousands of uncharacterized clinical variants from databases like ClinVar through our PIML framework, we will predict which specific mutations drive pathogenic aggregation and intra-condensate demixing, thereby uncovering novel therapeutic targets for conditions such as ALS and Alzheimer's disease. Technologically, decoding this grammar will supercharge synthetic biology. Researchers will be able to utilize our models for the rational design of designer IDRs, engineering bespoke condensates to compartmentalize metabolic pathways, buffer synthetic circuits against cellular noise, or sequester targeted toxins. 

By leveraging NCEMS support, this Working Group will establish a transdisciplinary blueprint for integrating massive, siloed datasets (genomics, biophysics, and clinical pathology) using advanced artificial intelligence, fundamentally advancing our capability to understand and engineer the emergent mesoscale architecture of the cell.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
Our proposed synthesis project is deeply committed to Open Science principles, transparency, and reproducible team science, ensuring that all findings and resources are freely accessible to the global community. Following the FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data principles, the completely harmonized dataset—integrating DisProt, PhaSepDB, SASBDB, BMRB, and ClinVar—will be deposited into Zenodo with comprehensive, machine-readable metadata. 

To maximize the utility of our Physics-Informed Machine Learning (PIML) framework, all source code, model weights, and data-processing pipelines will be made publicly available via GitHub under a permissive open-source license (e.g., MIT License). We will provide extensive documentation, including containerized environments (Docker) and interactive Jupyter Notebooks, allowing independent researchers to seamlessly reproduce our analyses. Furthermore, we will develop and host an interactive, open-access web portal. This platform will enable researchers globally to input arbitrary protein sequences or clinical mutations and receive instant predictions regarding the sequence's structural ensemble parameters, propensity for phase separation, and predicted condensate material properties. 

In line with the NCEMS mission to train the future data-savvy workforce, this Working Group places a heavy emphasis on trainee development. Postdoctoral researchers and graduate students will be heavily involved in the project, receiving cross-disciplinary mentorship spanning AI, statistical mechanics, and structural biology. To extend this training impact to the broader scientific community, we will host annual virtual hackathons and open-access coding workshops. These events will train the next generation of bioscientists in advanced data harmonization techniques and physics-informed AI, cultivating a collaborative ecosystem capable of tackling the next frontiers of biological emergence.

[Budget and Resources]
The proposed data synthesis and AI-driven modeling project requires dedicated NCEMS support, as it represents a community-scale effort that extends far beyond the resources, scope, and technical expertise of any single laboratory. Funding is requested exclusively to support synthesis, computational infrastructure, collaboration, and open science dissemination; no funds are allocated for de novo experimental data generation or laboratory equipment. 

The primary budget allocation will support the future data-savvy workforce: funding is requested for two full-time postdoctoral researchers and two graduate students. These trainees will be co-mentored by the multidisciplinary principal investigators and will serve as the primary execution engine for the massive data harmonization, statistical mechanics modeling, and development of the physics-informed AI architecture. 

Substantial resources are requested for computational infrastructure. We require funding for high-performance computing (HPC) time and cloud-based graphical processing units (GPUs) essential for training and validating large-scale deep learning models on multimodal biophysical datasets. Additionally, funds are requested to support the cloud hosting, maintenance, and long-term sustainability of the interactive, open-access web portal that will serve our tools to the community. 

To stimulate cross-disciplinary collaboration, the budget includes travel and accommodation expenses for bi-annual, in-person Working Group meetings at the NCEMS facility. These intensive sessions are critical for bridging the vocabularies of polymer physics, clinical pathology, and artificial intelligence, ensuring project alignment and rigorous peer feedback. Finally, funds are allocated for open-access publication fees to guarantee that all findings are freely disseminated, and for travel grants to allow our trainees to present their methodologies at national conferences and host the proposed open-science coding bootcamps.

Biomolecular condensates represent a fundamental paradigm of mesoscale emergence in cellular biology, transitioning from individual biomolecular interactions to functional, non-stoichiometric organelles with highly tunable material properties. Central to this liquid-liquid phase separation are the intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) of proteins. Theoretical frameworks rooted in polymer physics—such as the sticker-and-spacer model—have established that the valence and patterning of specific amino acids (e.g., aromatics, charged residues) govern the thermodynamic stability and viscoelasticity of these condensates. However, a major long-standing puzzle remains: how do evolutionary pressures constrain the sequence grammar of highly flexible IDRs to maintain optimal mesoscale emergence, and how do missense mutations disrupt this delicate balance to trigger pathological solid-like aggregation, as seen in neurodegenerative diseases? 

To address this compelling scientific question, our proposed NCEMS Working Group will execute a community-scale synthesis of publicly available genomic, biophysical, and clinical datasets. This transdisciplinary project strictly utilizes existing data, moving beyond the traditional single-protein focus to uncover universal rules of phase separation. We will integrate and harmonize diverse public data sources, including IDR sequence databases (DisProt, MobiDB), condensate repositories (PhaSepDB, CD-CODE), large-scale biophysical archives containing Small-Angle X-ray Scattering (SAXS) and Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) structural ensembles (SASBDB, BMRB), and comprehensive clinical mutation registries (ClinVar, gnomAD).

By synthesizing deep evolutionary sequence alignments with structural and biophysical data, we will map the multidimensional functional constraints placed on IDRs. First, we will train predictive models to decode the universal 'grammar' of conserved disorder, quantifying how specific patterns of hydrophobic clustering, electrostatics, and transient helicity are preserved across millions of years to maintain optimal condensate fluidity. In strict adherence to Open Science principles, all harmonized databases, physics-informed AI models, and reproducible analysis pipelines will be released publicly through an interactive, open-source web portal. Furthermore, this working group will provide vital training for the next-generation workforce, immersing graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in a highly collaborative environment that bridges statistical mechanics, biophysics, and advanced data science.

[Background and Significance]
The phenomenon of mammalian metabolic suppression, observed most dramatically during hibernation and daily torpor, represents a quintessential example of biological emergence at the mesoscale. During these periods of extreme physiological stress, cellular systems undergo profound reorganizations to survive hypothermia, ischemia, and nutrient deprivation. Molecular inputs—ranging from genomic variation to transcriptomic plasticity—integrate to produce remarkable mesoscale outcomes, such as the dynamic remodeling of mitochondrial networks, the partitioning of subcellular energy, and the recalibration of circadian-metabolic coupling. While isolated studies have mapped individual molecular components of these adaptations in specific models (e.g., bears, ground squirrels, and bats), the broader evolutionary and systemic rules governing this plasticity remain largely unresolved. A central, long-standing puzzle in evolutionary genomics and molecular biology is whether the genetic architecture enabling this emergent cellular flexibility is a deeply conserved ancestral state across all mammals, arose convergently in specific lineages, or was uniquely shaped by complex demographic histories, including archaic introgression.

Addressing this fundamental mystery requires a departure from traditional, siloed experimental paradigms. Generating new data in a single-lab setting is insufficient to capture the trans-mammalian complexity of metabolic suppression. Instead, a community-scale synthesis of the vast, disparate repositories of publicly available multi-omics data is imperative. In alignment with the mission of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS), this proposal seeks to catalyze a multidisciplinary working group to integrate massive transcriptomic and genomic datasets spanning diverse mammalian lineages, including both extreme metabolic adaptors and non-hibernating outgroups such as primates. 

By leveraging advanced Artificial Intelligence (AI) and data science frameworks, our transdisciplinary team will bridge the critical knowledge gap between single-molecule alterations and mesoscale emergent properties. We will synthesize high-coverage whole-genome sequencing (WGS), bulk and single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq), and time-series multi-tissue expression data strictly sourced from public repositories. This synthetic approach will allow us to systematically dismantle the regulatory logic of hibernation. Furthermore, exploring whether latent transcriptomic pathways for metabolic suppression remain dormant in non-hibernating mammals, such as humans and other primates, holds transformative potential. Characterizing these pathways not only answers evolutionary mysteries but could also yield unprecedented insights into managing human metabolic disorders, ischemic injuries, and the fundamental limitations of cellular energy balance. This working group will transcend individual capabilities, providing a cohesive, data-driven framework to understand how nature engineers resilience at the molecular and cellular mesoscale.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
Our working group will systematically interrogate the evolutionary origins and molecular architecture of metabolic suppression through four interconnected research questions, driving specific hypotheses centered on mesoscale emergence:

1. What are the shared mesoscale gene regulatory networks (GRNs) governing metabolic suppression across disparate mammalian hibernators?
Hypothesis: Obligate and facultative hibernators share a deeply conserved, core pan-mammalian gene regulatory network that orchestrates subcellular energy partitioning. We posit that this core network dynamically uncouples circadian clock transcription factors from standard metabolic outputs during hypothermia, thereby preserving mitochondrial ATP production and buffering cellular oxidative stress at the organellar level. By reconstructing these GRNs, we expect to identify universal regulatory hubs responsible for mesoscale survival during extreme physiological suppression.

2. To what extent is the genetic architecture for extreme metabolic flexibility conserved in non-hibernating mammals, particularly primates?
Hypothesis: Non-hibernating mammals possess intact, albeit transcriptionally dormant, latent regulatory nodes for metabolic suppression. We hypothesize that evolutionary divergence and adaptation to homeothermic environments led to the epigenetic or trans-regulatory silencing of these networks, rather than their complete genomic decay. Identifying these latent pathways in primates could reveal untapped cellular capacities for metabolic flexibility, addressing a long-standing puzzle in evolutionary biology regarding the loss versus suppression of ancestral traits.

3. How do circadian clock components functionally couple with metabolic pathways to orchestrate mesoscale emergence during hibernation?
Hypothesis: Temperature-dependent modulation of circadian clock transcription factors fundamentally alters the amplitude and timing of downstream mitochondrial gene expression. We propose that the shift from an active state to a hibernating state relies on a specific "transcriptomic phase shift" in which circadian regulators decouple from global metabolic drivers but maintain targeted control over localized, mesoscale energy conservation mechanisms within critical tissues (e.g., adipose, liver, and muscle).

4. What role did structural variation, archaic introgression, and complex demographic histories play in shaping the genomic architecture of metabolic traits in extant mammalian lineages?
Hypothesis: The evolutionary trajectory of metabolic plasticity was significantly shaped by complex demographic events, including the introgression of archaic genomic regions. We hypothesize that specific structural variations and introgressed alleles in both hibernating lineages and primate outgroups harbor critical cis-regulatory elements. These elements modulate the responsiveness of upstream metabolic regulators (e.g., PPARG), ultimately influencing a species' capacity for physiological adaptation. Using advanced demographic modeling, we will determine if "ghost" lineages contributed to the extant genetic diversity underlying metabolic trait variation.

By uniting evolutionary genomics, chronobiology, and machine learning, these questions will delineate the pathways from genomic sequence to emergent mesoscale survival strategies.

[Methods and Approach]
To achieve our objectives without generating new experimental data, our approach relies entirely on the synthesis and integration of massive, publicly available multi-omics datasets. The project will be executed across four distinct, computationally intensive phases, leveraging the transdisciplinary expertise of our NCEMS Working Group in evolutionary genomics, ecological physiology, and AI-driven data science.

Phase 1: Data Curation and Cross-Species Harmonization
We will systematically mine public repositories (e.g., NCBI Sequence Read Archive, Gene Expression Omnibus, and Ensembl) to aggregate high-coverage whole-genome sequencing (WGS), bulk RNA-seq, single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq), and time-series transcriptomic data. The phylogenetic scope will encompass diverse hibernators (e.g., ursids, ground squirrels, bats) and non-hibernating outgroups, with a specific focus on primate lineages. We will deploy containerized bioinformatics pipelines (via Nextflow and Docker) to standardize quality control, sequence alignment, and transcript quantification across species, creating a harmonized, pan-mammalian omics database explicitly designed to map orthologous regulatory regions and gene expression profiles.

Phase 2: Evolutionary Genomic Modeling via Deep Learning
To investigate the evolutionary history and demographic architecture of metabolic regulatory nodes, we will employ Approximate Bayesian Computation integrated with Neural Networks (ABC-NN). This AI-driven modeling approach will utilize the harmonized WGS data to simulate thousands of evolutionary scenarios, pinpointing signatures of natural selection, convergent evolution, structural variation, and potential archaic introgression. The ABC-NN framework will identify whether the genomic loci controlling metabolic suppression represent deeply conserved ancestral states or derived adaptations, specifically evaluating the genetic architecture of primate outgroups to detect latent, conserved regulatory elements.

Phase 3: AI-Driven Gene Regulatory Network (GRN) Inference
To connect genomic variation to transcriptomic plasticity, we will train multi-layer Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) on the integrated cross-species and multi-tissue transcriptomes. GNNs are uniquely suited to capture complex, non-linear relationships in highly dimensional data. We will use these models to infer dynamic, pan-mammalian GRNs, mapping the hierarchical cascade from upstream circadian clock transcription factors and metabolic regulators to downstream effector genes. This approach will identify critical regulatory hubs that coordinate synchronized transcriptomic shifts across different tissues (e.g., liver, muscle, adipose) during metabolic suppression.

Phase 4: Mesoscale Feature Extraction and System Integration
The final phase focuses on mesoscale emergence by correlating the inferred GRN modules with subcellular phenotypic data extracted from scRNA-seq and time-series experiments. We will computationally model how transcriptomic phase shifts alter the timing and amplitude of mitochondrial gene expression, predicting changes in organelle-level ATP production and oxidative stress buffering. By contrasting the active vs. hibernating network states against primate transcriptomes, we will definitively test for the presence of latent hibernation networks in non-hibernators. This comprehensive, in-silico synthesis will strictly adhere to the NCEMS mandate, pushing the boundaries of data integration to unlock new biological paradigms.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This community-scale synthesis project will fundamentally transform our understanding of mesoscale biological emergence, specifically how mammalian cells orchestrate profound metabolic suppression. 

Scientifically, the expected outcomes include the generation of the first comprehensive, pan-mammalian map of Gene Regulatory Networks (GRNs) associated with extreme metabolic flexibility. By deploying multi-layer Graph Neural Networks and ABC-NN modeling on cross-species multi-omics data, we will resolve the long-standing evolutionary puzzle of whether hibernation traits arose convergently or stem from a deeply conserved ancestral state. Crucially, our analysis of primate outgroups will definitively establish whether latent transcriptomic pathways for metabolic suppression remain intact in non-hibernators. Discovering such dormant networks could have extraordinary translational impacts, offering novel biomolecular targets for treating human metabolic disorders, minimizing ischemia/reperfusion injury during surgeries, and enhancing organ preservation.

Methodologically, this project will yield highly innovative, open-source AI and data science frameworks explicitly tailored for cross-species multi-omics integration. The customized GNN and ABC-NN pipelines developed here will serve as foundational tools for the broader scientific community to tackle other complex traits of mesoscale emergence. 

Furthermore, this synthesis project will tap into diverse new talent by heavily prioritizing workforce development. Trainees, including graduate students and postdoctoral researchers embedded within the working group, will gain unparalleled cross-disciplinary training. They will bridge the distinct fields of evolutionary genomics, chronobiology, ecological physiology, and machine learning, emerging as the next generation of data-savvy scientists uniquely equipped to handle massive biological datasets. Ultimately, this proposal aligns perfectly with the NCEMS mission, answering novel questions and solving biological mysteries entirely through the rigorous, collaborative synthesis of existing public data.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
Our working group is staunchly committed to the highest standards of open science, transparency, and reproducibility, aligning strictly with NCEMS mandates and community-created FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) principles. 

Given the purely computational nature of this synthesis project, ensuring the reproducibility of our data integration and AI modeling pipelines is our paramount objective. All analytical workflows, including data harmonization scripts, Nextflow pipelines, Approximate Bayesian Computation Neural Network (ABC-NN) architectures, and Graph Neural Network (GNN) models, will be containerized using Docker and Singularity. This ensures that any researcher, regardless of their local computational environment, can perfectly replicate our analyses.

All custom code, algorithms, and detailed computational notebooks (e.g., Jupyter, RMarkdown) will be version-controlled and hosted on publicly accessible GitHub repositories under an open-source license (e.g., MIT or GNU GPL). Upon the publication of findings, all codebases, integrated pan-mammalian omics datasets, inferred Gene Regulatory Networks (GRNs), and trained AI model weights will be permanently archived in Zenodo, guaranteeing the assignment of unique, persistent Digital Object Identifiers (DOIs). 

We will pre-register our core hypotheses and methodological approaches on the Open Science Framework (OSF) to maintain rigorous analytical transparency. Furthermore, we commit to disseminating all project outcomes through gold open-access, peer-reviewed journals and will promptly deposit manuscript preprints on bioRxiv to accelerate community access to our findings. To maximize the utility of our generated resources, we will also host a series of open-access webinars and provide comprehensive, step-by-step documentation and tutorials. This will empower researchers globally to apply our cross-species integration frameworks and AI models to their own multi-omics investigations into mesoscale emergence.

[Budget and Resources]
The requested budget is strategically designed to support the human capital, computational infrastructure, and collaborative networking required to execute this massive data synthesis project, adhering strictly to the NCEMS mandate of funding in-silico, multidisciplinary synthesis without experimental data generation.

Personnel (60%): The majority of the budget will fund workforce development and training. We request full support for two postdoctoral researchers and three graduate students. These trainees will be cross-trained at the nexus of evolutionary genomics, mesoscale physiology, and AI. They will be responsible for data harmonization, AI model development (GNNs and ABC-NNs), and transcriptomic network inference. Partial summer salary support is requested for the Principal Investigators to oversee the integration of cross-disciplinary methodologies and mentor the trainees.

Computational Infrastructure (25%): Synthesizing high-coverage WGS, scRNA-seq, and time-series data across dozens of species requires substantial computational power. We request funds for cloud computing credits (e.g., AWS or Google Cloud Platform) to facilitate the storage of terabytes of multi-omics data and to train complex, multi-layer neural networks on high-performance GPU clusters. This infrastructure ensures the rapid iteration and scalability of our AI-driven models.

Working Group Meetings and Collaboration (10%): To foster robust transdisciplinary collaboration, we request funds to support biannual, in-person working group meetings hosted at NCEMS facilities, supplemented by monthly virtual coordination sessions. These funds will cover travel, lodging, and logistics, ensuring continuous conceptual alignment among experts in chronobiology, ecological genomics, and data science.

Dissemination and Open Science (5%): Funds are allocated to cover article processing charges (APCs) for publishing our findings in high-impact, gold open-access journals. Additionally, minor funds are reserved for the maintenance of open-access databases and cloud hosting for our interactive public data portals.

These condensates, driven by liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), govern critical subcellular processes ranging from gene regulation to cellular stress responses. While the physical chemistry of LLPS is increasingly studied, a long-standing puzzle remains: how do evolutionary constraints at the atomic scale—specifically sequence coevolution and intrinsic allosteric gating—dictate the thermodynamic parameters required for mesoscale droplet formation across varying cellular environments? To answer this, our Working Group proposes a community-scale synthesis project that bridges molecular evolution, computational biophysics, and structural biology. Currently, investigations into protein phase separation remain siloed. However, there is an unprecedented volume of publicly available data ready for integration. We will synthesize massive multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) from genomic databases (e.g., Pfam, UniProt), predicted structural ensembles from the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, public molecular dynamics (MD) trajectories, and curated phenotypic databases of phase-separating proteins (e.g., PhaSePro, LLPSDB). No new experimental data will be generated; instead, we will leverage these public resources to build a unified predictive model of mesoscale emergence. Our multidisciplinary team will employ a three-tiered computational strategy. First, leveraging information theory and statistical models of coevolutionary sequence information (Potts models, Direct Coupling Analysis), we will extract evolutionary constraints and coupled networks within intrinsically disordered regions and RNA-binding domains of condensate-forming proteins. Second, we will map these coevolutionary constraints onto structural ensembles and public MD trajectories. By applying multi-ensemble contact analysis, graph theory, and random forest machine learning, we will uncover how these evolutionary linkages encode temperature-sensitive and stress-responsive allosteric switches. Finally, we will integrate these atomic-level biophysical networks with macro-level phase separation databases to identify the generalized rules governing how localized molecular changes propagate into mesoscale phase transitions.
