Simultaneously, the proliferation of high-throughput genomics, structural proteomics (such as the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database), and massive molecular dynamics (MD) repositories has generated an immense, untapped wealth of public data. However, these datasets are highly fragmented and siloed. Evolutionary biologists primarily analyze multiple sequence alignments to detect coevolution; biophysicists simulate structural dynamics to uncover allostery; and cellular biologists characterize condensates phenotypically. To resolve this fragmentation, our proposed Working Group seeks to execute a transdisciplinary, community-scale synthesis project. Aligned precisely with the NCEMS mission, we will leverage publicly available data to construct a unified paradigm explaining the emergence of mesoscale biological condensates. We conceptualize LLPS not merely as a physical polymer chemistry problem, but as an evolved, allosterically regulated biological phenomenon governed by information theory. By synthesizing massive genomic sequences, predicted structural ensembles, equilibrium and non-equilibrium MD trajectories, and curated phenotypic databases, we will map the architecture of evolvability and the dynamic structural shifts underlying LLPS. This community-scale synthesis transcends the capabilities of any single research laboratory, requiring the seamless integration of statistical mechanics, bioinformatics, computational biophysics, and machine learning. Furthermore, resolving the mesoscale ontology of allostery and phase separation will catalyze novel strategies for predicting cellular responses to environmental stressors and navigating the intricate landscape of biomolecular self-assembly. By merging these disparate scientific domains, our Working Group will delineate the sequence-to-droplet pipeline, yielding unprecedented, deep insights into the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties at the mesoscale. This systems-level understanding fulfills the foundational vision of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences, paving the way for advancements in de novo protein design and the engineering of autonomous biological materials.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This synthesis project is fundamentally driven by three primary research questions, each addressing a distinct layer of the atom-to-mesoscale hierarchy to unravel the emergence of biomolecular condensates. 

Question 1: How do coevolutionary constraints and information-theoretic sequence linkages encode the propensity for mesoscale phase separation? We hypothesize that the intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) and the interacting modular domains of phase-separating proteins contain highly conserved, coevolving networks of residues that dictate the precise valency and interaction strength necessary for LLPS. By traversing the landscape of evolvability using statistical models of coevolutionary sequence information, we expect to find that the energetic parameters governing condensate formation are deeply entrenched within sequence coevolution, serving as the hidden evolutionary blueprints for mesoscale architecture.

Question 2: In what ways do temperature-sensitive and stress-responsive allosteric contact modes gate the transition from soluble proteins to liquid-like condensates? We hypothesize that environmental triggers—such as thermal stress inducing lower critical solution temperature (LCST) behaviors—provoke highly specific, localized conformational changes that propagate through a protein's allosteric network. This propagation fundamentally alters the protein's phase boundaries. We predict that specific residue-residue contact states act as discrete thermodynamic switches, effectively lowering the critical concentration required for spontaneous mesoscale self-assembly and driving physiological adaptations like amyloid aggregation.

Question 3: Can the integration of atomic-scale coevolutionary networks and dynamic structural ensembles yield a robust, predictive machine learning model for biomolecular condensate emergence? We hypothesize that by synthesizing distinct data modalities—coevolutionary potentials derived from Potts models, dynamic contact maps abstracted from massive molecular simulations, and macro-scale phase separation observations—we can construct a generalizable AI/ML framework. This framework will be capable of predicting a protein's propensity to undergo LLPS, and its responsiveness to specific environmental triggers, solely from its primary sequence and predicted structural dynamics.

Exploring these three critical questions will resolve the long-standing mystery of how localized atomic fluctuations and historical evolutionary constraints dictate global cellular phenomena. The answers will dramatically transform our understanding of how nature fine-tunes the physical properties of biological liquids to optimize physiological functions. Furthermore, it will shed light on how subtle genetic mutations or environmental perturbations can drastically alter condensate solubility, leading to aberrant physiological states. Our synthesis-driven approach systematically connects the theoretical nodes between genetic information, physical structural form, dynamic allostery, and emergent mesoscale states, establishing a comprehensive new paradigm for molecular and cellular biology.

[Methods and Approach]
Our research design strictly adheres to the NCEMS mandate: it is a community-scale synthesis relying entirely on publicly available data, with no new experimental data generation. Our multidisciplinary approach is structured into three interconnected analytical tiers that integrate diverse scientific perspectives.

Tier 1: Evolutionary Landscape Synthesis. We will aggregate massive multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) from extensive genomic databases such as Pfam and UniProt. Our focus will be on the thousands of known and computationally predicted phase-separating protein families curated in public repositories like LLPSDB and PhaSePro. Utilizing information theory and statistical mechanics—specifically Potts models and Direct Coupling Analysis (DCA)—we will extract long-range coevolutionary constraints. This process will identify evolutionarily coupled networks and functionally neutral variants within both ordered domains and intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), effectively mapping the evolutionary landscape of condensate-forming proteins.

Tier 2: Biophysical and Allosteric Integration. We will bridge sequence data with structural dynamics by leveraging predicted structural ensembles from the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database and aggregating public molecular dynamics (MD) trajectories from repositories such as MoDEL. Coevolutionary constraints identified in Tier 1 will be mapped directly onto these 3D ensembles. We will apply multi-ensemble contact analysis and advanced graph theory to dissect complex residue-residue interaction networks. Utilizing random forest machine learning models trained on these contact networks, we will identify temperature-sensitive and environment-responsive allosteric gating mechanisms. This will reveal how specific structural modes trigger the large-scale conformational shifts indicative of liquid-liquid phase transitions.

Tier 3: Mesoscale Predictive Modeling. The final tier synthesizes the atomic-level biophysical networks with macro-level phase separation outcomes. We will train advanced deep learning architectures, integrating the DCA-derived energetic potentials and MD-derived dynamic contact matrices as primary predictive features. The phenotypic phase behavior from LLPSDB will act as ground truth labels for model training. This framework will employ rigorous cross-validation and feature-importance extraction to uncover the generalized biophysical rules governing how localized evolutionary and structural features propagate into mesoscale phase transitions.

This transdisciplinary methodology requires deep expertise across completely distinct fields—molecular evolution, computational biophysics, structural biology, and data science. It demonstrates the absolute necessity of a collaborative NCEMS Working Group. Only through this transdisciplinary synthesis can we effectively merge statistical models of coevolution with mesoscopic field-theoretic analyses of liquid condensates to solve fundamental biological mysteries.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The primary outcome of this Working Group will be a first-of-its-kind, multi-scale predictive framework that seamlessly connects primary sequence coevolution to mesoscale phase separation. By bridging the gap between evolutionary information theory and computational biophysics, we will solve the long-standing puzzle of how allosteric regulation and atomic-level constraints coordinate to produce emergent biomolecular condensates. We will deliver a comprehensive, open-access database mapping the evolutionary and structural determinants of over 10,000 potential phase-separating proteins, significantly accelerating the functional annotation of understudied genes.

This project will fundamentally transform molecular biology by providing a quantitative, predictive tool for understanding how genetic variations alter the physical properties of cellular liquids. This offers profound insights into both physiological adaptation and pathological transitions, such as aberrant amyloid aggregation linked to disease. Furthermore, the methodological innovations developed—synthesizing Potts models with dynamic structural contact networks—will establish a highly innovative new analytical strategy for data-driven discovery in the biosciences. 

Crucially, the project will have a profound broader impact through the cultivation of a highly trained, diverse cohort of data-savvy biological scientists. By structuring our team and mentorship models around the principles of Discipline-Based Diversity Research (DBDR), we will ensure that trainees from diverse backgrounds are fully integrated into cutting-edge computational research. These trainees will become deeply experienced in navigating and integrating vast public datasets across distinct biological scales, ultimately enriching the future scientific workforce and ensuring the long-term vitality of transdisciplinary synthesis research.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
Our Working Group is uncompromisingly committed to the principles of Open Science and reproducible, transparent team research. The sheer scale of integrating genomic, structural, and molecular dynamics datasets necessitates a robust framework for data management, which will be strictly guided by FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) principles from inception to completion. 

All synthesized datasets, aggregated multiple sequence alignments, derived evolutionary coupling matrices, and generated multi-ensemble contact maps will be systematically curated and deposited in open-access repositories such as Zenodo and Dryad, utilizing comprehensive, community-standard metadata. To ensure complete methodological transparency and reproducibility, all computational pipelines, machine learning algorithms, and data extraction scripts will be developed using version control (GitHub) and packaged within containerized environments (Docker/Singularity). 

Analytical workflows will be automated using Snakemake to guarantee that the broader scientific community can execute, validate, and adapt our models seamlessly across different computing environments. Furthermore, interactive Jupyter Notebooks detailing the step-by-step extraction of evolutionary constraints and the training of our deep learning models will be made publicly accessible. We will publish all findings in open-access peer-reviewed journals. Finally, we will actively disseminate our synthesized databases through a dedicated, interactive web portal, enabling researchers globally to explore the ontology of allostery and phase separation without requiring specialized computational expertise.

[Budget and Resources]
The requested budget is meticulously designed to support the collaborative infrastructure, massive computational demands, and workforce training integral to this NCEMS synthesis project. Approximately 30% of the budget will fund the facilitation of the transdisciplinary Working Group, covering travel, accommodation, and logistical support for biannual, intensive in-person collaborative sprints at the NCEMS facility, supplemented by resources for continuous virtual coordination.

A significant portion of the budget (35%) is dedicated to essential computational resources. We request funds for high-performance cloud computing environments (e.g., AWS or Google Cloud) and substantial cloud storage necessary to synthesize, transfer, and process terabytes of public molecular dynamics trajectories, massive AlphaFold structural ensembles, and extensive genomic sequence alignments. 

Crucially, in alignment with our commitment to training the future workforce and advancing Discipline-Based Diversity Research (DBDR), 30% of the budget provides comprehensive support for the recruitment, stipends, and specialized cross-training of a diverse cohort of graduate students and postdoctoral researchers. These funds will enable trainees to participate seamlessly across the collaborating laboratories, gaining unique expertise at the intersection of evolutionary bioinformatics, AI, and FAIR data management. The remaining 5% of funds are allocated for open-access publication fees and the long-term hosting and maintenance of the public-facing interactive database. This budget clearly demonstrates a computational and collaborative need that far exceeds the operational capacity of any individual laboratory, strictly requiring NCEMS support.

The transition from individual genetic variations to complex cellular phenotypes is governed by the mesoscale organization of metabolic networks. While decades of population genetics have identified thousands of loci under natural selection or archaic introgression—often linked to diet, climate, and pathogen response—we lack a fundamental understanding of how these distributed, population-level genetic changes synergize to produce emergent metabolic properties at the cellular level. Simultaneously, systems biology has developed robust tools to model cellular metabolism, but these frameworks rarely incorporate the rich evolutionary history of human populations. This project proposes a massive, community-scale synthesis of publicly available genomic, transcriptomic, and metabolomic data to bridge this gap, unifying evolutionary genomics and systems biology through the lens of artificial intelligence.

Our collaborative working group will synthesize data from global genomic repositories (e.g., 1000 Genomes Project, Simons Genome Diversity Project, archaic hominin genomes) with multi-omic physiological databases (e.g., GTEx, Human Cell Atlas, and Metabolomics Workbench). We will tackle this synthesis in three integrated phases. First, we will deploy interpretable deep learning architectures, including Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), to perform high-resolution inference of natural selection and archaic introgression across global populations. These AI models will be trained on extensive neutral coalescent simulations to identify complex evolutionary signatures specifically within genes encoding metabolic enzymes, transporters, and regulatory networks.

Second, we will map these evolutionarily divergent haplotypes onto context-specific Genome-Scale Metabolic (GSM) models of highly specialized cell types, such as adipocytes and macrophages. By integrating expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) data to constrain reaction bounds in the GSMs, we will employ optimization-based stoichiometric modeling to simulate how selected genetic variants collectively rewire metabolic fluxes. This will allow us to predict emergent mesoscale phenomena, such as the spontaneous reorganization of lipid biosynthesis pathways in extreme climates or metabolic polarization shifts in immune cells.

Finally, we will validate these in silico metabolic predictions by synthesizing matched public single-cell transcriptomics and mass spectrometry-based metabolomics datasets, cross-referencing population-specific metabolic profiles with our GSM-derived flux distributions. 

This project directly addresses the NCEMS mandate to explore mesoscale emergence by demonstrating how independent mutations interact within complex stoichiometric networks to yield novel biochemical phenotypes. By leveraging only existing public data, this collaboration merges deep learning, population genetics, and genome-scale modeling—a synthesis beyond the capacity of any single laboratory. Adhering to open science principles, all trained AI models, context-specific GSMs, and reproducible analytical pipelines will be hosted publicly. Furthermore, this working group will train a new generation of interdisciplinary postdoctoral fellows and graduate students, equipping them to navigate both generative AI and mechanistic systems biology to solve long-standing puzzles in molecular evolution.

[Abstract]
The transition from individual genetic variations to complex cellular phenotypes is governed by the mesoscale organization of metabolic networks. While decades of population genetics have identified thousands of loci under natural selection or archaic introgression—often linked to diet, climate, and pathogen response—we lack a fundamental understanding of how these distributed, population-level genetic changes synergize to produce emergent metabolic properties at the cellular level. Second, we will map these evolutionarily divergent haplotypes onto context-specific Genome-Scale Metabolic (GSM) models of highly specialized cell types, such as adipocytes and macrophages. By integrating expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) data to constrain reaction bounds in the GSMs, we will employ optimization-based stoichiometric modeling to simulate how selected genetic variants collectively rewire metabolic fluxes. This will allow us to predict emergent mesoscale phenomena, such as the spontaneous reorganization of lipid biosynthesis pathways in extreme climates or metabolic polarization shifts in immune cells.

This project directly addresses the NCEMS mandate to explore mesoscale emergence by demonstrating how independent mutations interact within complex stoichiometric networks to yield novel biochemical phenotypes. By leveraging only existing public data, this collaboration merges deep learning, population genetics, and genome-scale modeling—a synthesis beyond the capacity of any single laboratory. Adhering to open science principles, all trained AI models, context-specific GSMs, and reproducible analytical pipelines will be hosted publicly. Furthermore, this working group will train a new generation of interdisciplinary postdoctoral fellows and graduate students, equipping them to navigate both generative AI and mechanistic systems biology to solve long-standing puzzles in molecular evolution.

[Background and Significance]
A central challenge in the molecular and cellular biosciences is understanding mesoscale emergence: how independent molecular components, such as scattered genetic variants, interact across networks to produce entirely new biochemical and physiological properties. Human evolutionary genomics has made tremendous strides over the past two decades in cataloging loci subjected to natural selection and archaic introgression. By analyzing global genomes, researchers have identified adaptive signatures driven by environmental pressures such as diet, climate extremes, and pathogen exposure. Many of these adaptations localize to genes encoding metabolic enzymes and transporters, suggesting that environmental pressures frequently drive the remodeling of cellular metabolism. However, a significant knowledge gap persists: we fundamentally lack a mechanistic understanding of how these distributed, population-level genetic changes synergize across metabolic pathways to produce emergent, network-level metabolic properties at the mesoscale.

Simultaneously, the field of systems biology has developed mathematically rigorous frameworks, such as Genome-Scale Metabolic (GSM) modeling and optimization-based stoichiometric analysis, to simulate the complex interplay of hundreds of biochemical reactions. These models accurately predict metabolic fluxes and cellular behaviors under various constraints. Yet, GSM frameworks have historically remained isolated from population genetics. They typically model a 'reference' cellular state, completely ignoring the rich, population-specific evolutionary variations that dictate metabolic plasticity in the real world.

This proposal addresses this transdisciplinary gap by launching a massive, community-scale synthesis of publicly available data. We hypothesize that genetic adaptation is rarely isolated to single enzymes; rather, selective pressures act on distributed nodes within metabolic networks, driving coordinated shifts in biochemical fluxes. Uncovering these mesoscale phenomena requires integrating the statistical power of evolutionary genomics with the mechanistic rigor of systems biology. 

By leveraging the vast amounts of publicly available multi-omic data—including whole-genome sequences (e.g., 1000 Genomes, Simons Genome Diversity Project), archaic hominin sequences, transcriptomic data (e.g., GTEx, Human Cell Atlas), and metabolomic profiles (e.g., Metabolomics Workbench)—we will map evolutionary history onto metabolic topology. We propose a novel computational pipeline that relies on interpretable deep learning models, specifically Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), to extract non-linear evolutionary signatures without relying heavily on computationally exhaustive forward simulations. These insights will be directly fed into context-specific GSM models of key specialized cells, such as alveolar macrophages and adipocytes, which are highly sensitive to immune and climatic pressures, respectively.

This research fulfills the NCEMS mission by using entirely existing public data to answer long-standing mysteries regarding human metabolic adaptation. It goes beyond the capabilities of any single laboratory by requiring the fusion of population genetics, deep learning, and metabolic engineering. Ultimately, this working group will demonstrate how mesoscale emergence in cellular biology can be decoded by treating the metabolic network not as a static map, but as a dynamic landscape shaped by thousands of years of human evolution.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This working group will synthesize massive public datasets to explore mesoscale metabolic emergence through the lens of human evolutionary history. Our research is structured around three primary, interconnected scientific questions and their corresponding hypotheses:

Question 1: How do polygenic evolutionary adaptations manifest as emergent flux rerouting within mesoscale metabolic networks?
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that natural selection and archaic introgression do not randomly target isolated genes, but rather act selectively on distributed regulatory and catalytic nodes within highly connected metabolic subnetworks (such as lipid biosynthesis and central carbon metabolism). By integrating expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) with optimization-based stoichiometric modeling, we predict that these distributed genetic changes synergize to achieve coordinated, network-level flux optimizations. This systems-level rerouting allows cells to maintain homeostatic viability while shifting output to meet specific environmental demands (e.g., optimizing polyunsaturated fatty acid production in extreme cold environments).

Question 2: To what extent do diverse evolutionary pressures—such as climatic extremes versus pathogen exposure—drive distinct topological reorganizations in the active metabolic networks of specialized cell types?
Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that distinct environmental stressors drive highly specialized, cell-type-specific metabolic emergence. Specifically, we project that selective pressures related to thermal and dietary stress (e.g., high-fat diets in Arctic populations) will map onto distinct sub-network topologies in adipocyte GSMs, altering energy storage and lipid composition. Conversely, pressures from pathogen exposure will map onto macrophage GSMs, rewiring pathways associated with M1/M2 polarization (e.g., arachidonic acid and pyruvate metabolism). By mapping evolutionarily divergent haplotypes to context-specific GSMs, we anticipate uncovering the precise biochemical nodes responsible for cell-type-specific metabolic reprogramming.

Question 3: Can generative deep learning frameworks, when trained on neutral coalescent simulations, accurately identify epistatic and synergistic genetic modules within these metabolic networks from unannotated genomic data?
Hypothesis 3: Traditional summary statistics often fail to capture complex, multi-locus epistatic interactions critical for mesoscale metabolic emergence. We hypothesize that interpretable deep learning architectures, specifically Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), can implicitly compute complex long-range linkage disequilibrium and pairwise heterozygosity to identify hidden synergistic modules. By employing dimensionality reduction and SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) value analysis on our trained CNNs, we hypothesize that the network features most indicative of positive selection will highly correlate with co-regulated clusters of metabolic enzymes, thereby predicting which genomic loci act in concert to shift metabolic fluxes.

These questions directly align with the NCEMS goal of answering novel questions about biological emergence at the mesoscale. By addressing them, we will decode the mechanistic links between genotype, evolutionary history, and emergent cellular phenotypes, establishing a new paradigm for how public data can be synthesized to reveal the rules of molecular organization.

[Methods and Approach]
Our methodology is strictly computational and synthesis-driven, utilizing no newly generated experimental data. We will integrate methods from population genetics, deep learning, and systems biology across three distinct, tightly coupled phases.

Phase 1: Deep Learning for High-Resolution Evolutionary Inference
We will synthesize global genomic data from the 1000 Genomes Project, the Simons Genome Diversity Project, and archaic genomes (Neanderthal and Denisovan). To identify signatures of natural selection and archaic introgression within metabolic genes, we will utilize Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). A demographic model generator will simulate neutral coalescent data, acting as the 'fake' input for the GAN, while real genomic windows will act as the 'true' input. The CNN discriminator will be trained to identify spatial genomic architectures that deviate from neutral demography, pointing to selection or introgression. We will ensure interpretability by utilizing SHAP values and dimensionality reduction on the hidden layers of the CNN, allowing us to map the neural network's learned features back to traditional population genetic statistics (e.g., extended haplotype homozygosity, linkage disequilibrium). We will extract all high-confidence loci associated with metabolic enzymes, transporters, and transcription factors regulating metabolism.

Phase 2: Context-Specific Genome-Scale Metabolic Modeling (GSM)
Once evolutionary targets are identified, we will transition to mechanistic systems biology. We will reconstruct context-specific GSM models for adipocytes and alveolar macrophages using the BiGG Models database and literature-derived metabolic pathways. To link the genetic variants from Phase 1 to our GSMs, we will synthesize matched eQTL data from the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) project. By mapping how specific selected haplotypes alter the expression of metabolic enzymes in relevant tissues, we will mathematically constrain the reaction bounds (Vmax) of our steady-state stoichiometric models. Using flux balance analysis (FBA) and flux-sum variability analysis via bilevel optimization frameworks, we will simulate the metabolic landscape of these cells under varying environmental constraints. This allows us to observe mesoscale emergence in silico: predicting how selected mutations collectively reroute metabolic flux, alter resource allocation, and shift thermodynamic boundaries to produce distinct metabolic phenotypes.

Phase 3: Multi-Omic Validation and Synthesis
To validate our in silico predictions of emergent metabolic rewiring, we will synthesize independent, publicly available single-cell transcriptomics (from the Human Cell Atlas) and mass spectrometry-based metabolomics datasets (from the Metabolomics Workbench). We will cross-reference the observed metabolomic profiles of specific human populations (e.g., lipidomics data from populations adapted to extreme cold) with the flux distributions predicted by our evolutionarily-constrained GSMs. Concordance between our model predictions and the multi-omic public data will validate the mechanistic pathways by which evolution shaped these mesoscale networks.

This transdisciplinary pipeline requires the precise integration of population genetics, deep learning, and systems biology. By merging these isolated data silos, the working group will uncover how multi-locus evolutionary pressures dictate emergent metabolic phenotypes, entirely fulfilling the NCEMS mandate for innovative, community-scale data synthesis.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This community-scale synthesis project will fundamentally advance our understanding of mesoscale emergence by bridging the chasm between evolutionary genomics and mechanistic systems biology. 

Scientific Outcomes: First, we will produce an open-access 'Atlas of Evolutionary Metabolic Landscapes,' detailing how natural selection and archaic introgression have rewired the stoichiometric networks of specialized human cells. Second, we will output context-specific Genome-Scale Metabolic (GSM) models that inherently account for population-level genetic diversity, replacing the outdated 'single-reference' paradigm in metabolic modeling. Third, we will release novel, interpretable deep learning architectures (GANs and CNNs) explicitly optimized to detect epistatic, multi-locus evolutionary signatures within complex regulatory networks.

Broader Impacts: Beyond human evolutionary biology, the frameworks developed here will have profound impacts on biotechnology and precision medicine. Understanding how scattered genetic changes seamlessly reorganize lipid or central carbon metabolism can directly inform computational strain design in metabolic engineering, reducing the design-build-test cycle by leveraging nature's evolutionary optimization. In medicine, unraveling population-specific metabolic architectures will provide vital insights into differential susceptibilities to metabolic syndromes and autoimmune disorders across diverse populations.

Training and Workforce Development: Fulfilling the NCEMS mandate to train the next-generation workforce, this project will cross-train a cohort of postdoctoral fellows and graduate students. Trainees entering with backgrounds in pure computer science will learn stoichiometric modeling and population genetics, while systems biologists will gain fluency in generative AI and demographic simulations. By fostering this transdisciplinary expertise, we will cultivate a new generation of data-savvy scientists uniquely equipped to utilize public data to solve complex biological puzzles at the mesoscale.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
Our working group is deeply committed to the highest standards of open, reproducible, and team-based science, fully aligning with NCEMS core principles. All synthesized data, code, and analytical workflows will be made strictly publicly available under FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) principles.

Code and Workflow Sharing: All deep learning architectures, Python-based genome-scale metabolic modeling scripts, and data integration pipelines will be hosted on a public, version-controlled GitHub/GitLab repository. To guarantee computational reproducibility across different hardware environments, we will containerize all software dependencies using Docker and Singularity. Complex, multi-step analytical pipelines—such as transitioning from coalescent simulations to GAN training, to GSM flux balance analysis—will be orchestrated using standard workflow managers like Nextflow or Snakemake.

Data Availability: All processed, intermediate, and final datasets—including the context-specific GSM JSON/SBML files, trained neural network weights, and harmonized eQTL/metabolomic matrices—will be deposited in Zenodo with assigned DOIs to ensure long-term preservation and citeability. We will not use any proprietary or restricted-access data that cannot be shared in summary or processed formats under appropriate data use agreements.

Dissemination and Community Engagement: We will prioritize publishing all findings in open-access peer-reviewed journals and will deposit manuscripts on preprint servers (e.g., bioRxiv) prior to review. To maximize the utility of our 'Atlas of Evolutionary Metabolic Landscapes,' we will develop interactive, web-based Jupyter Notebook tutorials demonstrating how the broader scientific community can query our synthesized datasets and run custom flux balance analyses on our population-specific metabolic models.

[Budget and Resources]
To successfully execute this community-scale synthesis project, the working group requires NCEMS support that significantly exceeds the capacity of any single lab. The budget is carefully designed to support the necessary personnel, computational infrastructure, and collaborative logistics.

Personnel: The core budget will support three postdoctoral fellows and three graduate students over the grant period. These trainees will be distributed across the distinct domains of the project: one team focusing on generative deep learning and AI-driven evolutionary inference, one on optimization-based systems biology and GSM reconstruction, and one on multi-omic data synthesis and metabolomic validation. This structure ensures deep domain expertise while mandating cross-training and collaborative execution.

Computational Resources: Given the massive scale of the public data (thousands of whole genomes, single-cell transcriptomes, and high-resolution metabolomics), we require substantial computational resources. The budget includes allocations for high-performance cloud computing (e.g., AWS or Google Cloud Platform) equipped with GPU instances for training the computationally intensive Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). Additionally, cloud resources will be used to execute the large-scale bilevel optimization algorithms required for the metabolic flux modeling across thousands of genetic permutations.

The transition from individual genetic variations to complex cellular phenotypes is governed by the mesoscale organization of metabolic networks. While decades of population genetics have identified thousands of loci under natural selection or archaic introgression—often linked to diet, climate, and pathogen response—we lack a fundamental understanding of how these distributed, population-level genetic changes synergize to produce emergent metabolic properties at the cellular level. Simultaneously, systems biology has developed robust tools to model cellular metabolism, but these frameworks rarely incorporate the rich evolutionary history of human populations. This project proposes a massive, community-scale synthesis of publicly available genomic, transcriptomic, and metabolomic data to bridge this gap, unifying evolutionary genomics and systems biology through the lens of artificial intelligence.

Our collaborative working group will synthesize data from global genomic repositories (e.g., 1000 Genomes Project, Simons Genome Diversity Project, archaic hominin genomes) with multi-omic physiological databases (e.g., GTEx, Human Cell Atlas, and Metabolomics Workbench). We will tackle this synthesis in three integrated phases. First, we will deploy interpretable deep learning architectures, including Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), to perform high-resolution inference of natural selection and archaic introgression across global populations. These AI models will be trained on extensive neutral coalescent simulations to identify complex evolutionary signatures specifically within genes encoding metabolic enzymes, transporters, and regulatory networks.

By integrating expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) data to constrain reaction bounds in the GSMs, we will employ optimization-based stoichiometric modeling to simulate how selected genetic variants collectively rewire metabolic fluxes. Furthermore, this initiative will serve as a premier training ground for the next generation of data-savvy scientists. Postdoctoral and graduate trainees integrated into the Working Group will receive cross-disciplinary mentorship in multi-omics integration, computational biophysics, and reproducible team science, equipping them to lead the future of synthetic biology and molecular data science.

[Background and Significance]
The fundamental processes of cellular life depend on the emergent properties of mesoscale structures—supramolecular assemblies such as the nuclear lamina, sarcomeres, and stress granules that exist temporally and spatially between individual biomolecules and whole organelles. While recent decades have seen an explosion in omics data characterizing microscale molecular events, the mechanisms governing how these individual kinetic rates (transcription, translation, folding, degradation) coalesce to maintain or destabilize mesoscale assemblies remain poorly understood. This knowledge gap is particularly acute in the context of physiological stress and biological aging, where cellular environments undergo drastic, system-wide perturbations. Under these conditions, the classic assumption of tight correlation between mRNA abundance and steady-state protein levels frequently fails. Instead, cellular survival hinges on complex, multi-layered regulatory networks that buffer mesoscale structures against proteotoxic insults. Understanding this buffering capacity is a long-standing puzzle in the molecular and cellular biosciences.

Traditionally, single-investigator laboratories have generated critical but siloed datasets. Transcriptomic studies reveal stress-induced gene expression programs, while translatomic (ribosome profiling) and proteomic studies document variations in synthesis and steady-state abundances. Furthermore, specialized approaches utilizing in vivo isotopic labeling (e.g., SILAC, SILAM) have charted the diverse turnover rates of individual proteins. Despite this wealth of publicly available data, there has been no comprehensive, community-scale effort to synthesize these disparate modalities into a unified dynamic model of mesoscale structural integrity. The absence of such synthesis prevents us from recognizing the emergent thresholds—the exact kinetic 'tipping points'—where the uncoupling of protein synthesis and degradation precipitates the abrupt collapse or pathological aggregation of mesoscale complexes.

This proposal directly addresses the NCEMS mission by catalyzing a transdisciplinary Working Group to synthesize vast amounts of existing, publicly available data. We focus on the Integrated Stress Response (ISR) and aging-related cardiovascular degeneration as quintessential models of mesoscale failure. For example, in cardiomyopathies linked to LMNA mutations or in stress-induced endothelial dysfunction, the architectural integrity of the nuclear lamina and cytoskeletal network degrades over time. By integrating single-cell transcriptomics, translation dynamics, turnover rates, and biophysical metrics of protein disorder, we aim to uncover how intrinsic molecular plasticity and regulated turnover collectively act as a shock absorber for the cell. 

Our synthesis approach will shift the scientific paradigm from static correlative analyses to a dynamic systems perspective of molecular emergence. By rigorously applying artificial intelligence, machine learning, and dynamic modeling to integrated data sourced from public repositories such as GEO, PRIDE, and the UK Biobank, this project promises to reveal universal network principles governing mesoscale proteostasis. Crucially, this initiative strictly adheres to the mandate of utilizing only existing data to answer novel biological questions, leveraging transdisciplinary expertise to yield deeper, broader insights into cellular vulnerability and resilience without the generation of new experimental data. The significance lies in creating a universally applicable predictive framework for mesoscale biological emergence.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
Our Working Group will leverage community-scale data synthesis to address three compelling scientific questions regarding the emergent dynamics of mesoscale proteostasis networks. By integrating vast publicly available datasets, we aim to uncover how microscale kinetics dictate the stability of supramolecular assemblies during stress and aging.

Question 1: How do translation dynamics and intrinsic protein turnover rates interact to buffer the structural integrity of mesoscale complexes during the Integrated Stress Response (ISR)?
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that the structural stability of mesoscale assemblies, such as stress granules and the nuclear lamina, is not maintained by steady-state transcript abundance, but by a precise, emergent equilibrium between dynamic translation rates and post-translational degradation. Specifically, we posit that subunits of these complexes characterized by high intrinsic structural disorder possess highly tuned, rapid turnover rates that allow for immediate, adaptive stoichiometric remodeling upon ISR activation. This discordance between mRNA and protein half-lives provides a quantifiable buffering capacity that sustains mesoscale functionality when transcriptional pathways are transiently disrupted by hypoxia or metabolic stress.

Question 2: What are the mathematical and kinetic determinants that define the “tipping point” of mesoscale complex collapse during chronological aging and prolonged physiological duress?
Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that biological aging progressively erodes the translational and degradative buffering capacity of the cell, leading to a mathematically definable phase transition—or tipping point—where mesoscale proteostasis fails. Through dynamic systems modeling of synthesized multi-omics data, we anticipate identifying specific kinetic thresholds where the uncoupling of mRNA abundance, ribosome occupancy, and protein degradation inevitably precipitates pathological disassembly or toxic aggregation. We expect to demonstrate that this kinetic divergence is the primary driver of emergent mesoscale failure rather than a single deterministic genetic mutation or linear pathway alteration.

Question 3: Are the principles of mesoscale network failure conserved across diverse models of aging-related cardiovascular and vascular disease?
Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that despite differing etiologies, diverse cardiovascular pathologies—such as LMNA-related dilated cardiomyopathy and stress-induced endothelial dysfunction—share a universal kinetic signature of mesoscale collapse. By integrating in vitro iPSC-derived cardiomyocyte models with large-scale human proteomic biobanks (e.g., UK Biobank), we will test the hypothesis that the systemic uncoupling of the proteostasis network converges on a highly conserved set of molecular vulnerabilities within the sarcomere and nuclear envelope. We anticipate that machine learning models trained on integrated omics data will reveal these shared network nodes, linking microscale kinetic instability to emergent phenotypic failure.

These research questions cannot be addressed through localized, isolated experiments. They require the transdisciplinary integration of proteomics, translational dynamics, computational biophysics, and large-scale precision medicine datasets. By exclusively employing data synthesis and advanced computational modeling, our collaborative effort will decode the long-standing mysteries of emergent mesoscale stability, fundamentally advancing our understanding of cellular survival under stress and providing a robust conceptual foundation for future therapeutic interventions.

[Methods and Approach]
Our analytical framework relies entirely on the synthesis of publicly available datasets, integrating multi-omic information to map mesoscale emergence. The approach is structured into three integrated phases: Data Acquisition and Harmonization, Computational Systems Modeling, and Artificial Intelligence (AI) Driven Pattern Recognition.

Phase 1: Multi-Omic Data Acquisition and Harmonization
We will systematically harvest matching and highly comparable datasets from public repositories including the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO), Proteomics Identifications Database (PRIDE), and large-scale population resources like the UK Biobank. The synthesis will specifically target: 1) Transcriptomics (bulk and scRNA-seq) to capture baseline and stress-induced mRNA abundance; 2) Translatomics (Ribosome profiling/Ribo-seq) to quantify subcodon translation efficiencies and active translons; 3) Global Proteomics for steady-state protein abundances; 4) In vivo/in vitro protein turnover datasets (pulsed SILAC, dynamic SILAM) to define precise synthesis and degradation kinetics; and 5) Structural databases (e.g., MobiDB, AlphaFold) to quantify intrinsic protein disorder. To enable cross-study integration, we will develop an automated harmonization pipeline using standard identifiers and applying robust batch-correction algorithms (e.g., ComBat, Harmony) to mitigate technical variations across disparate studies. This pipeline will map all kinetic data onto predefined mesoscale assemblies (e.g., nuclear lamina, sarcomeres) using established ontology networks (Gene Ontology, Reactome).

Phase 2: Dynamic Systems Modeling of Mesoscale Buffering
To test our hypotheses regarding the buffering capacity of proteostasis networks, we will transition from static correlative analyses to dynamic kinetic modeling. We will construct Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) models that represent the flux of synthesis, folding, and degradation for individual subunits of mesoscale complexes. By populating these models with our synthesized kinetic parameters (translation efficiency, protein half-lives), we will simulate the dynamic response of these complexes to simulated ISR perturbations (e.g., simulated hypoxic or metabolic stress). We will perform bifurcation analysis to mathematically identify the “tipping points”—the critical thresholds of kinetic uncoupling where buffering capacity is overwhelmed, leading to simulated complex disassembly or aggregation.

Phase 3: AI-Driven Pattern Recognition in Cardiovascular Models
To apply our framework to physiological aging and disease, we will utilize machine learning algorithms to uncover conserved signatures of mesoscale collapse. Using Random Forest and Gradient Boosting architectures, we will train predictive models on our integrated multi-omics matrices derived from iPSC-cardiomyocyte stress models and endothelial cell arrays. The objective is to predict the emergent stability of the LMNA and sarcomeric complexes based purely on upstream microscale kinetic features. These models will subsequently be validated against population-scale plasma proteomic data (e.g., UK Biobank) to confirm whether the kinetic vulnerabilities identified in vitro manifest as systemic proteomic signatures in patients with dilated cardiomyopathy and vascular dysfunction. 

By leveraging the diverse scientific perspectives of our Working Group—spanning translation dynamics, cardiovascular precision medicine, and computational systems biology—this approach moves far beyond the capabilities of a single lab. It provides a robust, transdisciplinary method for decoding mesoscale emergence using purely synthetic, community-scale data.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This Working Group project will deliver transformative insights into the emergent properties of molecular and cellular biology, producing outcomes with broad utility across multiple disciplines. 

First, we will produce the first comprehensive, multi-omic kinetic atlas of mesoscale proteostasis networks, documenting the interconnected rates of translation, turnover, and degradation for structural complexes across healthy, stressed, and aging states. By shifting the paradigm away from static snapshots of mRNA-protein correlations toward dynamic kinetic modeling, we will provide the scientific community with a fundamentally new understanding of how molecular buffering systems function during the Integrated Stress Response (ISR).

Second, our dynamic systems models will deliver mathematically defined “tipping points” that predict when mesoscale complexes—such as the nuclear lamina and sarcomeres—will undergo pathological collapse or aggregation. This addresses a major long-standing puzzle in cellular biology: why certain molecular assemblies fail catastrophically under chronic stress while others adapt. These predictive models will establish a robust foundation for identifying novel, emergent vulnerabilities in cardiovascular diseases, including LMNA-linked cardiomyopathies and age-related vascular dysfunction.

Finally, the impact of this synthesis will extend far beyond the immediate findings. By creating an open-source, standardized computational pipeline for integrating disparate transcriptomic, translatomic, proteomic, and structural datasets, we will provide an invaluable analytical strategy for the broader biosciences community. This methodological innovation directly supports the NCEMS mission to develop innovative analytical strategies. Furthermore, the cross-disciplinary collaborative nature of this project will forge new conceptual bridges between systems biology, cardiovascular precision medicine, and structural proteomics, ensuring that our insights catalyze a new wave of transdisciplinary research into emergent mesoscale phenomena.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
Our Working Group is deeply committed to the gold standard principles of open, reproducible, and team-based science, strictly aligning with NCEMS community policies. To ensure maximum transparency, we will pre-register all analytical protocols, data inclusion criteria, and hypotheses on the Open Science Framework (OSF) prior to the execution of computational analyses.

All harmonized, multi-omic datasets generated through our data synthesis efforts will be fully annotated utilizing FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) principles. These curated datasets will be deposited in public repositories such as Zenodo and Dryad upon manuscript submission. To ensure computational reproducibility, all code, machine learning architectures, and ODE models will be version-controlled and hosted in public GitHub repositories under an MIT open-source license. We will utilize containerization technologies (e.g., Docker, Singularity) to package our analytical pipelines, ensuring that external researchers can identically reproduce our computational environments and results regardless of their local computing infrastructure.

To facilitate broad accessibility, we will develop an interactive, web-based R-Shiny application. This portal will allow researchers without extensive computational expertise to query the synthesized kinetic atlas, visualize translation and turnover dynamics, and simulate stress-induced network tipping points for their mesoscale complexes of interest.

Furthermore, all research outcomes will be disseminated as preprints on bioRxiv concurrently with submission to open-access, peer-reviewed journals. By embedding these rigorous open science practices into the core of our operations, we ensure that our synthetic methodologies, codebases, and data products serve as enduring, accessible resources that empower the global scientific community.

[Budget and Resources]
The requested budget is structured entirely around supporting the transdisciplinary synthesis activities, computational infrastructure, and personnel required for the Working Group, with zero funds allocated for new experimental data generation. 

Personnel Support: A significant portion of the budget is allocated to support two postdoctoral fellows and two graduate students. These trainees will form the core data-science task force. They will be cross-trained in multi-omics integration, dynamic modeling, and cardiovascular biobank analysis by the principal investigators. This directly fulfills the NCEMS mission to train the future data-savvy workforce. Funds will cover their stipends, benefits, and protected time dedicated exclusively to this synthesis project.

Working Group Meetings & Travel: We request support for bi-annual, in-person Working Group 'synthesis sprints' at the NCEMS facility. These intensive, multi-day collaborative sessions are vital for overcoming the limitations of remote coordination, allowing our diverse experts in proteomics, translational dynamics, and clinical omics to rapidly iterate on complex mathematical models and harmonize conceptual frameworks.

Computational Infrastructure: Given the massive scale of data synthesis—particularly the integration of high-throughput Ribo-seq, proteomics, and UK Biobank cohorts—we require funding for high-performance cloud computing resources (e.g., AWS or Google Cloud). This will support the storage, processing, and machine learning training required for phase 3 of our approach, as well as the hosting of our open-access interactive web portal.

Open Science & Dissemination: A modest allocation is reserved for open-access publication fees, ensuring all findings are freely available, and for dedicated server maintenance to guarantee the long-term availability of our containerized pipelines and databases. By leveraging NCEMS support, this project will bridge distinct biological disciplines and build a sustainable, open-source resource for the biosciences community.

title: A Bayesian Synthesis Framework for Predicting the Emergence of Mesoscale Ribonucleoprotein Compartmentalization from Public Spatial Transcriptomic and Single-Molecule Datasets
title_norm: a bayesian synthesis framework for predicting the emergence of mesoscale ribonucleoprotein compartmentalization from public spatial transcriptomic and singlemolecule datasets
abstract_text:
The unexpected appearance of mesoscale biological properties—such as the formation of localized subcellular translational hubs and membrane-less ribonucleoprotein (RNP) condensates—bridges the critical gap between stochastic single-molecule interactions and deterministic cellular phenotypes. Despite vast amounts of publicly available data at both ends of this spatial spectrum, our understanding of mesoscale emergence remains deeply fragmented. Single-molecule biophysical studies capture the high-resolution kinetic, stoichiometric, and reaction-diffusion properties of multivalent protein-RNA and protein-DNA interactions. Conversely, highly multiplexed spatial transcriptomics maps the subcellular compartmentalization of thousands of RNA species across whole cells and tissues. Currently, these two disjoint data modalities are rarely synthesized, leaving a crucial analytical blind spot in the molecular and cellular biosciences.

This proposed NCEMS Working Group will synthesize publicly available single-molecule tracking (SMT), single-molecule localization microscopy (SMLM), and multiplexed spatial transcriptomics (e.g., MERFISH, seqFISH) datasets to elucidate the biophysical rules governing the emergence of mesoscale RNP compartmentalization. We propose to develop a transdisciplinary predictive framework that merges rigorous Bayesian single-molecule inference with large-scale spatial multi-omics integration algorithms. Our collaborative approach strictly leverages existing public data to solve the long-standing puzzle of how transient, multivalent microscale interactions scale up to form stable mesoscale structures across diverse physiological and disease states, such as neurodevelopment and cancer microenvironments.

Our methodology proceeds in three integrative phases. First, utilizing advanced probabilistic modeling and Bayesian inference tools originally designed for single-photon and single-particle tracking, we will extract fundamental kinetic parameters, dissociation constants, and multivalent stoichiometric profiles of key RNA-binding proteins from public biophysical data repositories. Second, we will embed these microscale biophysical priors into a unified, scalable predictive algorithm—extending existing embedding and integration frameworks like Harmony—to analyze broad public spatial transcriptomic datasets. Third, we will calculate in situ thermodynamic probability landscapes to model how dynamically forming multivalent complexes drive specific RNAs into mesoscale compartments, effectively mapping single-molecule reaction-diffusion kinetics onto whole-cell spatial transcriptomic coordinates.

This community-scale synthesis relies fundamentally on NCEMS support, as it goes far beyond the scope of a single laboratory. It demands the deep integration of diverse scientific domains: computational multi-omics, single-molecule tracking, statistical optics, and biophysical chemistry. By bringing together researchers across these fields, we will deliver an open-source computational platform that uncovers how localized molecular biophysics dictates higher-order cellular architecture.

In strict adherence to open science principles, all harmonized multi-scale datasets, Bayesian models, and deep integration pipelines will be made freely available. Furthermore, the Working Group is deeply committed to training the next generation of data-savvy scientists. Trainees will receive cross-disciplinary mentorship, learning to bridge the analytical divide between the physics of photon-arrival statistics and the computational scale of genome-wide spatial omics. Ultimately, this project will pioneer innovative analytical strategies to decode the physical emergence of mesoscale biological organization from publicly available data.

Our collaborative approach strictly leverages existing public data to solve the long-standing puzzle of how transient, multivalent microscale interactions scale up to form stable mesoscale structures across diverse physiological and disease states, such as neurodevelopment and cancer microenvironments.

Our methodology proceeds in three integrative phases. First, utilizing advanced probabilistic modeling and Bayesian inference tools originally designed for single-photon and single-particle tracking, we will extract fundamental kinetic parameters, dissociation constants, and multivalent stoichiometric profiles of key RNA-binding proteins from public biophysical data repositories. Second, we will embed these microscale biophysical priors into a unified, scalable predictive algorithm—extending existing embedding and integration frameworks like Harmony—to analyze broad public spatial transcriptomic datasets. Third, we will calculate in situ thermodynamic probability landscapes to model how dynamically forming multivalent complexes drive specific RNAs into mesoscale compartments, effectively mapping single-molecule reaction-diffusion kinetics onto whole-cell spatial transcriptomic coordinates.

This community-scale synthesis relies fundamentally on NCEMS support, as it goes far beyond the scope of a single laboratory. It demands the deep integration of diverse scientific domains: computational multi-omics, single-molecule tracking, statistical optics, and biophysical chemistry. By bringing together researchers across these fields, we will deliver an open-source computational platform that uncovers how localized molecular biophysics dictates higher-order cellular architecture.

In strict adherence to open science principles, all harmonized multi-scale datasets, Bayesian models, and deep integration pipelines will be made freely available. Furthermore, the Working Group is deeply committed to training the next generation of data-savvy scientists. Trainees will receive cross-disciplinary mentorship, learning to bridge the analytical divide between the physics of photon-arrival statistics and the computational scale of genome-wide spatial omics. Ultimately, this project will pioneer innovative analytical strategies to decode the physical emergence of mesoscale biological organization from publicly available data.

[Background and Significance]
The fundamental challenge in molecular and cellular biology today is understanding how molecular parts list spontaneously organize into functionally complex, emergent architectures. At the heart of this challenge lies the mesoscale: the structural tier existing between individual biomolecules (nanometers) and whole organelles (micrometers). Among the most striking examples of mesoscale emergence is the compartmentalization of ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes into specialized membrane-less organelles, such as stress granules, processing bodies, and localized translational hubs. These mesoscale domains are critical for regulating gene expression, cellular stress responses, and developmental trajectories. Aberrations in these structures are frequently implicated in severe pathologies, including neurodegenerative diseases and malignant tumor microenvironments. 

Despite their biological importance, our predictive understanding of RNP condensation remains severely limited by a profound analytical divide. On one hand, single-molecule biophysics offers remarkable insights into the fundamental interactions driving RNP formation. Public repositories of single-molecule tracking (SMT) and single-molecule localization microscopy (SMLM) data harbor vast amounts of underutilized information regarding the fast, stochastic reaction-diffusion dynamics, valency, and concentration-facilitated unbinding events of RNA-binding proteins (RBPs). On the other hand, the genomics community has produced massive, high-dimensional spatial transcriptomics datasets using highly multiplexed in situ hybridization techniques (e.g., MERFISH, seqFISH). These datasets map the static, steady-state subcellular localization of thousands of RNA species but lack biophysical depth. 

Currently, these two powerful fields—statistical optics-based biophysics and computationally driven spatial genomics—operate in silos. There is no existing mathematical or computational framework that synthesizes stochastic single-molecule kinetics with whole-cell spatial RNA coordinate mapping. As a result, a critical analytical blind spot persists: we cannot yet predict how specific biophysical microscale rules scale up to generate the mesoscale RNA compartmentalization observed in spatial transcriptomic atlases. 

This proposal addresses this gap by directly aligning with the NCEMS mission to leverage artificial intelligence and data science for community-scale data synthesis. We propose the first comprehensive, multi-scale synthesis framework that utilizes only existing, publicly available data to unify single-molecule probabilistic inference with high-dimensional spatial omics embedding. By systematically integrating these disjoint datatypes, we will uncover the biophysical principles driving the emergence of mesoscale properties. 

The significance of this work is twofold. First, it solves a long-standing puzzle regarding how multivalent protein-RNA interactions manifest as stable, compartmentalized cellular phenotypes. Second, it develops an entirely novel, cross-disciplinary analytical strategy that projects fundamental thermodynamic and kinetic constants onto genomic-scale structural maps. This transdisciplinary synthesis is beyond the capabilities of any single laboratory. It necessitates a Working Group that seamlessly integrates expertise in single-cell and spatial computational biology, single-molecule biophysical chemistry, and rigorous statistical optics. Ultimately, this predictive framework will allow researchers to mathematically link nanometer-scale single-photon arrival statistics to the micrometer-scale subcellular geography of the transcriptome, redefining our understanding of cellular organization.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
Our Working Group will execute a community-scale synthesis of publicly available data to address three critical research questions regarding the physical emergence of mesoscale RNP compartmentalization. These questions are designed to bridge the analytical gap between molecular biophysics and spatial omics, testing explicit hypotheses derived from statistical mechanics and systems biology.

Research Question 1: How do the microscale kinetic parameters of RNA-binding proteins predict the steady-state mesoscale spatial distribution of the transcriptome?
Hypothesis 1: The subcellular compartmentalization of RNA species observed in multiplexed spatial transcriptomics is not random but governed by the reaction-diffusion kinetics of multivalent regulatory proteins. We hypothesize that by employing Bayesian inference models on public single-molecule reaction-diffusion (smRD) data, we can extract biophysical priors (e.g., binding affinities, off-rates, diffusion coefficients) that accurately predict the clustering and compartmentalization of target RNAs in corresponding public MERFISH and seqFISH datasets. We posit that high-affinity, slow-diffusing RBP states correlate directly with dense mesoscale transcriptomic hubs.

Research Question 2: What is the role of multivalent stoichiometry and concentration-facilitated unbinding in driving cell-state-specific RNA compartmentalization?
Hypothesis 2: Multivalency-enabled ternary complexes act as thermodynamic sinks that drive the phase separation and mesoscale organization of RNPs. Drawing on public single-molecule tracking and localization data, we hypothesize that changes in the stoichiometric ratio and multivalent interactions of RBPs across different physiological states (e.g., neurodevelopmental stages or cancer microenvironments) shift the thermodynamic probability landscape. By computationally integrating this biophysical data with state-specific spatial transcriptomics, we predict we can model concentration-facilitated unbinding events that explain how specific transcripts are dynamically recruited to or released from mesoscale compartments during cellular state transitions.

Research Question 3: Can we map continuous single-molecule reaction-diffusion dynamics onto discrete, high-dimensional spatial transcriptomic coordinates to create a unified 'in situ thermodynamic landscape'?
Hypothesis 3: High-dimensional multi-omics integration algorithms can be adapted to co-embed biophysical kinetic profiles with spatial transcriptomic mapping. We hypothesize that extending dimensionality reduction and data integration frameworks (such as the Harmony algorithm) to incorporate probabilistic biophysical parameters will enable the construction of an 'in situ thermodynamic landscape.' In this landscape, local transcript density acts as the boundary condition for the Bayesian reaction-diffusion model. This will allow us to calculate the probability of RNP compartment emergence at any given sub-cellular coordinate, effectively linking the stochastic nature of photon-arrival biophysical measurements to the spatial certainty of transcriptomic maps.

By addressing these questions solely through the synthesis of existing data, we aim to validate a predictive model of mesoscale emergence. The successful proof of these hypotheses will demonstrate that complex, higher-order cellular structures are mathematically predictable emergent properties arising from localized single-molecule thermodynamic and kinetic rules. This framework will provide the molecular and cellular biology communities with a transformative theoretical tool capable of inferring dynamic biophysical states from static transcriptomic snapshots.

[Methods and Approach]
Our community-scale synthesis project strictly utilizes publicly available datasets, involving no new experimental generation. The methodology is organized into three integrative phases requiring deep transdisciplinary collaboration across computational genomics, single-molecule biophysics, and probabilistic modeling.

Phase 1: Bayesian Inference of Microscale Kinetics from Public SMT/SMLM Data
We will curate a comprehensive repository of publicly available single-molecule tracking (SMT) and single-molecule localization microscopy (SMLM) datasets from databases such as SMTracker, Zenodo, and the NIH 4D Nucleome Data Portal. Focusing on key multivalent RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) implicated in phase separation (e.g., FUS, TDP-43, G3BP1), we will apply advanced probabilistic modeling to extract kinetic parameters. Leveraging tools related to Bayesian single-molecule reaction-diffusion (Bayes-smRD) and single-photon single-particle tracking (SP2T), we will analyze raw photon arrival data and discrete coordinate trajectories to infer robust biophysical priors. This computational step will quantify diffusion coefficients, kinetic on/off rates, and the stoichiometric distributions of RBP complexes without the artifactual bulk averaging present in standard biochemical assays. These parameters will serve as the microscale foundation for our synthesis.

Phase 2: Spatial Integration and High-Dimensional Embedding
Simultaneously, we will harmonize publicly available subcellular spatial transcriptomics data (e.g., MERFISH, seqFISH+) sourced from the SpaceTx consortium and the Brain Initiative Cell Census Network (BICCN). Because these datasets exist across highly varied formats and biological states (e.g., murine neurodevelopment, human glioblastoma), we require robust algorithmic integration. We will extend computationally efficient integration architectures, conceptually similar to the Harmony algorithm, to project these diverse spatial transcriptomic coordinates into a shared embedding space. However, instead of integrating solely across technological modalities, we will implement a novel co-embedding strategy that registers local spatial RNA density with the stoichiometric and multivalent binding probability distributions extracted in Phase 1. 

Phase 3: Thermodynamic Mapping and Predictive Modeling
In the final synthesis phase, we will map the microscale biophysics onto the mesoscale transcriptomic geography. We will treat the spatially resolved RNA counts from Phase 2 as steady-state endpoints driven by the reaction-diffusion processes quantified in Phase 1. By developing an 'in situ thermodynamic landscape' model, we will calculate the localized probability of multivalent ternary complex formation across the cellular volume. This involves constructing a non-equilibrium statistical mechanics framework where local transcript density dictates the concentration-facilitated unbinding and recruitment rates of regulatory proteins. We will validate our predictive framework by computationally predicting the location and density of specific RNP compartments (e.g., stress granules or nucleoli) based solely on transcript coordinates and biophysical priors, comparing our predictions against independent publicly available multiplexed immunofluorescence and transcriptomic co-staining datasets.

Feasibility and Rigor: Our approach is entirely computational and data-driven, leveraging the distinct but complementary expertise of our Working Group. Rigor will be ensured through cross-validation against withheld public datasets and the application of strict, standardized quality control metrics for both the biophysical inference and spatial integration pipelines. NCEMS support is vital to provide the computational infrastructure and collaborative environment necessary to execute this transdisciplinary synthesis.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This Working Group will deliver a suite of transformative outcomes that address the fundamental biological puzzle of mesoscale emergence while fundamentally advancing computational methodology in the molecular and cellular biosciences.

First, we will produce a unified computational synthesis framework that successfully bridges the gap between single-molecule biophysics and spatial genomics. This framework will be the first of its kind to mathematically link the stochastic, microsecond-scale dynamics of protein-RNA interactions with the static, whole-cell subcellular spatial mapping of the transcriptome. 

Second, we will generate a massive, synthesized multi-scale dataset. By annotating existing public spatial transcriptomic atlases with high-resolution thermodynamic and kinetic biophysical parameters, we will provide the scientific community with a novel 'in situ thermodynamic map' of the cell. This resource will allow researchers to predict dynamic molecular behavior directly from static, highly multiplexed genomic imaging data. 

The broader impacts of this project are substantial. By elucidating the biophysical rules governing RNP compartmentalization, our findings will offer critical insights into cell-state transitions underlying both normal physiology (e.g., neural differentiation) and pathology (e.g., cancer cell states, neurodegenerative proteinopathies). 

Furthermore, this project will significantly impact the scientific workforce. By executing this project through a collaborative NCEMS Working Group, we will cross-train a cohort of postdoctoral and graduate trainees. These early-career researchers will develop a highly unique, dual-fluency in statistical optics/biophysics and high-dimensional computational genomics. This training will address a critical shortage in the data-savvy scientific workforce, equipping the next generation to pioneer holistic, multi-scale approaches to biological complexity.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
Our Working Group is resolutely committed to gold-standard Open Science principles, ensuring that all synthesized data, code, and analytical pipelines generated during this project are completely transparent, accessible, and reproducible.

Code and Software Availability: The entirety of our novel Bayesian inference frameworks, integration algorithms, and thermodynamic predictive models will be written in open-source languages (Python, R, and C++ for GPU-accelerated steps). All code will be actively maintained on a public GitHub repository under an MIT open-source license. To guarantee computational reproducibility, we will package our multi-scale integration pipelines into Docker and Singularity containers, allowing any researcher to deploy our environment with identical dependencies.

Data Accessibility: Following FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) principles, all harmonized intermediate datasets and the final multi-scale synthesized atlases will be deposited into public repositories such as Zenodo and the Open Science Framework (OSF). These deposits will be accompanied by exhaustive metadata detailing the provenance of the original public datasets (SMT/SMLM and Spatial Transcriptomics), the specific preprocessing steps applied, and the versioning of the analytical tools utilized.

Documentation and Protocols: We will provide rigorous documentation, including extensive Jupyter Notebook and RMarkdown tutorials that step users through the analytical workflow—from raw photon-arrival statistics and transcript spatial coordinates to the final localized probability landscapes. 

Team Science: We will adopt an open, collaborative team science approach. Working Group meeting notes, decision logs regarding data inclusion criteria, and preliminary synthesis models will be made publicly available on our OSF project page, fostering real-time community engagement and external peer review throughout the project lifecycle.

[Budget and Resources]
This community-scale synthesis fundamentally requires NCEMS support, as the computational demands and transdisciplinary integration vastly exceed the resources of any single investigator or existing bilateral collaboration.

Personnel and Training Support: A significant portion of the budget will support two postdoctoral fellows and two graduate trainees. These trainees will be co-mentored by Working Group members, facilitating deep cross-pollination between the computational genomics, Bayesian biophysics, and single-molecule microscopy domains. NCEMS funding ensures dedicated time for these early-career scientists to focus entirely on dataset synthesis and multi-scale algorithmic development, serving as the core drivers of our workforce training mandate.

Computational Resources: Synthesizing millions of single-photon biophysical traces with billions of spatial transcriptomic coordinates requires substantial computational power. Funds are requested for cloud computing resources (e.g., AWS, Google Cloud) equipped with high-performance GPU clusters. This infrastructure is essential for running the computationally intensive Bayesian reaction-diffusion inferences and the high-dimensional spatial embedding algorithms at scale.

Working Group Convenings: To effectively integrate these disparate scientific disciplines, we request support for bi-annual, in-person Working Group meetings at the NCEMS hub. These multi-day intensive collaborative sessions are critical for bridging field-specific vocabularies, troubleshooting analytical bottlenecks in the synthesis pipeline, and ensuring cohesive team science practices. 

Dissemination and Open Science Costs: Modest funds are allocated to support open-access publication fees, the hosting of large synthesized datasets on robust repositories, and the organization of a virtual community workshop in Year 2 to train external researchers on how to utilize our newly developed multi-scale integration software. 

By centralizing these resources through NCEMS, we will efficiently catalyze a transdisciplinary synergy that maximizes the value of existing public data to solve fundamental mysteries of mesoscale biological emergence.
